News.title: UK weather live: Britain braces for second 80mph storm as Austen continues before Boelo
News.content:
The Met Office has issued 'danger to life' weather warnings for Storm Austen, with more set to come into force over the weekend as Storm Boelo arrives

Storm Austen is causing travel chaos with airports closed, flights cancelled and train services disrupted - and Brighton's iconic West Pier has now partially collapsed.

The Met Office has issued several weather warnings for wind covering Wales and much of England today. Further wind warnings will come into force tomorrow in Northern Ireland, Scotland and the north of England, while a new amber warning has now been issued for 34 areas ahead of Storm Boelo, the second named storm to hit the UK in a matter of days.

Flood warnings were issued too, along parts of the Dorset Coast and South Devon Coast. The Environment Agency urged people in affected areas to "move to higher ground" and "protect yourself and loved ones".

All Channel Islands airports were closed and flights have been cancelled at Exeter and Southampton airports. CrossCountry, Great Western and South Western train services are among those hit by severe disruption. Some 31,000 homes are without power in the south-west.

A yellow wind warning covering south-west England, the south coast, parts of Wales and Herefordshire runs until 5pm today, potentially bringing gusts of up to 70mph. Another yellow wind warning covers a much wider area across England and Wales, including London, the Midlands, the North West and parts of Yorkshire. That warning is in place until 9pm today.

News.title: Man City charges LIVE: Three punishments facing club as Kyle Walker forced to backpedal
News.content:
The latest news and updates on Manchester City's ongoing 114 financial charges case against the Premier League

Hello and welcome to the Manchester City 114 financial charges blog on Mirror Sport!

It has now been over a month since City were found guilty by an independent panel of all financial breaches brought forward by the Premier League.

The process of an appeal hearing and one for their potential sanctions have both started with City continuing to deny any wrongdoing. News.title: Andy Burnham issues request to Donald Trump for Ukraine to use Starlink
News.content:
Andy Burnham issues request to Donald Trump for Ukraine to use Starlink

In a call to US President Donald Trump, Prime Minister Andy Burnham stressing the need for Ukraine to have the best chance to defend itself, Downing Street has said tonight

View 3 Images President Donald Trump and Prime Minister Andy Burnham spoke today (Image: AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson)

Andy Burnham has underlined the importance for Ukraine to have full access to Starlink so they can continue to defend themselves against Russia’s full-scale invasion in a call with Donald Trump, Downing Street has said.

‌



‌



The US President had denied instructing tech billionaire Elon Musk to restrict connectivity to Starlink's military-grade counterpart, Starshield, before saying the tycoon had "put it back".

‌



The satellite internet service is operated by SpaceX, Mr Musk's aerospace company. It provides high-speed broadband globally and is used by Ukraine for military communications and drone operations.

‌



Last week, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said he has been "betrayed" by Trump and ally Musk, who "deliberately" blocked his country's access to the military-grade version overnight. Yesterday, he said it had not been fully restored, despite Trump's claims the matter was resolved.

View 3 Images Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said access to Starshield had not been fully restored. (Image: AP Photo/Geert Vanden Wijngaert)

The Prime Minister this afternoon raised the issue directly with the US president after restrictions placed on Kyiv's use of the satellite communications system.

‌



Ukraine relies on Starlink to help intercept Russian missile and drone attacks, but faced speed limits last week that significantly curtailed its ability to do so.

Mr Musk has suggested the order to impose caps on the system came from the White House, though the Wall Street Journal reported that the tech billionaire was behind the slowdown.

‌



In a readout of the conversation between the UK and US leaders on Friday, a No 10 spokeswoman said: "The Prime Minister spoke to the President of the United States of America Donald Trump today.

View 3 Images Tycoon Elon Musk is an ally of the US President (Image: AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson)

‌



"The Prime Minister underlined the importance for Ukraine to have full access to Starlink so they can continue to defend themselves against Russia's full-scale invasion.

"The Prime Minister recognised the work of President Trump to bring Putin to the negotiation table and the leaders agreed to work together, alongside international partners, to bring an end to the blood."

‌



Mr Zelensky said that Ukrainians could die if the unrestrictive service was not restored. There was confusion about who ordered the slowdown on October 14 and an informal investigation inside the White House was conducted.

Asked on Friday, Trump said: "If there is a problem, I will get it straightened out."

‌



He then added: "I have not spoken to him [Musk]. I might have to, but I have not. I've heard it was fixed, but if it's not, I'll speak to him."

The Wall Street Journal has reported that last week, Mr Musk capped the speeds at which Ukrainian hardware could stay connected to the satellite-based network, rendering some offensive drones and interceptor drones virtually useless.

Article continues below

The internet slowdown followed several statements by the Trump administration and Mr Musk that Ukrainian officials saw as hostile to the country, leading Kyiv to immediately suspect the order came either from the president or the world's richest man.

News.title: Man and dog killed after being hit by bus in Bristol as police launch appeal
News.content:
Man and dog killed after being hit by bus in Bristol as police launch appeal

The man, a pedestrian in his 70s, was critically injured and died at the scene alongside a dog after being hit by a bus, police have said.

View Image The man, a pedestrian in his 70s, died alongside a dog in Bristol (Image: PA)

A man and a dog have died after being hit by a bus in Bristol.

Officers were called to the junction of Stockwood Road and Hollway Road at around 11pm last night (October 22) after the crash.

The man, a pedestrian who was in his 70s, was critically injured and died at the scene, police said. A dog was also killed in the incident.

While formal identification is yet to take place, his next of kin have been informed and will be supported by a specialist family liaison officer, Avon and Somerset Police has confirmed.

The bus driver, a man in his thirties, has been arrested and remains in custody while enquiries continue, the force said.

Officers are currently seeking any witnesses or those with CCTV or dashcam footage who may be able to assist.

A statement from Avon and Somerset Police said: "We are appealing for witnesses and dashcam footage after a pedestrian died after he was involved in a collision with a bus in Bristol last night (Thursday 22 October).

"The collision happened at the junction for Stockwood Road and Hollway Road at around 11.10pm. The road has since reopened after enquiries were carried out at the scene.

"The pedestrian, a man in his seventies, was critically injured and died at the scene. While formal identification is yet to take place, his next of kin have been informed and will be supported by a specialist family liaison officer.

"Our thoughts are with them at this traumatic time. A dog also died in the incident.

"The driver of the bus, a man in his thirties, has been arrested and remains in custody while enquiries continue.

"Any witnesses and those with CCTV and dashcam footage from around the time of the incident are asked to contact us on 101 quoting reference number 5226345957 or complete our online appeals form.”

News.title: Three dead and five injured after gas explosion at coal mine in Turkey
News.content:
Three dead and five injured after gas explosion at coal mine in Turkey

At least three people have died and five more are injured following a methane gas explosion at a privately-owned coal mine in the Kilimli district of Zonguldak in Turkey

View Image A methane gas explosion occurred at a privately owned coal mine in the Dereiçi area of ​​Gelik town (Image: TV100)

An explosion in a Turkish coal mine has left three people dead and five injured.

‌



‌



The blast, caused by a build-up of methane gas, happened at a privately-owned mine in the Kilimli district of Zonguldak at around 10am local time.

‌



Paramedics and fire crews were sent to the scene, where two people pulled from the mine were initially confirmed dead and five injured workers were taken to hospital.

‌



The death toll has since climbed to three, according to local news reports.

Zonguldak Governor Osman Hacıbektaşoğlu visited the scene and told reporters the explosion had been caused by methane gas.

‌



Some relatives of the miners reportedly collapsed in front of the hospital where their loved ones were being treated, TrtHaber reports.

Rescue teams were dispatched to the area immediately after the incident and are continuing their work, Interior Minister Mustafa Çiftçi said in a statement. He added that necessary checks were being carried out at the mine and officials were closely monitoring the situation.

Article continues below

“I pray to Almighty God for mercy upon our deceased miner brothers, for patience and condolences to their grieving families and loved ones, and for a speedy recovery for the injured,” he said. “May God never again allow our noble nation to experience such pain.”

Meanwhile, Justice Minister Akın Gürlek announced that an investigation has been launched. He said: "Regarding the explosion that occurred as a result of methane gas accumulation in a mining operation in the Kilimli district of Zonguldak, the Zonguldak Chief Public Prosecutor's Office has launched an immediate investigation.

News.title: Reform 'newspaper' sent to millions features councillor who called for mosque ban and praised Tommy Robinson
News.content:
Reform 'newspaper' sent to millions features councillor who called for mosque ban and praised Tommy Robinson

EXCLUSIVE: Nigel Farage’s party featured Councillor Phil Tierney in its campaign newspaper, despite his calls for all mosques to be shut and for Muslims to be banned from office

View 2 Images Reform councillor Phil Tierney called for Muslims to be banned from office (Image: Facebook)

Reform's new "newspaper" sent to millions of people features a councillor who said Muslims shouldn't hold public office and that all mosques should be shut.

‌



‌



Nigel Farage’s party sent out a campaign newspaper, called "The Reformer", as the party tries to stabilise after collapsing in the polls.

‌



The so-called newspaper shows Councillor Phil Tierney, who described himself as Islamophobic and signed a petition urging the Government to "halt the political persecution of Tommy Robinson".

‌



Mr Tierney shared a post on X in July 2025, saying: “I am Islamophobic.” He also reposted an image saying that “no communist or Muslim should be allowed to hold any office”, branded Islam a “plague on this wonderful earth” and called for all mosques in the UK to be closed.

Nigel Farage could miss out on dozens of seats due to anti-Reform tactical voting at next election READ MORE :

Close Nigel Farage ally appears to admit £5million Brexit comment slip up in undercover footage READ MORE :

View 2 Images Reform councillor Phil Tierney features in the 'Reformer', fifth along from the right by the heading 'Clean Up Britain' (Image: Reform UK )

In May the party said it was "thoroughly investigating these allegations", but months later Mr Tierney is pictured alongside the caption “Cleaning Up Britain”.

‌



He is a councillor for Chelmsley Wood in Solihull where Reform has 17 seats, with the Tories on 24.

The latest revelations come with Mr Farage already facing pressure after a documentary by ITV Exposure and Hardcash Productions, appeared to show Reform figures making sexist, racist and other concerning comments.

‌



In a further blow, this week The Mirror revealed Reform could miss out on dozens of seats across the country at the next general election due to anti-Reform tactical voting, according to new research.

The survey commissioned by Electoral Calculus also found anti-Reform sentiment had grown over the last 12 months - as the right-wing party faces scandals on multiple fronts.

‌



Bridget Phillipson, Chair of the Labour Party, said: “There is clearly a rotten culture of racism in Reform. Nigel Farage isn’t just tolerating these toxic views. He’s now putting them up in lights. As ITV’s investigation exposed, this is prevalent in Farage’s party, yet he refuses to act.

“For once in his life, Farage should hold his hands up. He should take action against his councillor's disgusting views and apologise for giving him so much prominence in his so-called newspaper.”

‌



There was also fury from the Tories. A Conservative spokesperson said: “Reform claimed they had improved their vetting.

"Yet they are distributing a national newspaper to millions of households promoting a councillor who shared posts supporting Tommy Robinson and claiming Muslims shouldn’t hold public office. Nigel Farage clearly doesn’t have what it takes to get his house in order.”

Article continues below

Reform UK did not respond to a request for comment.

News.title: Met Police chief condemns vile racists who 'AI'd suicide vest' on PC celebrated for supporting women
News.content:
Met Police chief condemns vile racists who 'AI'd suicide vest' on PC celebrated for supporting women

PC Fiona Shaik Umar was subject to 'vile' racism online after she was given an award by the Metropolitan Police Federation on Wednesday for supporting female police officers

View 5 Images The officer joined the Met Police after her daughter asked whether women like her could serve with the force (Image: LinkedIn)

The Met Police commissioner has condemned racist abuse directed towards a decorated officer, after she was awarded for her work supporting women in policing.

‌



‌



Sir Mark Rowley condemned "vile" abuse directed at PC Fiona Shaik Umar, who was honoured with the Outstanding Contribution to Women in Policing Award on Wednesday. She has received "all sorts" of misogynistic and racist abuse, he said, since she received the award during the Police Federation annual conference.

‌



Despite having dedicated her career to helping develop the service, the Met chief added that during the "online tirade", she was denigrated by vicious trolls who posted AI images of her wearing a suicide vest.

‌



To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

Reform launches racism probes into politicians after undercover TV investigation READ MORE :

View 5 Images PC Fiona Shaik Umar was subject to vile abuse (Image: LinkedIn)

Speaking to BBC Radio 4's PM programme, he said the federation had made the award a "really positive thing, but added it was hijacked by vile racists. He said: "The federation put out this really positive thing about this award, and the online tirade of vileness, of racist, anti-Islam and all sorts of other abuse, and misogynistic, was horrific.

‌



"At one extreme, somebody did an AI-generated image and put a suicide bomb on her," he added. "I mean, the stuff out there is just vile."

The chief added that female officers, especially those hailing from minority ethnic backgrounds, are more likely than others on the force to suffer online abuse. PC Umar said she was "truly humbled" to receive the award, which recognised her for developing the Hijab Project.

‌



View 5 Images The PC was honoured for her initiative helping female police officers (Image: LinkedIn)

Her project was a vital force for changing uniform options for women among Met Police officers to meet the needs of Muslim women officers serving in the force.

‌



She said in a video shared by the federation that she was inspired to enter the Met after her daughter asked whether "women like you" could do the job. She said: "I'm truly humbled to receive this award because I'm super passionate about the work I do around representation and inclusion for women in policing.

"I never thought about a career in the police until my daughter at the time said to me, 'Can women like you do that job?', and I was really offended because obviously she'd never seen anyone who looked like me being a police officer."

‌



View 5 Images Sir Mark Rowley said women and minority police officers are subject to the worst abuse (Image: Yui Mok/PA Wire)

"And it's because of that that I have continued to do this work and to try and create a space for women who look like me in policing across the UK."

‌



Paula Dodds, Chair of the Metropolitan Police Federation, hailed the mum as an "incredible police officer" who was being celebrated for "outstanding work". In a statement, she called out the "vile racist abuse" suffered by the PC, which she said had come from "cowardly keyboard warriors".

View 5 Images The Met Police federation has stood by the celebrated PC (Image: LinkedIn)

‌



She said: "PC Fiona Shaik Umar is an incredible police officer who has been rightly recognised for her outstanding work. That's what we should be celebrating."

"Not discussing the vile racist abuse directed towards her by cowardly keyboard warriors. The same people who don't have an ounce of her courage or her sense of duty. We stand in solidarity with the Commissioner in his condemnation of the torrent of abuse she has sadly had to endure.

Article continues below

"We are supporting Fiona and will continue to unashamedly celebrate the work of her - and our colleagues of all backgrounds. The disgusting bigots will not win."

News.title: 'Radical' call to finally fix prison rehabilitation crisis as poll shows public backing
News.content:
'Radical' call to finally fix prison rehabilitation crisis as poll shows public backing

EXCLUSIVE: A new report by Community trade union and Serco found 55% think rehabilitation needs to be fixed, more than the 46% who favour longer sentences

View 2 Images Ministers face calls to show courage to tackle a prison rehabilitation crisis (Image: Tony Nicoletti/Daily Record)

Ministers face calls to show "political courage" and fix the prison rehabilitation crisis after polling showed voters prefer that to longer sentences.

‌



‌



A report by Community Union and Serco has called for prisoners to get a legal entitlement to rehabilitation behind bars - and for cuts to education funding to be reversed. It warns the current system is failing to turn criminals' lives around - meaning many are in and out of jail.

‌



Polling seen by The Mirror shows 55% of adults want rehabilitation fixed - more than the 46% who think sentences should be longer, and 36% who think prison life should be harder. A poll of 1,999 adults by PF Global found 85% agree that a prison sentence should be both a punishment and a means of rehabilitation.

‌



Andy Burnham defends emergency kit list and gives verdict on stockpiling wine READ MORE :

John Healey told to extend free breakfasts to SEND children in secondary school at Budget READ MORE :

View 2 Images Justice Secretary Alex Norris has been urged to create a legal requirement for rehabilitation

Gavin Miller, national secretary for justice and custodial at Community Union, said: "We have an antiquated system. The justice sector is so, so far behind the times.

"If you've got somebody who's been sentenced who genuinely wants to break the cycle, this would give them the leverage to say, 'You need to give me this. I don't want to be back here'.

‌



"As a society, I think we've got an obligation to try and support that. And that helps everybody, and even if you go into the commercial argument, it helps the public purse.

"We've got to come up with some radical ideas if we're going to get reform. Otherwise, what we're going to do is tiptoe into the next crisis."

‌



He said the Tories underinvested in the prison sector, delivering just 500 new prison places in 20 years. Mr Miller said: "Now, if we just build new prisons, we're going to fill those prisons. What we need to do is find a way to encourage rehabilitation, to encourage a way of breaking the cycle."

The report warns that years of overcrowding, staff shortages and rising violence has left many prisons struggling. It said that rehabilitation is a postcode lottery, with huge variation between jails, stating: "The problem is not a lack of belief in the importance of rehabilitation, but a lack of capacity to deliver it."

‌



And it concludes: "Political leaders must find the political courage to talk about and make the big decisions required to reform our long-struggling prison system, break the cycle of crises and deliver a rehabilitation system that prisoners, prison staff and the wider public deserve and expect."

Research by PF Global also found 71% of the public believe being a prison officer is more difficult than most public sector jobs. And 55% believe prison officers are not sufficiently valued by society.

‌



The report calls on the government to explore a legal duty for minimum rehabilitative entitlements in each sentencing plan. It also says prison governors should have more freedom over recruitment and how their jails are run.

It also calls for teaching and learning hours to be restored and better data collection on how rehabilitation programmes are working. In January the government admitted it expects education delivery hours in prisons to fall by 20-25% because of rising costs.

‌



Olivia Walsham, Director at PF Global, said: "Our research underlines the jeopardy currently facing the prison system. It is operating at capacity, struggling to deliver the effective rehabilitation that the public expects and in doing so is perpetuating a cycle of offending that does nothing for prisoner outcomes nor public safety.

"If policymakers were to be bold and focus not only on the amount of time spent in prison, but what happens whilst people are there to reduce reoffending, our findings show that they would have the public backing to do so."

‌



A Ministry of Justice spokesperson said: “We inherited prisons on the brink of collapse but we’re pulling every lever to restore order. We run a range of schemes to give prisoners the skills and experience they’ll need after release, including finding a job.

"This report recognises good work at HMP Warren Hill and we’re committed to sharing good practice across the estate.

Article continues below

“But we know there is more to do, which is why former Home Secretary Amber Rudd is leading an independent review to deliver safer prisons, cut reoffending, and keep the public safe.”

News.title: Storm Austen brings power cuts and travel disruption as more wind and rain forecast
News.content:
More than 15,000 homes are without power as Storm Austen continues to batter southern England and Wales, with more bad weather expected this weekend.

The first named storm of the season brought gusts of up to 84mph (135km/h) to Jersey, while in southern England the wild weather disrupted travel with fallen trees blocking railway lines and roads.

In Brighton, part of the iconic West Pier - an abandoned structure that first opened in 1866 - collapsed into the sea.

On Saturday, Storm Boelo is forecast to bring more strong winds and heavy rain. The Met Office has put in place an amber warning for wind on Saturday and Sunday to cover parts of Scotland, northern England and Northern Ireland.

Austen made landfall in the south-west overnight and tracked eastwards throughout the day. All schools on Jersey and Guernsey closed for the day and some in Cornwall were closed or started later than normal.

Ahead of the worst of the storm on Thursday afternoon, families were evacuated from a holiday park in Perranporth, Cornwall. Among them was Hannah Dawson-Turk, who told the BBC "the night before last, it sounded like our caravan was going to be ripped apart".

"The storm is very loud outside now, and the waves look huge from our windows," she said from a nearby hotel.

The National Grid said engineers had restored power to more than 60,000 properties since Storm Austen began.

Some ferry services between the UK and France were cancelled, while National Rail advised many routes were travelling at slower speeds.

In Brighton, onlookers filmed as a section of the West Pier fell into the sea as it was pummeled by large waves.

Stephen Royle, who lives opposite, said the waves rolling in were "enormous" and he is "shocked" by how much of the pier ended up in the sea.

The pier closed to the public in 1975 and fell into disrepair, but the ruined structure became a symbol of Brighton for some.

News.title: Meghan says she was informed about 'disturbing allegations' against her father in 2018
News.content:
The Duchess of Sussex has said she was informed about "disturbing allegations" about her estranged father in 2018.

In a statement, Meghan said a letter containing allegations against Thomas Markle was sent to the Metropolitan Police that year and subsequently shared with her.

Her comments come after reports that images of child sexual abuse allegedly belonging to her father had been found at his former home in the Philippines.

Thomas Markle, who is 82 and based in the US, denies possessing any such images.

Commenting after the allegations, first reported by The Sun newspaper, external, the duchess said: "I am deeply distressed at the news that has come to light in the last 24 hours, and my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed."

She said that when she received the letter outlining allegations against her father, she was "given assurance that these were being investigated".

She added she hoped it could be understood why she had kept her distance from her father and did "not allow him to have contact with our children".

This was "to protect them", Meghan said, adding that she had "trusted that the authorities were doing the same for other families".

She described the allegations as "more sickening than one could ever imagine" and said her "sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children".

News.title: Meghan statement offers answers after years of questions about her relationship with father
News.content:
Before today's allegations and the statement from the Duchess of Sussex there was not much at all between Meghan and her father.

Quite when the duchess last saw her father Thomas isn't clear. By the time her engagement was announced in 2017, a once-close relationship had cooled.

He had moved to Mexico following his retirement in the US and then, as he spoke freely to the media before and after her 2018 wedding, the relationship went into the deep freeze.

He said she barely called as he underwent heart surgery, the duchess's people briefed that she had. Then they went silent as he complained in interview after interview that he no longer saw his daughter, had never met Harry nor, later, his grandchildren.

Now Meghan has told us why.

Thomas Markle gave the first, very large, hint that things would be different within weeks of the announcement of Meghan and Harry's wedding.

Instead of accepting the embrace of the Palace - and the media silence that involves - he happily went rogue, giving comments, sometimes commentary, to various media outlets. He had what appeared to be a paid photoshoot whilst claiming that he was being harassed by the media, withdrawing from the wedding just days beforehand as he underwent heart surgery.

There was no lack of drama.

The interviews and comments never really stopped. Markle was a regular on some broadcast outlets, often complaining that he had no contact with his daughter and son-in-law or, later, his grandchildren.

From Meghan came neither comment nor guidance as to why she had cut contact with the father with whom she had once been so close.

And into that vacuum rushed theory and supposition - that Meghan was embarrassed by her father, that she and Harry felt their privacy had been compromised by him and so would no longer give him material to recycle, that the old man who was so close to the popular news outlets that tormented them was no longer part of the life they wanted to lead.

News.title: Bayern Munich manager Kompany taken to hospital after collapsing at training
News.content:
Bayern Munich manager Vincent Kompany was taken to hospital after collapsing as he watched the club's second team train on Friday.

The 40-year-old had been unwell with a virus and missed the pre-match news conference on Tuesday prior to Bayern's Champions League game against Arsenal.

The former Manchester City and Belgium defender was subsequently on the touchline for the match on Wednesday.

Reports in Germany say Kompany is in a stable condition in hospital.

"Vincent Kompany required medical attention after collapsing during an FC Bayern reserve team training session on Friday," said a statement from the Bundesliga club., external

"The first-team head coach was watching the second string's session.

"Kompany is undergoing thorough examinations in hospital and will remain under medical care.

"His coaching staff will oversee training and match activities until further notice."

Bayern's next game is against Freiburg in the German top flight on Sunday.

"Vincent Kompany's health is our top priority. We at FC Bayern will do everything we can to ensure his speedy recovery," said Bayern sporting director Max Eberl.

"Vinnie is receiving all the necessary medical care and support, and all the time he needs.

"His coaching team, in whom we have complete confidence, will take over his duties. All of us at FC Bayern wish Vinnie a speedy recovery."

Aaron Danks, one of Kompany's assistants, took the pre-match news conference for Bayern before the Arsenal game.

German football journalist Taufig Khalil told BBC Radio 5 Live that Kompany had been "suffering with the virus for about a week".

He added: "The thing started last weekend on Saturday against Leipzig, and that's the first time we saw Vincent Kompany [when] he didn't look very well.

"He didn't do the press conference after, and Max Eberl told us that he's suffering with a virus.

"Everybody was really surprised that Vincent Kompany was standing there with his black jacket in the pouring rain of Munich on Wednesday night against Arsenal. Everybody expected Aaron Danks to be there.

"The problem was that maybe you couldn't bench Vincent Kompany, the game was too important for him.

"Bayern Munich just told us that he's in stable conditions. There was a helicopter involved in the whole thing, which landed on the training ground at Bayern Munich, but he was not brought into the hospital by helicopter. They brought him with a medical car and he will be now there."

News.title: Watch: Prince William on how he once dreamed of becoming 'DJ Xara'
News.content:
The Prince of Wales has revealed he once dreamed of becoming a policeman or a DJ.

Speaking on BBC One's The Graham Norton Show, Prince William said he thought being a policeman was "quite cool," before going through a phase where he wanted to be a DJ.

Billing himself as "DJ Xara" - with an X - he told the host he "wasn't very good", falling short of the calibre needed to play school parties.

The Prince made a surprise appearance on the show which airs on Friday evening, as part of a special edition to mark the Earthshot Prize, an initiative he set up in 2020 to tackle global environmental issues.

He was joined on the sofa by Cate Blanchett, Robert Irwin and Hannah Waddingham, who are all involved with the prize.

Read more about the prince's appearance here.

News.title: Burnham suggests stocking up on tinned food and bottled water
News.content:
The prime minister has advised people to stock up on tinned food and bottled water in order to be prepared for emergencies.

With storms battering the UK, and in the wake of online disruption caused by a major security flaw, Andy Burnham said "unexpected events seem to be becoming more and more common".

The government has drawn up recommendations for households to have three days' worth of bottled water and tinned food to deal with a crisis such as a war, an online attack or a natural disaster.

Burnham added: "It's not about panicking... It's about just taking sensible measures to have enough in the house to tide you over should there be a difficult situation."

At Labour's conference last month, Housing Secretary Angela Rayner joked that her emergency box, external would include a bottle of wine.

She said she'd include: "Mascara, concealer, I don't know, a bottle of Sauvignon Blanc, a tin of baked beans because you've gotta have some baked beans, and I like a good tin of custard as well so I think that'll keep me going for a while."

Asked whether he agreed with her, Burnham told BBC Radio 5 Live's Matt Chorley: "Well, I'm not sure a bottle of wine is your best first port of call if you're in a slightly crisis situation, but it probably helps when you've done the hard work.

"But I'll stick to the basics I think - I do like my beans, so I have plenty of those in the cupboard, and soup.

"I think those are the kind of things that I would recommend people to have, as well as Twiglets, I'm not sure I can get by for too long without those."

Last month, the National Audit Office (NAO) warned Britain's food supply chain is at risk given the growing threat of cyber-attacks and the climate crisis and said the Department for Food, the Environment and Rural Affairs (Defra) had not done enough in recent years to improve supply chain resilience.

The chief executive of the Cold Chain Federation, which represents firms transporting temperature-controlled foods, also told the BBC the UK is being targeted by Russian cyber-hackers who "know that there are pinch points in the food supply system".

Speaking at a wildfire resilience summit in Liverpool, Burnham denied the government had failed to properly prepare, saying: "No, we're having the conversation with people about being better prepared because we're living in a world where unexpected events seem to be becoming more and more common.

"Obviously, weather events, and we're in a situation today where the UK is facing storms and obviously, we feel for the people without power in Cornwall right now.

"It is just having those supplies in the house to get you through those moments. So we are having that conversation about resilience."

News.title: GP says she was forced out of job after raising concerns about gender treatment
News.content:
Although Doyle at first denied to the tribunal he knew Hall before this, it emerged during the tribunal that he had previously had a number of mentoring meetings with the GP.

The GMC investigation was not taken forward. However, the NHS launched an investigation into Redvers, bringing in an external investigator.

The tribunal heard she was called to what she described as a "brutal" four-hour interrogation.

"It was oppressive, very upsetting. I didn't feel I had the chance at all to explain what had happened," she said. "I broke down at one point".

She said she was off sick for several months as a result and received treatment for trauma.

Other colleagues who were interviewed as part of the investigation into Redvers also complained about the process and the NHS upheld most of their complaints.

The investigation concluded the CEO and trust should apologise to Redvers.

It also warned that Redvers' treatment would have a "broader negative impact" on the willingness of staff to raise concerns.

In 2023, a year after the grievance outcome, when a trans campaigner suggested in an NHS meeting that she was transphobic, Redvers told the tribunal she felt the NHS did not do enough to support her. She felt she had no choice but to leave her job as a safeguarding GP.

"I just felt there's no way I could carry on working in this organisation," she told the BBC.

At about that time, a group of parents, school governors and social workers began raising concerns about WellBn and Hall.

The co-founder of campaign group PSHE Brighton, Rachel Cashman, said: "It is a travesty that Sarah Redvers was punished for doing her job safeguarding and expecting the best standards of care for gender distressed children."

Redvers is now waiting for the outcome of her employment tribunal. She may not get the judgment for several months.

She described what has happened as "personally and professionally difficult" and said the NHS "needs to remember that patients come first" and it should "listen to staff who raise legitimate concerns."

In a statement NHS Surrey and Sussex said: "We engaged professionally and supportively with the Employment Tribunal. We recognise that some employment processes should have been handled differently and have apologised whilst Dr Redvers was employed with us, before, and during the hearings. We await the findings of the tribunal to make any further comment."

NHS England said: "When concerns about prescribing practices by an individual GP were escalated to NHS England national directors in 2023, they met directly with an affected family and asked regional professional standards leads to undertake formal investigations.

"Wider concerns were subsequently identified, and the WellBN practice was asked to stop providing a specialised prescribing service. Further new information led to NHS England and NHS Sussex initiating an independent patient safety investigation in 2025."

Dr Sam Hall and WellBN have been contacted for comment.

In response to the investigation report in June, WellBN said it recognised "the seriousness and sensitivity of the matters raised" and that its priority remained providing "compassionate, safe and effective care for all patients".

News.title: Freed US citizen was tortured in Russian jail, former Ukrainian prisoners say
News.content:
Khyliuk, a journalist, was held in the earliest days of the invasion, when Russian troops advanced towards the capital Kyiv.

He said he knew Hubbard's health was declining over the months they were initially held in nearby cells because he heard his complaints and the guards calling him more often to see the prison doctor.

Khyliuk described broken windows and biting cold, with detainees using time out of their cells to huddle together in the bathroom for warmth.

"It was very difficult conditions in Novozybkov, worse than in the next prison. It was very cold there in winter, terribly cold," he said.

Both men encountered the retired English teacher again at their next prison, Pakino, where Shyshko says Hubbard's condition worsened.

"There was not a single spot on his knees or on his feet without rot," he said.

"Everything was rotten. We all had scabies. It was very, very difficult for him. I even bandaged him once at the medical centre, because the doctor didn't want to do it. He just couldn't do it himself, and I had to help. He was quite weak then and he almost couldn't move."

They detailed a harsh regime and a meagre diet of porridge, bread and potatoes, with a daily routine of beatings and humiliation, being forced to run or hold stress positions.

"There's a handler with a dog, who lets go so it can bite you on the buttocks, on the elbow, or bite your leg. Then these wounds fester very badly," Shyshko said.

Khyliuk claimed that soon after their transfer to Pakino, Hubbard was hidden to conceal his condition from a team of International Red Cross visitors.

"I would like to say that an international humanitarian organisation that receives a lot of funding could do better. They saw only what was shown to them and they were happy with that," he said.

The International Committee of the Red Cross said in a statement that "in any situation where the ICRC has been granted access, we request to see every individual and assess the conditions they are held in. We continue our discussions with parties to the conflict on this issue."

Khyliuk said Hubbard disappeared from the prison in 2024 and he thought he must have been released. Khyliuk was returned to Ukraine in August 2025 in a prisoner exchange.

He likened their treatment to the regime of Soviet leader Joseph Stalin.

"Russian captivity is a torture machine. From the first second of your detention, they do everything to suppress you, to intimidate you. This is torture in all its manifestations, from psychological to physical. Beatings, hunger, cold, lack of any information, lack of the opportunity to communicate even with other prisoners".

Khyliuk said he was pleased to see Hubbard finally released and heading to the US.

"I understand what it is like to be in terrible captivity. Moreover, it was not his war. He ended up in the wrong place and at the wrong time," he said.

But he described the timing as "shameful PR of the US president, who is losing votes in elections to Congress".

Shyshko said he hoped one day their torturers would face justice.

"Evil must be punished, and so it will be. I have hope for that".

News.title: First personalised cancer vaccine cuts risk of disease returning in major trial
News.content:
Shares in the drugmakers MSD (known as Merck in the US) and Moderna have surged since both companies first hinted at the success of the vaccine in the summer.

But investors sold off stock on Thursday after financial analysts said the results were not quite as strong as those seen in an earlier, much smaller trial.

Both companies said they were now "engaging with authorities" suggesting they could file for approval from medicine regulators as soon as next year.

Widespread NHS use will also depend on cost, given that each individual patient will need to have their tumour genetically analysed and a personalised vaccine made for them.

The trial will continue so that the patients involved can be monitored â both to see if the cancer returns over time and to assess whether the drug ultimately helps them live longer.

Professor Alan Melcher from the Institute of Cancer Research in London, who wasn't involved in the research, described the results as "very impressive".

"It is an important proof of principle for the field, although we shouldn't get ahead of the evidence," he said.

"We can't assume from one melanoma trial that the same approach will work across all cancers, and longer follow-up will be important to understand the effect on overall survival."

The full trial results are due to be presented at the European Society of Medical Oncology (ESMO) cancer conference in Madrid on Saturday.

They have yet to be published in a peer-reviewed medical journal, where they can be scrutinised by independent experts.

News.title: Green councillors face Labour deadline to disown Zionism policy
News.content:
Labour is set to decide whether to end power-sharing with Green councillors after demanding they disown their party's policy that Zionism is a form of racism.

The BBC has been told Green groups have been given until Sunday to respond to the demand, after which Labour's ruling National Executive Committee (NEC) will decide whether the party will continue with local deals to share power.

Green groups in some areas have publicly stated they do not agree with the policy or have distanced themselves from it, reducing the likelihood the pacts will end.

But in other areas Green councillors are yet to specify where they stand on the issue, meaning local alliances appear more vulnerable to collapse.

The issue is the most acute in nine local authorities where Greens are key partners in power-sharing arrangements, such as making up majorities that enable budgets to be passed and policy decisions to be made.

These include Sheffield City Council, Warwick District Council and Lewes District Council, three authorities where Labour and the Greens are in direct coalition.

The other areas where the Greens play a key role are: West Oxfordshire District Council, Stafford Borough Council, Havant Borough Council, Broadland District Council, Derbyshire Dales District Council and Wealden District Council.

In other areas, Green councillors are not central to local alliances continuing to function. These include Runnymede Borough Council, where Green councillors have left the local ruling alliance folllowing Labour's ultimatum.

In some areas, such as Lewes, Wealden, Broadland, West Sussex and North Somerset, local Green groups have distanced themselves from their party's Zionism policy, or said they do not agree with it.

But other Green groups are yet to publicly respond to Labour's demands, meaning there is greater uncertainty over the future of their co-operation with the party.

In Stafford, the power-sharing arrangement means the Greens have one cabinet member on the authority, councillor Tony Pearce, who holds the climate change portfolio.

Councillor Pearce has been contacted for comment but has not yet responded.

The leader of the Stafford Green group, Doug Rouxel told the BBC they were "formulating a response" to Labour's letter which they would like to put to party members first.

Labour confirmed the if the Greens refused to reject the Zionism policy, a process would then be triggered to remove Pearce from his cabinet position in Stafford.

Elsewhere, the leader of the Labour group on the Green-led Lewes District Council has resigned from the party, following his own party's ultimatum.

Chris Collier, who has been contacted for comment, will now sit as an independent cabinet member on the Labour-Green alliance that was formed to run the council in May 2023.

The BBC has been told Collier did not agree with the tone of Labour's ultimatum to the Green Party over the Zionism policy.

News.title: Trump says Burnham 'getting it done' after Jackdaw decision
News.content:
Burnham announced the decision to approve the drilling of the Jackdaw gas field earlier this week.

Jackdaw is situated 150 miles (241km) east of Aberdeen and is operated by Adura, a joint venture between Shell and Norwegian state energy firm Equinor.

Ministers said the first gas could be produced by the end of this month, helping heat millions of homes, and also announced the creation of a new energy wealth fund.

Environmental campaigners say the decision would hamper efforts to tackle climate change and make "no meaningful difference" to UK energy security.

Based on official forecasts for the amount of gas the UK will need over the next decade, that suggests Jackdaw has the potential to meet around 1.6% of total projected national gas demand between 2026 and 2036.

Operators say it could be connected to the Great British gas network within weeks and could produce gas for the next 11 years.

Trump responded to the decision on Friday, but appeared to confuse oil and gas.

He said: "They're opening up the North Sea oil. I've been after them to do that for two years."

Trump added: "Andy is getting it done, and I guess it's against the liberal principle, but he knows what's right. It's going to make UK a very wealthy country."

In a discussion on Friday, Burnham and Trump spoke about the decision to approve Jackdaw.

The two leaders "agreed on the significant benefits this will bring to the UK, boosting the economy and supporting jobs for British workers", a statement from Number 10 read.

It added that Trump and Burnham "welcomed the continued collaboration between UK and US companies, especially on nuclear power".

Earlier this week, on Wednesday, Trump said the decision was "great news for the wealth and prosperity" of the UK.

Writing on his Truth Social platform, Trump urged the UK to go "full blast" and called the North Sea "one of the greatest and most prosperous areas of oil in the world".

A decision is yet to be taken on whether production can begin at Rosebank, the UK's largest known untapped oil field, which is located off the coast of Shetland in the North Atlantic.

News.title: Man dies after car crashes into Lidl supermarket
News.content:
A man in his 30s has died after a car crashed through the entrance of a Lidl shop in Wolverhampton.

Police were called to the supermarket in Finchfield Hill shortly before 18:00 BST on Friday.

West Midlands Police said the man was pronounced dead at the scene and a number of other people were treated for injuries.

West Midlands Fire Service said it dispatched four crews to the incident at 17:51 BST with two crews still at the scene at 20:05 BST.

The car had crashed through the entrance of the shop, smashing the glass, and remained just inside the doors on Friday night as emergency services remained at the scene.

Tina Bonev, who witnessed the crash, said it was "absolutely terrifying" and there had been "shock and confusion" in the aftermath.

News.title: Police yet to receive £2m after A66 crash, says commissioner
News.content:
A police force has still not received the Â£2m it was promised by the government in the wake of a car crash that led to the deaths of seven people, including two police officers, the local police and crime commissioner (PCC) says.

Cleveland PCC Matt Storey said Cleveland Police was still waiting for the extra funding promised by the home secretary in August.

Shabana Mahmood pledged the cash in light of challenges faced by the force following the deaths, which followed a pursuit on the A66 at South Bank, near Middlesbrough, on 22 August. Five young men were also killed.

The Home Office said the force would receive the Â£2m it had been promised by the end of November.

During the fatal crash, a Volkswagen Passat in which the five young men were travelling hit an oncoming marked Cleveland Police vehicle on the dual carriageway near Middlesbrough at about 03:39 BST.

Officers PC Matthew Blades, 37, and PC Tom Clough, 38, died at the scene.

The occupants of the VW Passat, which was travelling the wrong way down the A66 at South Bank - Michael Robert Cahill, 23, Jakub Matusiak, 23, Makai Saddington, 18, and 17-year-olds Theo Rae and Cole Robert Worthy - were also killed.

On the morning of the crash, Cleveland Police said it received several reports of two vehicles being driven dangerously around the town and a Volvo XC60 had been seen ramming properties.

Further arrests were subsequently made in connection with organised crime, including the following weekend after another vehicle ramming.

News.title: Trial set for men accused of synagogue bomb plot
News.content:
Two Iranian men have appeared in court over an alleged plot to target the Jewish community in Manchester with a homemade bomb.

Salam Ahmadyan, 36, of Liverpool, and Rahman Salehi, 34, of Salford, are accused of conducting hostile reconnaissance at Heaton Park Synagogue, which was subject to a fatal attack last year, along with the Jewish Museum in Cheetham Hill.

The pair, who arrived illegally into the UK on boats, are charged with engaging in conduct in preparation for terrorist acts on or before 20 September. They deny the charges.

They appeared via videolink at the Old Bailey and a trial date was set at Manchester Crown Court for 15 June 2027.

It is alleged Ahmadyan and Salehi were in contact with an Iranian national who directed and co-ordinated the planned attack, with the third party most likely operating within Iran.

The men are accused of getting instructions to make a chlorine bomb and acquiring liquids, components and equipment required in order to manufacture or assemble an improvised explosive device.

They are also accused of using the internet to identify and research potential targets, acquiring images, plans and maps of potential targets and conducting reconnaissance of potential locations for attack.

The pair deny the charges against them.

The trial is estimated to last five weeks. The next court hearing is due to take place on 16 April next year.

Melvin Cravitz, 66, and Adrian Daulby, 53, were killed when Jihad Al-Shamie, 35, drove into the gates of Heaton Park Hebrew Synagogue on 2 October last year, and began a knife attack while wearing a fake suicide belt.

News.title: Ex-Tory campaign chief and his wife receive suspended sentences over election bets
News.content:
The Conservatives' former director of campaigning and his wife have received suspended prison sentences after they admitted to cheating at gambling by placing bets on the date of the 2024 general election.

Anthony Lee used "inside information" emerging from a private meeting called by then-Prime Minister Rishi Sunak to bet on the general election date months before it took place, Southwark Crown Court heard.

Lee and his wife Laura stood to win more than Â£23,000 had their cheating not been uncovered, the court heard.

Lee was sentenced to 10 months and two weeks' imprisonment, suspended for 12 months, while his wife was sentenced to four months and two weeks' imprisonment, suspended for a year.

Amy Hind, a former Tory party employee who was working as an NHS business support manager, was also sentenced to six months' imprisonment, suspended for a year, after previously pleading guilty to cheating on the date of the election.

Judge Tony Baumgartner, sentencing the three of them, said their conduct "risked undermining" the confidence the public has in the Conservative Party "as an institution", "undermining trust in the democratic process" and the "integrity of the gambling system".

The trio were among several people charged with betting offences by the Gambling Commission.

The trials of other defendants will take place next year and in 2028.

Former Conservative MP Craig Williams, who was Sunak's closest parliamentary aide at the time, pleaded guilty in June and will be sentenced at a later date.

News.title: PM defends Gogglebox appearance after Badenoch criticism
News.content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has defended his decision to appear on a celebrity episode of Channel 4 hit show Gogglebox after opposition leader Kemi Badenoch said she was "amazed" he had time to do it.

Badenoch told BBC Breakfast that "even as a junior minister or as a secretary of state, I never had time to go on Gogglebox" and it "takes hours to do".

The Conservative leader was responding after Burnham was revealed in the line-up of a celebrity episode of the show in aid of Stand Up To Cancer - which will air later.

"I'm proud to support Stand Up To Cancer. I make no apology for trying to lead with a bit of lightness and at times a bit of humour, that's the way I go at things," Burnham said.

The former Greater Manchester mayor will appear on the programme alongside friend Steve Rotheram, the Labour mayor of the Liverpool City Region.

Speaking to BBC Radio 5 Live, Burnham continued: "It is always a moment in the annual calendar where we support Stand Up To Cancer through Gogglebox," Burnham said of the recurring charity special.

"Steve and I are proud to do it.

"I'm trying to give the country a lift - trying to give the county some hope.

"That's always my approach and it's what I'm trying to do.

"It may not appeal to everybody when it comes to Gogglebox.

"It's Stand Up To Cancer night and I've always been somebody who puts my shoulder behind the fight against cancer."

News.title: Jury convicts man of rape, murder 14 years after UNC student’s death
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

A man accused of killing a North Carolina college student 14 years ago was convicted Friday of first-degree murder, rape and other charges after prosecutors told jurors that forensic evidence was “screaming his name.”

Faith Hedgepeth was a 19-year-old sophomore at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill when she was beaten to death in her off-campus apartment in September 2012. Miguel Salguero Olivares was arrested nine years later after being pulled over for driving while intoxicated and providing a DNA sample that prosecutors say matched evidence from the crime scene.

Salguero Olivares, 33, did not testify during the trial, and his attorneys rested their case without calling any witnesses. Jurors deliberated for six hours over two days before convicting him of murder, rape, sexual offense and burglary.

In closing arguments Thursday, defense attorneys accused investigators of having “tunnel vision” in assuming that their client was a monster and not a “19-year-old boy” who had consensual sex with the victim days before her death. Prosecutors, meanwhile, urged jurors to rely on DNA evidence instead of distractions from the defense team.

“We know who did it. The forensic evidence is screaming his name,” said prosecutor Angela Garcia-Lamarca, who described the “uncurable agony” Hedgepeth's family has endured.

“When the defendant brought that bottle down on her head and she started to bleed, that was the start of a bleeding that still hasn’t stopped,” she said. “He sentenced her to death. He sentenced everybody else who loved her to life. There was no one there to protect her. There was no one there to stop him — until now. Y’all are here. You’re here now, and you can stop him.”

Prosecution suggests victim spurned defendant's advances

Nearly two dozen witnesses testified for the prosecution, including crime scene technicians, state and local law enforcement, a DNA expert and Hedgepeth's friends.

Hedgepeth's roommate, Karena Rosario, testified that she was drunk and sick when Hedgepeth drove them home from a club around 2 a.m. that Sept. 7. She said she later called a friend to pick her up, leaving Hedgepeth in the apartment alone. She returned hours later to find her roommate’s body.

Prosecutors suggested Salguero Olivares may have attended a barbecue hosted by Hedgepeth’s neighbor that night, unsuccessfully hit on the young women in the parking lot and then returned, embarrassed and angry, after Rosario left. No witnesses corroborated that theory, but Garcia-Lamarca told jurors, “You don’t have to believe that to know he’s guilty.”

An autopsy showed Hedgepeth suffered extensive skull fractures and cuts to her face and head, and she was also badly beaten on her arms and legs.

“He beat her until her skull cracked like an egg,” special prosecutor Lisa Coltrane said in her portion of the closing arguments. “That is what the last moments of this vibrant young woman’s life was.”

Forensic evidence was a focus

Experts testified that the defendant’s fingerprints and palm print were found on a wine bottle at the scene and that his DNA was found in Hedgepeth’s body, on a note written on a fast-food bag found at the scene and on a rum bottle covered in blood that investigators identified as the weapon in the killing.

Erin Ermish, a forensic scientist with the state crime lab, said DNA swabbed from Hedgepeth’s body was 170 septillion times more likely to be a mixture of DNA from Hedgepeth and Salguero Olivares than from Hedgepeth and an unknown individual. One septillion is a 1 followed by 24 zeros. In contrast, NASA estimates the entire universe contains only 1 septillion stars.

Ermish also said the DNA mixture from the top of the rum bottle was 48.6 tredecillion times more likely to be from Hedgepeth and Salguero Olivares than from two unknown, unrelated individuals. One tredecillion is a 1 followed by 42 zeros.

The defense highlighted investigation mistakes

Defense attorneys questioned Rosario’s account of that night, the processing of the crime scene and the reliability of some DNA evidence. They pointed out that police failed to search some areas of the apartment and later lost some possible blood evidence and emphasized that DNA from sexual intercourse can remain for days afterward.

“Maybe he was living the same life as other 19- and 20-year-old children that we’ve heard about in this case,” defense attorney Jason Murphy said. “Maybe he had too much to drink, maybe he forgot about an encounter.”

But Coltrane dismissed that as “noise.”

“No matter what kind of mistakes were made or things that were missed, it doesn’t erase the palm print; it doesn’t somehow lift the DNA out of Faith,” she said. “They didn’t talk to every single person in Chapel Hill, and it doesn’t matter. They still got the guy because he left his DNA like confetti all over that room.”

News.title: Trump boasts he ordered DOJ to sue Alaska to get election result tossed out if they lose
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Donald Trump says he ordered the Department of Justice to sue the state of Alaska in an effort to block the results of a U.S. Senate election from being certified, unless the incumbent Republican wins.

Government attorneys filed a lawsuit Friday arguing that the presence of Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. on the ballot would confuse voters who support the sitting senator, Daniel S. Sullivan, in the unusual matchup of two candidates with the same name up against a Democratic candidate.

“I’m the one that said do it,” Trump told reporters Friday. “They have two Dan Sullivans.”

Trump’s admission of an extraordinary intervention in the nation’s elections follows the president’s threats to overhaul election administration and assert federal control before critical midterm elections with the balance of power in Congress, and fate of his final years in office, at stake.

Voters might “inadvertently vote” for the wrong candidate, according to the Justice Department. “To guard against this danger, it is vital that Defendants not certify any election result that may be impacted by voter confusion,” government attorneys wrote in court filings on Friday.

open image in gallery Donald Trump told reporters that he instructed the Justice Department to sue Alaska to prevent the loss of a Trump-backed Republican incumbent in a close Senate race ( Reuters )

That “voter confusion” could tilt the election in favor of the Democratic nominee, Mary Peltola, thanks to Dan J. Sullivan’s “frivolous” campaign, according to the Justice Department.

Recent polling suggests the Republican incumbent is neck and neck with Peltola, a former Democratic congresswoman.

The Trump administration is seeking a court order that would prevent the state from certifying results if “Senator Sullivan does not win the election,” claiming that “had all votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan been cast instead for Senator Sullivan and Alaska’s rank-choice process played out accordingly, Senator Sullivan would have won the election.”

“The Democrats put up a guy,” Trump told reporters Friday. “I don’t think he ever voted before. All of a sudden he decides to run.”

The lawsuit was filed one day after Attorney General Todd Blanche said he would not rule out dispatching the Justice Department to block states from certifying election results.

“Yes, of course there’s scenarios we could all come up with, hypothetically — some ‘doomsday’ scenario, for example,” he told reporters Thursday. “I don’t think it’s proper to make any kind of conclusory statements about what could happen in the future.”

open image in gallery Dan J. Sullivan, left, is challenging incumbent Senator Dan Sullivan, right, for a U.S. Senate seat in Alaska, an unusual matchup that prompted the Trump administration to intervene ( Sullivan for Senate/Getty )

open image in gallery Democratic candidate Mary Peltola, a former congresswoman, is polling closely alongside the incumbent Republican ( Reuters )

While it’s “never” the Justice Department’s intention to “improperly interfere with elections or the state confirmation process or certification process,” he told reporters, “to say that there’s no circumstances that we would ever do that, of course, I’m not going to say that,” he said.

“But am I planning my days around the election to be somewhere to not certify? Of course not,” he added.

Days earlier, Blanche — the president’s former criminal defense lawyer — stated that he “works for President Trump.”

“There was this misperception that there’s this separation and independence between the Department of Justice and the White House, and everybody likes to champion that, and they accused me of not suffering from independence,” he told The New York Post’s podcast. “I don’t.”

David Becker, executive director of the nonpartisan nonprofit group Center for Election Innovation & Research, said the lawsuit “represents an unprecedented intervention by the federal government.”

“This is purely a matter of state law, and the administration has absolutely no authority to tell Alaska when or how to certify the results of its Senate election,” he said in a statement.

"The DOJ attempting to intervene at this late stage is entirely against department policy, as there is no legitimate enforcement of federal law here, and it raises serious concerns about political interference,” he added. “I cannot recall an administration ever attempting to stop the certification of an election — and certainly not 11 days before polls close.”

Former Alaska state elections attorney Libby Bakalar called the government’s argument “laughably bad, almost to the point of sanctionably frivolous,” while Notre Dame Law School election law professor Derek Muller called the argument “one of the worst ones I’ve ever seen.”

The issue has also already been litigated in Alaska’s courts.

In June, the Alaska Division of Elections removed Dan J. Sullivan from primary ballots, saying his candidacy was “for the purpose of confusing or misleading voters.”

But he appealed that decision, and an Anchorage Superior Court judge overturned the lower court. The argument that his candidacy is designed to “confuse or misguide voters is not supported by a preponderance of evidence,” Judge Thomas Matthews in a 32-page analysis.

The state appealed, but the decision was upheld, and the state did not seek an appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court.

In the primary, Peltola finished first with 49.5 percent of the vote, followed by Dan S. Sullivan with 41.4 percent and Dan J. Sullivan with 2.5 percent.

Harry Child, a spokesperson for Alaskans for Mary, called the lawsuit a “despicable political threat to overturn an election.”

According to the campaign, the lawsuit was “designed by Senator Dan Sullivan’s allies to suppress the voices of Alaskans because Sullivan is terrified he’ll lose the seat that has allowed him to enrich himself at Alaskans’ expense for over a decade,” Child told The Independent.

A spokesperson for Senator Sullivan’s campaign said they will “let the DOJ complaint run its course.”

“Alaskans can tell the difference between a Democrat sideshow and Senator Sullivan’s strong record of delivering for Alaska, a record he’ll keep building on for the next six years,” campaign spokesman: Nate Adams told The Independent.

News.title: Employee error blamed for toxic chemical leak that sent 60 people to hospital in Ohio
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

A chemical leak that sent 60 people to the hospital and forced hundreds of people to flee their homes has been blamed on an employee error.

Mayor Wade Kapszukiewicz announced the cause of the tank leak at a news conference on Friday and said that all remaining evacuation orders in Toledo, Ohio.

The chemical leak happened Tuesday night when an employee of MC Tank Transport “introduced a temperature level to the tank in the process of trying to transfer the liquid" that caused a chemical reaction, the mayor said.

MC Tank Transport said the tank contained glycidyl methacrylate, which it described as “an industrial chemical used to make certain plastics, paints and coatings perform better.”

open image in gallery A plume of smokes rises from MC Tank Transport Inc., where a chemical tank exploded overnight, prompting hundreds of residents to evacuate or shelter in place amid concerns about a potential toxic release, Wednesday, Oct. 21, 2026 ( AP )

The evacuation orders were lifted after the company finished venting the tank that ruptured. That allowed a hazmat team to enter the site and test safety levels.

“At this time, we do feel confident that the site is safe," Toledo Fire and Rescue Battalion Chief Blake Molnar said.

Dr Brian Kaminski, vice president of medical affairs for ProMedica hospitals, said about 60 patients were treated at the hospital, most suffering relatively minor symptoms. A small number of patients who had underlying health conditions were admitted, he said, and all patients were expected to recover.

The company has “accepted responsibility” for what happened, the mayor said.

open image in gallery The U.S. EPA on the scene near MC Tank Transport Inc. ( AP )

“There was no fire, there was no explosion. There was a very serious chemical reaction, which now happily has run its course, and we’re now finally able to return to some level of normalcy here in our community," he said.

Based on data that officials have seen so far, the amount of the chemical in the air didn't reach levels high enough to have “a long-term meaningful impact on human health,” according to Kapszukiewicz.

However,, some wuestions remain unanswered at the investigation is ongoing, he added.

News.title: AP Interview: Coast Guard swimmer says he fought waves, darkness to rescue 16 people from ocean
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Strapped into a harness, Josh Law was lowered from a U.S. Coast Guard helicopter into the rough Pacific Ocean in the pitch black night, far off the Mexican coast.

The force of the helicopter blades pummeled the water, whipping up spray and turbulence. The Coast Guard rescue swimmer couldn’t hear anything over the noise or see anything in the darkness. Waves of 6 to 8 feet (1.8 to 2.4 meters) pummeled him.

All he could do was follow the searchlight from the helicopter with the hope it would lead him to the more than two dozen people flung into the cold waters some 140 miles (225 kilometers) off the coast of Mexico’s Baja peninsula. He would personally rescue 16 of them.

“I was experiencing exhaustion at that point," Law, 24, told The Associated Press in his first interview since the rescue. "We had very little sleep. But what I was experiencing was nothing compared to what they were at that point ... I just had to keep that in mind.”

Over the next two hours in the predawn hours of Oct. 16, Law was the sole person in the water who would get the people whose boat had capsized out of the water. Eleven others were never found. The Coast Guard called off its search late Sunday.

Law described the dramatic operation to save lives along a remote route frequented by migrant smuggling boats. What the boat was doing out there and where it originated from are part of a federal investigation. It was unclear if the vessel got lost, had engine failure, was swept out to sea or meant to go that far. Only what were believed to be pieces of the boat were found. All who were rescued are Mexican, the Mexican consulate said.

The Coast Guard said U.S. Customs and Border Protection was investigating and interviewing the survivors, but the agency did not respond to multiple inquiries on whether the vessel was a migrant smuggling boat.

The alarm sounded, rousing the Coast Guard crew members from their sleep

The mayday call came in around 1 a.m.

Someone said their boat was sinking in the middle of the Pacific Ocean off the coast of Ensenada, Mexico.

Within minutes, the alarm sounded at the U.S. Coast Guard Air Station in Ventura, northwest of Los Angeles, rousing Law and his colleagues from their sleep.

Helicopter pilot Lt. Miyako Miller checked flying conditions and planned the flight route that would take the crew of four over the vast ocean south of the U.S. border.

Law prepared his dry suit, fins and medical items, then put on a harness that would be hooked onto a cable to lower him down from the aircraft into the ocean.

By 2 a.m., they were taking off from the Coast Guard station in Ventura.

Pilot says she was guided by the stars

Miller wore night vision goggles to help her fly in the dark. She said she relied on the stars, with no moonlight that night.

As the crew approached the reported location of the sinking, Miller spotted a tiny flicker of light in the distance.

Then she spotted what looked like debris floating in the water, but it was difficult to distinguish what it was. Miller carefully navigated the helicopter over the area, lowering the aircraft until it was hovering about 40 feet (12 meters) above the water.

“I’m doing my best to maintain my references externally by looking outside through the night vision goggles," Miller said, adding that meanwhile “the flight mechanic is telling me where to position the helicopter.”

Some 250 miles (400 kilometers) southwest of Ensenada, Mexico, is Guadalupe Island, a biosphere reserve that is well known as a place brimming with great white sharks.

Law said he didn’t think about what was in the water as he hooked himself to a cable and zipped into the ocean, strapped in a harness.

There was no time to waste. While Law’s dry suit provided some warmth, he knew the others had already spent hours in hypothermic temperature waters.

Law said he was guided by a searchlight from the crew, which allowed him to catch a glimpse of the people in the water.

They were scattered across a wide area. Some were wearing life vests that had tiny lights that produced the flicker first spotted by Miller. Others clung onto one another, buoys and pieces of wreckage, shivering and treading water to stay afloat.

Law said he swam to them, flipped them on their backs, put his arm over them and pulled them up using the “buddy tow” technique. Kicking his legs to swim, he carried them to the spot where he could signal the flight mechanic to lower a basket for them to be picked up.

“With one hand, I’m holding the survivor. With the other, I am signaling to the helicopter and working with the device,” he said.

He placed them into the basket, one by one. Then it was hoisted up to the helicopter where the crew got each person into the aircraft before lowering the basket again.

Law’s dry suit slowly filled up to his knees with water, feeling like weights pulling on him as he swam.

Over the next 90 minutes, Law battled heavy waves while swimming back and forth.

With little fuel, the crew flew to San Diego where ambulances waited

With a packed helicopter and dwindling fuel, the crew decided to head to the Coast Guard station in San Diego where ambulances were waiting.

On the flight, Law treated three people with what he described as “bad” wounds, staunching the bleeding. Several of the injuries were “consistent with shark bites" and the Coast Guard provided life-saving first aid, the agency said in a statement Saturday.

Customs and Border Protection officers went to a hospital and said they would process the survivors according to immigration laws after they were medically cleared. Nearly half of those rescued have since been returned to Mexico, U.S. officials said.

Law and his crew returned to Ventura that morning — it was by far the longest rescue operation he had ever done, he said.

The search for the 11 others continued for another two days to no avail. The Coast Guard, alongside Mexico and the U.S. Navy, searched more than 2,441 square miles (6,322 square kilometers) for a combined 89 hours.

Migrants are increasingly turning to the risky alternative offered by smugglers to travel by sea to avoid heavily guarded land borders. Small boats called pangas leave Baja at night and sometimes travel hundreds of miles (kilometers) north.

News.title: Trump, seeking to help Maine Sen. Susan Collins, exempts some Canadian imports from his 50% tariffs
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

President Donald Trump, seeking to help Republican Sen. Susan Collins in a tough reelection battle in Maine, is exempting some imports — including plywood sheets, packing crates and some machinery — from the 50% tariffs he slapped on $20 billion worth of Canadian products over the summer. The changes will take effect Oct. 30.

The White House said the president was seeking to offset "the burden to U.S. commerce while better serving the public interest.''

Collins, locked in a tight race with Democratic challenger Troy Jackson, issued a statement saying she'd spoken with Trump's top trade negotiator, Jamieson Greer, and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick "about the toll tariffs are taking on Maine families, businesses, farmers, and growers.''

"Many of our farmers and growers rely on specialized equipment, packaging materials, and other products from Canada that are either unavailable from American suppliers or cannot be replaced without incurring significant expense,” Collins said. “I have asked for tariff relief for these important products and stressed the burdens additional costs impose on Maine businesses and families. I will continue working directly with administration officials to seek additional relief from tariffs and encourage a broader trade agreement with Canada, our neighbor, ally, and largest trading partner.”
