News.title: Amex slashes 3,500 jobs and joins other financial companies culling staff as some leaders admit it’s for AI
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

American Express revealed plans Friday to cut around 3,500 jobs – about 5 percent of its global workforce – as the company’s executives admitted that artificial intelligence was a factor.

The cuts mark Amex’s first major round of layoffs in nearly a decade. The credit card giant said the move would streamline operations while allowing it to continue investing in the business but did not specify which departments or locations would be affected.

Chief Executive Stephen Squeri said the company wants to reduce management layers, speed up decision-making and position for future growth, according to The Wall Street Journal.

AI is also a factor in the restructuring. Chief Financial Officer Christophe Le Caillec told CNBC that the changes would help American Express become “leaner, more agile, and also to prepare for AI.”

Amex’s layoffs come after other major staff cuts at banks and credit card companies, including Barclays and Citigroup, as financial firms become the latest white-collar industry to feel the intense impacts of AI.

open image in gallery American Express said the layoffs will help streamline operations, as well as help it ‘prepare for AI’ ( Getty )

Economists are increasingly concerned about the impacts of AI on millions of white-collar jobs, including customer service, bookkeeping, payroll and HR, The New York Times reported in June. Many of these jobs offer middle-class wages without requiring a college degree and are disproportionately held by women, according to the outlet.

An Axios-Generation Lab poll of 1,075 Americans ages 18 to 34 released in August found that 27 percent believe they or someone they know has lost a job because an employer replaced the position with AI.

Le Caillec spoke Friday about how American Express could rely more on AI in the future. “You don’t want to automate processes that are not optimally structured,” he said. “So what we’re doing here is to reduce layers and increase spans of controls, so that we can automate and take advantage of AI in the coming quarters and the coming years.”

The layoffs come as American Express reported higher profits and revenue in the third quarter as customers continued spending on its cards. The company posted net income of $3.71 billion, up 28 percent from $2.9 billion a year earlier.

The American Express cuts come a day after Barclays announced plans to cut 5,000 jobs, or about 5 percent of its global workforce, by the end of the year. Barclays Group CEO CS Venkatakrishnan said the job cuts reflect the bank’s investment in technology to simplify operations and improve efficiency.

"AI has an important role to play and may have a more important role to play in the future. We will employ the AI at scale," he said, according to the BBC. "But AI is the icing on the cake, not the cake. Because you need to do the infrastructure build to get the benefits of AI.”

About 60 percent of the job cuts will affect support functions, including developer roles, Barclays said.

Earlier this year, Citigroup cut about 10 percent of its workforce, around 20,000 jobs. HSBC also announced it is considering a multiyear plan to cut around 20,000 roles. Standard Chartered, meanwhile, has announced plans to eliminate 15 percent of its workforce, around 7,800 jobs, by 2030.

Melania Trump has claimed to have secured a ceasefire for the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky, where up to 2,000 residents are cut off from world and facing starvation.

Russia has agreed to pause all military action in Oleshky to allow for humanitarian aid to enter and to prepare a civilian evacuation through a designated safe passageway, according tot the White House.

The localised ceasefire will begin on October 29.

“The situation in Oleshky is dire. Oleshky is a frontline war city on the brink of disaster,” the First Lady said. “Oleshky’s remaining population is comprised primarily of elderly residents who urgently need medical attention, medicine, food, and clean water.

“The people of Oleshky have limited electricity, live amid mined roads, and endure regular military attacks. It was abundantly clear that without my intervention, the possibility to bring humanitarian aid into the city and to evacuate the elderly would be impossible.”

This comes as Donald Trump claimed that SpaceX CEO Elon Musk has restored Ukraine's Starlink access, even as Volodymyr Zelensky and Ukrainian sources said there had been no change in satellite internet speeds.

The US President refused to confirm reports that he had called Musk to ask him to restore the service for Ukraine's military, saying: "I ​don't want to comment ⁠on it, whether I called or whether somebody else called ... The bottom line - ‌he put it back."

News.title: Carrick weighs up stripping Bruno Fernandes of Man Utd captaincy
News.content:
A defiant Michael Carrick refused to rule out stripping Bruno Fernandes of the captaincy as the Manchester United manager told his players to cut out their public sniping and start doing their talking on the pitch.

Carrick struck a bullish tone as he came out fighting and moved to reassert his authority after a tumultuous past fortnight that has left him battling to save his job ahead of Sunday’s must-win game against Bournemouth at Old Trafford.

The United manager began his press conference on Friday afternoon with a stirring five-and-a-half-minute monologue in which he issued an emotional call to arms to his players to demonstrate the values of hard work, sacrifice, humility and resilience that define the club.

Referencing Sir Matt Busby, Sir Alex Ferguson, Sir Bobby Charlton, Ryan Giggs and Wayne Rooney, Carrick warned there could be no “entitlement” culture in echoes of complaints from his predecessor Ruben Amorim.

United are actively considering their options in the event Carrick cannot quickly arrest a shocking start to the season that hit a new low with Wednesday’s 4-1 humiliation by Como. The likes of Julian Nagelsmann, Eddie Howe, Unai Emery, Fabian Hürzeler and Antonio Conte are in the frame.

But Carrick insisted he was “100 per cent” convinced he was the right man to take United forward and, while he claimed the dressing room was “not divided”, he has had to contend with first defender Lisandro Martínez and then Fernandes venting in public.

Martínez was fined and publicly apologised for an extraordinary tirade at Jason Wilcox, the director of football, and the Old Trafford board last week before Fernandes appeared to call out Carrick’s tactics in the wake of the Como debacle.

Carrick responded at the time to having his set-up and approach questioned by suggesting tactics count for little if players are unprepared to run.

Asked if he would consider taking the captaincy off Fernandes, Carrick said: “I’m just saying I’ll always – whatever the situation is – do what’s best for the club.”

News.title: Oil hits five-month high amid fears of fresh strikes on Iran
News.content:
The price of oil has hit a five-month high amid fears Donald Trump will ramp up strikes in the Middle East following the midterm elections.

Brent crude, the international benchmark, climbed as much as 2.8pc to more than $116 a barrel, pushing down stock markets in the US and Europe.

It followed a New York Times report that the US and Israel had drawn up plans for renewed strikes against Iran after the midterm elections.

Oil has climbed more than 4pc this week, increasing pressure on stock markets at the same time as fears grow about the valuations of AI companies.

European shares fell on Friday, with the FTSE 100 down as much as 0.8pc, the Cac 40 in Paris down 1pc and the Dax in Frankfurt down 1.1pc.

On Wall Street, the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell as much as 1pc, while the S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite fell at a slower pace than the previous day.

Traders were rattled on Thursday after Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s chief executive, warned that a “scarcity of capital” was hampering the rollout of the technology.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq in New York dropped by 2.6pc on Thursday while the S&P 500 fell 1.2pc on its worst day since July.

Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta was one of the worse hit in the sell-off, as its shares finished trading almost 7pc lower.

Overnight, the sell-off spread into Asian markets. Japan’s Nikkei 225 dropped by as much as 2.3pc and was down more than 4pc on the week.

The Kospi index in South Korea declined as much as 4.1pc on Friday but recovered to be marginally higher as markets closed.

The stock market turmoil led to a jump in safe haven assets like bonds.

The yield on 10-year US Treasury bonds, a benchmark for the cost of borrowing for governments around the world, fell by the largest amount since March 2023.

News.title: Europe’s record-breaking summer heat estimated to have killed 50,000 people
News.content:
More than 50,000 people are estimated to have died across Europe as a result of this summer’s record-breaking heatwaves, according to research.

In the UK alone, researchers estimate there were 4,354 excess deaths this summer.

The number of excess deaths across Europe is double the number recorded in 2025 and it is also far higher than the previous record of 29,000 deaths. This was recorded in 2022 when the continent also endured exceptionally high temperatures, with the mercury hitting 40 degrees celsius for the first time in the UK.

According to the Met Office the UK saw its hottest ever summer this year with five widespread heatwaves and 40 days where the temperature was above 30 degrees celsius. Mainland Europe experienced its third hottest summer, with temperatures particularly high in the south and west.

Researchers from Imperial College, London and the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine (LSHTM) looked at 854 urban areas in 30 countries across Europe. Using temperature records and modelling based on the relationship between heat and mortality they estimated the number of heat-related deaths that occurred between June and August.

They said findings from previous years’ excess heat mortality modelling matched official figures released later by national health authorities.

Because the study only looked at urban areas – making up 40 per cent of the population of the countries studied – researchers believe the number of deaths is likely to be an underestimate.

According to the study, published in Nature Health, southern and western Europe were hardest hit. Italy experienced the highest number of excess deaths (13,303), followed by France (7,268), Spain (6,824), Germany (6,340) then the UK.

There were an estimated 22,000 deaths among those aged 85 and over but researchers pointed out that an estimated 6,000 people under the age of 65 are also likely to have died as a result of the heat.

Around a third of the deaths took place in late June, when average temperatures across Europe were more than 5°C above what would be expected during this time of year. Researchers say in early summer people were less likely to have acclimatised to the sweltering weather. This period was marked by both extremely high humidity and unusually high night-time temperatures, making it difficult for people to cool down.

Researchers also estimated that more than two thirds of the total excess deaths were attributable to climate change. Across the continent as a whole Europe was an average 2.9°C higher than would have been expected. However, in some places temperatures were as much as 12°C higher.

Dr Clair Barnes, extreme weather and climate change researcher at Imperial College, said extreme heat was having a severe impact on public health.

“It is yet another reminder both of the imperative of rolling out targeted interventions to protect those who are most vulnerable to this increasingly extreme heat, and of the growing need to rapidly transition away from fossil fuels to slow the pace of change and limit future warming.”

Dr Pierre Masselot, assistant professor of statistics and epidemiology at LSHTM and one of the study’s authors, said “climate change is everybody’s problem”.

“It is not just hot regions that are suffering any more with some parts of Western and Northern Europe experiencing extreme heat and historically high health burden. And the whole population is affected, as shown by the significant death toll among younger age groups.

“It is becoming increasingly clear our cities are poorly adapted to rising heat, and it is critical we improve our efforts towards adaptation. This means cooling the cities through more green spaces and less pollution, and providing health care for affected populations.”

News.title: Bournemouth thrash Milan to seal greatest win in club’s history
News.content:
Milan could not even point to being down to 10 men for the last hour as mitigation; long before, Bournemouth had treated the Rossoneri with contempt. When Ruben Amorim’s side trudged off, soaked and silenced, they had not mustered a single shot on target.

Few nights have better encapsulated the Premier League’s power. Bournemouth have never finished higher than last season’s sixth in the top flight of English football; AC Milan have won seven European Cups. But the Premier League’s financial clout is such that, each season, the bottom club earns more than the champions of Serie A.

The Premier League’s shared riches, allied to years of astute recruitment and management, have underpinned the Bournemouth’s ascent. Even Andoni Iraola’s departure has not stalled the progress at the Vitality Stadium; Marco Rose has relished the new European adventure.

Real Sociedad and Sturm Graz had already been toppled in Bournemouth’s first two European games. Now, Bournemouth have won their first three matches in Europe. Despite middling Premier League form, Rose’s ambitions will extend far beyond securing a berth in the knockout stages of the Europa League. On this evidence, Bournemouth are legitimate contenders to win the competition, and earn a berth in next season’s Champions League.

“It’s a special night for the club,” Ryan Christie, Bournemouth captain, said. “It’s mega – in terms of the story of the club, it’s ridiculous.”

Evanilson, perhaps, was Bournemouth’s standout player against AC Milan, combining intricate linkup play with a constant threat in front of goal. Centre-back Antonio Silva, controlling play from deep while marauding forward, also possessed a calmness that any of Milan’s beleaguered team lacked.

His side’s fate swiftly sealed, Amorim did not bother to summon Luka Modric or Christian Pulisic. Bournemouth’s own bench showed the depth that the club now possesses. Rayan showed off his trickery and directness; Adli – a substitute for substitute Alex Toth, who suffered a hamstring injury – then ensured that Bournemouth secured the margin of victory that their dominance deserved.

News.title: Harry Brook hits historic double century – but England still lose to Sri Lanka
News.content:
Good morning and welcome to the fourth match of the autumn tri-series in Pakistan. After two wins for the hosts, the two touring sides face each other for the first time in Rawalpindi, the last match here before the circus leaves for Lahore. England and Sri Lanka played each other only last month in this format, England winning at Chester-le-Street and the Oval by a distance, those victories sandwiching a narrow defeat at Headingley where, if you remember, Harry Brook’s side were cruising until Jos Buttler ripped his left hamstring. He did eventually come back out to bat on one leg as his rattled team-mates flapped and fell to Asitha Fernando, Dilshan Madushanka and Eshan Malinga.

On Tuesday against Pakistan, England again were flying with both ball and bat but they let the middle-order rebuild, losing control of the rate. Their two most experienced white-ball bowlers, Adil Rashid, who looked rusty after breaking his hand in August, and Sam Curran, who missed the end of August and all of September following groin surgery, went for 6.87 and eight runs an over respectively. Then, after a promising opening partnership, Ben Duckett top-edged a pull, Tom Banton flicked straight to midwicket and Will Jacks later fell in identical fashion when well-set to marshal the chase. Arafat Minhas ended up with six for 40, bowling Harry Brook with a beauty, and there will be more trial by spin today.

Although there was some talk of England failing in end-of-days Bazball fashion, it most reminded me of the teething troubles of Eoin Morgan’s side in 2015 and 2016 when they were experimenting with players, viz this Rose Bowl collapse. We have to acknowledge that Joe Root, the best player of spin, was undone by one that kept low from Naseem Shah and both Brook and Jordan Cox lost their wickets to very good deliveries from Arafat, a bowler, on a feast day. Dunith Welllalage will return to try to replicate his line of attack today but he is a bowler that England know well. He has had his days against them but they have also given him some tap in the past.

News.title: Health authorities race to investigate first human death linked to Shamonda virus
News.content:
A French man has become the first person to contract Shamonda virus, a disease previously only found in animals and spread through midges.

The patient, who had a weakened immune system, has since died, according to the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC).

Shamonda virus was first identified in Nigeria in the 1960s and has this year been detected in farm animals all across Europe.

It was confirmed to have spread to the British Isles in September, after being found in a cattle herd on the island of Jersey. There have also been cases in Ireland.

The French patient, who was immunocompromised, died earlier this month while infected with the virus, but it is unclear if the infection contributed to his death, the ECDC said in a statement.

Investigations into whether the virus caused or contributed to the patient’s death and how the infection was acquired are ongoing.

Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, the director of the World Health Organization (WHO) said in a statement on X that he was “in contact with French authorities, who are collecting information to better understand the source of infection.”

He added the patient was “immunocompromised, which made them more vulnerable to infection and severe disease.”

There was “no health risk to the general public identified at this time”, the French health and agriculture ministries said in a joint statement.

Dr Ben Brennan, Group Leader and Senior Lecturer, MRC-University of Glasgow Centre for Virus Research, University of Glasgow, said: “This is an important scientific finding, as it is the first reported human infection with Shamonda virus [..] at present, there is no evidence that Shamonda virus causes widespread human disease, although further investigation is needed to understand its ability to infect people.”

In animals, Shamonda virus attacks the central nervous system and can lead to severe inflammation and haemorrhage. It can also lead to miscarriages.

Affected horses have been reported to exhibit seizures, lethargy, fever, muscle twitching, and difficulty walking.

Authorities are also still trying to ascertain whether the man himself was infected by a biting midge – the route of transmission between animals – or if he could have been infected by close contact with livestock.

It is thought he was infected in eastern France, where the virus had been circulating in midges and animals earlier in the year.

“Despite decades of circulation of the Shamonda virus in Africa and Asia, no human cases had been documented until now. This is therefore an exceptional case occurring in a severely immunocompromised patient,” French health authorities said in a statement.

The UK Plant and Health Agency said some of the neurological signs of the disease in horses resemble West Nile fever, human cases of which reached a record high on mainland Europe this year.

News.title: What happens when you get malaria during pregnancy?
News.content:
Huge strides have been made in recent years in combating malaria but one group is more at risk than ever before: pregnant women.

They are uniquely vulnerable to the disease and because sub-Saharan Africa shoulders the burden of global cases the continent’s rapidly growing population means far more women are exposed today than at the turn of the millennium.

According to a recent study, 52 million pregnant women in Africa face the threat of malaria each year, up from 37 million in 2000.

And the toll is heavy: malaria in pregnancy kills at least 10,000 mothers and 210,000 infants every year.

Malaria in pregnancy is uniquely dangerous, and the disease acts very differently to how it does in someone who is not pregnant.

“Pregnant women are one of the most vulnerable groups to malaria, it can lead to severe anaemia, immune suppression, and in the worst cases, mortality,” Lottie Renwick, global campaign director at Malaria No More UK told The Telegraph.

Malaria parasites infect and feed on red blood cells, dividing and multiplying in the bloodstream. This makes them easily detectable through a simple blood test, which allows life-saving treatment to be administered quickly.

But in pregnancy, the parasites are notoriously evasive.

Instead of floating in the bloodstream, they colonise in the placenta – the organ that feeds and sustains the baby.

Sports.title: Leclerc tops first USA practice as upgraded Ferrari shows early promise
Sports.content:
Charles Leclerc showed early promise in an upgraded Ferrari car to pip Red Bull's in-form Max Verstappen to the fastest time of first practice at the United States Grand Prix.

Ferrari, McLaren and Red Bull all introduced fresh revisions to their cars for the opening hour of running at the Circuit of the Americas, which is staging the first leg of the sport's second of three end-of-season triple headers.

Ferrari's package features changes to their car's floor, sidepod and diffuser and showed speed on both the medium and soft tyres around the undulating COTA lap, with Leclerc ultimately setting the session's pace on the latter with a best lap of 1:36.052.

Verstappen, the winner of the last two races, finished 0.084s behind Leclerc although lost a quicker lap on the softs which was two tenths faster than the Ferrari due to a track limits violation at Turn 19.

Lando Norris was third in a McLaren car which also features changes as they bid to return to form after a difficult run of races saw them slip into the clutches of Red Bull in the Constructors' Championship battle for third.

World championship leaders Mercedes do not have fresh upgrades in Austin. But both of their drivers are back to running the package first introduced two races ago in Malaysia after George Russell reverted to the older-spec last time out in Singapore.

Russell finished fourth, 0.326s behind, in opening practice with title-leading team-mate Kimi Antonelli fifth on a weekend the Italian could clinch 2026's world title if he wins on Sunday and his team-mate and Lewis Hamilton do not score sufficient points to stay in mathematical contention.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Lewis Hamilton gives an insight into his costly decision to override Ferrari's strategy call in Singapore.

Hamilton was only sixth fastest in Friday's first session, half a second away from team-mate Leclerc, after his soft-tyre run did not come together. Oscar Piastri was seventh in the second McLaren.

Sky Sports F1's Martin Brundle said: "It does look so close at the front.

"McLaren look in there too, Mercedes found some time. Ferrari you'd have to say just had an ounce of an advantage but it is early doors."

Sports.title: Cordina: I've been offered Pacquiao fight on AJ-Fury card
Sports.content:
Welsh boxer Joe Cordina has told Sky Sports that he has been offered a fight with Manny Pacquiao as part of the undercard for the blockbuster all-British heavyweight clash between Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury on December.

The 34-year-old has confirmed that he has agreed to fight the boxing icon at the Principality Stadium in his birth city of Cardiff, but that no contracts have been signed as of yet.

Sky Sports have approached Pacquiao's team for comment.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports' John Dennen spoke to Dana White about what we can expect from the Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua fight

"I've been offered the fight," said Cordina, a two-time super-featherweight world champion. "They asked me if I'd fight Pacquiao: this is what the deal is, otherwise they're going to offer it to someone else.

"'Of course', I said, 'No problem'. I've won world titles, and don't get me wrong, I want to win more. But, for me, the name of Manny Pacquiao at this present moment is bigger than any name in boxing.

"He's an eight-division world champion, a legend. But a global superstar like him will be gone in the next year or so.

"So for me to be able to share the ring with someone who I grew up watching before I even started boxing, it would be an honour."

Image: Manny Pacquiao is an eight-division world champion and bona-fide legend in the sport of boxing

Cordina added: "Don't get me wrong, it's nowhere near done. I haven't been sent a contract, I haven't been sent anything and I haven't been told yet it's happening.

"I've been offered it, I've said yes, agreed everything and I'm now just waiting for them to either tell me yes or no?

"I'm training as if I am fighting Manny Pacquiao. I've been training for the last four or five weeks.

"If the phone rings, I know I'm ready."

In terms of the prospect of facing the 47-year-old Pacquiao a decade or so on from his prime, Cordina pointed to the Filipino's most recent fight against Mario Barrios in July of 2025 that ended in a draw.

"They had a draw but, to be honest, I thought he [Pacquiao] nicked it," Cordina said of the WBC welterweight title clash.

"I've seen loads of people be like, 'Why are you fighting Manny Pacquiao? He's an old man'.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Manny Pacquiao showed he's still got his lightning speed during his training for his comeback fight against Mario Barrios last year. Credit: @mannypacquiao

"But the last thing to go is power. You see him on the bags and he's still got speed, he's still sharp and his footwork is still there. Yes, his timing might be off - he hasn't been in the ring for a year and a half - and that might be the thing that is his undoing.

"But he's had so many fights; he's an eight-division world champion, he knows his way around the ring, he's not a novice. He's been around the block; he's boxed everybody."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports' Michael Bridge has more on the timing for Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua's fight at Cardiff's Principality Stadium on Friday 11 December - with the ringwalk expected to place at 1am in the early hours of Saturday

As for potentially being on the same bill as Joshua and Fury, Cordina hopes the long-anticipated fight lives up to the billing, while he also doesn't buy Joshua as an underdog.

"You can never write off a heavyweight anyway, but especially when it's Anthony Joshua," Cordina said.

"It only takes one shot from him, and you're in Barney Rubble [trouble].

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Anthony Joshua makes his predictions for his fight against Tyson Fury on December 11

"They're both going to go out there and go straight at it; they're going to meet in the middle of the ring and just have a crack.

"Whether it goes down like that or not, I don't know, but that's what I'd like to happen, to see them have a shootout like in a Western.

"It'd be an anti-climax otherwise. This fight has been talked about for years - and it's probably come five years too late.

"I just believe that can't be a bore fest. They've got to go out there and go at it."

Sports.title: Trump states Paris concerns - 'NFL could have postponed Steelers-Saints'
Sports.content:
US President Donald Trump has said the NFL "could have probably postponed" Sunday's game in Paris between the Pittsburgh Steelers and New Orleans Saints due to street protests in the city.

France is bracing for more demonstrations Saturday against the high cost of living, with museums closing and the government deploying a larger security presence to prevent a repeat of last week's violent unrest.

The game on Sunday - the first ever NFL regular-season game held in France - is taking place at Stade de France in Saint-Denis, just north of the capital.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Phoebe Schecter has been impressed by the Pittsburgh Steelers' ability to keep winning despite below-par performances, with QB Aaron Rodgers continuing to lead the way

"I think maybe it's looking like tomorrow is going to be a bad day in France, so you worry about it," Trump told reporters.

"I would have said the NFL could have probably postponed that match, because France is really in trouble."

The US State Department issued a security alert late on Thursday, saying: "Numerous groups submitted plans for protests on Saturday October 24. Americans in Paris for the NFL game on Sunday October 25, should also exercise caution and be aware of their surroundings.

"While permits may be filed for demonstration routes, last-minute changes can happen and protests can occur outside planned routes."

Image: NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell has yet to suggest there will be any change to the planned Sunday kick-off in Paris

NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell said this week that preparations were made in consultation with US and French authorities.

Street protests, he said, "are not unusual in France". The league did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Trump's remarks.

Soccer team Paris Saint-Germain's game against Lyon has been moved from Sunday to Monday evening at the request of Paris police.

Image: PSG's game against Lyon scheduled for Sunday has been moved to Monday night

The game was scheduled for Sunday night in Parc des Princes.

Steelers quarterback Aaron Rodgers said on Friday that "the NFL is alert to what's going on".

He added: "This game means a lot to the NFL. If it was unsafe, then I'm sure we wouldn't be here."

A weekend event for Steelers fans was cancelled on Thursday because of security concerns.

Sports.title: When Carra met Chelsea boss Alonso
Sports.content:
Sky Sports' Jamie Carragher sat down for a wide-ranging interview with Chelsea manager Xabi Alonso in which the pair discussed his appointment at Stamford Bridge and his aims for the season, as well as looking back at their time playing together at Liverpool.

Why did you choose to join Chelsea?

"It was about the timing. For me, it was the right timing after Leverkusen. After Madrid, I had my time off and I wanted to have that good feeling, that good connection about where to go.

"I had no link to Chelsea, but with the potential that was here, a few things could change and I thought we could start the journey together.

"I had a feeling that the very strong base of the squad was very good and with some updates, some improvements, some new signings, we could have a solid team. And that it was going to be a project.

"It's not that, in year one it's already done; we know it might take some more years, but the first year is important. It's just starting but, so far, the feeling that we could be aligned taking decisions is going to be important."

Chelsea

Tottenham Hotspur Saturday 24th October 5:00pm Kick off 5:30pm

Did you think about the Chelsea ownership coming into initial talks?

"From outside, I had the view of what I read, what I saw about the team, but then you get to know the people, you get to know their analysis, the things they have done, the things they thought could be done better, where we were and where we wanted to take the club.

"Knowing that, in many processes, many decisions, I was going to be part of it, was important. There is the ownership, the sporting director and me, but we are always connected and we have good communication.

"That's basic, to take responsibility. Things after can go well or not go well because this is football, but in the end, you want to feel part of it."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights from the Premier League match between Everton and Chelsea.

Was Chelsea's managerial history something you thought about?

"No, it was not a worry because I know what you need to get results, but I had the feeling we were on the same page.

"We knew that where we want to be next year or in two years will take time and this is the process of building things the right way and that's why the first phase we have improved in the team has been good.

"It's just seven games, but we have a clear direction of what we want. Zero worry about this. This is football, you need to get the results. But to have the feeling we are doing things in the right way and that we have a plan is as important for me as the results."

Is winning the Premier League, getting back into the Champions League in the plan?

"In the medium to long-term, yes. We know that takes time and many right decisions. We won't make all the right decisions but, for me, being involved in the key decisions is as important as the rest.

"This is the ambition of the club. This club has won Champions Leagues and Premier Leagues not so long ago and we want to be back there, but we are not stupid to think this has to come right now. Time will tell when that can come."

This club has won Champions Leagues and Premier Leagues not so long ago and we want to be back there

Is the set-up different to your previous experiences?

"My experience in Germany is different from my experience in Spain and now. In Germany, you work very closely with the sporting director every day. That's very different from England.

"I had that relationship with Simon Rolfs where he was in the office with me every day, but not to say 'You need to do this!'

"It was to chat about the momentum of one player or a player is in a bad mood or we have had talks. Normal things. In the end, this close relationship made us a very good tandem, and it worked really well.

"At Chelsea, Sam (Jewell), Paul (Winstanley), Joe (Shields) are really close to the team as well."

What are your early memories of joining Liverpool?

"I remember not many English players used to watch LaLiga, but you were one of the ones watching LaLiga, Barcelona and Real Madrid, of course, but Atletico, Deportivo La Coruna.

"We used those games to talk more about football. We started getting to know each other and you were football mad, I was football mad.

"I learned as well that you need to earn the respect of the guys that were there. You need to have a proper impact on Stevie [Gerrard] Carra, Didi Hamann, Sami Hyypia. I knew I needed to earn my place, I need to earn my respect.

"Happily, it didn't take too long. It didn't take as long as it could coming from Real Sociedad, being 21. It was quite quick.

"I remember Bolton was proper, with Sam Allardyce. Gary Speed tackled me and said 'Welcome to the Premier League!'

"One of the first games was against Norwich at home and we won 3-0 and I played a very good game. Then people start respecting you and saying 'He can play' and, little by little, you start making your own things in the club and you get the respect of the established and local players.

"That was very important because, if not, you can struggle with the adaptation at the beginning."

Image: Xabi Alonso won the 2005 Champions League with Liverpool

What are the biggest differences between when you came to the Premier League as a player to what you see now as a manager?

"I would say the gap between the top clubs and the rest, 20 years ago, was much bigger than it is. The players are more complete. You hardly see a player that is not so fit or not so prepared physically.

"Tactically, the gameplans are really sophisticated nowadays. I'm still getting into the tempo of the Premier League because, for me, it has been a change. I try to learn as quickly as possible, but now it's very sophisticated, even the squads are so complete.

"Something has not changed: the energy that is created in the stadiums. For me, it feels the same. At the noise... we were playing against Everton and the noise and energy that was created in this stadium, that has not changed.

"For me, it's very different to the sounds of the Bundesliga or Spain. My first game against Fulham we played in the Premier League, I said 'This smells like the Premier League!'"

What do you mean about still getting up to speed?

"Before, you knew the top teams could play. But you knew, with the other teams, if you were going to press a little bit, even with one less player, normally they would play long and you would have to be ready.

"Now, that's not enough. Now, you need to prepare what's going to be the trigger point from one side; find solutions to that, so all the teams are much more complete.

"The game is much more sophisticated in the way that it has developed a lot. Teams have solutions and very good patterns."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player A look at some of the best goals Spurs have scored against Chelsea over the years.

Is there a certain methodology behind Spain's football success?

"Yes, there is a big methodology, but it has been built for 20 years. It is not something that has been built in two years.

"For example, Luis de la Fuente has been part of the youth national teams for a lot of time and he knows them very well. These players have played together for a long time and when they were 17,18, they were already playing together and they became elite players playing together.

"Now, they have this connection. You see that they are so dominant in how they play and this has a lot to do with the work the clubs do.

"I am from Real Sociedad and the way they work there, they put a lot of focus on the young players and they give them the potential. But I have to be honest, here at Chelsea they work really well and I'm really impressed with some of the young players we have.

"As well, I see the English team - they are getting there. With Thomas Tuchel, they nearly got to the final, they got to the semis. This England team is getting close. You see the players and they are very good players. They need to take the next step to develop to be winning something. They are not too far."

Why do England not produce the types of players that can control big games?

"To reach such control in the Premier League is very difficult. I think you have to be a top, top team and top players if you are able to control the game in such a manner to be so dominant.

"We are not the quickest, but we need to think quick and the players they need to think quick. That's why they develop game intelligence, awareness.

"Rodri, for example, is one step ahead, one metre ahead. How? Training, habits. The same way Sergio Busquets used to do that. He was not the quickest, but he was the smartest on the pitch and that's a pattern that is repeated in Spain because of the collective purpose of the development of the team."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Chelsea boss Xabi Alonso says keeper Emi Martinez is 'doing good' but will be out of action for a few weeks after undergoing surgery on his jaw.

What are the differences between the top managers you worked under and what did you take from them?

"Each one was really important at that stage of my career. For example, being 21/22 at Liverpool, if I had Carlo Ancelotti, it's different to when I had Ancelotti when I was 30 at Real Madrid.

"At that time, I needed a lot of tactical input, I needed a lot of explanation and Rafa Benitez was very good at that. After, I became more mature as a player.

"I then went to Madrid and I was mainly with Jose Mourinho and with Ancelotti, but that's about competing, about your mentality. I was a good player, but I could get better. It was about competing, about a winning mentality, about being tougher and I got more mature in Madrid.

"My last spell in Munich was like, after the university degree you want to have a Masters. I worked with Pep. I was so curious about why they played so well and I wanted to be inside.

"That last stage of my career in Munich made my transition to try to become a coach. I started thinking about the processes, how things happen, how you need to work and I paid a lot of attention in those years because I knew the end was getting closer and, at the end, I was going to try eventually to try to become a coach."

Did you ever speak to those managers about becoming a coach?

"With Ancelotti and with Pep. I remember my last year with Ancelotti, he invited me to do a team talk in pre-season. Pep had many midfield players where he had a good connection. For me, that was no surprise that I was so interested in the end to try to eventually become a coach."

When did you start having your own ideas?

"For me, it was more about how did I feel with a group? How did I feel talking to a group? The connection I had with the players, how I managed telling people they weren't going to play. If those decisions stress you so much, you know the job is so hard and can be so demanding.

"If you understand them as part of the job and you enjoy them somehow, that's when you can take the job naturally. I felt it. After, let's talk about football.

"I was a midfielder, so I was about control: how to control the game, how to give it more balance, how to have distances, how to not be up and down. That was how I started, but after it's about adapting to the players you have, the league where you are.

"For example, I went to Leverkusen and the team was in a difficult position. We became a very counter-attacking team. I saw the team and said 'Now we are in a difficult position and it's not about trying to play the nicest game, it's about competing'.

"We changed the system, we were very compact, defending tight and very good on the counter-attack and we ended up playing the semi-finals of the Europa League and qualifying. I have ideas and what I like, but you try to adapt as well."

Watch the full interview on Sky Sports Premier League at 7.30pm on Sunday October 25

Sports.title: Hatton leaves LIV Golf to add name to growing list
Sports.content:
Tyrrell Hatton has confirmed he is to leave LIV Golf, becoming the latest star name to announce his departure from the breakaway league.

Hatton's announcement, posted on social media on Friday, comes on the same day Ian Poulter also announced that he would not be re-signing with LIV, and two days after Louis Oosthuizen.

LIV Golf saw Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF) end their funding earlier this season but have since secured investment from BC Partners Credit, as they look to relaunch and continue in 2027.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Geraint Hughes explains what is next for LIV Golf and what will happen to their players after they filed for bankruptcy

The league filed for bankruptcy protection in September with a Chapter 11 petition, which they said was to "preserve the company's business" as it attempts to restructure, with players left to decide whether they wish to re-sign with LIV.

Hatton has opted against doing so, writing on his Instagram story: "Wanted to confirm that I will not be part of LIV 2.0. A big thank you to everyone for their continued support.

"I am excited for what the next chapter of my career holds. Looking forward to seeing you all in Abu Dhabi."

Earlier in October, Jon Rahm also reached a separation agreement to leave LIV Golf and Sergio Garcia exited his contract with the circuit.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Inci Mehmet explains why Jon Rahm is to quit LIV Golf after deeming the terms offered for the proposed relaunch of the breakaway series 'unacceptable'

Only a handful of players are currently publicly committed to re-signing with LIV ahead of their initial deadline later this month.

BC Partners Credit retain the right to extend or waive the October 25 player deadline, while LIV Golf attorney Robert Fitzgerald said earlier this week that they should know by the end of the month whether it will be ceasing operations or moving forward.

Sports.title: Hamilton eyes staying in F1 into 2030s to race in African GP
Sports.content:
Lewis Hamilton has set his sights on staying in Formula 1 into the 2030s in order to fulfil his dream of racing in Africa.

Formula 1 last week announced the addition to its calendar of an African Grand Prix in Rwanda but did not provide a firm date for the first staging of the event, saying instead it will take place in the "early 2030s".

Hamilton, who turns 42 in January, will be 45 at the start of F1's 2030 season. Despite the seven-time world champion accepting there is no guarantee he will still be on the grid at that stage, he is retaining hope of competing in what will be the sport's first race in Africa since 1993.

Speaking ahead of this weekend's United States Grand Prix, Hamilton said: "I'm now forced to stay a bit longer because we have a race in Africa and that has been my dream to race in Africa.

"So, I'm going to have to keep fighting to stay fit. If I can keep punching out results over the next years, we will keep it going."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Rwandan president Paul Kagame says it's an 'honour and privilege' following the news that the Rwandan circuit is set to host a Grand Prix from the early 2030s

Hamilton is driving his second season for Ferrari and is known to have a contract with the team until at least the end of the 2027, with a potential option to remain with the Italian squad in 2028 too.

His future beyond that point with Ferrari and in F1 remains uncertain, but Hamilton's former team-mate Fernando Alonso has shown what's possible, with the Spaniard set to embark on another season with Aston Martin next year at the age of 45.

Hamilton: Approach Rwanda with humility

The announcement of a 10-year deal for Rwanda to host the event was met with criticism from some quarters, with Amnesty International labelling the agreement as "a sportswashing prize for the Rwandan authorities."

Appearing to react to some of the criticism that followed the announcement, Hamilton launched a passionate plea for the new event to be approached "with humility".

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Lewis Hamilton, Max Verstappen and George Russell react to rumours that Rwanda is on course to host Africa's first F1 race since 1993 South African Grand Prix in Kyalami

"I don't get to choose where we go," Hamilton said. "Naturally, there are problems all over the world today, so I've seen many of the stories. But I think we really have to approach it with humility.

"There's a lot that we don't know. Growing up in England, they never taught us anything about Africa. It needs to be on the curriculum. A lot of the problems they have there are still results of colonialism and the West intervening.

"But if you go and see the people, you see so many designs that are out there today from top brands that come from Africa. It's got all the richest resources. I really hope, and I still have hope, that Africa unites. I know there are many people who don't want that to happen because they would be so powerful if they did. But I'm still hopeful that at some stage they will.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player South African Formula 1 presenter and content creator Nqobile Khwezi says it's an 'absolute delight' for Rwanda to be chosen to host a brand-new African Grand Prix from the early 2030s

"And, yeah, of course, going there doesn't mean that you neglect the things that are happening there. So hopefully many people start to educate themselves a little bit more about what is happening there and what has happened there for hundreds of years. I hope that does spark the conversation.

"And then I guess I'll finish it off with this: I think we need to make sure we're pushing to free Congo, free Sudan, free Syria, free Palestine. I think there's a lot of peace that I'm hoping we get to at some stage."

Rwanda's history in sport

'Visit Rwanda' are front-of-shirt sponsor for Aston Villa, having signed a multi-year deal worth £20m a season in the summer. The move was criticised by Amnesty International as "sportswashing" by the country to deflect from its human rights record.

DR Congo has accused Rwanda of arming rebel groups and committing human rights breaches and last year urged Arsenal, PSG and Bayern Munich to review their deals with the country in 2025.

Arsenal ended their eight-year deal with Rwanda at the end of last season after pressure from supporter groups. The club's LGBTQ+ group, the Gay Gooners, told Sky Sports News at the time that it had raised concerns with Arsenal over the partnership since 2021.

PSG extended their deal with Rwanda until 2028, while Bayern ended their commercial deal but extended a deal to focus on an academy in the country.

Felix Jakens, Amnesty International UK's head of campaigns, said in a statement: "Rwanda is buying into the world's biggest sports to polish its image and deflect from its appalling human rights record.

"A 10-year Grand Prix 'presented by Visit Rwanda' is a sportswashing prize for the Rwandan authorities.

"Arsenal, Aston Villa, the cycling world championships and now Formula 1 - Rwanda is buying into the world's biggest sports to polish its image and deflect from its appalling human rights record.

"Formula 1 says sport can be 'a positive force for good'. That rings hollow if F1 shrugs off who it is partnering with. Rwanda's authorities are prolific in arbitrary detention, torture and the repression of free speech - these are abuses at home.

"Beyond its borders, we are seeing bloodshed in the Democratic Republic of Congo, and Rwanda is playing a significant role in fuelling the conflict and related human rights abuses - both through its support to the M23 armed group and the direct actions of Rwanda's military in eastern Congo.

"Formula 1 must not be a bystander. It should use its influence with the Rwandan authorities to push for change, rather than lend its brand to a PR exercise."

Sports.title: Ipswich v Nottingham Forest: Premier League – live
Sports.content:
now 16.06 EDT 46 min: Philogene hares after a long pass down the left. Forest are very fortunate Milenkovic is immediately switched on; the defender blocks a low cross. Share

1m ago 16.04 EDT Ipswich get the second half started. No changes yet. Share

8m ago 15.57 EDT Half-time postbag. “There’s always one relegated team per season which is too good to go down. I don’t think it’ll be Forest this season, because they really do look too good to go down, but it could be them if they don’t start putting away their chances. Sports.title: Carrick delivers 5min 27sec monologue and says he will hold brolly to keep everyone dry
Sports.content:
Michael Carrick began his Friday media conference with an extraordinary 5min 27sec monologue that cited Manchester United’s values of “humility”, “resilience” and “earning the right to win”, in what could be read as a public address to his players after the season’s dismal start.

The head coach, whose job is under threat, later stated “100%” he could turn United’s form around and sought to underline his selfless attitude by saying he would hold an umbrella for “everyone else to stay dry” while he got wet.

The downpour on Carrick intensified on Wednesday when Bruno Fernandes questioned his tactics after United’s 4-1 Champions League loss at Como and the coach did not rule out dropping the midfielder or stripping him of the captaincy when Bournemouth visit on Sunday. “I’ll always do what’s best for the football club,” he said. “The most important thing for me is the team, first and foremost – the squad, the dynamics in the squad.”

Carrick decided to make his speech, delivered without being asked a question, after events in Como and Lisandro Martínez’s criticism a week earlier of Jason Wilcox for the signings by the director of football.

United have won only two of 11 games and started the current round of fixtures in 13th. Carrick said: “We need to respect what it takes to be here, respect what it takes to win, what you have to do to win. I’m not entitled to be here. Entitlement cannot be at this football club. We’re not entitled to win. We’ve won in the past, we’ve got an incredible history, but that doesn’t mean you’re entitled to just win.”

Carrick, a highly decorated United player for 12 years until 2018, cited two of his former teammates. “Ryan Giggs, arguably one of the greatest to play for this club, it was never about Ryan Giggs, it was about Manchester United. Wayne Rooney was top goalscorer of this football club. His biggest thing was playing for the team, sacrificing for the team, and what was good for Manchester United.

“Sir Alex Ferguson, the best manager of all time, the greatest for me … his main priority was Manchester United. Going back to Sir Matt [Busby], Sir Bobby [Charlton], the resilience was beyond belief of what they showed and the way they rebuilt this football club,” referring to the aftermath of the Munich disaster. Carrick insisted he could embody these values and transform United’s campaign. “One hundred per cent, yeah,” he said, before confirming he had spoken to the hierarchy and players about the crisis.

“There’s always conversations going on. It’s pretty obvious how we’re all feeling. The responsibility for me to be in this position is to lead.” Warming to his theme, he said: “I’ll hold that umbrella for me to get wet and for everyone else to stay dry. That’s the position I’m in and it’s a privileged position.”
