Sports.title: Man Utd chief was axed over manager pick as ANOTHER civil war breaks out in boardroom
Sports.content:
Man Utd chief was axed over manager pick as ANOTHER civil war breaks out in boardroom

Manchester United's boardroom is once again divided over the club's next steps as a decision looms over the future of struggling manager Michael Carrick

View 3 Images Uncertainty over Michael Carrick's future at Manchester United is reportedly a factor in the club's latest 'civil war' (Image: Denis Doyle/Getty Images)

Michael Carrick's current predicament at Old Trafford has led to a case of deja vu for Manchester United. Reports of 'civil war' in the boardroom are all too familiar for a team that found itself in a very similar situation not long ago.

‌



‌



United's struggles for on-field results have recently bled into the media via both players and Carrick himself. However, that feeling of discontent is seemingly not limited to the dressing room as those in the upper echelons allegedly clash, too.

‌



Lisandro Martinez took aim at the club's hierarchy for not doing enough in the transfer window following a recent Champions League loss to Atletico Madrid. Captain Bruno Fernandes then questioned Carrick's tactics following a 4-1 defeat at Como, leading to comments from the manager suggesting his players weren't working hard enough.

‌



The Daily Mail has now reported on a growing rift between director of football Jason Wilcox and head of recruitment Christopher Vivell. This is said to be largely in relation to whom the club should appoint as Carrick's successor if he is fired, which is exactly the kind of disagreement that previously led to a massive change at board level.

Erik ten Hag sent on immediate scouting mission in new role days after tearing Man Utd apart READ MORE :

Wilcox's predecessor, Dan Ashworth, also left the club under a cloud of controversy in December 2024. Ashworth arrived at Old Trafford to much excitement in the summer of that year, given his superb work in the same role at Newcastle.

However, United co-owners INEOS decided to part ways only five months into his tenure. The Athletic later reported this was at least partly down to indecision over whom should replace Erik ten Hag when he was sacked in October 2024.

‌



Ashworth was reported to have played a prominent role in Ten Hag's contract extension that year but supposedly had limited involvement in Ruben Amorim being appointed as his replacement. Instead, chief executive officer Omar Berrada took the reins in negotiating that appointment as a clear divide emerged.

3 View 3 Images United director of football Jason Wilcox was recently criticised by defender Lisandro Martinez (Image: Kieran McManus/Shutterstock) 3 View 3 Images Director of recruitment Christopher Vivell is reportedly in disagreement with Wilcox over whom should manage United next (Image: Ronny Hartmann / AFP via Getty Images)

‌



Make sure you don't miss the best Man Utd coverage by making the Daily Mirror one of your Google preferred sources.

United paid £4.1million to terminate Ashworth's contract early, just one month after Amorim was appointed. It was viewed by fans as a terrible use of funds for a club that's grown too accustomed to waste in the post-Sir Alex Ferguson era.

‌



Carrick will lead United out once again at home to Bournemouth on Sunday. However, there's no getting away from the sentiment it's a case of 'when' and not 'if' the club moves on, with the team failing to win any of its last seven games.

As things stand, a number of potential successors have been bandied about at United. Eddie Howe, Julian Nagelsmann and Antonio Conte are each reported as candidates, helped by the fact they're all currently free agents without a club.

A new manager won't rid United of that feeling of disharmony at boardroom level, however. And while Carrick's job is the main talking point up for discussion at Old Trafford, it may not be long before other changes are made among the hierarchy, too.

Sports.title: Jamie Carragher pinpoints Mikel Arteta change as he bids to end 92-year Arsenal hoodoo
Sports.content:
Jamie Carragher pinpoints Mikel Arteta change as he bids to end 92-year Arsenal hoodoo

Mikel Arteta has seemingly taken a more expansive approach this season with Jamie Carragher noticing the change and asking a question of the Arsenal boss

View 2 Images Jamie Carragher has posed an intriguing Arsenal question to Mikel Arteta (Image: (Photo by GSI/Icon Sport via Getty Images))

Jamie Carragher has noticed a more attacking approach from Mikel Arteta that presents a significant dilemma for the Arsenal boss. The Gunners played out an enthralling 2-2 draw with Bayern Munich in the Champions League on Wednesday evening, ensuring they have just one defeat in all competitions this season.

‌



‌



That loss was particularly humbling against Brighton in the Premier League but Arsenal have since responded with two very different wins. Some excellent attacking football was on display in their turnaround win over Leeds United before eventually grinding down Nottingham Forest and winning 1-0 at the City Ground.

‌



The 2-1 win over Chelsea also showed the Gunners as a dynamic attacking force and Carragher has noticed that change, which seemingly also makes them more susceptible to conceding. He wrote in His column for The Telegraph: "In Arsenal’s case, the consensus is that improving on last season’s title requires playing more adventurously while finding the extra ingredients needed to win the Champions League. Wednesday’s 2-2 draw with Bayern Munich was a step in the right direction.

‌



"It was an end-to-end, entertaining game in the Allianz Arena. Arsenal’s late equaliser was a work of art which undermined the accusation they do not produce enough silky, attacking football.

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

Make sure you don't miss the best Arsenal coverage by making the Daily Mirror one of your Google preferred sources.

‌



"Even so, as it stands, it is difficult to make a compelling argument that Arsenal will win the Champions League without more stardust upfront.

"They lack the weapons of the other European contenders, especially Paris St-Germain, so when the moment of truth comes against the very best in the knockout rounds, the likelihood is Arteta’s side will lack the necessary ammunition."

‌



"It would have been fascinating to watch Arsenal in the parallel universe in which Vinícius Júnior signed, because it’s unlikely he would have been tracking back at the City Ground last weekend. Arteta demands his attackers embrace defensive responsibilities. That’s his make-up. Tactically, he remains more like Jose Mourinho than Wenger."

Back-to-back European champions PSG are quite clearly their biggest competition, demonstrated by their attacking dominance when scoring four goals against both Barcelona and Manchester City. On their way to last season's final, the Gunners conceded just two goals in the knockout stages. It was clear their defensive solidity is the strongest weapon at Arteta's disposal but that is yet to work in Europe, forcing him into a big tactical decision.

‌



View 2 Images Vinicius Junior was pursued by Arsenal in the summer transfer window

Making his team more expansive could be beneficial in some areas but also a risk during a season in which Arsenal are clear title favourites and have the chance to retain their crown for the first time in 92 years.

‌



On Arsenal's style, Carragher added: "The fundamental question for Arteta right now is what can and should he do about it? Stick with a successful blueprint that has earned admiration and won the Premier League, or make the necessary tweaks which might make Arsenal more loved and a better watch every week, but also more vulnerable?

"Staying on the current path he will almost certainly win another Premier League title. Shifting the balance more from defence to attack risks compromising the characteristics which have made Arsenal so dominant domestically."

‌



How much do Arteta and Arsenal fans really crave a change given the road to further Premier League glory is so clear?

When Arteta took over he had to find a different way to get past Jurgen Klopp’s Liverpool and Pep Guardiola’s Manchester City. The fact that they are no longer an obstacle may be one of the reasons why there is a feeling he can afford to play with more risk.

Sports.title: Dalton Smith must ensure dream does not become a nightmare in tough Alberto Puello test
Sports.content:
Dalton Smith must ensure dream does not become a nightmare in tough Alberto Puello test

Our man Barry McGuigan runs the rule over Dalton Smith as he prepares to defend his WBC super lightweight title in front of his home crowd in the Steel City

View Image Sheffield Wednesday fan Smith salutes the crowd at Hillsborough before taking on Alberto Puello (Image: Richard Bierton/Every Second Media/Shutterstock)

What a moment for Dalton Smith, defending his WBC super lightweight title in front of his home crowd in Sheffield.

‌



‌



That’s the stuff dreams are made of. He is, however, facing former champion Alberto Puello, who is looking to turn Smith's big night into a nightmare.

‌



Smith shot to prominence in January, stopping Subriel Matias inside five rounds in New York. In his previous fight, Matias gained a majority decision to take the belt from Puello. So this closes out the round robin.

‌



It’s a huge test for Smith. The Dominican doesn’t fight like Matias, who comes right at you. He’s a southpaw with a good chin and plenty of smarts.

Matias beat Puello by holding the centre of the ring and sitting on him, backing him up against the ropes. And then there was only a fag paper between them.

FOLLOW OUR FIGHTING FB PAGE! Latest boxing and MMA news, analysis and much more via our dedicated Facebook page

‌



Smith does not fight that way. Indeed, both Smith and Puello like to hit on the counter, so this could be the opposite of what we saw in New York.

Matias was perfect for Smith. The one thing Smith does not like is initiating. He did not have that concern with Matias.

‌



In an absolute barnburner, Matias brought it to him. And to his credit, Smith made it an unbelievable fight, trading some seriously heavy blows.

He survived some tricky moments in the third and fourth before breaking through with a couple of big right hands in the fifth. The first stunned Matias, the second finished him.

‌



Puello is not that guy. If he uses that sticky jab and keeps his distance, this could be a long night for Smith.

‌



As the away fighter, Puello knows that he has to win by a margin on the cards. He is not a big puncher so he will be looking to go the distance.

Puello has fast feet and hands, and has the greater experience having held two versions of the world title. Smith must arguably show us something different to prevail. He might even find himself behind and then have to go and get Puello.

‌



That is not his thing, which is the danger for him in this fight. Puello is aware of Smith’s strengths. He understands that he wins by being on his toes.

It will be fascinating to see how Smith copes with a more technical fighter who isn’t easy to pick off. If Smith lands with a good shot he can beat anybody. But at this level the target is not always easy to find.

Sports.title: Hallgrimsson urges UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland drew 1-1 with Israel in a behind-closed-doors contest in Serbia; there were allegations of spitting by an Israeli player at half-time, while the Israeli government criticised the Irish players for bowing their heads during the national anthem

Republic of Ireland: Heimir Hallgrimsson calls on UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future after tense draw

Ireland's head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson has called for UEFA to keep his team and Israel separate in future

Heimir Hallgrimsson has called on UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future.

The Ireland boss was speaking following his side's 1-1 UEFA Nations League draw with Israel behind closed doors in Serbia.

The games between the two nations this international break were overshadowed by politics, with the Football Association of Ireland (FAI) urged to boycott the internationals amid ongoing conflict in the Israel-Gaza War.

This continued in Serbia, as Ireland fitness coach Damien Doyle was allegedly spat on by an Israeli player at half-time, according to reports in the stadium.

Irish media reported that the incident took place as the teams went down the tunnel. Ireland boss Hallgrimsson confirmed there was an allegation, but he admitted he didn't see it and declined to comment further on it.

However, when asked if the two countries should be playing each other again, he told RTE Sport: "No, they shouldn't. That's not ours to decide - that's UEFA who decides that. Obviously, there's a big support for Palestine in Ireland. There's not many countries that support Palestine as much as Ireland does.

"I wouldn't wish any national team to go through what we've gone through in these two weeks, so maybe UEFA just needs to step in and do something."

Sky Sports News has contacted UEFA for comment.

Israeli Government accuses ROI of 'moral blindness'

The Israeli Government have accused the Ireland football team of "moral blindness" for bowing their heads during their national anthem.

For the second time in a week, the Irish players, coaching team and FAI all bowed their heads while the Israeli national anthem was played pre-match.

Image: Republic of Ireland players bowed their heads during the national anthem

The official Israeli Government X account posted: "While some use the football field as their political theatre, for us this is personal.

"1939: Irish players raised their arms in salute to Nazi Germany.

"2026: Irish players bowed their heads during Israel's anthem.

"Different generations. The same moral blindness.

"Today, Israel's players wear black armbands to remember those brutally massacred by Hamas on October 7 - including former professional footballer Lior Asulin.

"Some of us have skin in the game. Others just make a show of it."

Sky Sports News has contacted the FAI for comment.

Two Israeli journalists banned for post-match press conferences

Meanwhile, prior to the match, UEFA confirmed that two Israeli journalists were banned from the post-match press conferences, after Saturday's pre-match Ireland press conference descended into chaos.

The media access for Ireland was cut short after an Israeli journalist alleged that Israeli players had claimed Irish players had racially abused them during the match in Hungary last weekend.

The journalist alleged that a derogatory term had been used, which Sky Sports has chosen not to repeat. The term is not associated with antisemitic or anti-Israeli abuse.

An Irish press officer refuted the allegation, saying: "That's completely untrue," before bringing the news conference to a premature close.

After the press conference ended abruptly, Serbian police were called following an allegation of assault by an Israeli journalist, who said a microphone had been taken from them by an FAI press officer.

Sky Sports News understands that no further action was taken by police.

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland draw with Israel in second Nations League meeting
Sports.content:
Match report and reaction as Republic of Ireland drew 1-1 with Israel in behind-closed-doors contest in Serbia; Troy Parrott's first-half penalty was cancelled out after the break; sides clashed at half-time

Republic of Ireland 1-1 Israel: Troy Parrott scores again as sides draw second controversial Nations League meeting

The Republic of Ireland drew 1-1 with Israel in the second controversial Nations League fixture between the sides.

Troy Parrott's first-half penalty was cancelled out by Dor Peretz after the break in the behind-closed-doors game in Serbia.

The Republic's 'home' fixture was held on neutral territory at the 4,500-seat TSC arena in Backa Topola, due to "operational challenges that could impact on the delivery of the game on home soil" according to a June Football Association of Ireland (FAI) statement.

Both sides wore black armbands. The Republic's, the same as in Hungary to acknowledge - as the Football Association of Ireland chief David Courrell explained before that contest - "all lives lost" in the ongoing Israel-Hamas conflict.

Israel's armbands - which read "7.10" - were to commemorate the October 7, 2023 Hamas-led attack on southern Israel, their official X account confirmed.

The pitch featured no sponsored content or branding, just UEFA graphics with slogans like "football for all", a decision taken by the FAI.

Image: The referee pleads with the benches in Serbia

Tensions rose at half-time after a fracas broke out in front of the tunnel and players from both sides engaged in a heated argument, with the Israeli Government later accusing Irish players of "moral blindness" for bowing their heads during Israel's national anthem, as they did in Monday's first match.

Officials broke up a second altercation in three minutes of added time, and there were more heated words exchanged after the final whistle.

On the pitch Parrott, who has now scored 10 times in his last seven competitive internationals, fired the Republic in front from the spot in the 39th minute before Dor Peretz drew the sides level two minutes after the restart.

The result puts Ireland third in Nations League Group B3, level on points with second-placed Kosovo.

Hallgrimsson calls on UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future

Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson has called on UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future.

Speaking after the 1-1 draw, Hallgrimsson also declined to comment on the half-time fracas between the two sides.

When asked if the two countries should be playing each other again, he told RTE Sport: "No, they shouldn't. That's not ours to decide - that's UEFA who decides that. Obviously, there's a big support for Palestine in Ireland. There's not many countries that support Palestine as much as Ireland does.

"I wouldn't wish any national team to go through what we've gone through in these two weeks, so maybe UEFA just needs to step in and do something."

On the half-time incident, he said in his post-match press conference: "I was there. I'm not going to comment on it. It's something that a disciplinary committee is probably going to look at."

Sky Sports News has contacted UEFA for comment.

Two Israeli journalists banned for post-match press conferences

Meanwhile, prior to the match, UEFA confirmed that two Israeli journalists were banned from the post-match press conferences, after Saturday's pre-match Ireland press conference descended into chaos.

The media access for Ireland was cut short after an Israeli journalist alleged that Israeli players had claimed Irish players had racially abused them during the match in Hungary last weekend.

The journalist alleged a derogatory term was used - which Sky Sports has chosen not to repeat. It is not a term associated with being antisemitic or anti-Israeli.

An Irish press officer refuted the allegation, saying "that's completely untrue", and brought the news conference to a premature close.

After the press conference ended abruptly, Serbian police were called due to an allegation of assault by an Israeli journalist who had the microphone taken from them by an FAI press officer.

Sky Sports News understands there was no further action was taken by police.

Sports.title: Ireland news conference cut short after tense exchanges with Israeli media
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland vs Israel is being played in Serbia as the FAI moved the game to a neutral venue for "operational reasons" in June following widespread calls for a boycott; protests briefly halted Ireland's draw with Austria on Thursday over opposition to Sunday's Israel fixture

Republic of Ireland vs Israel: Heimir Hallgrimsson's press conference cut short after tense exchanges with Israeli media

Republic of Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson's pre-match press conference ahead of Sunday's match against Israel in Serbia ended abruptly after a tense exchange with Israeli media.

The media access was cut short after an Israeli journalist alleged that Israeli players had claimed they were racially abused by Irish players during their match in Hungary last Sunday.

The journalist alleged a derogatory term was used - which Sky Sports has chosen not to repeat. It is not a term associated with being antisemitic or anti-Israeli.

An Irish press officer refuted the allegation, saying "that's completely untrue", and brought the news conference to a premature close as one of his colleagues remonstrated with the reporter.

Image: Ireland's players bowed their heads before facing Israel in the reverse fixture last week

Hallgrimsson later labelled the accusation a "verbal attack" during a separate briefing for members of the Irish press.

The exchange in the main press conference took place after Hallgrimsson was also asked a question about a co-pilot who attacked a pilot and tried to hijack a flight travelling from Dubai to Tel Aviv earlier this week.

The reporter's question was shut down by the FAI press officer.

Sky Sports News understands there are no open UEFA investigations at this stage from the previous meeting between Israel and Ireland last weekend.

The FAI are conducting their own investigation into whether striker Adam Idah was racially abused by Israeli supporters during their 3-0 UEFA Nations League win but have yet to make an official complaint to UEFA.

Image: Protesters interrupted Ireland's draw with Austria by throwing tennis balls onto the pitch with Palestine flags on them

Despite the high-profile nature of the fixture, members of the Irish media later reported that there was no UEFA delegate present at the news conference.

Sky Sports News was told a UEFA match delegate does not have to attend press conferences. The duty is left to the venue media manager, whose job it is to report anything if there is an incident.

Sunday's match is being played in Backa Topola, Serbia, as the FAI moved the game to a neutral venue for "operational reasons" in June following widespread calls for a boycott.

Sky Sports News has approached the FAI for comment.

Sports.title: Ireland held by Austria despite Parrott double as protests interrupt game
Sports.content:
Troy Parrott scored twice but the Republic of Ireland were forced to settle for a 2-2 draw after Austria came back in the second half of their Nations League encounter at the Aviva Stadium in Dublin.

The contest was twice interrupted in the opening 45 minutes, first due to what campaign group Stop the Game later referred to in a statement as a "limited tennis ball protest", when - around the 20th minute - tennis balls wrapped in stickers featuring the Palestinian flag and the text '#StopTheGame' were launched onto the pitch.

The match paused a second time when an invader carrying what appeared to be a Palestine flag entered the pitch and was promptly tackled and carried off by security.

The protests came after Ireland's decision not to boycott their game against Israel last week - although goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu did make himself unavailable.

Ireland are due to face Israel again on Sunday.

Image: Tennis balls with Palestine flags were throw onto the pitch

Before the protests, Parrott scored a sensational 12th-minute opener, and then added a penalty on the stroke of half-time.

A pair of substitutes proved Ireland's undoing after Alexander Prass halved the deficit in the 71st minute and Michael Gregoritsch drew the sides level six minutes later.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's men had a chance to top Group B3 with a victory, but they sit third behind Austria and Kosovo at the halfway point of the group stage.

Hallgrimsson made three changes, including the reintroduction of Finn Azaz, who was greeted warmly when his name was announced over the PA system before the match.

Bazunu was back in the squad, while Liam Scales and John Egan were awarded starts.

There was a significant security and police presence outside the stadium, where a small group of protesters also gathered before kick-off.

There was an audacious early effort from Sasa Kalajdzic, who tried to catch Caoimhin Kelleher off his line with a lob from midfield, before Ireland enjoyed a couple of attacking spells deep in the visitors' half.

Image: Parrott is congratulated after scoring his second goal against Austria

It was a brilliant opener from Parrott, who realised he was on his own after bringing down Adam Idah's glanced-on header from a goal kick.

The Real Betis striker was sandwiched in a triangle of white shirts, before nutmegging Philipp Lienhardt and evading every other challenger with a mazy run before planting the ball past Florian Wiegele and into the bottom corner.

Image: A protestor was carried off the pitch during the game

Kelleher denied Patrick Wimmer and there were a few more promising spells for Austria before Parrott doubled their lead.

Ryan Manning won the penalty after he was clipped in the box by Nicolas Seiwald. Parrott stepped up after a VAR check and blasted it past the Austria 'keeper.

Austria cut the deficit after Liam Kitching was caught out and Austria worked the ball to the unmarked Prass, who blasted the ball beyond Kelleher. The offside flag was initially raised, but the decision was reversed after a VAR check.

The Brentford goalkeeper then failed to stop Gregoritsch's free-kick as Ralf Rangnick's side fought back for a point.

Ireland captain Dara O'Shea was denied by an excellent leaping Wiegele save, Gregoritsch directed a shot over the crossbar and both sides fended off attempts at a late winner.

Sports.title: Hallgrimsson admits 'toughest days' of career after Ireland beat Israel
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland beat Israel 3-0 in their controversial Nations League fixture at a neutral venue in Hungary.

Players did not shake hands with each other before their meeting at the Nagyerdei Stadion in Debrecen and there was no exchange between Ireland captain Dara O'Shea and Israel's Manor Solomon.

Ireland players also appeared to bow their heads while Israel's national anthem was played out before kick-off.

Black armbands were worn by Ireland players, which Football Association of Ireland (FAI) chief executive David Courell said was a gesture to recognise "all lives lost" in the Israel-Gaza conflict.

Goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu was the only player who chose not to play after the squad voted to proceed with the match on Saturday amid calls for the game not to go ahead.

Goals from Troy Parrott, Adam Idah and Jack Moylan sealed the victory for Heimir Hallgrimsson's side.

Moylan celebrated his goal by kissing and raising his black armband before kissing his badge.

Hallgrimsson: I couldn't be more proud of the players

Republic of Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrimsson:

"It has been some of the toughest days of my coaching career, but its not about me.

"The game, the desire the players showed to make a statement on the pitch - they are football players, they wanted to show on the pitch, make that talking with their feet.

"What they did was impressive. In tough times that's when you find your leaders, there were so many players that stepped up in these tough times. The energy levels they showed was impressive.

"The performance was good given all the preparation, the lack of training, all of our meetings were about something other than football.

"I couldn't be more proud of the players.

"By playing I know we are making some people unhappy. By playing we are making others happy. Winning probably pleases everyone, but there will still be people angry that we played the game.

"I hope we can settle that slowly down and stay together as a team. I wish people in Ireland continue supporting these boys, because they certainly deserve it."

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland slip to deserved defeat in Kosovo
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland slipped to a 1-0 defeat away to Kosovo in their Nations League opener in Pristina.

The build-up to the League B3 encounter had been overshadowed by the controversy around upcoming fixtures against Israel, which Republic boss Heimir Hallgrimsson had admitted many of his squad members were uncomfortable about playing.

Chiedozie Ogbene had fired an early chance over before Kosovo responded to finish the first half strongly at the Fadil Vokrri Stadium.

The home side saw two shots cleared off the line and Ireland goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher then clawed away a header from Vedat Muriqi as Hallgrimsson's side got to the break on level terms.

Ireland - who are scheduled to play Israel in Hungary on Sunday and then again in a 'home' tie at another neutral venue in Serbia seven days later - dug in for the second half but were eventually undone with seven minutes left when Kosovo captain Muriqi bundled the ball in from close range.

Udinese defender James Abankwah was handed a first competitive start as part of a back five, with in-form Real Betis striker Troy Parrott the lone forward and Dara O'Shea taking the captain's armband.

Image: The Republic of Ireland have won two of their six games in 2026 so far

Ireland created what ended up being their only real clear chance in the 22nd minute. Abankwah got away down the right and ran into the Kosovo penalty area before cutting the ball back to Ogbene, who sent a curling effort over the crossbar.

Kosovo, who are in League B for the first time, went close on the half-hour mark when a cross from the left found its way through to Muriqi, whose angled shot was cleared off the line by Jayson Molumby.

Veldin Hodza then saw his 10-yard strike blocked in front of goal by O'Shea before Kelleher got up to claw away a looping header from Muriqi, which was set for the top corner.

Ireland made a positive start to the second half, with a deep cross from the right by Abankwah finding Parrott at the far post and his header was gathered by Kosovo goalkeeper Arijanet Muric.

Image: Vedat Muriqi scored the winner for Kosovo

Kosovo, though, continued to carry a threat themselves. Baton Zabergja sent a 20-yard effort just wide of the top corner, which again got the home supporters into full voice.

Muriqi forced Kelleher into another smart reaction save from an angled shot at the near post before Kosovo eventually made the breakthrough in the 83rd minute.

Ermal Krasniqi's shot was deflected onto the crossbar and Muriqi reacted quickest in a crowded six-yard box to nod the ball over the line.

Kosovo should have got a second late on when substitute Krasniqi dragged his shot wide after being set up by Muriqi following a break onto a long ball.

Ireland pay price for 'off day'

Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrimsson told RTE:

"[Kosovo are] a good team, momentum with them, crowd with them, and to be honest they deserve the win.

"There was nothing that we didn't know about how they would play, where their threats would be, but [it was] an off day for a lot of our players and [it is] a tough place to come to if you have an off day, so a deserved win for Kosovo."

Hallgrimsson added: "We were the team that needed to defend today and didn't connect in possession or passes, not as sharp as we have done.

"We have to quickly find out the reason that we had an off day. We can all do better than we did today.

"It is a two-day turnaround for the next one, so we better be quick…and do better than this versus Israel. They are probably in the same position as us [having lost to Austria]."

Asked if the controversy from playing the fixtures against Israel had impacted on his team's performance against Kosovo, Hallgrimsson said: "I couldn't say now. It is difficult to measure that one."

He added: "This is the situation, we have to cope with it. And like I said before the game, this camp is a test of character.

"We need to do better in that area than we did here today. We knew that we needed to win the duels, win the one-vs-ones, but sadly they had the upper hand on all the basics."

What it means and next fixtures

Sports.title: Why have the Republic of Ireland's two games against Israel become so controversial?
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland will face Israel in a men’s football fixture for the first time since 2005 in this international break, but there have been calls for the two UEFA Nations League games not to be played at all.

Both meetings - the first played in Debrecen, Hungary on Sunday and the second scheduled for the Serbian town of Backa Topola on October 4 - have been overshadowed by politics, with the Football Association of Ireland (FAI) urged to boycott the internationals amid ongoing conflict in the Israel-Gaza War.

Uncertainty over the games going ahead might have subsided, but the tensions between the two nations have not.

Heimir Hallgrimsson, the Republic of Ireland head coach, has been accused of "stupidity and hypocrisy" by the Israel Football Association after last week suggesting his team would be "playing against genocide" when facing Israel, while his players are not ruling out their own protests ahead of the games.

The Athletic examines the key issues ahead of the first meeting this weekend.

Why have these games caused controversy?

This has been a contentious issue rolling down the tracks ever since the 2026-27 Nations League draw was made in February. Group B3 saw the Republic of Ireland pitted against Kosovo, their opening opponents this evening, and Austria, but it was the prospect of facing Israel which created immediate unease.

The Football Association of Ireland (FAI) had overwhelmingly approved a motion that called on UEFA to ban Israel from its competitions just four months earlier due to violations of the governing body's statutes, including "the organisation of clubs in illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank without the consent of the Palestinian Football Association".

The Nations League draw duly reignited the row. Irish politicians, including the FAI member Joanna Byrne, were quick to call for a boycott of the Israel games in the following days and protests ensued when Qatar visited Dublin's Aviva Stadium for a friendly in May. Tennis balls featuring the Palestine flag were thrown on the pitch by supporters, twice causing brief interruptions.

Image: Tennis balls with a Palestinian flag on were thrown onto the pitch in Dublin during protests in May 2026

The FAI had already confirmed its plans to go ahead with the Israel games by then, and that decision was formally approved at an EGM in July.

That saw only 32 votes in favour of a boycott, with 75 members voting for the games to be played. The FAI had argued that boycotting games would cause "significant and lasting harm to Irish football" due to the likely disciplinary sanctions from UEFA.

A measure of the opposition to the Republic of Ireland facing Israel also came with the acceptance that the "home" fixture would not be played in Dublin. The FAI cited "operational challenges (that) could impact the delivery of the game on home soil" and the decision was eventually made in late June, with the support of UEFA, to move the game to Backa Topola, a small town in northern Serbia, on Sunday week.

No tickets for the game will be made available to Ireland fans.

The FAI has subsequently revealed that a request to see the two nations kept apart in future competition draws has been rejected by UEFA.

"The answer I got was very clear," FAI chief executive David Courell told reporters on September 18. "That would not be possible because Ireland and Israel have never been in direct conflict."

What is the political backdrop?

The Republic of Ireland has consistently outlined its backing for the Palestinian people since the conflict with Israel began almost three years ago, joining Norway and Spain when officially recognising a Palestinian state in 2024. Taoiseach Micheal Martin has also made his stance clear, accusing Israel of committing "genocide" last year in comments reported by the Irish Mirror.

The conflict in Gaza began after Israel responded to attacks by Hamas militants on October 7, 2023, which saw around 1,200 people, mostly civilians, killed in Israel and 250 taken hostage. The war has subsequently seen 73,000 people killed, according to figures from the Gaza Health Ministry and used by the UN.

Strained relations between the Republic of Ireland and Israel have continued this year. Two Israeli government ministers were the subject of travel bans in June, while foreign minister Helen McEntee also confirmed Ireland's intent to limit goods trading with settlements in the Israeli-occupied West Bank this summer.

Image: Taoiseach Micheal Martin

A meeting between the Republic of Ireland and Israel on a football field this weekend has subsequently taken on enormous significance against such a backdrop.

There are similarities in Ireland's political stance with those of Norway, who faced similar calls for a boycott when Israel travelled to Oslo last October. The Norwegian Football Federation (NFF) had aligned itself with its government and said in a statement leading up to Israel's visit that the "tragic humanitarian suffering in Gaza" had made the fixture challenging.

That World Cup qualifier, won 5-0 by Norway, saw thousands take part in a protest march to the stadium.

Who has opposed the games taking place?

Moving a home game 1,500 miles away has not stopped the objections building ahead of the two teams meeting on Sunday. More than 160 Irish sportspeople signed an open letter asking their national team to boycott the Israel games under the banner of the Irish Sport for Palestine Group, who have also run the "Stop the Game" campaign that protested outside of the Irish team hotel in Dublin on Monday.

"This is a significant moment and with this moment you have an opportunity to do the right thing," the letter said.

Kevin Kilbane, the former Republic of Ireland international who holds 110 caps, has also been unequivocal in his views. "The Republic of Ireland should not be playing Israel… not while Israeli forces are committing genocide," he wrote in a column for the Irish Times.">he wrote in a column for the Irish Times.

Amnesty International also issued a fresh statement on Tuesday that said UEFA risked letting football "rubber-stamp apartheid" by allowing Israel's continued participation in its club and international competitions. A spokesperson for the Israeli FA responded to that by saying: "Their obsession with the idea of Israel as a state is incurable, as is their need of attention."

The Irish media, meanwhile, has faced its own dilemmas in the coverage of the Israel games. RTE, the public broadcaster behind Ireland's boycott of the Eurovision Song Contest in the last two years due to Israel's continued involvement, has stripped back its coverage. Contractual obligations will be met, RTE confirmed in a statement, but there would be no studio coverage or commentators sent to either fixture.

Image: Kevin Kilbane, former Ireland international, has spoken out

What have the key stakeholders said ahead of this weekend?

Relations between the two nations have grown increasingly hostile in the last week. Hallgrimsson appeared in front of the media to announce his squad for the upcoming friendlies and made pointed remarks when asked how his players would focus on football.

"We're not playing with genocide, we're playing against genocide," the former Iceland head coach told reporters. "We're playing against Israel, we're not playing with Israel."

The reaction to those words, in a social media post from the Israel FA account, raised temperatures further still. "We have contributed to the world and humanity in countless fields, earning an impressive number of Nobel Prizes along the way," it read. "Unfortunately, we have not yet found a cure for stupidity, ignorance and hypocrisy displayed by @IrelandFootball team coach. We're not playing with ignorance, hypocrisy and stupidity, we're playing against the coach who embodies them."

Martin, who was among the world leaders attending the UN General Assembly in New York, was then drawn back into debate on Tuesday. "I think those are unacceptable remarks. They should be withdrawn. Israel can't keep denying what the world knows and what the world understands."

The FAI has not addressed Hallgrimsson's comments publicly, but the Republic of Ireland's head coach said on Wednesday that he had been "grateful for the support" he had received.

"Maybe from a leadership point of view, it was not clever from me to take the attention (away) like this. It's a tricky time for us," Hallgrimsson said in his pre-match press conference ahead of facing Kosovo.

The same extends to his players, too. Dara O'Shea, the Ipswich Town defender, said, according to the BBC, that he and the rest of the players would come together on Friday to "openly discuss" the prospect of a protest ahead of the first Israel game in Debrecen on Sunday.

Image: Dara O’Shea, left, and head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson during Wednesday’s press conference

Why are the games being played in Hungary and Serbia?

Hungary has acted as an adopted home for Israel since the start of the conflict. They first played there in November 2023, when resuming their attempts to qualify for Euro 2024 when hosting Switzerland at the Pancho Arena in Felcsut, a small village 26 miles west of Budapest.

Victor Orban, who lost his position as Hungary's prime minister this year, had been a long-standing ally of Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu and claimed Hungary to be the "safest country in Europe" for Jews.

The World Cup 2026 qualifiers against Estonia, Norway and Italy were all held in Debrecen, which has also previously hosted European games for Israeli sides Maccabi Haifa and Maccabi Tel Aviv.

The Republic of Ireland's choice of Backa Topola, Serbia, is less clear. Dublin ceased to become an option, even behind closed doors, as the opposition to Israel visiting became clear, which left limited options for relocation.

It needed to be a nation sympathetic to Israel to avoid further protests and Serbia, neighbouring Hungary to the south, has forged strong diplomatic relations. According to the Associated Press, Serbia's president Aleksandar Vucic inaugurated an assembly factory for Israel-made drones last week, with plans for three more production sites.

A switch to Serbia was reliant on UEFA approval and it will be Backa Topola's home of the TSC Arena where this story ends on October 4.

Sports.title: 'Brutal, searing and punishing heat' - Babb on playing for Ireland at USA '94
Sports.content:
While none of the home nations qualified for the 1994 World Cup, the Republic of Ireland did.

It was a second successive appearance at the tournament for the Boys in Green, who were again led by 1966 World Cup winner Jack Charlton.

At Italia '90, the weather had been hot - but at USA '94, it was a different kettle of fish altogether.

The iconic image of Charlton launching an open bottle of water in the direction of Andy Townsend and Tommy Coyne always provides a reminder of that.

Image: Jack Charlton led the Republic of Ireland at Italia '90 and USA '94

He clashed with FIFA over their policy that bottles could not be thrown to the players on the pitch, so took to throwing the contents instead before FIFA later relented and allowed water bags to be thrown.

"They trust me to do what is right for them and I will continue to do it," Charlton said. "We have been right in pursuing this matter and FIFA's change of heart proves that."

Charlton was rarely seen without his white baseball cap that summer. Steve Staunton famously even wore one during the national anthem before the second group game against Mexico.

One of the players in the Ireland squad that summer was Phil Babb. The defender, then 23, had just completed his second full Premier League season at Coventry.

He made his international debut in a 0-0 friendly draw with Russia in March 1994, then played in the next four friendlies leading up to the tournament.

Image: Phil Babb played in all four of the Republic of Ireland's games at the 1994 World Cup

Nothing was set in stone, but he knew he would at least have a decent chance of being included in Charlton's 22-man squad, so started to physically prepare himself.

"A coach at Coventry asked me if I wanted to do anything specific - we ended up doing 12-minute sessions in a sauna!" Babb recalls, with a smile.

"We were doing burpees, press-ups, just trying to acclimatise to that intense heat. We did about six sessions - but I wouldn't recommend it for anyone now!

"I was a fit lad and had played pretty much all the Premier League games Coventry had played that season. I adapted to the heat pretty well, but I know some of the older lads really struggled."

Babb started alongside Paul McGrath in the heart of defence for Ireland's tournament opener at Giants Stadium in New Jersey.

Image: Ray Houghton's stunning strike earned a shock 1-0 win over Italy

That Saturday, they shocked an Italy side that featured Paolo Maldini, Franco Baresi and Roberto Baggio. John Aldridge's stunner sealed a memorable 1-0 win.

It was an achievement made all the more impressive by the fact the Azzurri went on to finish as runners-up - but also given the fact it was played in temperatures exceeding 30C.

"When we walked out onto the field, about two hours before kick-off, you could tell it was going to be absolutely roasting," he recalls.

"You could tell that straight away and we didn't stay out long. I just checked the grass to see which studs I wanted, then I went straight back in. I know some of the lads were walking around and taking the atmosphere in, but I thought: 'This is too hot'.

"I didn't go out for a warm-up with the rest of the lads, either. I stayed in the changing room. It was built for NFL, so they had a 40m sprint track. I warmed up in there and waited until we went out. It was brutal, it was searing, it was punishing.

"It affected everyone's game. You were saturated after just 10 minutes walking onto a pitch, so you had to conserve energy at the right times.

"Recovery was very basic and there was very little ball work because of the demands of the actual games and the fluids you lose. When you're that dehydrated, it's quite difficult. You want a drink, but you don't feel hungry and that is a key part of the recuperation."

Image: Babb, whose Ireland were knocked out by Dennis Bergkamp's Netherlands, joined Liverpool later that summer

Thirty-two years on from that tournament, football has evolved exponentially.

Sports science has taken on a key role in the game and, this summer, is likely to play into the way teams approach games tactically due to the heat. A slower tempo is expected in many.

Charlton was not prepared to facilitate the same in 1994, though.

"We only played one way, so if you tried to go off-piste, Jack would certainly let you know!" adds Babb.

"We had one style of play, with a lone striker. If it wasn't Tommy Coyne, it might have been Niall Quinn up there and we'd be putting long balls up to him, with either willing runners out wide or the midfield bombing on.

"That was the Irish way back then. Tommy ran tirelessly, to the point where he actually collapsed with heat exhaustion on the plane home.

"I think Jack's sports science was a barrel of Guinness in his room and he'd call the lads in and have a pint! I'm sure there's a high calorific content in that, so maybe he was ahead of his time!"

In spite of that, Babb's memories of the tournament are largely positive.

"I enjoyed it, I have to admit! I'd rather play in the searing heat than a wet Tuesday night in Hull," he says.

"I was a fit lad and it was quite easy for me playing alongside Paul McGrath, who was imperious in that tournament. I learned a lot from him and how he conserved his energy.

"I felt I got stronger because I got used to it. I guess our 0-0 draw against Norway would probably attest to the heat and the style of play.

"It all comes down to the individual. Footballers are supreme athletes now and they leave nothing to chance, so I think they'll cope a lot better than we did in the mid-90s."

The methods may have moved on since Charlton was throwing water onto the pitch, but Babb's memories from USA '94 provide a reminder this World Cup will be a battle against more than just the opposition.

Sports.title: Aussie boxing legend Jeff Fenech hospitalised as he faces fresh new health battle: 'He's always a fighter'
Sports.content:
Australian boxing legend Jeff Fenech has been hospitalised with heart problems, with his NRL star son-in-law Bradman Best revealing the family’s concern ahead of his Kangaroos debut.

The four-weight world champion, 62, was admitted to Strathfield Private Hospital around 10 days ago after suffering severe fatigue, breathing difficulties and feeling unwell.

Fenech has since had a blood clot removed from his wrist and undergone tests to investigate whether a potentially life-threatening staph infection has returned.

A recurrence has not been confirmed.

Best, who has a baby daughter with Fenech’s daughter Kayla, disclosed the hospital stay while discussing the boxing great’s influence on his career.

The Newcastle centre is preparing to make his Australian Test debut against Fiji on Sunday, but took time to acknowledge Fenech’s health battle.

Jeff Fenech, 62, has been hospitalised after suffering heart problems, fatigue and breathing difficulties

Bradman Best paid tribute to his father-in-law ahead of his Australian Test debut

Fenech has reportedly had a blood clot removed from his wrist and undergone tests for a possible recurrence of a serious infection

‘Jeff has been massive for me, I just want to give a quick shout-out to him,’ Best said.

‘He’s actually in hospital at the moment.

‘I’m thinking of him. He’s tough, he’s always a fighter.’

Best said Fenech had become an invaluable source of advice as he worked towards representing Australia.

‘Jeff has done a lot for me in my career,’ he said.

‘I was visiting him last week and he’s always giving me tips on what to do and how to be better.

‘It’s special having a father-in-law like that who’s a four-time world champion.

‘He’s an icon in Australia and it’s special having a bond like that with him.’

Tim Tszyu’s preparations for his world-title clash with Erislandy Lara have been disrupted by his trainer’s hospitalisation

Fenech became one of Australia’s greatest boxers, winning world titles across four weight divisions during a career that earned him the nickname ‘The Marrickville Mauler’

Asked whether Fenech’s condition was serious, Best remained hopeful.

‘Yeah, he will be right. He’s always a fighter. He’s been in there with a few heart problems and stuff, but he’ll be good.’

The hospitalisation has also interrupted Tim Tszyu’s preparations for his planned WBA middleweight world-title clash with Erislandy Lara.

Fenech became Tszyu’s head trainer in July, helping guide him to a unanimous decision victory over American star Errol Spence Jr.

Tszyu credited the veteran trainer with helping inspire that result, which set up his pursuit of a world championship in a second weight division.

With Fenech sidelined, fellow trainer Basil Nassis has taken charge of Tszyu’s work in the gym.

The Lara bout is expected to take place in Australia in November or December, according to the reports.

Fenech hopes to recover in time to be involved, although the Telegraph reported he is unlikely to perform padwork during the build-up.

The latest scare follows two major heart operations.

In October 2019, Fenech underwent emergency open-heart surgery in Thailand while preparing Jack Brubaker for a fight against Tszyu.

He needed another six-hour open-heart operation in 2024 during a serious infection.

Sports.title: British boxing has a world beater in the ascendancy. Daniel Dubois is starting to look like a monster - and he's ready for Oleksandr Usyk, Anthony Joshua, Tyson Fury or anyone else, writes JEFF POWELL MBE
Sports.content:
British boxing has a world beater in the ascendancy. Daniel Dubois is starting to look like a monster - and he's ready for Oleksandr Usyk, Anthony Joshua, Tyson Fury or anyone else, writes JEFF POWELL MBE

'Bring him on,' roared Daniel Dubois when asked if he would like a third fight against the greatest boxer of his generation who has beaten him twice.

Oleksandr Usyk, who is in a state of limbo somewhere between vacating all the heavyweight tiles and semi-retirement, is a genius so may not fall readily into the trap baited on the banks of the Thames in the dark hours of this Sunday morning.

Ukraine's war hero will have watched Dubois annihilate the gallant Fabio Wardley and recognised that Dynamite Daniel is no longer the callow youth he wiped the canvas with a couple of times during his reign as the undisputed world champion.

Promoter Frank Warren is not given to understatement but when he said 'Daniel has matured now' he was only scratching the surface of the transformation.

It may be a stretch to compare Dubois with the once terrifying Sonny Liston but to those rivals wearing the other belts he needs if he is to become undisputed then he is starting to look like a monster.

'I want them all,' said WBO champion Dubois. He was referring to the winner between Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua in December, who will thereby hold a WBA title, as well as IBF and WBC champions Filip Hrgovic and Ajit Kabayel.

Daniel Dubois knocks down Fabio Wardley during his annihilation on Saturday night

Dubois has declared himself ready to fight anyone in the heavyweight division

Their availability, especially that of AJ or the Gypsy King, will be determined no doubt by there being many more millions in the Aladdin's Cave from which Saudi Arabia has helped finance the welcome flux of mega-fights of late.

If so then Warren is promising a 2027 bursting with monthly heavyweight spectaculars as lustily anticipated as Dubois' second demolition of Wardley . At the rapid conclusion of which another packed O2 crowd was switching its allegiance from a love affair with Fabio's romanticised emergence from white collar boxing to realisation that Britain has a world beater in the ascendancy.

One who may be growing, also, into more of a box office star than the monosyllabic Liston ever was. If his accurate bravura prediction of a 'bash and smash' slaughter of Wardley and his most jovial media conference yet which followed are anything to go by.

Having nursed his confidence in the Dubois family cocoon Daniel now has a mansion of his own to live in and a selection of race cars to drive. No more Mister Shy Guy but none the less likeable for that.

The transition to full manhood was rounded off over the two fights with Wardley. This included recovery from two early knockdowns in the first Fight Of The Year battle to a brutal 11th round stoppage victory.

And now the onslaught triggered by a staggering right hand blow only 17 seconds after the first bell which imposed an eight count on the ropes. Followed by an overwhelming TKO in round two. Wham, bam and thank you man. No criticism this time of a delay in calling it off. In flew the white towel, in jumped referee Steve Gray.

Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua fight each other in December - and Dubois wants the winner

There has been some nagging at the edge of Dubois' triumph. Suggestions that Wardley came back too soon after the second-half beating in May. But if five-and-a-half months is not sufficient time to recover then how long would be? The immortal Joe Louis used to fight once a month, for heaven's sake.

Wardley, honest man that he is, blamed himself. Having lived to fight another day he vows to do better enough to launch a comeback campaign for another world title. Meanwhile Dubois, at 29 last month, heads for the stratosphere as champion of the next generation of heavyweight boxing.

As the new monster of the prize-ring? It took The Greatest Of All Time to stop the Liston beast In his awesome tracks. Might Usyk be the Muhammad Ali in waiting for Dubois? Maybe. Perhaps not since he is the older legend now. It would be fascinating finding out.

The tombstone on Sonny Liston's grave in Las Vegas describes him simply as A MAN. Frank Warren is right about Dubois becoming exactly that.

Sports.title: Former heavyweight world title contender boxer dies 'suddenly' aged 40: Denis Boytsov, once set to fight Tyson Fury, was unable to speak for 11 years after mysterious 'attack'
Sports.content:
A former world No 2 heavyweight boxer once primed to fight Tyson Fury has died aged just 40, after 11 years of care following an 'attack' in which the perpetrators were never found.

Russian Denis Boytsov pulled out of a fight with Fury in December 2012 and was considered the world's second-best heavyweight behind Wladimir Klitschko. He had a 36-1 record when his career was cut short in 2015.

Boytsov suffered serious head injuries in a Berlin subway tunnel and had to be placed into a medically induced coma because of swelling on the brain.

A statement on the boxer's website suggested he was the victim of an attack linked to his boxing career. 'It is possible that this attack was linked to the boxer's sporting activity,' the statement said. 'Around two years ago, Boytsov was receiving threats constantly.'

His wife Olga Litvinova was left deeply upset and suggested Boytsov may have been the victim of an attempted 'assassination' after that series of threats.

Now, 11 years on, Boytsov's family have revealed he died 'suddenly' this week after many years in care. His father says the cause of death was a detached blood clot.

Russian boxer Denis Boytsov died this week from a detached blood clot at home

Boystov is pictured in his boxing gear in hospital after the 'attack' on him in 2015

'A blood clot broke off,' Nikolai Boytsov told Russian news agency TASS. 'There was nothing they could do; it was instant death. Three minutes and that was it.

'This happened at home. His wife fed him and started turning him to the side. He suddenly broke down, started shaking, turned blue. And his whole life was over.'

Brother Maxim Boytsov revealed Denis had been unable to speak in the 11 years following the Berlin incident. Boytsov underwent extensive treatment in Germany and then back in his homeland.

'No, we didn't communicate. He just nodded yes and no. But he understood everything. I courted him for ten years. But it didn't work out,' said Maxim.

Boytsov's funeral is set for today in the Russian region of Oryol.

British former heavyweight boxer David Price - who once beat Fury in 2005 - revealed Boytsov's punching power was much stronger than that of Anthony Joshua, having trained with both.

Boytsov's wife Olga was by his side as he died in Russia this week

Boytsov was due to fight Tyson Fury in 2012 and was considered a top heavyweight fighter

'I sparred a Russian called Denis Boytsov in Germany once. He only hit the top of my head, but he was a powerful puncher,' Price told the Daily Star.

'I think he got his career cut short, he got absolutely battered and left for dead, he couldn't fight again. But I remember him being a really powerful puncher.'

Sports.title: Britain's only female boxing referee faces backlash as she REFUSES to accept fighter's towel being thrown in twice - moments before technical knockout by a brutal headshot at the O2 Arena
Sports.content:
Britain's only female boxing referee faces backlash as she REFUSES to accept fighter's towel being thrown in twice - moments before technical knockout by a brutal headshot at the O2 Arena

It is the best-known sign of submission in sport - but a boxing referee at the O2 Arena on Saturday night twice refused to accept a heavyweight fighter 'throwing in the towel' before he was brutally beaten.

Heavyweights Adam Olaniyan and Dan Garber were fighting in London on the undercard of Daniel Dubois' victory over Fabio Wardley - with Bradford fighter Garber, 41, beaten by technical knockout (TKO) in the second round.

But focus after the fight has instead been on referee Amy Pu, after she allowed Garber to undergo more punishing headshots even after his team had tried to stop the fight. Pu, the UK's first and only female professional boxing referee, kicked a towel thrown by Garber's team out of the ring to allow the fight to continue.

Garber had been dismayed by his team's attempts to submit and Pu elected to continue on with the fight. Seconds later, Olaniyan, 20, unleashed a flurry of further punches which sent Garber to the canvas to end the contest. Garber's team had thrown in another towel but that was also ignored before Pu stopped the punishment.

Garber could be seen receiving oxygen ringside after the fight.

It is rare for referees to overrule the decision of the boxer's corner to end a bout but is allowed within the sport's rules. British Boxing Board of Control (BBBofC) regulations state that the towel does not automatically end a fight and referees are left with the authority on when to do so.

Referee Amy Pu finally steps in to end Adam Olaniyan's fight against Dan Garber on Saturday

Garber's team twice tried to throw in the towel to stop the fight but Pu refused the submission

But fans were unimpressed by Pu's decision-making, with footage of her kicking the white towel out of the ring going viral after being posted by broadcasters DAZN.

'Ref nearly got dan garber killed. Kicking the towel out idiot,' one viewer wrote on X.

Another fan said: 'Dan Garber receiving oxygen after referee Amy Pu inexplicably refuses the corner's towel and allows Olaniyan to pile more damage in. Rules should be changed to make the towel coming in an automatic fight ended. Refs don't know what's been happening in the gym.'

And another picked apart Pu's record, writing: 'Bbbofc referee Amy Pu has been mostly terrible all night, two stoppages called earlier than they needed to be, kicking the towel out to let Dan Garber take more punishment, this is not new for her.'

Originally from Taiwan, Pu took up boxing in her 30s in London and later became a professional referee in 2024. She has spoken about isolated issues of suffering from racism and sexism in the male-dominated world of boxing.

'On the professional side, I have to say the reaction has mostly been really positive,' Pu told the BBC earlier this year. 'During the amateur days, there were some odd comments and stuff. I think one of the hesitations I had before turning professional was also for that reason.

'People have just been so supportive, knock on wood, I haven't really had any criticism directed at me because of my sex or because of my race.

'I'm really grateful and I hope that it continues, that people should see me as a referee. They can give me stick as a referee, not as a female Asian referee.'

Rising star Olaniyan's record now stands at 5-0 in his short professional career, while Garber has 14 victories to 10 defeats.

Garber, for his part, did not appear disappointed with Pu's decision-making. Writing after the fight on Facebook - instead focusing on the money he had made and being able to 'buy a third house'.

He said: 'What an experience, took the fight last week and we knew what we was up against but no excuses.

'Maybe this is the end now for me, time waits for no-one. Bought 2 houses out of boxing and tonight gets me a 3rd, it’s been a massive part of my life. If it is the end then what a way to go out in front of 20,000.'

Sports.title: Stunned inside 17 SECONDS and over in two rounds: Brutal Daniel Dubois was explosive in deciding his Fabio Wardley rematch and is now the undisputed champion-elect, writes JEFF POWELL MBE
Sports.content:
To hell with the romance. Stuff the slow starts. Never mind most of the O2 shouting against him.

Daniel Dynamite Dubois exploded into the ring with such power and brutality that he might have sent a tsunami along the Thames.

What he did beyond doubt last night, and what cannot be contested by Fabio Wardley or the three other world heavyweight belt wearers, was announce himself as the undisputed champion-elect.

White-collar Wardley was disabused of any notion he might regain the WBO title he lost to Dubois five months ago.

He was stunned in 17 seconds by Dubois's first booming right-hander of a red-hot night. And so the pain continued unabated.

'Fabio is a great boy, coming in for the second time, but it was my time, and my era,' said Dubois. 'I had my intentions, bad intentions, from the beginning.'

Daniel Dubois brutalised Fabio Wardley in their rematch as he wrapped things up in two rounds

This time there was no delay in Wardley's corner throwing in the towel. No point in the referee delaying the inevitable.

Dubois's sledgehammer blows rained down like missiles, with none travelling in the opposite direction.

One of the rival world champions was here to see the ferocity in person. Filip Hrgovic, who had disposed of Moses Itauma recently, sounded somewhat shell-shocked.

Agit Kabayel may be in no rush to meet Dubois. Nor, perhaps, will the winner of December's WBA clash between Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua.

This was an enormous statement by a man whose courage had been questioned but who will now be favourite to hunt them all down in his quest for the succession to Oleksandr Usyk as the undisputed champion.

'I'm the champion now, and I want to get some big fights in,' said Dubois. 'At this stage in my career, big money, big fights.'

The next generation of heavyweights has arrived.

So the irresistible force and the immovable object came to blows again at the O2. Dubois had risen from the canvas twice in the spring to claim his second world heavyweight title. Wardley, who neglected to finish him off, paid such a bloodied price that he left us wondering how he had stayed on his feet.

After being dropped in the opening seconds in their first fight, Dubois delivered revenge this time around

Their mutual hammering in Manchester had left us greedily wanting more at the O2.

Both pledged to put the savagery on after-burner second time around. Forget the concerns for their health.

In the parlance of the first promotion, Don't Blink was the warning to all those in attendance. These two had spent their careers knocking people out for fun or sometimes being stopped themselves.

No one expected this fight to go the distance. Not the fighters themselves. 'Me early,' predicted Dubois. 'Me earlier,' said Wardley.

'Twelve rounds?' opined promoter Frank Warren. 'No chance.'

The majority of the crowd were with the underdog, roaring Wardley into the ring. Partly from their feeling for romance, with a white-collar boxer breaking into the highest echelons of the heavyweights.

Dynamite Daniel's reception was more subdued. Even a hint hostile. Wardley hoped for a first-round knockdown, but that went to Dubois.

The first right of the night had Fabio reeling on the ropes for an eight count. More hell followed.

Dubois may have found greatness and is the undisputed champion-elect in the next generation of heavyweights

It was all over in round two. Wardley was brave as always, but his corner could not let him keep taking sledgehammer blows without reply.

'I just came in and I didn't execute the game plan properly,' Wardley admitted. 'I hold my hands up to that; that is entirely down to me.'

'A little white-collar boy like me could never have dreamed like this,' he added, reflecting on a sold-out O2 despite defeat.

Dubois may have found greatness with this mammoth performance.
