World.title: Liberia: PLP Elevates Zarwolo to Two Top Posts as Party Eyes New Political Framework With Bility’s CMC
World.content:
MONROVIA, Liberia — The People’s Liberation Party (PLP) has appointed education policy expert Tonzeah N. Zarwolo to two senior leadership positions, a move that could position him to help shape the party’s policy direction as it explores political collaboration with Musa Hassan Bility’s Citizens Movement for Change (CMC).

Zarwolo, a former PLP National Youth Chairman, has been named National Vice Chairman for Political Affairs and Acting National Secretary General, according to two appointment letters dated October 22, 2026.

The appointments come as the PLP engages in discussions with Bility’s CMC about a possible political collaboration intended to offer an alternative to the country’s established political blocs, the Coalition for Democratic Change (CDC) and the ruling Unity Party (UP).

While neither appointment letter explicitly links Zarwolo’s elevation to the discussions, his combination of political, administrative and education policy experience could make him a significant figure in developing the principles and policy priorities of any proposed arrangement.

A Possible Role in Policy Development

Zarwolo’s professional background could be particularly relevant if the proposed collaboration moves beyond political consultations toward developing a formal policy document.

An education policy expert, he has worked on national education projects involving the United States Agency for International Development (USAID) and CODE Canada. He is also a university lecturer.

That experience could provide a foundation for contributing to discussions on education reform, public-sector performance, institutional accountability and national development priorities.

Zarwolo’s appointment as National Vice Chairman for Political Affairs could place him in a position to coordinate discussions on behalf of the PLP, while his role as Acting National Secretary General could give him a hand in documenting decisions and coordinating the party’s internal processes.

However, there is no confirmation in the appointment letters that he has been assigned to lead or draft a policy document for the proposed collaboration.

The Search for a Different Political Arrangement

The PLP’s reported discussions with Bility’s CMC come amid wider efforts by Liberian opposition parties to determine how they might cooperate ahead of the 2029 general and presidential elections.

In September, the CMC withdrew from a proposed opposition coalition process convened by former President George Weah, arguing that the draft arrangement did not adequately reflect its objectives. The party has emphasized the need for cooperation built around a clear reform agenda rather than political unity alone.

That position underscores a central question for any alternative political framework: whether participating parties can agree not only on political cooperation but also on a defined program for governing and addressing Liberia’s challenges.

For the PLP and CMC, a formal arrangement could require decisions on policy priorities, accountability mechanisms, internal decision-making, the roles of participating parties and how commitments would be communicated to the public.

Zarwolo’s policy background could be relevant to that process, particularly if the parties seek to develop proposals grounded in sectoral experience and implementable public policy rather than a general declaration of political unity.

Zarwolo Accepts Both Appointments

Zarwolo thanked the Political Leader, Tapple Doe, Bernard Blue Benson, National Chairman, David Woods Beyan Sr. National Vice Chair for Administration and the wider PLP membership for the confidence placed in him.

“I hereby formally accept these appointments and assure the Party of my unwavering commitment to discharging my responsibilities with diligence and loyalty,” he said.

He pledged to work with the party’s leadership and fellow partisans to advance its collective vision and strengthen its ideals.

World.title: Liberia: Commerce Minister Designate Plan Meets a Market That Isn’t Waiting
World.content:
MONROVIA — Stephen M. Yekeson Jr. told senators Wednesday that he wants to be “judged by what is delivered.” His confirmation statement gives the Senate one promise it can test within 100 days, and many more it cannot.

By Rodney D Sieh

Appearing before the Senate Committee on Commerce and Industry, the acting Commerce and Industry Minister set out a vision to have Liberia “produce more of what Liberia consumes” by 2029. He pledged to protect consumers, enforce Liberian-only business sectors and cut the cost of moving goods “between the ship and the shop.”



His firmest commitment: within 100 days, the ministry will publish weekly prices for rice, fuel and cement in all 15 counties. Beyond that, the statement leans on verbs such as “work with,” “engage” and “address,” with few numbers, dates or budgets attached. Set against the problems now pressing on traders and households, the distance between promise and mechanism is where the scrutiny belongs.

A stronger dollar that isn’t reaching the market

Yekeson’s most striking admission was that prices have kept rising “in spite of a stronger Liberian Dollar.” The Liberian dollar was Africa’s best-performing currency in September, closing the month at about L$172 to US$1.

Small traders in Monrovia say the gains are not passed on. They report that some wholesalers still price stock at about L$190 to the dollar while the market rate sits near L$170, a gap of nearly 12 percent.

On October 6, Yekeson announced a five-point plan under which the ministry would work with the Central Bank to require supermarkets, wholesalers and retailers to post the bank’s daily exchange rate. That measure does not appear in his Senate statement. Instead, he cites a “reengineered” Price Analysis Department and a better-resourced Inspectorate. Whether the posting rule is still coming, and when, is a question the committee should put to him.

Fuel: a review, but no formula

Fuel is where the Senate already has its own findings. A Senate probe found that diesel rose from L$840 to L$1,235 a gallon between October 2024 and September 2026, a 47 percent increase. Gasoline climbed from L$775 to L$985 over the same period. The probe also found that Bea Mountain paid nothing on 16.4 million gallons of diesel.

The senator leading that inquiry proposed that the Liberia Petroleum Refining Company (LPRC) publish its full pricing formula every week. Yekeson’s statement moves in that direction but stops short. He promises to review pricing with the LPRC, and says regulated prices should be “transparent, rule-based and regularly reviewed,” reflecting verified import costs, duties, transport and a reasonable margin.

He does not commit to publishing that formula. His weekly price list would show what motorists pay at the pump, not how the figure was reached. He also names the LPRC, a petroleum body, as his partner in reviewing rice and cement pricing, a pairing he did not explain.

Rice: a global squeeze is coming

The next test may arrive before his 100 days are up. World rice prices are up about 67 percent on the year and hit a 26-month high in early October.

At home, the price of the staple was last fixed in March. After an emergency meeting with six major importers, the ministry announced that a 25kg bag would stay at US$14.00 wholesale and US$14.50 retail.

With import costs climbing, importers are likely to push for an increase. Yekeson’s formula of verified costs plus a reasonable margin may justify one. His weekly price list will then put any rise in public view, county by county. The Senate should ask him now whether US$14.50 can hold, and on what basis it would change.

An Inspectorate that barely registers

Yekeson promises inspectors will pursue “hoarding, collusion, false invoicing and short measures.” The ministry’s own figures suggest little enforcement capacity today.

At a budget hearing last week, he reported that the ministry had collected about US$4.12 million by September 30. Of that, inspectorate fees and fines brought in roughly US$48,700, about 1 percent. He acknowledged those collections could improve.

The pledge is also not new. In 2024, his predecessor Amin Modad rolled out a rebranded Inspectorate Division to keep vendors from selling rice above the government ceiling. The committee should ask how many inspectors the ministry has, how many cases it opened this year, and what money comes with “resourcing” them.

Small business: right diagnosis, no deadlines

On Liberian enterprise, Yekeson’s diagnosis matches what traders report. He has said that women make up 75 percent of traders reporting financial constraints.

His answers are sensible but undated:

* Procurement set-aside. The law already reserves a quarter of qualifying public procurement for Liberian-owned small businesses. He promises to publish compliance “agency by agency,” but gives no date.

* Credit. A credit guarantee programme will come “only with the requisite approvals and clear fiscal safeguards,” a signal that no money is yet set aside.

* Late payment. He will “engage” concessionaires and “report progress,” with no target for how quickly government and companies must pay.

* Business registration. Service centres exist in seven counties, with nationwide expansion planned for 2027. His “every county” pledge carries no date.

* Liberians-only sectors. He will enforce the reservation of rice and cement retail, fuel stations and sand supply through ownership checks. He did not say how many such businesses are now foreign-owned.

The 2029 goal to “produce more of what Liberia consumes” has no baseline or target. He has also warned that a stronger currency can cut what farmers and processors earn, a tension his import-substitution plan does not address.

Questions of record

Yekeson told senators he will disclose all relevant interests, comply with the Code of Conduct and recuse himself where conflicts arise. He did not say whether he still holds shares or roles in South Atlantic Capital Group or Panchariya Group West Africa, where he previously served as CFO and president, respectively.

His appointment has also revived older questions. Smart News Liberia reported that his name appeared in a 2013 Liberia Anti-Corruption Commission asset verification that raised questions about deposits totaling more than US$300,000. His statement did not address it.

What the Senate should hold him to

Yekeson’s statement is the work of someone who knows the market’s pressure points. The question for senators is whether they will confirm the diagnosis or demand the mechanisms.

Five commitments would turn the speech into a record that can be checked:

1. Weekly county-level prices for rice, fuel and cement, published by the 100-day mark.

2. A date for the rule requiring traders to post the Central Bank’s daily exchange rate.

3. Publication of the full fuel pricing formula alongside pump prices.

4. An agency-by-agency report on the 25 percent procurement set-aside, with a deadline.

5. Full disclosure of his remaining business interests before confirmation.

He has offered quarterly reports to the committee. If confirmed, the first should show progress on each.

World.title: Liberia: Economist Samuel Jackson Appeals to Court for Permission to Travel Abroad Amid Health Concerns
World.content:
Jackson (center), who is seeking court permission to travel abroad for medical treatment, remains barred from leaving Liberia. He was seen being assisted by two men at the courthouse.

MONROVIA — Liberian economist and political commentator Samuel Jackson has appealed to Criminal Court “A” Judge Onesimus Barwon for permission to travel abroad for specialized medical treatment, citing concerns about his deteriorating health as he faces charges in connection with the death of his wife.

By Victoria Wesseh

Jackson was seen struggling to walk on the grounds of the Temple of Justice in Monrovia on Thursday, October 22, prompting renewed attention to his reported health condition.



The economist is seeking medical leave to obtain treatment outside Liberia but remains barred from leaving the country as his legal proceedings continue.

Jackson is facing charges in connection with the March 2026 death of his wife, Ntombi Khumalo Jackson, a South African attorney who was found dead in their Monrovia home.

Jackson told authorities that he discovered his wife semi-conscious in their bedroom after returning home from a television talk show engagement.

Khumalo Jackson, who was born in Gauteng, South Africa, was the founder of NK Attorneys. Her death attracted widespread public attention, particularly after images allegedly showing bruises and other injuries on her body circulated on social media.

Reports indicated that she suffered severe head injuries and required emergency brain surgery.

The circumstances surrounding her death have since become the subject of legal proceedings involving her husband.

Jackson’s request for permission to travel abroad for medical treatment now presents the court with a matter requiring consideration alongside the conditions imposed on him as the case proceeds.

The court’s decision on his request was not immediately available.

World.title: Liberia: War Victims, Survivors Protest at Court Office, Capitol as House Chairman Pledges to Put Court Bill Before Plenary Tuesday
World.content:
Some of the protesters at the war crimes court office. Credit: Anthony Stephens/New Narratives.

Hundreds of war victims, survivors and justice advocates protested at the war crimes court office and the Capitol Building, demanding approval of legislation to establish the long-awaited court.

A disagreement erupted at the Capitol after a lawmaker said a legislative committee had decided to exclude economic crimes from the proposed court. Protesters objected, prompting another lawmaker to assure them that both categories of crimes would be covered.

The House Committee Chairman pledged to bring the matter before plenary Tuesday, as the government’s timetable for establishing the courts faces uncertainty.

By Anthony Stephens, senior justice correspondent with New Narratives

Hundreds of victims and survivors of Liberia’s civil wars, joined by justice advocates, protested Thursday outside the government office overseeing the establishment of a war crimes court, temporarily disrupting operations, before moving to the Capitol Building, where a senior lawmaker pledged to place the long-delayed legislation before the House plenary on Tuesday.

The peaceful demonstrations drew people with disabilities, rural women, elderly victims and survivors, young people, and traditional and religious leaders. For hours, protesters gathered outside the Office for the Establishment of the War and Economic Crimes Court, holding placards demanding justice. One read: “REAL PEACE IS NOT THE SILENCE OF GUNS. REAL PEACE IS DISPENSING JUSTICE AND ENDING IMPUNITY. WE CALL ON THE EXECUTIVE AND LEGISLATURE TO GIVE THE PEOPLE JUSTICE & ACCOUNTABILITY NOW…”



“What’s going on wrong? We are suffering,” said Korpo Dennis, president of the Women in Peacebuilding Network, her voice cracking as she broke down in tears, burying her face in her lappa, a traditional cloth wrapped around her waist. Addressing Jallah Barbu, the office’s executive director, Dennis questioned why President Joseph Boakai had not raised the issue at the United Nations General Assembly, as she said he had promised. “He na come, we can hear nothing. We want answer today or else, we will sleep on this street.”

The protests underscored mounting frustration over Liberia’s failure to establish a court to prosecute atrocities committed during its civil wars, more than two decades after the fighting ended. Despite repeated government commitments and consultations, competing bills remain before lawmakers, leaving uncertain when those accused of wartime crimes will face prosecution.

Dennis’s organization was among the women’s peace groups widely credited with helping pressure Liberia’s warring factions to end the conflicts.

Barbu told protesters he remained confident that Boakai had not abandoned his commitment to establishing the court. Prevented from entering his office, along with other staff, he unsuccessfully attempted to reach House Speaker Richard Koon by telephone.

He then contacted James Verdier, the speaker’s chief of staff, who assured protesters that the legislation would be approved. Unsatisfied, the protesters moved to Capitol Hill to press lawmakers directly.

Kula Fofana, Boakai’s press secretary, did not respond to a request for comment on the protesters’ concerns.

“It has taken us too long,” said Jeremiah D. Cooper, a member of the Group of 77, an organization representing people with disabilities. “The same Liberian people who voted for you are the same Liberian people demanding that you pass certain documents in the interest of the country,” he added. “You people say you will not do it. Why?”

Jeremiah D. Cooper, one of the protesters.

But the gathering soon exposed a disagreement over whether the proposed court would prosecute both war crimes and economic crimes.

Prescilla A. Cooper, a Montserrado County representative and member of the House Committee on Claims and Petitions, told protesters that a joint legislative committee tasked with harmonizing the competing bills had agreed to proceed with legislation establishing a war crimes court, leaving economic crimes to be handled separately by the Liberia Anti-Corruption Commission.

The protesters rejected her account, insisting that economic crimes allegedly committed during Liberia’s civil wars must also fall within the proposed court’s jurisdiction.

Justice advocates have long argued that including economic crimes would allow the court to order convicted warlords and other perpetrators, including institutions found responsible, to pay restitution to victims and communities harmed by their actions.

Prince Toles, chairman of the House Committee on Claims and Petitions, sought to reassure the protesters, saying he shared their position that the legislation should establish a War and Economic Crimes Court.

“We signed it in 2024 (the joint resolution). We signed it 5G. But this one, we will give it 20G,” Toles said, referring to the Legislature’s earlier support for establishing the court. “If people did not rob the system, all of us would have lived better. I want to tell you that we are with you.”

“We will bring this matter before plenary,” Toles said. “But if they ask us to bring a paper signed by the different stakeholders, I will just propose that you draft something for us temporarily. Bring it here tomorrow (Friday), then I will put it on the floor on Tuesday.”

Plenary, the full membership of either legislative chamber, is its highest decision-making body. Toles’s pledge does not guarantee a vote or passage Tuesday.

House leaders subsequently invited protest organizers to a meeting.

“We feel a little bit relieved that it will work,” Peterson Sonyah, executive director of the Liberia Massacre Survivors Association, said by phone afterward. “We are impressed with the discussion. We are planning to be there on Tuesday.”

The protests came as Liberia approaches a deadline in its plans to establish the courts.

Under a 36-page roadmap submitted to Boakai in July 2025 , the court office projected that the National Anti-Corruption Court would be operational by November 2026, followed by the War and Economic Crimes Court in November 2027.

With neither court’s establishing legislation approved, the timetable faces uncertainty. The roadmap also envisaged completing trials by 2031, after which the war crimes court would transition to a residual mechanism.

Liberia is also preparing to assume the rotating presidency of the United Nations Security Council in December, a moment justice advocates say will draw international attention to the country’s unfinished accountability efforts.

A FrontPage Africa/New Narratives survey of 1,150 people across 11 counties found that 91 percent supported establishing the court, while 89 percent said they would not vote for lawmakers opposing it.

The survey was not scientifically sampled. Only 4 percent of respondents reported awareness of lawmakers’ consultations on the proposed court.

The legislative process has been complicated by six competing proposals.

They include a War Crimes Court bill from the Liberian National Bar Association ; a separate proposal from civil society organizations working with the Independent National Commission on Human Rights ; and two bills introduced by Senate President Pro Tempore Nyonblee Karnga-Lawrence and Senator Joseph Jallah , one proposing a War Crimes Court and another a Special Economic and Corruption Crimes Court.

The remaining two bills were prepared by the court office , proposing a War and Economic Crimes Court and a separate National Anti-Corruption Court. Boakai subsequently forwarded both proposals to the Legislature .

The senators’ proposals drew criticism from justice advocates , who warned that provisions concerning jurisdiction and appeals could weaken wartime accountability.

In June, more than 40 House members attended a two-day technical deliberation in Buchanan, Grand Bassa County , organized by the court office and its partners to examine the legislation.

Separately, the Senate Committee on Judiciary, Human Rights, Claims and Petitions began consultations on the competing bills , seeking to resolve differences over senior appointments, prosecutorial independence and appeals.

The committee also outlined plans to harmonize the proposals , with further consultations and hearings expected before the legislative session ended.

Neither chamber approved the legislation before lawmakers departed for their constituency break.

The Legislature was scheduled to return October 9, but a dispute over lawmakers’ benefits delayed the House’s reopening. Regular business resumed October 13.

For Sonyah and the other organizers, Tuesday will test the assurances they received. They intend to return to the Capitol to see whether the matter reaches plenary — and whether the proposed legislation retains both war crimes and economic crimes.

This story was a collaboration with New Narratives as part of the Investigating Liberia project. Funding was provided by the U.N. Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights and the European Union. The funders had no say in the story’s content.

World.title: Lavushimanda DEBS cites career guidance gap
World.content:
Lavushimanda District Education Board Secretary (DEBS) Beatus Nshenda has observed that most learners from rural schools end up choosing wrong careers because of lack of exposure to other professions.

Mr Nshenda says the limitation in career choices by most school leavers is because they chose to become like the people they interact within their localities.

He was speaking today when he addressed learners during the first career’s Day for Mununga Day Secondary School held at the school.

“Some of you don’t even know what you want to become when you complete school because you are not exposed to other professions,” he said.

And Mr Nshenda said Careers Day in schools is an important event that gives learners exposure to diverse professionals.

He says careers day also connects classroom learning to real world jobs and inspires learners to early career planning.

The DEBS further said the purpose of careers day is to help learners understand the different career opportunities so that they make proper choices in future and avoid ending up in wrong careers where they may be frustrated.

He added that education is the foundation of every opportunity one can get in life, adding that learners must put education first even if they may want to become farmers or entrepreneurs.

Mr Nshenda encouraged learners to take education seriously, set clear goals and choose careers according to their interest.

And Mununga Day Secondary School Head Boy Chipo Kunda said he is grateful to the school authorities for organising a careers’ day.

He said the event has given learners a clear picture of different professions.

“We are grateful for this day because we have learnt a lot from professionals from different departments,” he said.

Another grade 11 pupil, Kezia Wingabile said her dream of becoming a lawyer will be achieved as she has insight of what it takes to study law.

“Some of us will come back and show you that we have achieved what we learnt at this careers day,” she said.

And Evance Kolala, another grade 11 pupil said the careers day has opened his mind and made him understand what he will become in future.

“I want to be a police officer and I have learnt what it takes and what I should have in order to become one,” he said.

The Mununga Day Secondary school first ever careers day saw people from various government departments such as Agriculture, Health, Information, the judiciary, engineers from the local authority and others giving career talks to the learners.

Other people who spoke to the learners at the event were from the Tanzania Zambia Railway Authority (TAZARA) and the Tanzania, Zambia Mafuta (TAZAMA) as well as engineers.

World.title: Mukubesa calls for child-focused growth
World.content:
Ministry of Finance and National Planning Permanent Secretary for Budget and Economic Affairs Mwaka Mukubesa says Zambia’s Grow Zambia Agenda must translate economic growth into improved living conditions for vulnerable citizens, particularly children.

Mrs Mukubesa said economic growth would only be meaningful if its benefits reached all citizens and improved access to essential services such as education, healthcare and nutrition.

She was speaking today at Kabwata Orphanage and Transit Centre in Lusaka when she handed over donated foodstuffs, bedding and other essential supplies to support children at the institution ahead of Zambia’s 62nd Independence anniversary.

Mrs Mukubesa said the donation was in line with this year’s Independence theme, “Zambia @62 Our Journey, Our Growth, Our Future,” which calls for reflection on the country’s development journey and a renewed commitment to an inclusive and prosperous future.

She said the government’s Grow Zambia Agenda, which seeks to accelerate economic growth, unlock productive potential and create employment opportunities, should ensure that vulnerable groups are not left behind.

Mrs Mukubesa stressed that investing in children’s welfare, education, healthcare, nutrition and protection was essential to building the country’s human capital and securing its future prosperity.

“The children we nurture today are the citizens, innovators, entrepreneurs and leaders who will shape our country tomorrow,” she said.

She said the donated items were intended to provide practical assistance to the centre and improve the comfort and well-being of the children under its care.

Mrs Mukubesa added that, beyond material assistance, children needed access to quality education, adequate nutrition, healthcare and psychosocial support to enable them to develop their abilities and reach their full potential.

She said the Ministry remained committed to supporting responsible financial planning and the allocation of public resources towards policies and programmes that addressed the needs of vulnerable populations.

Mrs Mukubesa has urged Zambians to work together in building a prosperous nation where every child had an equal opportunity to learn, develop and contribute to national development, regardless of their circumstances.

Meanwhile, Ministry Director of Economic, Human Resource and Administration, Nalituba Mwale said every child deserved an opportunity to develop their potential and contribute meaningfully to the country’s future.

Mrs Mwale said independence is not only about celebrating the country’s freedom but also reflecting on the collective responsibility to ensure that every child had an opportunity to succeed.

She urged communities to work together to protect children, nurture their abilities and create a future where no child felt forgotten or left behind.

Mrs Mwale encouraged the children at the institution to remain hopeful, continue learning and pursue their dreams despite the challenges they might face.

She also commended caregivers for their dedication to supporting vulnerable children and urged them to continue with their work of providing care and guidance.

And Founder and Director of Kabwata Orphanage and Transit Centre, Angela Miyanda, has urged the Permanent Secretary to present issues affecting children at the institution that may require assistance.

Mrs Miyanda said the occasion was significant as the country prepares to celebrate its independence tomorrow.

Mrs Miyanda said Independence Day serves as a reminder of the importance of peace, noting that some of the children at the centre are refugees.

She said the presence of refugee children at the institution highlights the importance of appreciating the peace Zambia enjoys.

World.title: Veep welcomes President Hichilema’s Vice-Chairpersonship to COMESA
World.content:
Vice President Mutale Nalumango says President Hakainde Hichilema’s election to the Vice-Chairpersonship of the Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa (COMESA) will support the country’s vision for the grow Zambia agenda.

Mrs Nalumango says the Grow Zambia Agenda is an export-based programme, and COMESA provides an important platform for Zambia to advance its agenda, as trade requires working with other nations.

She added that COMESA also plays a role in advancing the African Continental Free Trade Area, Therefore, taking a leading role in the organisation is a positive development.

Speaking during the Vice President’s question time in Parliament, Mrs Nalumango noted that COMESA is an opportunity for Zambia to benefit from the vast market represented by member countries.

“His vision and recognition for his economic acumen should be appreciated. His leadership will help strengthen COMESA by bringing to the table the kind of leadership that is needed,” she noted.

Meanwhile, she further stated that providing land for COMESA is also very important because it will facilitate the development of infrastructure, indicating that under the Grow Zambia Agenda, this includes energy trading, interconnectivity and other infrastructure needed to support economic growth.

“We need leadership that can bring member states together and encourage them to work towards linking our regions through improved infrastructure,” she said.

And Mrs Nalumango says the maize export market is open, indicating that exports are already permitted within the existing arrangements.

She explained that arrangements are already in place for maize exports to countries such as Kenya and the Democratic Republic of the Congo, which have placed orders, while the government is considering Malawi as another market.

The Vice President has clarified that there is no load shedding in the country, but that the power interruptions being experienced in parts of Lusaka are due to ZESCO scheduled maintenance and other works.

Mrs Nalumango explained that the work being undertaken goes beyond routine maintenance, indicating that substantial investment and work are required to expand and improve the country’s electricity network.

“There are areas where people are experiencing interruptions to their electricity supply, but these interruptions are not necessarily the result of load shedding,” she said.

She highlighted Zambia’s long-term objective to achieve wider electricity coverage by around 2030 or 2031, saying that it requires considerable work on transmission lines and distribution networks, thereby resulting in temporary disruptions to electricity supply.

World.title: Lions club donates wheelchairs, supplies to UTH
World.content:
The Lions Club of Sunningdale has donated 10 wheelchairs, kitchenware and associated cleaning products at University Teaching Adult Hospital (UTH) Emergency Ward.

Speaking at the handover, UTH Senior Medical Superintendent, Charles Mbewe welcomed the Club’s gesture expressing that it will improve access to emergency care by providing mobility to patients that are unable to move.

Dr Mbewe said the donation demonstrates the vital role that service organisations play in supporting and complementing government efforts to enhance healthcare delivery.

“We are particularly encouraged by the Lions Club’s commitment to serving communities and supporting those in need,” he said.

Dr Mbewe further pledged to put the donations to good use by meeting the needs of patients who depend on the services offered at the emergency department.

Meanwhile, Lions Club President, Jonathan Maliki stated that the club responded to the needs of the hospital as it understands that a wheelchair can make a difference.

“From our visits we have observed a serious shortage of equipment and supplies and decided to extend this gesture,” he said.

Mr Maliki stated that the donation will make a difference because without enough functional wheelchairs, patient’s lives are endangered.

World.title: Government urges Local Leaders to Drive Grow Zambia Agenda
World.content:
Government has urged Mayors, Council Chairpersons and Councillors across the country to take an active role in spearheading development projects and advancing the Grow Zambia Agenda.

Cabinet Office Permanent Secretary for Special Duties, Wisdom Bwalya says civic leaders should prioritise development and avoid unnecessary conflicts that may hinder progress in their respective districts.

Mr Bwalya said this in Chongwe district when he officially closed a five-day training workshop for a cohort of newly elected civic leaders at Chalimbana Local Government Institute.

He also presented certificates to participants, who included Mayors, Council Chairpersons, Councillors and traditional leaders.

He emphasised that all leaders serving in councils, regardless of how they were appointed or elected, had a common responsibility of promoting development and should therefore be treated equally.

The PS urged the civic leaders to embrace one another and work collectively towards addressing the needs of the people in their respective communities.

He also acknowledged the important role traditional leaders play in resolving conflicts and supporting local development initiatives.

Meanwhile, Chalimbana Local Government Institute Principal James Paipi said the training was designed to equip the newly elected civic leaders with the knowledge and skills required to effectively discharge their responsibilities.

Mr Paipi said the training had brought together various categories of councillors, including those elected from wards, traditional leaders and representatives appointed through the mixed-member proportional representation system.

And Chongwe Mayor Frederick Saashi said the participants would apply the knowledge acquired during the training to improve the performance of their respective local authorities.

Mr Sashi described the training as an eye-opener that had enhanced the participants’ understanding of their civic responsibilities.

The Mayor assured that the participants would return to their respective districts with valuable knowledge to support effective service delivery and local development.

World.title: Chongwe Council relocates illegal CBD traders
World.content:
Chongwe Municipal Council has started relocating traders operating illegally within the Central Business District (CBD) to designated temporary trading areas at the Showgrounds.

Chongwe Municipal Council Assistant Public Relations Manager Cecilia Musonda says some vendors had been trading on Chongwe Primary School grounds and along the road frontage of Mount Meru Filling Station along Great East road.

Ms Musonda said the relocation exercise follows concerns over the use of undesignated trading spaces, which have contributed to disorder, obstruction of public spaces and challenges in maintaining sanitation and hygiene.

She said the practice also interferes with the proper use of public infrastructure and poses potential risks to public health and safety.

Ms Musonda explained that the Showgrounds had been identified as a suitable temporary trading area because it has functional ablution facilities and a water supply to support trading activities and promote hygiene.

She added that the council had rehabilitated the shelter at Chongwe Old Market to provide temporary trading space for some of the affected vendors.

“The intervention would help ease pressure on the available trading spaces as the Council mobilises resources towards completing the new Chongwe Modern Market, which is being constructed by the Zambia National Service (ZNS),” she said.

The Assistant Public Relations Manager

said the modern market project had made considerable progress and remained a key priority for the Council.

“Upon completion, the facility is expected to accommodate a significantly larger number of traders in a more organised and suitable trading environment,” Ms Musonda said.

She emphasised that the relocation exercise was intended to balance traders’ economic activities with the need to enforce compliance with applicable laws and regulations, maintain order and ensure that public spaces were used for their intended purposes.

Ms Musonda appealed to all traders to cooperate with the relocation exercise and conduct their businesses only in designated trading areas.

World.title: Chilanga acting DC calls for digital learning
World.content:
Chilanga Acting District Commissioner Maureen Chilende has urged schools to embrace technology for the development of digital skills for learners.

Speaking when she officiated at the Great Scholars Academy Private School’s Ninth Graduation Ceremony, Ms Chilende said the world of technology is rapidly changing, hence schools must evolve to acquire new knowledge and skills in technology and science.

Ms Chilende commended Great Scholars Academy for establishing a computer laboratory saying it will enable learners to acquire digital skills.

She encouraged learners to use technology innovatively and to carry out problem-solving research for the betterment of the country.

“We are living in a world where digital skills are increasingly important in almost every profession. Our learners must be prepared to use technology responsibly and productively,” Ms Chilende said.

Ms Chilende noted that the Great Scholars Academy Private school is an example of how the Government’s vision of Public-Private Partnerships (PPP) in the education sector can be reflected.

She added that private schools supplement the government’s efforts in the education sector by expanding access and creating opportunities for children.

World.title: Chilengi urges private sector to complement Government’s efforts
World.content:
Minister of Health Roma Chilengi has called on private sector companies to invest in the upgrade of mental health facilities to promote quality health service delivery.

The call follows Finsbury Reinsurance Limited’s contribution of more than K400,000 towards the refurbishment of B Ward at Chainama Hills Hospital.

Professor Chilengi says corporate social responsibility initiatives are important in complementing government efforts to strengthen healthcare delivery and improve conditions for patients and healthcare workers.

He made the remarks during the official handover of the refurbished B Ward at Chainama Hills Hospital, undertaken by Finsbury Reinsurance Limited under its corporate social responsibility programme.

Professor Chilengi said the contribution demonstrated how Zambian companies could respond to community needs and create a lasting social impact beyond their core business operations.

He challenged other companies to emulate Finsbury Reinsurance Limited, saying increased private sector participation could significantly improve conditions at the mental health institution.

He said the Government values partnerships with the private sector, civil society and other stakeholders in advancing the country’s development agenda.

Professor Chilengi also commended the hospital’s management and staff for continuing to care for patients under difficult working conditions.

Speaking at the same event, Finsbury Reinsurance Limited Chief Executive Officer and Managing Director, Webster Twaambo, said the company had spent more than K400,000 on items and renovation works at the hospital.

Dr Twaambo said the contribution included 20 metal beds, 10 benches, replacement of ceiling boards in the dining area, roofing of a shelter, repairs to the water reticulation system and repainting of the ward.

He explained that the support was intended to improve the safety, comfort and dignity of patients, healthcare workers and visitors at the institution.

Dr Twaambo highlighted that the contribution marked the beginning of the company’s commitment to supporting Chainama Hills Hospital and called on other institutions to contribute towards improving mental health services.

Meanwhile, Chainama Hills Hospital Senior Medical Superintendent, Margaret Chibowa, thanked Finsbury Reinsurance Limited for selecting the institution as a beneficiary of its corporate social responsibility initiative.

Dr Chibowa said the contribution would help create a better environment for patients and demonstrate that healthcare workers’ efforts are recognised and appreciated by the wider community.

And Chainama Hills Hospital Principal Hospital Administrator, Cecilia Chisaka, expressed gratitude to the Minister of Health for officiating at the handover ceremony, saying his presence demonstrated the Government’s commitment to strengthening healthcare delivery.

She added that the refurbishment of B Ward was a meaningful investment in the well-being, dignity, safety and comfort of patients, and thanked Finsbury Reinsurance Limited for its contribution towards improving the hospital’s facilities.

World.title: Congo-Kinshasa: As Ebola Spreads to 8th DR Congo Province, Families Battle to Feed Themselves
World.content:
A health worker carries a stretcher into an Ebola treatment centre in the DR Congo.

Geneva — Hunger in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DR Congo) is undermining efforts to combat Ebola as the deadly disease has expanded across borders and also to an eighth province of the huge central African country, the UN said on Friday.

Families facing Ebola in the DR Congo, which has a population of more than 105 million, can find that protecting themselves from the virus can also mean losing the means to feed their children, according to the UN’s World Food Programme (WFP).

“Today, the outbreak has spread to an eighth province, reaching communities already under immense pressure,” David Stevenson, the WFP's DRC country director, said during a UN press conference.

“As it spreads, hunger continues to undermine the measures needed to contain it.”

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

And earlier in the week, the World Health Organisation (WHO), on Oct. 20, said that Nigeria has confirmed one imported case of Ebola Bundibugyo virus disease in the Federal Capital Territory (FCT).

It became the fifth country to detect the virus since the DRC declared an outbreak on May 15.

The spread of the disease comes as agencies fighting the escalating Ebola virus in the DRC constantly battle to win the trust of local communities, according to international groups in the field calling for the protection of health workers.

Stevenson said that the WFP has two critical roles: helping families seek care without sacrificing food and providing the logistics backbone that keeps the wider response moving.

“Without sustained support, we risk leaving families unable to follow health guidance when it matters most.”

The WFP official explained that in Ituri’s Mungbwalu, the epicentre of the outbreak, Francine Birungi Amoti has lost a child to Ebola.

“She is raising her six surviving children and another baby entrusted to her care. Violence has cut her off from her fields.

“She told me, ‘If you go, you may not even return alive, and I do not have money to buy food at the local market. So we stay at home, and WFP helps us enormously.’”

For Francine, food assistance means feeding the children in her care when reaching her fields could cost her life.

'INSECURITY AND HUNGER'

“This is what a crisis on top of a crisis looks like: disease and bereavement, compounded by insecurity and hunger,” said Stevenson.

He also cited the case in North-Kivu’s Butembo, where Isabelle Kyakimwa arrived at an Ebola treatment centre without strength.

“As she recovered, she told us: ‘Food is important for us as patients because it helps us regain the strength to keep going.’

Close 

Her words show what food assistance brings to a treatment centre: regular, safe, nutritious meals that support recovery, dignity, and continuity of care.

“Food does not treat Ebola. Medical teams do,” said Stevenson.

“But their work takes place amid severe food insecurity and continued violence that repeatedly displaces families, destroys livelihoods and complicates access to care.”

He said food assistance is vital to supporting patients through that care and that WFP needs $115 million over the next six months, including $79 million for hot meals and dry rations.

World.title: Kenya: Calls for Penalties Follow 12-Story Building Collapse
World.content:
A building under construction collapsed in the Eastleigh neighborhood of Nairobi.

Nairobi — Nairobi Governor Johnson Sakaja has called for tougher penalties against rogue developers and the restoration of prosecutorial powers to county governments following the collapse of an incomplete 12-storey building in Eastleigh.

Sakaja said weak penalties for violating construction regulations undermine enforcement efforts and allow developers to compromise building safety, putting lives at risk.

Speaking as he led multi-agency rescue operations at the site along 1st Avenue, 9th Street, the Governor urged professional bodies representing architects, engineers and quantity surveyors to take action against developers who dismiss qualified experts after obtaining construction approvals.



He said some developers engage licensed professionals to secure approvals but subsequently remove them from projects and proceed with construction using unqualified personnel, undermining safeguards intended to ensure buildings meet approved designs and safety standards.

"We have formally written to the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions, and we hope our request will be considered. Counties must be empowered to take firm action against rogue developers who disregard building regulations and put lives at risk," Sakaja said.

The Governor questioned the deterrent effect of existing penalties, noting that some developers found guilty of violating construction regulations could face fines as low as Sh5,000.

"Even when such offenders are arrested and taken to court, the penalties can be as low as Sh5,000, which is not a sufficient deterrent," he said.

Sakaja argued that restoring prosecutorial powers to county governments would strengthen enforcement and enable authorities to take firmer action against developers who disregard approved construction plans and safety requirements.

He called on professional associations representing architects, engineers, quantity surveyors and builders to collaborate with county governments in identifying and investigating cases where qualified professionals are withdrawn from construction sites under questionable circumstances.

The Governor said the bodies should take appropriate disciplinary action against professionals found culpable, adding that experts responsible for building design, supervision and safety must be allowed to discharge their duties without interference.

Sakaja also reiterated the need for developers to obtain occupation certificates before putting buildings into use. He said structures must undergo the necessary inspections to establish that they are safe and fit for occupation.

According to the Governor, developers are required to secure county approvals, engage qualified professionals and sign indemnity forms committing them to comply with approved plans and construction standards.

However, he said some developers disregard these commitments after obtaining approvals, compromising the integrity of construction projects.

The calls for stronger enforcement came after an incomplete 12-storey building collapsed in Eastleigh, triggering a multi-agency search and rescue operation amid fears that people were trapped beneath the rubble.

The building was still under construction, with the ground floor occupied at the time of the collapse.

Nairobi City County emergency response teams were coordinating operations alongside the National Disaster Operations Centre, the Kenya Red Cross, the Kenya Defence Forces and other agencies.

Heavy machinery had been deployed to clear debris and create access to sections where victims could be trapped, as additional resources were mobilised to support the rescue effort.

Sakaja urged families and members of the public with information about missing persons to report to designated centres established by rescue teams at the scene.

Close 

Residents were also advised to share information through the county's emergency hotlines, 1508 and 1199.

"Our health teams are on standby to provide immediate medical attention and support rescue efforts as soon as victims are reached. We are doing everything possible to ensure the operation proceeds as quickly and safely as possible," he said.

The collapse has renewed scrutiny of building safety enforcement in Nairobi, particularly compliance with approved construction plans, the engagement of qualified professionals and inspections at different stages of development.

Sakaja said stronger legal powers, tougher penalties and closer collaboration between county governments and professional bodies were necessary to hold developers accountable and prevent similar incidents.

He maintained that restoring county prosecutorial powers would complement existing inspection and enforcement mechanisms by strengthening the ability of local authorities to pursue violations of construction regulations.

World.title: Rwanda: Kagame Defends Strict Dress Codes Amid Rwanda's Dressing Controversy
World.content:
Rwandan President Paul Kagame has defended cultural expectations on dressing, arguing that societies have their own standards of acceptable behaviour which should not be abandoned simply because other countries embrace different ways of life.

Speaking on Thursday while addressing more than 10,000 young Rwandans at BK Arena in Kigali during the "Meet The President" session, Kagame said dress codes should be understood within the context of the places people visit and the values of the society in which they live.

"If you are going to the beach, by the water, where people go to relax, there is a certain way you can dress and behave that may be different from other places. That is perfectly acceptable. But imagine someone coming here dressed as though they were at the beach. Would that work? Wouldn't you all turn around and wonder, what happened to this person?" Kagame asked.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

His remarks come amid a growing debate in Rwanda over restrictions on women's dressing, following incidents in which women have faced scrutiny over their clothing in public spaces.

The debate intensified after a video circulated showing police officers forcefully handcuffing a young woman wearing a miniskirt at a bus park in Rubavu.

The Rwanda National Police subsequently cleared the woman of wrongdoing and detained the officers involved pending disciplinary review.

The incident also drew criticism from human rights advocates and public commentators, who argued that cultural values should not be used to justify police intimidation, harassment or arbitrary enforcement of dress standards against women.

Addressing the wider debate, Kagame said the expectations should apply to men as well, arguing that discussions about dressing are often unfairly directed at women.

"By the way, this is not just about women. Most of the time, these things are made to be about women, but the same applies to men. Even now, imagine we are sitting here, and a man suddenly walks in, as though he has just come from the gym, wearing shorts, with nothing on his upper body, and comes to sit among us. People would ask, what happened to this person? Did he forget where he was going?" he said.

Kagame argued that societies should be allowed to maintain their own social standards rather than adopt practices from other countries without considering whether they fit local values.

He said people's willingness to participate in a particular social setting could also depend on the expectations established by those organising it.

"Now, if we had all agreed to come dressed that way, then perhaps that is how it would be. But some people would not come. Isn't that so? Some would simply decide not to attend, saying, we are not going to be part of that," he said.

The Rwandan leader said communities have ways of regulating behaviour through shared expectations and self-regulation, adding that practices accepted elsewhere should not automatically be embraced by Rwandans.

"There is a way society regulates itself, including through self-regulation. But when you simply say, we have seen this elsewhere, so let us do the same here, and you bring it into our society, society may tell you, we have not reached that point yet. Perhaps we were moving in that direction, but we are not there yet," Kagame said.

He called for disagreements over cultural values to be handled through dialogue rather than hostility, saying people should be able to reach an understanding when differences emerge.

"That should not create any hostility. There should be a way of regulating these things so that people can come to an understanding," he said.

Kagame compared society's response to unfamiliar practices to the body's reaction to a foreign object, which it gradually attempts to remove.

"It is like a foreign body. I think those of you in the medical profession know this. When a foreign object, a fragment of something, enters the body, the body tends to reject it. It keeps pushing it out. Even when a thorn gets stuck in your skin, if you leave it there for some time, it begins to work its way out. Eventually, you find it near the surface and remove it. Society works in much the same way," he said.

He added that tensions can arise when individuals seek to introduce practices that conflict with the established values of a community, while other members of that society resist the changes.

"A healthy society, with its own way of functioning, when something unfamiliar is introduced into it, gradually, little by little, that society begins to push it away. There is then a struggle between someone trying to change society to fit something they have brought from elsewhere, and society itself saying, do not bring these things here, and pushing that person away. But there should be no conflict. That is how these things should work," Kagame said.

Close 

He urged young people to reflect on the values they want for themselves and the direction in which they want their society to develop.

"Young people like you should keep these things in mind. Think about them. Understand what it is that you want for yourselves," he said.

Kagame also called for open discussions about changing social norms, urging young Rwandans to question practices that are becoming more common but which they consider inconsistent with their culture or harmful to society.

"Even here, in our discussions, people should be able to raise these questions and say, there are things we have seen becoming increasingly accepted in our society, yet they are not part of our culture. They do not even bring us any benefit. Why should we accept them, especially when they are things that harm people? Why?" he asked.

World.title: Nigeria: Health Is Economic Infrastructure - Why Nigeria Must Invest in Health
World.content:
blog

Listen to this article 8 min The recently concluded World Health Summit in Berlin, themed "From Crisis to Resilience: Innovating for Health", reinforced a key message: health spending is an investment, not just an expense. Yet Nigeria's 2026 Appropriation Bill proposed ₦2.48 trillion for health out of ₦58.47 trillion, about 4.2% of the budget. That is less than a third of the 15% target African governments agreed to in the 2001 Abuja Declaration.

Closing this gap requires recognising health as an investment in economic growth, much like roads and power. Nigeria's growth ambitions depend on people being healthy enough to participate in the economy. Health should therefore be treated as economic infrastructure in the country's development priorities and budget decisions.

What the evidence actually supports

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Egypt's experience illustrates the potential economic returns of health investment. At the summit session Funding the Future: Unlocking the Economic and Fiscal Returns of Health Innovation, Khaled Abdel Ghaffar, Egypt's Minister of Health and Population, described a $240 million early-detection programme reaching 60 million people, followed by affordable generic treatment. It was projected to save $7 billion by 2030, a 688% return.

However, these are projections, not a confirmed result. For Nigeria, achieving comparable gains would require screening capacity and reliable medicine supplies that are not yet available at the same scale. Martin Seychell, Deputy Director-General at DG INTPA at the European Commission, cautioned that better outcomes depend on how the money is spent.

"We should not make the mistake of simply gauging and assessing efforts simply on the basis of how much money we are investing in health budgets. Because we know, of course, if you underinvest, you will not get good outcomes. But it doesn't follow that if you just increase the health budgets without a clear strategy, you will get better outcomes."

Nigeria's clearest return is household income

One of the clearest benefits for Nigeria is the funds families could keep if healthcare were more affordable. At the Health as an Investment: Preparing Systems & Societies for the 21st Century session, Dr Githinji Gitahi, Group CEO, Amref Health Africa singled out Nigeria when discussing the high out-of-pocket health expenditure, noting that what people pay out of pocket is "ridiculously higher than the government spends."

People pay about 71.9% of current health expenditure out of pocket. An analysis of the 2023/24 General Household Survey found that 45.5% of households faced catastrophic health spending, meaning health costs accounted for at least 10% of their household budget. These bills can force families to borrow, sell belongings or cut spending on food and education.

During the Strategic Health Economy session, Dr Ezekwesili recalled that evidence showing that malaria cost Africa about 2% of its GDP "changed the conversation" with ministers and described the disease as a "productivity tax on the economies." The Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare estimates that malaria reduces Nigeria's GDP by more than $1.1 billion each year, while Nigeria accounts for 27% of global cases.

At the same session, Dr Satoshi Ezoe, Japan's Assistant Minister for Global Health, explained that Japan reached universal health coverage in 1961 while still recovering from the Second World War, and argued that "we laid the foundation by making UHC, which led to socioeconomic development."

Nigeria is one of the first eight countries in the UHC Knowledge Hub, a Japanese initiative with the World Health Organization and the World Bank that brings health and finance ministries together to plan for universal coverage. Successful coverage should mean fewer families are pushed into hardship by medical bills and fewer workdays lost, not enrolment figures alone.

Who captures the value?

The economic case for health investment extends to building local industries and creating employment opportunities. Yet Africa captures little of the value from the health products it uses, as Dr Obiageli Ezekwesili, founder and chief executive officer of Human Capital Africa, told the summit during the session The Strategic Health Economy:

"[Africa's] capacity in terms of... global manufacturing... it's less than 5%. Then you look at... competitiveness... how much value does Africa gain from the health value chain -- also insignificant...

Nigeria aims to increase local production of essential health products to 70% by 2030. The Presidential Initiative for Unlocking the Healthcare Value Chain is supported by tax and duty waivers on pharmaceutical inputs and about $2 billion in financing commitments.

However, packaging imported products locally is not the same as making them locally. Manufacturers still rely on imported active pharmaceutical ingredients to produce medicines, leaving them exposed to foreign-exchange fluctuations and price volatility.

Local production also needs skilled workers, as does the wider health system. Nigeria has 95,456 registered doctors but only 60,551 with active practising licenses, while its 2024 National Policy on Health Workforce Migration requires wider implementation.

The role of policy in enabling health workers to deliver care also features in the summit session Health as an Investment: Preparing Systems & Societies for the 21st Century, where Dr Githinji Gitahi, Group CEO of Amref Health Africa, stressed its importance for community health workers.

Making investment accountable

Funding also must reach the services it is meant for. At the Health as an Investment: Preparing Systems & Societies for the 21st Century session, Dr Gitahi warned that prevention and vaccination budgets "are the first to be cut" when fiscal space tightens, because their results are less visible.

Nigeria shows the risk: in 2025, only ₦36 million of the ₦218 billion appropriated for federal health capital projects was released. For Nigeria, the value of health investment lies in the industries it builds and the workers it equips. Realising that value requires funding, procurement and regulation to support these goals.

Close 

The following steps could help put this into practice;

The Office of the Accountant-General and Budget Office should include health infrastructure in quarterly cash plans and publish how much funding is released.

The National Health Insurance Authority (NHIA) and state schemes should automatically enrol eligible conditional cash transfer beneficiaries and publish whether enrolment reduces their out-of-pocket spending. In addition, the NHIA, the National Primary Health Care Development Agency (NPHCDA), and state governments could consider offering qualified Nigerian manufacturers multi-year purchasing agreements with clear standards for price, quality, and delivery. Reliable demand would make it easier for manufacturers to invest.

Incentives under the Presidential Initiative for Unlocking the Healthcare Value Chain (PVAC) and NAFDAC approval pathways should reward verified local production, including making ingredients and meeting quality standards. Annual reporting should show which products are replacing imports.

Health belongs in Nigeria's growth strategy for the same reason ports and power do: the economy depends on it. That case must be reflected in funding released on time, stronger local production and affordable, quality care. Nigeria needs to spend more on health, use the funds strategically and measure whether people and the economy are better off.

World.title: South Africa: How Nurses Are Learning to Administer the New HIV Prevention Injection
World.content:
South Africa's rollout of lenacapavir, a six-monthly HIV prevention injection, requires nurses to learn, adapt and find ways to make it work for patients.

After 26 years in nursing, Sister Keitumetse "Tumi" Senokwane still had something new to learn about giving injections.

The six-monthly HIV-prevention jab, lenacapavir, often referred to as just LEN, presented a unique challenge.

"You know, lenacapavir is different. As much as I've got experience with injections, the needle size is different from the subcutaneous (beneath the skin) injections we are used to, and the solution is quite thick," says Senokwane. "Because we were not used to it, the practical training helped us to get used to it." She practised withdrawing the yellow liquid, using cooking oil as a stand-in.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

That kind of preparation matters because lenacapavir for HIV prevention is being introduced at a time when South Africa still has a substantial need for effective HIV prevention options. The country had an estimated 140 000 new HIV infections in 2025. Modelling suggests that scaling up lenacapavir to 1.4 million to 2.1 million initiations a year by 2030 could avert an average of 32 200 to 51 700 infections annually.

But realising lenacapavir's potential will depend on more than getting the injection into clinics. It also requires nurses to administer it correctly, answer patients' questions, and adapt services to their needs.

Getting to grips with lenacapavir

Senokwane is a professional nurse and site manager at Maria Rantho Community Health Centre and Phedisong 1 Clinic in Tshwane, which are participating in the Wits RHI Len4PrEP study.

"LEN4PrEP is an implementation research study, so looking at how we can deliver the product in a real-world setting," says study investigator Dr Catherine Martin.

The researchers recruited 1 544 participants between November 2025 and June 2026, with follow-up continuing until June 2027. The study began several months before South Africa's national rollout of lenacapavir on 5 June 2026, when the injection was launched at 360 public health facilities across six provinces.

By 8 October, 76 922 people had initiated LEN nationally, including 36 733 in 133 facilities in Gauteng, according to health department spokesperson Foster Mohale.

For Senokwane and her colleagues, administering lenacapavir meant learning a new HIV prevention method.

Nurses first had to complete a compulsory Nurse-Initiated Management of Antiretroviral Therapy (NIMART) course, which provides a theoretical foundation for managing HIV and antiretroviral treatment. This was followed by practical training in preparing and administering LEN.

Training also covered eligibility, side effects, HIV testing and counselling, with videos and clinical mentorship providing additional support.

Mohale says feedback from early-rollout clinics, nurses and patients would help the department refine its training and guidelines.

At the study clinics, nurses also had to adapt the service to patients' needs and fit the new injection method into existing care.

The one-stop shop

The Department of Health's lenacapavir implementation guidelines emphasise counselling clients on their HIV prevention options and helping them choose a method that suits their needs.

At the study clinics, nurses incorporated LEN into existing sexual and reproductive health services, allowing clients to access HIV prevention alongside services such as family planning and STI screening and treatment during a single visit.

"You will get all services in one room like a one-stop shop," says Senokwane.

"Maybe you are here for lenacapavir, but we also check whether you are on a family planning method. If not, we will give you information and provide a family planning method for you, where we screen you for STIs, and then if you've got some infections, we also treat you," she says.

The LEN4PrEP study also used a mobile clinic to bring HIV prevention and sexual and reproductive health services to young people in their communities.

"So many of our clients already know us. They know how we treat them and the quality of service we provide," she says.

Initial LEN consultations took longer as nurses explained the available prevention methods and how soon each would offer protection against HIV.

"We give you the information and explain how each method works, how long until it is effective. Participants would like to know when they are going to be protected from HIV if they take this specific method," says Senokwane.

At the Southern African HIV Clinicians Society's Long-Acting Antiretroviral Treatment Conference in Johannesburg in September, Wits RHI's Professor Saiqa Mullick, Director of Implementation Science, shared early findings from the LEN4PrEP study.

She reported that convenience was a major reason participants opted for the lenacapavir jab. They valued not having to take a daily pill or make frequent clinic visits, while the injection offered greater privacy for some. It also attracted people new to PrEP, alongside existing users seeking a method that better suited their lives.

Pre-exposure prophylaxis, or PrEP, refers to antiretroviral medicines taken to prevent HIV infection. When used as prescribed, oral PrEP has been shown to reduce the risk of HIV infection from sex. For several years now, HIV prevention tablets have been widely available in South Africa's public healthcare system, although uptake has been somewhat muted with only around 350 000 people taking the tablets in mid-2025, according to estimates from Thembisa, the leading mathematical model of HIV in South Africa.

Of the 1 538 participants whose method choices were reported, 85.8% selected the lenacapavir shot, compared with 13.7% who selected the prevention pills and 0.5% who chose not to use PrEP.

"People want options that fit into their lives," Mullick told delegates.

Sticking the landing

Patients could also choose where in the body to receive the injections: the upper arm, buttocks, abdomen or thigh.

Among the 1 319 participants who started LEN, Mullick says approximately 50% of women preferred the buttocks, while about 51% of men preferred the upper arm. The ongoing study will explore both men and women's reasons for injection-site preferences.

For nurses, the challenge was to administer the injections correctly while making the process as efficient as possible.

Lenacapavir requires getting two injections during the same visit. Patients also need to take two lenacapavir tablets on the day of their first injections, followed by another two tablets 24 hours later. These tablets form part of the initiation dose before they continue with injections every six months.

Senokwane says a Wits RHI pharmacist taught her a way to withdraw the solution while keeping the vial upright, rather than turning it upside down.

"That was the best method for me because it worked faster," says Senokwane.

"So with that method, you pull up 1.5 ml of air into the syringe and inject the needle into the vial. [The syringe] draws at least one ml by itself, without assistance, which allows the nurse to multitask. And then you also save time because you are able to prepare two injections at the same time," she says.

But efficiency was only part of the learning curve. Because lenacapavir is a thick solution, it needs to be injected slowly.

"I wish I knew that you can't inject it fast," Senokwane said. The thick solution required a slower injection technique to reduce leakage.

Slow administration was included in nurses' initial training, but its importance in minimising leakage was reinforced as they gained practical experience and shared lessons with colleagues.

Dr Martin says that in the early stages of implementation, nurses consulted experts, including those involved in clinical trials, on how to manage leakage at the injection site.

"As local experience grew, they learnt to reassure participants that minor leakage could occur and to assess more substantial leakage to determine whether further follow-up was needed."

Answering patient concerns

Patients were also concerned about the side effects of lenacapavir.

Lumps or small nodules at the injection site are a common side effect of lenacapavir. In one clinical trial, which included 2 140 participants who received lenacapavir, roughly 64% developed subcutaneous nodules at the injection site.

"Most of the clients were curious about the nodules. They were worried about whether they would be able to continue with their normal activities, especially those who wanted to exercise," says Senokwane.

"They wanted to know how long the nodule would last and whether they would get another one when they came back for their second injection. Usually, by the time they came for their next injection, the nodule would have disappeared."

Others were worried about the pain.

"We advise them that if the nodule comes with pain, just use a warm or cold compress, or you can even use a painkiller," explains Senokwane.

Mullick says addressing these concerns and discussing them with clients in advance is part of making the injection work for patients in practice.

"This might seem something relatively small, but from an implementation perspective, it contributes considerably to the person receiving the product."

Close 

Making it work in real time

As nurses became more familiar with administering lenacapavir, the clinics also refined how they moved patients through the service, from the initial consultation to receiving the injection.

Patients first met a navigator who explained the available services. After registration, an HIV test and a check of their vital signs, they saw the research nurse.

The clinics later began using the waiting time more effectively, with navigators introducing patients to PrEP and other services before their consultations.

Initially, appointments could take about an hour and a half. As the clinics refined their workflow and nurses became more familiar with the process, Senokwane says visits took about an hour or less.

"Training manuals and guidelines provide all the theoretical knowledge and framework for delivering lenacapavir," Martin explains.

"But, that real-world experience gives you a little bit more insight into things that you can only learn by working with clients."

Each one teach one

Senokwane's experience eventually helped her become a mentor to other nurses.

"The mentorship was really very important. We've got support from our pharmacist, and then we've got support from our sub-investigator at site. So everyone needs to be mentored until you are really 100% sure that you can do it on your own," she says.

When non-research nurses started providing lenacapavir in June at the study sites, she went there to demonstrate the technique. Some nurses she had trained also helped their colleagues.

"They were always grateful that we really helped them. So they really appreciated it. The more you practice, the better you become," says Senokwane.

Lessons from the clinics also informed training. Videos demonstrating how to prepare and administer lenacapavir were produced by Wits RHI, alongside webinars. Martin says the videos would be incorporated into future training.

"It's always helpful to see something in practice. With a new product, although it can be explained theoretically, it is helpful to actually see a provider and a client interaction," she says.
