World.title: Why Meta is charging to post more hyperlinks
World.content:
Why Meta is charging to post more hyperlinks

You're reading a newsletter from The Indicator from Planet Money. Once a week, we curate our favorite stories and insights on business, finance, economics and why they matter. Subscribe here to get it in your inbox every Friday.

Outside of Atlanta, two gas stations got into a price war. The Atlanta TV station WSB-TV reported that, over the course of a day, prices dropped from $2.54 down to $1.44, $1.39 and eventually down to just 97 cents. When drivers took notice, the traffic jam began and police intervened. BUT while it was happening, one driver said she only spent $15 to fill up her truck. It usually costs $90. "Look at God, baby! Look at God!" she said.

In our team's Slack, co-host Wailin Wong responded to the low prices, "make it up on volume!?" Jeff Guo wrote, "how is this real." But like, actually. How is this real?

Coming up:



Why Facebook is charging you to post hyperlinks

How fake data centers can still drive up electricity costs

How one man is dealing with a rental car agency

News We're Watching

Why websites make it hard to leave

What To Know: Social media sites don't love it when users leave. If you've ever used Instagram, it's not the easiest place to post links. You need to include them in bios, or through a special button on stories. Well now, if you run a Facebook page, you can only post TWO hyperlinks for free per month. $49.99/month will get you a Meta One Advanced plan, allowing you to include eight hyperlinks in posts or reels. With the $499/month Max plan, you can post an unlimited amount. Ashley Gullen, who runs a game design company, posted on Mastodon, a decentralized social media platform, "Facebook achieving absurd new heights of enshittification" in response to the news. This isn't totally unique. Nieman Lab did a whole study finding that posting links hurts news publishers on X.

toggle caption i Tony Avelar/AP Photo

Why are companies doing this?: Attention is money for social media sites. They want to keep you inside their walls! David Evans, managing director at BRG, a consulting firm, wrote a simple explanation as to why platforms want you to stay on their site: "Attention platforms use content to get consumers to spend time on their platform and sell marketers the ability to expose these consumers to messages."

Sponsor Message

Even FAKE data centers could be driving up electricity costs - The Wall Street Journal

What To Know: Developers are desperate to get their data centers up and running. They need it to help power their precious AI and whatever other computing is needed. BUT, developers won't just say, "This is the only location we'll accept for this project." No, they'll put out requests to all sorts of locations for their centers. The problem is, utilities are still considering data centers that likely WON'T GET BUILT in their electricity forecasts. Energy research firm Wood Mackenzie estimates that only a mere 23% of data-center requests are considered "high confidence," according to The Wall Street Journal. The rest are speculative!

How this affects YOU: Electricity costs could rise even if the data centers don't get built. Hoowwwwww does that work now? Because utilities are still planning for expected demand. They can't just suddenly integrate a wildly power-demanding data center without new substations or transmission lines. It's possible for the utility to pass on some of those grid investments onto consumers, even if the data centers never come to pass. Some power markets also set prices based on future demand so… There are lots of ways these projects could mess with your electricity bill.

Sponsor Message

Another oil reserve gets tapped - U.S. Department of Energy

It's your weekly update on diesel prices! This week, the Trump administration has found a NEW way to try and lower prices, which seems to be a core issue ahead of the midterms. This time, the U.S. Department of Energy has authorized an exchange from the Northeast Home Heating Oil Reserve. It would release roughly a third of the reserves for heating oil. The Chief Energy Advisor for Gulf Oil thinks it won't make a difference on prices.

toggle caption i Screenshot of a post on X by @tomkloza/X

What's interesting, this reserve has only been tapped ONCE, and that was after Hurricane Sandy. According to the DOE's history, that's the sort of thing it was meant for. "The intent was to create a buffer large enough to allow commercial companies to compensate for interruptions in supply during severe winter weather." Here, the DOE will loan out up to 315,000 barrels of heating oil in hopes of lowering prices. It's called an exchange because borrowing entities, like a regional heating oil retailer, would be required to replace the same volume at a premium ahead of next year.

Today's Indicator

Why Oracle's debt load could be your problem

If you HAVEN'T listened: We keep hearing about the AI boom that's propping up the U.S. economy. Well, Oracle is a part of that story. The enterprise software company has moved into building out data centers to serve the AI industry. Now, they have a huge deal with OpenAI worth $300 billion over five years. Here's the problem. Oracle has been spending freely with the assumption that this OpenAI deal will deliver. But what if it doesn't? Oracle already has $169 billion in total debt and a growing credit risk. They're one link in an interconnected chain of enormous tech companies. If that link breaks, it could spell trouble for the economy.

Listen to the full episode

Sponsor Message

If you HAVE listened: Lindsay Tyler, credit analyst, explains in the piece that Oracle is making a bet on data centers. "The analogy might be you have 10 apartments, you've pre-signed leases with, for those 10 apartments, and you're thinking, 'Should I build another floor?'"

On the surface, this doesn't seem plausible. Isn't computing demand insatiable right now? Yeah, right now. But…



AI is getting so much more efficient to run. Research from Epoch AI found "the cost of achieving a given level of AI performance has fallen about 47% per quarter since 2023, or 13× per year."

The chips powering these AI models "have a useful lifespan of one to three years due to rapid technological obsolescence and physical wear."

Some economic historians like to compare the AI buildout to the railroads, but this one is different. Rails last longer than one to three years. The cost of shipping does not plummet 13x per year. And maybe Oracle is at the center of these economic forces colliding: a railroad-type investment boom building castles made of sand.

Rest of the Week

We can inflate away the national debt… at a cost

Piercing the American taboo of talking about income and class

Can a "Moneyball" system work for campaign funding?

Listener Mailbag

Context: Last week, we ran an episode full of consumer rage stories. One included a story about someone charged for damage to a rental car that was impossible to disprove. Stay to the end for a surprising twist.

Listener Jim Zerefos sent in a response from Colorado.

I share the frustration of the person who complained about dubious damage claims from a rental car company. I've been fighting Alamo for nearly a year now over a $1,600 damage claim. Alamo sent me photos of very minor damage taken AFTER our rental, but never provided photos from BEFORE our rental. [The car] had some 23k miles so seems possible (likely?) the scratches occurred some time before our rental.

Sponsor Message

My spidey sense here smells a scam: "rental companies now scan cars for damage and so are trying to find scapegoats for all prior damage"? Alamo's reaction to me (and my insurance company) has been to ignore us - never sending the "before" pics and never acknowledging that's an issue. They just keep sending us invoices. They now are threatening collection action and have banned me from renting from the Alamo rental family (as if I would). So, the story on the broader scam? Or story on which credit cards still offer primary rental damage coverage (which we THOUGHT we had)?

By the way, here at The Indicator, we reached out to the car rental company and they responded in a statement through a spokesperson from Enterprise Mobility: "Customer satisfaction is our top priority, and we are always open to further conversations with customers regarding damage claims. Our team is actively reviewing this matter through our escalation process and will reach out to the customer to share an update today."

And we already have an update: Jim tells us Alamo has since dropped the claim and will make no further collection efforts. Alamo's "risk" department instructed the Cleveland manager to drop the claim, according to Jim.

Jim's response: "Sad to see that you got more action in a day than my insurance company and I got in nearly a year."

In Our Spare Time

Co-host Wailin Wong is reading Under Story

This fall has yielded a bumper crop of big new fiction releases. My favorite from the last couple of weeks of reading is UNDER STORY by Chloe Benjamin. This novel is about a fungi expert who goes to Antarctica after a family tragedy. She's hoping to anonymously wash dishes at a research station. However, a strange light phenomenon and the arrival of her physicist ex-husband pull her back into the scientific world. This was an exciting, imaginative, and beautiful story about grief, family, parallel universes, trees, and mushrooms. (Bonus rec: This book also makes for a good pairing with Emily St. John Mandel's new novel, Exit Party.)

World.title: Trump to exempt some Canadian products from tariffs amid midterm pressure
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

U.S. President Donald Trump is poised to lift tariffs on some Canadian products — and hit others with new duties — as Republicans in border states lobby for relief from trade actions that have put them in a shaky political position ahead of November's midterms.

Maine Republican Sen. Susan Collins said on Friday that the Trump administration will scrap tariffs on some paper and plastic products, refrigeration and packaging equipment, agricultural machinery and seaweed and algae products, among others, after she relayed how damaging these levies have been for consumers and businesses in her state.

Trump hit these products with a 50 per cent tariff in August, apparently retaliating for Canada's countermeasures on some U.S. goods that were imposed after the president first launched his trade war last year.

While removing tariffs on some products important to a politically sensitive swing state, the White House said it would levy new Section 338 tariffs on products with certain valves, carpets and waste products "to continue addressing Canada’s discriminatory treatment of U.S. commerce."

The six-page list of new Canadian products facing the 50 per cent tariff also includes shampoos, cocoa powder products, window air-conditioning units, archery equipment and canoes less than 7.5 metres long, among others.

Collins said the Canadian products that are getting a tariff reprieve are "essential" to some Maine businesses and farms and cannot be easily replaced with U.S. alternatives.

She said, for example, Maine's blueberry growers rely on Canadian-made specialized harvesting boxes that work with existing processing equipment. Plus, a U.S. supplier of cardboard totes widely used in the agricultural sector recently stopped making that particular product, "leaving producers with no choice but to turn to Canada," she said.

"I will continue working directly with administration officials to seek additional relief and encourage a broader trade agreement with Canada, our neighbour, ally and largest trading partner," Collins said in a social media statement announcing the changes.

U.S. Sen. Susan Collins campaigns in Fryeburg, Maine, earlier this month. Collins, a Republican, is in a tight race with Democrat Troy Jackson. (Spencer Platt/Getty Images)

Collins, a 30-year veteran of the U.S. upper house, is in a pitched battle for re-election in Maine as she tries to hold off a Democratic challenger, Troy Jackson, who has made Trump's trade war with Canada a centrepiece of his campaign.

A moderate Republican who has sparred with Trump in the past, Collins had earlier pressured the administration to drop U.S. tariffs on products like road salt given her wintry state depends on Canadian supplies to keep the roads clear.

Another border state Republican Senate candidate, Michigan's Mike Rogers, has publicly called for an end to the trade war with Canada, saying the tariffs have raised prices at a time when inflation is already high.

Polls show Trump's dispute with Canada is deeply unpopular among American voters in both major parties.

The tariff climbdown comes on the same day Trump claimed that Canada "very much wants to make a deal" with the U.S. to restore trade peace, while falsely claiming Canada has been making "$90 billion a year" from the U.S.

That's an apparent reference to the U.S. trade deficit in goods with Canada, which Trump's own U.S. Trade Representative pegs at $48.3 billion US — much of it driven by U.S. refineries buying large volumes of Alberta oil at a discount to world prices. The U.S. consistently runs a trade surplus in services with Canada.

While suggesting a bilateral deal could soon be in hand, Trump has repeatedly made it clear he is wedded to his tariff policy.

At a Friday rally in Fort Myers, Fla., one of several deep-red states where he is trying to shore up the Republican vote, Trump said "tariffs" is still his "favourite word" because they've "made us rich."

WATCH | Carney says Canada can wait for 'another administration': Carney says Canada can wait for 'another administration' if necessary for U.S. trade deal | Duration closed caption 0:35 Prime Minister Mark Carney, speaking in Istanbul on Friday, said a trade deal with the U.S. could be signed 'this afternoon' if the Americans 'were there.' Carney said 'we don't care about the timing.'

Prime Minister Mark Carney, meanwhile, said during a bilateral visit to Turkey that Canada is open to a mutually beneficial deal with the U.S. that protects Canadian interests — but the government is in no rush.

"We could sign it this afternoon if the U.S. were there. If it has to be months from now or longer than that, or another administration, before a proper deal comes into place, we will do that," he said.

World.title: Loblaw CEO apologizes to 2 million shoppers for personal data hack, offers free credit monitoring
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The CEO of Canada's largest grocery retailer is apologizing to about two million shoppers for a data breach earlier this year where hackers accessed private information, including names, addresses, phone numbers, birthdates and purchase details.

Brampton, Ont.-based Loblaw operates about 2,500 stores nationwide under its namesake Loblaws banner, as well as numerous sub-brands including No Frills, Real Canadian Superstore, Zehrs and Fortinos.

In March, Loblaw announced that unauthorized activity took place "in certain Loblaw technology systems" around Feb. 23. In an email this week to impacted customers, the company says its internal investigation found an "unauthorized third party" accessed certain personal information.

"We know you trust us to protect your information, and we take that responsibility seriously," Loblaw CEO Per Bank states in the email seen by CBC News. "We're sorry for the concern this may cause, and are committed to supporting you and helping protect your information."

WATCH | Loblaw returns country-of-origin labels to produce: Loblaw stores returning produce country-of-origin labels after backlash | Duration closed caption 1:46 Just weeks after removing country-of-origin labels from the produce section of most provinces' stores, Loblaw reversed the decision after being contacted by CBC News, and in the face of a renewed trade war with the U.S. and customer backlash.

As a precaution, Loblaw says customers were logged out of applications that use the company's PCiD credentials. These include loyalty programs like PC Optimum, the PC Express online grocery service and the PC Financial portal.

The company is offering two years of free credit monitoring and identity restoration services through TransUnion. Impacted shoppers have until Feb. 28, 2027 to enroll.

Loblaw is also advising those who receive the email to "be cautious" about unexpected emails, calls or texts asking for personal information or asking you to click a link or download an attachment.

"Keep an eye on your accounts and report any suspicious activity to the appropriate organization," the CEO says in the email.

Understanding credit monitoring services

Consumers should know that credit monitoring services offer limited protection, warned Cat Coode, a Waterloo, Ont.-based privacy and data strategist.

"It only covers if someone is going to use your information in order to apply for a credit card or apply for certain government documents. It doesn't cover the spectrum of the things that you could do with that data," she told CBC News on Friday.

"The privacy issue can never be resolved … Once your data is available, it is available. ... You can change your credit card number, but you can't change your birthdate."

More than a 'slap on the wrist'?

All organizations in Canada have a legal obligation to keep the personal information they collect safe, says Maanit Zemel, a Toronto-based lawyer who specializes in internet, privacy and cybersecurity law.

"It's a regulatory obligation imposed by both federal and provincial privacy legislation."

Federally, there is the Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act. But Zemel calls PIPEDA, which officially came into force in 2001, "stuck in the 90s."

The government introduced Bill C-36, the Protecting Privacy and Consumer Data Act, in June. It proposes a major overhaul of Canada's private sector privacy framework, updating language to establish privacy as a "fundamental right" and replacing parts of PIPEDA.

The bill also requires companies to conduct a "privacy impact assessment" before transferring personal data outside of Canada.

If passed, Zemel says the new legislation will significantly up the consequences for companies found to have mishandled the personal data of customers.

"It's no longer going to be a slap on the wrist," he said. "There's going to significant consequences for a potential failure to comply with these requirements, including appropriate security safeguards."

World.title: Ukraine's restricted access to Musk's Starshield is costing lives, Carney says
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Prime Minister Mark Carney on Friday criticized a decision to restrict Ukraine's access to Elon Musk's military-grade satellite network, saying the move is costing lives.

"I search for the right adjective to describe whoever took this decision, or a group of people took this decision, against a country … that is literally fighting for the lives of its citizens against naked aggression," Carney said in Istanbul.

"So are we concerned? Yes, we are concerned."

Early last week, Ukrainian officials said they had lost some of their access to Starshield, the military version of Starlink, the global satellite communications system owned and operated by Musk's company SpaceX.

Ukraine employs Starshield to both track incoming missiles and jet-powered drones, and to guide interceptor and spy drones, while using Starlink for critical internal communications.

WATCH | Carney 'concerned' about reported Starlink slowdown: Carney says he is 'concerned' about reported Starlink slowdown in Ukraine | Duration closed caption 3:10 Prime Minister Mark Carney says he is concerned about the reported slowdown of SpaceX's Starlink satellite system in Ukraine, which created 'real consequences.' He says Canadians likewise 'do not want to be caught in a situation where we are reliant on one provider that may change their view' and compromise Canadian sovereignty.

Reuters reported last week that, according to two U.S. officials, the order to restrict the system came from inside the White House. The Wall Street Journal, meanwhile, reported on Wednesday that the restrictions were ordered personally by Musk.

Musk said that Starshield was owned and controlled by the U.S. government, and that an y restrictions are decided by the U.S. military and, ultimately, by U.S. President Donald Trump. The commercial Starlink system, he said, was not designed or authorized for mi litary use.

Trump has denied ordering the restrictions. On Friday, Trump said he's unaware of who did, and wouldn't tell even if he knew.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says that since Starshield's capacity had been restricted, his country has been unable to track drones and missiles travelling faster than 160 kilometres per hour.

Ukraine says Starshield not restored

Zelenskyy says those restrictions have complicated Ukraine's efforts to repel Russian missile and jet drone attacks — resulting in the deaths of civilians, including children.

Carney agreed with that assessment, saying it now "does seem clear" the restrictions have "real consequences, human consequences" and that some recent deaths in Ukraine are "direct casualties as a consequence of this reduced ability."

"I just refer in the last 36 hours to the attack at the centre of Kyiv," Carney said. "Kyiv, absolutely no dressing up on any sort of military or quasi-military target, just a direct attack on citizens and with immense human suffering. So this is real, this is concrete."

On Thursday, Trump said that Musk has since restored Ukraine's access to the satellite network. But Zelenskyy contradicted that claim in an interview with CNN saying "it still doesn't work."

Ukrainian military officials also said on Friday that the restrictions on Starshield remain in place.

Ukraine’s access to Starlink is still limited, President Zelensky tells me. “It limited our possibility to defend.” https://t.co/eusHc70JO5 —amanpour

In an interview with NBC's Meet The Press on Sunday, Zelenskyy was asked directly who he thought was to blame for the Starshield restrictions.

"It’s [the] opinion of our generals, of our government and of course my also opinion … that it was the message from American government to limit this speed, and technically SpaceX did it." Zelenskyy said.

The warning for Canada

The restriction of Starshield comes amid a low point in relations between Kyiv and Washington as Trump seeks to push Ukraine into accepting stronger concessions in a peace deal.

Trump has also been pressuring Ukraine to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries, although Starshield is not used on drones conducting those attacks as it does not operate over Russian territory.

Without mentioning Trump, Carney said that relying on an ally "that may change their view" puts Canadians at risk.

"Once you realize that, as we have, this government has, it leads to a series of decisions and partnerships that are necessary in order to diversify and to build up sovereign capabilities within Canada or with partners," he said.

Diversifying Canada's defence partnerships, Carney said, will take time "because we're starting from a position where we're highly, highly reliant on certain systems in certain countries."

Zelenskyy is already working to move away from his country's reliance on the U.S. satellite network, signing a letter of intent with Finnish companies Nokia and ICEYE on Thursday to develop Ukraine's own satellite communications network.

World.title: As Connor Hellebuyck heads to New Jersey, Winnipeg Jets GM will hold on to the 'good memories'
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Connor Hellebuyck era is over in Winnipeg after the Jets traded the all-star goalie on Friday.

The 33-year-old from Michigan is headed to the New Jersey Devils.

It ends a long, sometimes fractious drama that began when Hellebuyck told the team during exit interviews at the end of last season that he wanted to be moved.

Now that the trade is in the rear view, Jets general manager Kevin Cheveldayoff will endeavour to forget those times.

Hellebuyck gave many years of service to the Jets and the team's fans, and a "lot of good memories, and I choose to remember those," Cheveldayoff told reporters Friday, shortly after a blockbuster trade sent the all-star to the New Jersey Devils for six players.

"He was a big part of our family, and we accomplished some pretty good things. We obviously didn't accomplish the end-all goal that we all wanted [winning the Stanley Cup], but those [other] memories are always going to stay.

"That's what I talked to Connor about today when I called him and wished him all the best."

Coming to Winnipeg in exchange for Hellebuyck are forwards Dawson Mercer, Alexander Command and Nick Bjugstad and goaltender Nico Daws. The Jets also get New Jersey’s second-round pick in the 2029 NHL draft and seventh-round pick in the 2027 draft. (Winnipeg Jets)

In return for Hellebuyck, the Jets have acquired forwards Dawson Mercer, Alexander Command and Nick Bjugstad, goaltender Nico Daws, and New Jersey's second-round pick in the 2029 NHL draft and seventh-round pick in the 2027 draft.

Hellebuyck will return to Winnipeg with his new team on Nov. 10, when the Jets will host the Devils at Canada Life Centre.

Mercer, 24, was New Jersey's first-round pick (18th overall) in the 2020 draft, while Daws, 25, was New Jersey's third-round pick (84th overall) in the 2020 draft. They were teammates on Canada's 2020 gold-medal-winning junior team.

Command, 18, was New Jersey's first-round pick (12th overall) in the 2026 draft and is currently playing in the Swedish league.

Bjugstad, 34, was the Florida Panthers' first-round pick (19th overall) in the 2010 draft. He's currently on the long-term injured reserve, recovering from a torn pectoral muscle that required surgery.

Cheveldayoff said he's "very comfortable" with his end of the deal, particularly snagging Command, who was one player the Jets considered choosing in the 2026 draft had Viggo Björck not been available.

"We addressed some needs that we had in our forward group here right now. We added depth to the organization and we added assets that I can use now either for drafting or at the trade deadline," Cheveldayoff said.

"And at the end of the day, that's the goal I set out to try to accomplish. I certainly wished we could have done it five or four months ago, whatever … but here we are."

Hellebuyck is a three-time Vezina Trophy winner and 2025 Hart Trophy winner as NHL MVP who has made five appearances at the NHL All-Star Game.

He also backstopped the U.S. men's hockey team to an Olympic gold medal in February 2026.

He still had five years left on a seven-year contract when he requested his trade.

There was speculation it was because Hellebuyck and his family were targets of online harassment after the goalie and some Olympic teammates visited the White House.

U.S. President Donald Trump gave Hellebuyck the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the U.S.'s highest civilian honour, while anti-American sentiment was soaring in Canada due to Trump's tariffs and references to making Canada the 51st state.

Cheveldayoff told reporters in September that the harassment had escalated to the point where team security and local police were involved, with increased monitoring around Hellebuyck's Winnipeg residence.

Others speculated Hellebuyck's trade demands were prompted by the Jets' poor performance last season.

When the Jets re-signed him in 2023, it was seen as a commitment to build a squad that would consistently compete for the Stanley Cup.

Then the Jets missed the playoffs in 2025-26 for the first time in four seasons, after winning the President's Trophy for the league's best regular-season record in 2024-25.

Hellebuyck voiced strong frustration.

"What we did was unacceptable, and no one wants to be a part of that," he said.

Cheveldayoff said last month that the team was respecting Hellebuyck's request to keep the trade request quiet and was caught off guard when Hellebuyck went public on Aug. 27.

When he was a no-show for training camp in September, the Jets suspended him.

Hellebuyck notified the team on Oct. 2 that he planned to end his absence, but the Jets chose to enforce the full three-week suspension rather than immediately reintegrate him.

That suspension was set to expire on Friday.

Cheveldayoff last month said he was in no rush to make a trade, choosing instead to wait for the right offer.

He told reporters he didn't want "future assets" that may or may not work out. He wanted players who could offer immediate production to support those who had committed to the team.

He reiterated that on Friday, saying, "We weren't going to take a [draft] pick and a prospect."

People might think putting a goalie of Hellebuyck's calibre on the market would create a flood of offers, but it's not such an easy task, said Cheveldayoff, who talked to a lot of teams, and many who had a locked-in No. 1 goaltender offered nothing but sympathy.

"They said, 'Hang in there. I feel for you, buddy.' That's the sentiment I got from a lot of my counterparts who were sleeping easy at night, as opposed to wasting away a summer," Cheveldayoff said.

He said he told Hellebuyck's agent many times, "I can't force other teams to make offers or decide when they're going to make offers.

"Fortunately, I can now have some sleep."

World.title: Crime Stoppers had 'potentially one of the most harmful data breaches' Canada has seen. What's next?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Two days after an exclusive CBC investigation revealed the extent of the Crime Stoppers data hack in Canada, experts are now weighing the long-term implications of what could be among the country's most dangerous privacy failures.

"It strikes me as potentially one of the most harmful data breaches we've ever seen in Canada," said Michael Geist, a law professor at the University of Ottawa and the Canada Research Chair in Internet and E-commerce Law.

When it comes to the Canadian law, he says, both Crime Stoppers, the organization that collected the data, and Navigate360, the company it hired to manage it, could be held accountable.

"[How] Canadian privacy law functions is that the organization that collects the personal information is the one that's responsible," said Geist. "And even where they use third parties or subcontractors as part of what takes place, it's on them to ensure that no matter who gains access to the information, it has that appropriate level of protection."

However, enforcing those rules across borders — Navigate360 is U.S.-based — is notoriously difficult, he says, and the domestic penalties are weak.

"These kinds of incidents keep happening. There's a real urgency to addressing Canadian privacy law, which is woefully out of date," he said.

"And at the top of the list has been really weak enforcement."

Expert fears company doesn’t know leak's true scale

At the heart of the breach is Navigate360 and its tip management platform, P3. All Crime Stoppers chapters, including those in Canada and the U.S., relied on P3 to keep their data anonymous.

The information was stolen last March by hacktivist collective Internet Yiff Machine, who stated they wanted to disprove the company's claim that its platform was "anonymous" and "secure." CBC News analyzed a copy of the hacked data and found that more than 1.5 million tips submitted to Canadian Crime Stoppers programs over the last 25 years were exposed, along with tens of thousands of unredacted personal details.

CBC has reached out repeatedly to Navigate360 and shared the highlights of its investigation, but the company has not responded.

Adding to the controversy are accounts provided by the Toronto and Guelph Wellington Crime Stoppers chapters, where Navigate360 appeared to change its narrative about how much data had been stolen and what was affected.

According to a Wednesday statement from the Toronto chapter, Navigate360 initially told the organization that no Canadian data was taken, then said Toronto wasn't impacted, before finally revealing months later that years of Toronto data was compromised. Guelph Wellington shared a similar statement on Thursday.

Cybersecurity expert Ali Dehghantanha, who reviewed samples of the compromised data as part of CBC’s original investigation, said it was alarming that Navigate360's claims to Toronto Crime Stoppers appeared to change.

"They apparently received six different [accounts] in seven months from the vendor," he said, adding that this raises massive red flags about the company's ability to investigate the hack and fix the vulnerabilities that might have allowed it.

Dehghantanha, who has conducted digital forensics investigations for over a decade, said he is also very surprised at how quickly Navigate360 seemed to have returned its system to an operational state following the hack.

WATCH | More about the investigation: Crime Stoppers hack exposes personal information of tens of thousands of Canadians | Duration closed caption 3:40 A massive data breach leaked 25 years worth of unredacted personal information from Crime Stoppers, compromising the identities of thousands of Canadian tipsters. The Toronto branch of Crime Stoppers has asked the public not to send in tips until the issue is resolved.

Toronto Crime Stoppers said it was told about the leak on March 18; a week later on March 25, Navigate360 told the organization that the system was "safe and fully operational."

"It doesn't seem that there was a full investigation there," Dehghantanha said, "that you could do and you could say, 'Oh, only these clients have been impacted.'"

Internal memo advises against calling privacy commissioner

Meanwhile, Geist says tipsters whose information has been leaked may be limited in their options for justice.

"In terms of actual compensation to the affected individuals, current privacy law doesn't really focus on that," he added. "You've got to look to other mechanisms like class actions if what you're looking for is actual compensation."

Beyond that, another avenue could be to launch a privacy commissioner investigation — but Geist warns that could take years, and any recommendations for the future would not be legally binding.

WATCH | Ont. police suspend tip lines: Multiple Ontario cities suspend Crime Stoppers tip lines over massive data hack | Duration closed caption 1:58 Toronto, Halton and Guelph are among the Ontario cities temporarily pausing Crime Stoppers tip programs after a CBC News investigation revealed a massive data breach exposed 1.5 million tips over the past 25 years to possible exploitation by hackers.

He noted that even if Canada's privacy commissioner investigates the matter, it can only issue a "non-binding finding" directing a company to fix bad practices — it cannot force a company to compensate victims.

Still, even with those limited powers, the privacy commissioner may have already been top of mind for the Canadian Crime Stoppers Association (CCSA) in the months following the hack, according to a copy of a June 18 internal memo obtained by CBC.

"We currently do not believe that you are required, nor should you contact the privacy commissioner in your region at this time," instructs CCSA president David Forster, saying his organization has "previously assessed that they [the commissioner] do not have jurisdiction over Crime Stoppers."

Crime Stoppers is best known for its public appeals, often partnering with police, for help with unsolved crimes and to advance investigations — all with the promise of anonymity for tipsters who contact them. (Tyson Koschik/CBC)

CBC has reached out to the CCSA for comment on the contents of the memo. We have also contacted the Canada and Ontario privacy commissioners to ask whether they are investigating the data breach, if they have received any citizen complaints, and whether they actually have jurisdiction over Crime Stoppers.

We have also contacted the Canada and Ontario Privacy Commissioners to ask if they are investigating the data breach, if they have received any citizen complaints, and whether they actually have jurisdiction over Crime Stoppers.

In a public statement on Thursday, Forster offered reassurance to the public: "Navigate360 has advised us that third-party cybersecurity experts investigated the breach, identified vulnerabilities and completed remediation."Those measures strengthen protections for current and future tips, he said.

However, he noted: "They cannot undo the exposure of information already taken, which remains a serious concern."

World.title: Canadian woman dies in U.S. after fears of detainment prevented her from seeking medical care
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A 61-year-old Canadian woman living in the isolated U.S. town of Point Roberts, Wash., has died after refusing to seek medical care out of fears she would be detained or deported.

Paige Adamson made headlines last month when she was stopped at the Point Roberts border crossing, south of Tsawwassen, and interrogated for hours about whether she had unlawfully voted in a U.S. election.

The U.S. permanent resident was scheduled to appear at a deportation hearing before a federal immigration judge in Seattle on Nov. 4.

Point Roberts community support officer Annelle Norman said Adamson called her on Thursday night asking to borrow a pair of crutches from local nonprofit Circle Of Care.

"I took them over and found her literally debilitated on the sofa, in very, very bad pain," Norman said.

"She told me that she had slipped and fallen on her right side … she was relying on the help of a few friends to come and help her get up and take her to the bathroom."

Norman, who was also a friend and neighbour of Adamson, said she urged the distressed woman to call paramedics or visit the local Point Roberts health-care clinic.

"And she said, 'No, no, I'm afraid if I go, I won't be able to come back. They'll keep me or they'll deport me.'"

Point Roberts community support officer Annelle Norman says she urged Paige Adamson to call paramedics or visit the local health-care clinic. (CBC News)

Point Roberts is a U.S. pene-exclave at the southern tip of the Tsawwassen Peninsula, completely cut off by land from the rest of the country.

U.S. immigration lawyer Len Saunders said Adamson had mentioned not feeling well and needing to see a doctor. Residents of Point Roberts have to cross into Canada in order to get to other parts of Washington state or the U.S. and there was a risk she would be detained by ICE upon return to the U.S.

Adamson was a permanent resident of the U.S. who had been living in Point Roberts for more than 14 years and crossed the Canadian border countless times. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

"She was quite frankly scared about trying to drive up to Canada and come back in," Saunders said.

"There are no doctors where she lives. For all practical purposes, she was in detention," he said.

"I mentioned to her that I'd heard of people in the past maybe taking a boat or taking an airplane. But financially, I don't think she could afford it. She didn't have a lot of money."

Norman said she checked in on Adamson over the weekend, but her friend's condition had not improved.

"The next message that I got was on Monday, telling me to show up at her address," she said.

"She had died sometime in the hours previous."

In a statement, Whatcom County Sheriff public information officer Deb Slater said the death "appeared to be of natural causes."

Louise Trapp, operations manager with the medical examiner, said Adamson's body was in her office's care pending examination by a forensic pathologist.

'Absolute worst case outcome'

Adamson was a permanent resident of the U.S. who had been living in Point Roberts for more than 14 years.

According to Saunders, her status meant she was legally entitled to leave and enter the country while awaiting deportation proceedings, but border officials had the right to detain her if they saw fit.

"Officers have the right to take you into detention and send you on a one-way trip to the Northwest Detention Centre down in Tacoma," he said.

Immigration lawyer Len Saunders says Paige Adamson had been missing appointments with her doctor in Bellingham, Wash., due to fears of being detained or deported trying to cross the border. (Martin Diotte/Radio-Canada)

"I asked her to speak to the Peace Arch port-of-entry. I believe she had called them but was given no guarantees on what would happen … I could understand her concerns."

As a U.S. resident, accessing health care in British Columbia was not an option. CBC News reached out to U.S. Customs and Border Protection for comment but did not hear back before deadline.

Saunders said he couldn't believe it when he was advised of Adamson's death on Sunday.

"This is an absolute worst case outcome. Here's a lady with no prior immigration violations, no criminal convictions. She was about as squeaky clean as you could get," he said.



Adamson is survived by two sons, both residents of B.C.

World.title: Stop-motion movie Wildwood is a staggering masterpiece. It's a miracle it exists at all
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

There are the kinds of movies that switch something in your brain.

Movies that, after watching, make you skip the bus and inexplicably walk 10 kilometres home. Movies that make you stumble through your door, sit down and fumble out a piece of art — even if it's something remedial, unfinished and perhaps even ugly.

Ones that inspire you to make anything: it just needs to exist, because you're suddenly reminded how astounding it is that each and every one of us can perform a legitimate type of magic: artistic creation.

In this case, that spark of inspiration would be Wildwood, the newest dark-fantasy, stop-motion marvel from stop-motion powerhouse Laika. A 16-years-in-the-making animated behemoth from the studio responsible for Coraline, ParaNorman, Tim Burton's Corpse Bride and Kubo and the Two Strings. And given that pedigree, it's perhaps not too surprising to sit up and take notice when the studio puts out what it — and this critic — are touting as its obvious magnum opus.

That is, perhaps, to be expected, given the amount of work and waiting that's gone into Wildwood. Adapted from the 2011 novel of the same name, Laika's film is a passion project from CEO Travis Knight, one that has been in production for nearly the exact amount of time that he's run the company. The end result just so happens to be the longest, most expensive and one of the most ambitious such projects ever attempted. Which is quite a feat, given it is made in a medium already infamous for its time-intensive creation process.

But it is a process that's led to a stunning achievement of human ingenuity, crackling with so much raw beauty that it feels an understatement to call it one of the best animated movies ever made.

WATCH | Wildwood trailer:

Wildwood is so packed with casual displays of complicated artisanal mastery, it makes you stop and stare every time a character casually hops off a rock — given that animation sequence that must have taken weeks to execute — or when a murder of hundreds of jet-black, clay-constructed crows flit through a spellbinding murmuration that fills up the screen, in what feels like a natural phenomenon that couldn't possibly have been rendered by hand.

What's more, throughout the film, all these characters are physically breathing. Their chests are actually rising and falling due to an internal breathing mechanism Laika invented and maintained for the film's entire runtime — just to give it that one added bit of realism.

The visibly obvious effort it took to make all of these seemingly impossible scenes is the point; a not so subtle jab at generative AI that runs through both the medium and the narrative.

That is even as its story — of a young Prue (voiced by Peyton Elizabeth Lee) and her reluctant friend Curtis (the scene-stealing endearing Jacob Tremblay) travelling through a fantastical forest to save her kidnapped baby brother from magical kingdoms on the brink of war — doesn’t exactly sound all that original.

Because to believe some critics, if you’ve seen one Spiderwick Chronicles — or Labyrinth, Bridge to Terabithia, Where the Wild Things Are and on and on — you’ve seen 'em all.

That exact complaint — that Wildwood's done-to-death storyline is its weakest aspect — is already an established critique. This is even as its technical mastery is hailed: a reported $100 million US, more than 200 unique puppets, more than 1,000 artisans and one particularly jaw-dropping battle scene.

That last epic sequence utilizes 3,000 characters across a 12-minute runtime — and its sets, if laid end to end, would be taller than a small building. According to Laika, it required one worker whose entire job was tracking the evolving facial scars of the main character — just for that one scene alone.

Brendan the Bandit King, voiced by Mahershala Ali, appears in a scene with Prue. (Laika)

But according to some early watchers, Knight only afforded those resources for the — admittedly astounding — visuals, effectively sinking all the money into ingenuously crafted internal skeletons, functioning under-skin bicep muscles and fully articulated horses. And then he used the last two pennies to scratch out a script that reads something like Narnia 2: This Time it’s Personal.

Which is strange, given the end result. While it is true Wildwood could have subverted expectations, its stellar execution of the magical kingdom/children-in-peril genre comes together remarkably well. And for its supposed target audience of actual children, there’s a lower chance they've already been embittered by such tropes. More likely, Wildwood will likely become their core memory of such tales.

What's actually the most original aspect of its plot — at least for modern American animated cinema — is a truly shocking level of violence for what is a children's film: guns, swords, death, snarling teeth, blood-curdling threats, arrows in chests and blood trickling from mouths.

Along with the bone-chilling performances of Carey Mulligan as Dowager Governess Alexandra and — especially — Tom Waits as the genuinely terrifying coyote soldier Maksim, it is genuinely surprising how far Knight goes to explore the extremes of terror and emotion that do in fact come along with childhood.

Because now, more than ever, it is genuinely surprising anyone would use so much money to grapple with the realities of how unsettling and terrifying childhood can be. More often, when modern children's entertainment is mixed with true peril, it's released in the walled garden of tax-supported systems: leading Canada's past, uniquely interesting children's programs like Cybersix, The Odyssey or simply deeply disturbing PSAs .

When brought into modern American contexts, they're expected to ditch the harshness, as Apple TV did for the sunnily sanitized Time Bandits reboot). Or, like some fans already expect will happen to the almost identically terrifying Brothers Lionheart in its upcoming adaptation, the sensible business decision is to instead market dark fantasy as gritty drama to adults.

Which is what makes Wildwood's existence such a singular miracle; it is the result of a particular set of circumstances of its creation — the likes of which are unlikely to happen again. Laika is partially bankrolled by Knight's father, Nike co-founder Phil Knight, and the company's sole money-earning feature remains Coraline. Beyond the labour-, time- and cost-intensive production, every decision in Wildwood — from its alienating animation style, to the specificity of its genre and inherent violence — seems lab-designed to continue that money-losing pattern.

It is a message even cheekily, defiantly shown in the background: "Enjoy handmade art before it's gone forever,” penciled in on a street sign. Its a sort of clarion call for itself; a hidden Easter egg making an argument for a format that can't hope to last long. And, obviously, it's a shot across the bow of generative AI.

But Wildwood also feels designed to do what our current profit-focused system rewards the least: craft something challenging, memorable and aimed away from the lowest common denominator. It feels designed to celebrate human achievement. And it feels designed to celebrate humanity; what we are worth, and what we can do.

Which, of course, is to do magic.

World.title: Vivek Ramaswamy defends campaign ad featuring estranged mother of Amy Acton
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Republican Vivek Ramaswamy on Friday defended his campaign's ad featuring the estranged mother of Democratic rival Dr. Amy Acton in the closely watched race for Ohio governor.

Speaking at a campaign stop in northeastern Ohio, he said the , which features Acton's mother calling her "a liar," had nothing to do with childhood abuse.

"The irony is they're lying about an ad that is about lying," Ramaswamy said. "They're changing the subject because they don't want to answer for their own failures."

The  features Acton's birth mother, Donna Arthur, criticizing her and insinuating she has mental health issues. Arthur lost custody of her children after her husband, the children's stepfather, was indicted for raping Acton.

Acton is Ohio's former public health director and has made no secret of facing homelessness and abuse as a child. She has condemned Ramaswamy for the ad.

"I won't normalize somebody who has said that my childhood is just something I'm complaining about," she told Spectrum News.

A message seeking comment was sent Friday to her campaign.

Like 'hitting pay dirt': Trump

The ad has stirred significant reaction, including from U.S. President Donald Trump, who said it was like "hitting pay dirt."

WATCH | Ramaswamy faces backlash over ad: Ohio's Vivek Ramaswamy slammed for attack ad featuring opponent's estranged mother | Duration closed caption 2:14 Republican candidate for Ohio governor Vivek Ramaswamy has drawn backlash after releasing an attack ad featuring his Democratic opponent Amy Acton’s estranged mother. The ad fails to disclose that the mother remained married to the man who sexually abused Acton as a child.

At a campaign rally in Iowa on Thursday, Trump told the crowd Ramaswamy called him to ask for advice.

"You've got to ride with it," Trump recalled telling Ramaswamy, a biotech billionaire and former presidential candidate. Trump expressed jealousy that he didn't have such a strong ad to run during his own campaigns.

Other Republicans have been critical.

'Wrong to run this ad': governor

Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine criticized Ramaswamy and said the ad should be taken down.

"It's wrong to run this ad," DeWine said Thursday.

According to police and court documents obtained by The Associated Press, Cledith Arthur was arrested and charged with the rape of his stepdaughter, then 12, in July 1978, after Acton's biological father reported him to authorities. The abuse allegedly happened from December 1976 to April 1978.

Cledith Arthur pleaded not guilty. He was indicted by a grand jury that September, but failed to show at a court hearing and remained a fugitive until at least 1981. He has since died.
