ASUR Q3 Results at a Glance

Revenue rose 18.9% to 10.42 billion pesos (about US$557 million), and without construction services under the accounting rule IFRIC 12 it rose 12.6% to 7.83 billion pesos (about US$419 million). Construction revenue, which is matched by construction costs and does not change EBITDA, jumped 43.0% to 2.59 billion pesos (about US$139 million).

EBITDA, a measure of operating cash earnings, rose 1.7% to 4.72 billion pesos (about US$252 million), and operating profit rose 5.3% to 3.89 billion pesos (about US$208 million). Net income attributable to ASUR shareholders, which excludes minority interests such as the other owners of the Puerto Rico airport operator, rose 2.1% to 2.16 billion pesos (about US$115 million).

Earnings were 7.1960 pesos per share against 7.0486 a year earlier, which ASUR translated into US$3.9825 per ADS against US$3.9009. All other dollar figures here are our arithmetic at the Bank of Mexico rate of 18.7005 pesos per dollar for 22 October, so they differ slightly from ASUR’s own conversion at 18.0692 pesos per dollar.

El Economista reported that revenue came in above analyst expectations and EBITDA in line with them. Expectations are forecasts, and the filed figures are the only results.

Cancún Traffic Drops 8.8%

Cancún handled 6.13 million passengers in the quarter against 6.71 million a year earlier, a fall of 8.8%. International passengers dropped 13.3% to 3.53 million, while domestic passengers fell 1.8% to 2.59 million.

Across Mexico, traffic fell 4.6% to 9.08 million passengers, with international traffic down 11.8% and domestic traffic up 1.6%. The eight other Mexican airports carried 2.96 million passengers, up 5.5%, so the decline is concentrated in Cancún.

ASUR’s monthly table shows Mexican international traffic falling every month from March, by 10.0% in May, 12.1% in June, 11.5% in July and 13.6% in August, then 9.8% in September. For the first nine months, Cancún passengers are down 5.9% and the Mexican total is down 3.1%.

International passengers made up about 58% of Cancún’s traffic in the quarter, by our calculation from ASUR’s table. El Cronista, which calls Cancún Mexico’s second-largest airport, wrote that its traffic has not hit bottom and described it as the group’s worst-performing block.

Puerto Rico traffic fell 3.2% to 3.25 million, though September alone rose 3.1% after months of declines, while Colombia rose 5.2% to 4.68 million. Brazil and the other new airports carried 3.92 million passengers in September, up 1.4% on a pro forma basis, since ASUR owned them for only one month of the quarter.

Revenue Rises on Acquisitions

Acquired businesses supplied about 1.30 billion pesos (about US$69 million) of the 1.66 billion pesos (about US$89 million) revenue increase, our calculation from the filing. That is 456.4 million pesos (about US$24 million) from the US commercial operations, which we profiled in How Cancun’s Airport Group Ended Up Running the Shops at LAX and JFK, and 841.2 million pesos (about US$45 million) from Brazil and the other new airports in September.

Mexico revenue rose 3.1% to 6.68 billion pesos (about US$357 million) on a 32.4% jump in construction revenue, while without construction it fell 6.8% to 4.52 billion pesos (about US$242 million). Mexican EBITDA fell 9.5% to 3.16 billion pesos (about US$169 million).

Commercial revenue in Mexico, which covers shops, parking and similar income, fell 14.6% to 1.18 billion pesos (about US$63 million). ASUR links the drop mainly to lower passenger traffic.

Margins and Debt After the Brazil Deal

The adjusted EBITDA margin, which excludes construction revenue, fell to 60.3% from 66.7% a year earlier. Brazil and the other new airports added 313.2 million pesos (about US$17 million) of EBITDA in September, about 46% of their revenue excluding construction against about 70% in Mexico, our calculation.

On 1 September 2026 ASUR closed the purchase of CPC Aeroportos from Motiva for 5.1 billion reais (US$992.2 million), adding 17 airports in Brazil and one each in Costa Rica, Curaçao and Ecuador. We covered the agreement in Motiva Hands 20 Airports to Mexico’s Asur in a Closed Deal.

Total debt stood at 69.97 billion pesos (about US$3.74 billion) on 30 September, up from 27.49 billion pesos (about US$1.47 billion) at the end of 2025, while cash was 20.09 billion pesos (about US$1.07 billion). Net debt was 2.6 times trailing EBITDA against 0.2 times a year earlier, and interest cover fell to 5.2 times from 12.8 times.

Interest expense almost doubled, rising 95.6% to 871.7 million pesos (about US$47 million), which ASUR ties to two Mexican loans, US lease liabilities and the Brazil debt. A foreign-exchange loss of 803.5 million pesos (about US$43 million) was largely offset by a 719.2 million pesos (about US$38 million) gain on currency forward contracts.

New Bonds and Special Dividends

On 8 October ASUR announced that its Cancún airport subsidiary had placed US$900 million of senior notes at 6.711% due 2031 and US$900 million at 7.491% due 2036, rated BBB by S&P Global Ratings and BBB+ by Fitch Ratings. ASUR said the proceeds repaid in full the US$1.23 billion bridge loan for the Brazil deal and the 6.39 billion pesos (about US$342 million) bridge loan for the US airports, plus a 675 million pesos (about US$36 million) Santander loan and 3.0 billion pesos (about US$160 million) of a BBVA México loan.

Shareholders approved on 20 August two extraordinary cash dividends of 10 pesos per share (about US$0.53) each, payable on 30 November and 23 December 2026. With ten shares to an ADS, that is 100 pesos (about US$5.35) per ADS for each payment by our arithmetic, before any fees or taxes, and the dollar value will depend on the exchange rate at payment.

What It Means for You

For ASR shareholders the ASUR Q3 results combine revenue growth bought through acquisitions, falling Mexican traffic and a debt load that is far higher than a year ago, offset by two special dividends. This is a reading of the filing and not investment advice.

Travellers should note that these figures count passengers, not fares or cancellations, and Cancún still handled 6.13 million passengers in the quarter. Our What to Do in Cancún in October 2026 and Cancún city guide cover planning for the trip.

For wider context on the economy that feeds these airports, see our Mexico 2026 explained guide and our guide to who holds power in Mexico. Both place Mexican airports in the wider economy.

What Is Not Known

The ASUR Q3 results release does not say why international traffic at Cancún fell, or how much came from airline capacity, prices or traveller demand. It also does not break out passengers by country of origin, so the share of US travellers is not known.

Brazil and the other new airports counted for only one month, so a full-quarter picture of their margins and traffic is not yet available. The filing gives no full-year guidance that we found.

We did not review management’s remarks on the 23 October investor call, and the share-price reaction is not known. Dollar figures for pesos are our conversions at the Bank of Mexico rate of 22 October.

Frequently Asked Questions

What do the ASUR Q3 results show?

Revenue rose 18.9% to 10.42 billion pesos (about US$557 million) and net income rose 4.4% to 2.31 billion pesos (about US$123 million). Passengers fell 1.2% to 20.9 million.

How many passengers did Cancún airport lose?

Cancún passengers fell 8.8% to 6.13 million in the quarter, with international passengers down 13.3%. Domestic passengers fell 1.8%.

Why did ASUR revenue rise if traffic fell?

Acquisitions supplied about 1.30 billion pesos (about US$69 million) of the 1.66 billion pesos (about US$89 million) increase, our calculation from the filing. Construction revenue also rose 43.0%, though it is matched by construction costs.

How much debt does ASUR carry after the Brazil deal?

Total debt was 69.97 billion pesos (about US$3.74 billion) on 30 September, and net debt was 2.6 times trailing EBITDA. In October ASUR placed US$1.8 billion of bonds and used the proceeds to repay bridge loans.

Is ASUR paying special dividends?

Shareholders approved two extraordinary dividends of 10 pesos per share (about US$0.53) each, payable on 30 November and 23 December 2026. That equals about US$5.35 per ADS for each payment at the 22 October rate.

Where can I read ASUR’s own report?

ASUR furnished its 3Q26 results to the US Securities and Exchange Commission on 22 October 2026 and posts the full earnings release on its investor website. The release is in pesos, with dollar figures at ASUR’s own rate.

World.title: Chile Renews China Swap at US$7.5 Billion
World.content:
Aerial view of the Port of San Antonio on the central coast of Chile. (Photo: Serpentus, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

CHILE · CENTRAL BANK

Key Facts — The country Chile, a leading copper and lithium producer, runs its currency and foreign reserves through the Banco Central de Chile, its central bank.

— Why it matters A standing back-up line of about US$7.5 billion gives Chile an extra cushion if markets seize up, and it links its finances more closely to China, its main trading partner.

— Why now The central bank announced on Friday 23 October 2026 that it had renewed the agreement, which has run since 2015, for five more years.

— What happened The Banco Central de Chile renewed its renminbi-peso currency swap agreement with the People’s Bank of China, the central bank of China.

— The numbers The line is worth about US$7.5 billion, runs for five years and has a precautionary purpose, so it does not change Chile’s international reserves unless it is activated.

— What it means for you US investors and companies with Chilean exposure see a back-up line confirmed for five more years, with no stated change to reserves, interest rates or the peso.

— Still open The size of the line in yuan and pesos, whether it was ever drawn, and whether the new terms differ from the old ones.

— Power Index Chile ranks 3rd of 14 in Chile ranks 3rd of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 63.6 points (October 2026 edition).

Chile has renewed its China swap for five years, the central bank said on Friday 23 October 2026, keeping open a renminbi-peso line worth about US$7.5 billion. The agreement with the People’s Bank of China has been in place since 2015 and is described as a precaution that does not change Chile’s reserves unless it is used.

For US readers the news matters because Chile supplies copper and lithium to world industry and China is its main trading partner, so part of the safety net behind the Chilean peso sits with the Chinese central bank. It also arrives while Chile talks to Washington over tariffs, which we covered in Chile Admits Not All Goods Regain Zero US Tariff.

The central bank said the resources can be used, if requested, to help the stability of financial markets should that be needed. The versions of the announcement we found give only the dollar equivalent of about US$7.5 billion and no size in yuan or pesos.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Chile ranks 3rd of 14 with 63.6 points. Strongest pillar: state capacity & security (86); weakest: diplomatic & cultural influence (38). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

How the Renewed China Swap Works

A currency swap line is an agreement between two central banks to exchange their currencies if one side asks. CNN Chile described such lines as a back-up of foreign-currency liquidity that can be activated in episodes of market stress.

In this deal the two currencies are the Chinese renminbi, also called the yuan, and the Chilean peso. The central bank said the agreement has a precautionary purpose, so it does not change international reserves while the line stays unused.

Diario Financiero wrote that the agreement has aimed since it was first signed to ease payments in renminbi inside Chile. It said this lowers transaction costs for financing and foreign-trade payments denominated in the Chinese currency.

The same paper added that the agreement also seeks to let investors buy instruments denominated in renminbi directly in the Chinese market. That is a second stated purpose, besides the safety net.

Putting the US$7.5 Billion in Context

BioBioChile put Chile’s international reserves at about US$53.5 billion in September 2026, with more than US$30 billion of that held in US dollars. On that basis the swap line equals roughly 14% of reserves, which is our own calculation and not a central bank figure.

The line is not part of those reserves unless it is activated, so the comparison shows scale and not a sum. The central bank itself says that only activation would change the reserve level.

BioBioChile also noted that Chile holds a flexible credit line from the International Monetary Fund. That line was renewed in August 2026 at about US$11.8 billion, or about 8.7 billion special drawing rights, and the paper says the central bank has never used it.

Adding the two lines gives about US$19.3 billion of standby backing, our own sum of two arrangements with different counterparties and conditions. The central bank describes the China swap as precautionary, and no source reviewed says Chile is under market stress.

Not the Same as the AFP Swaps

BioBioChile stressed that this currency swap is a different instrument from the interest-rate swaps that have drawn attention because of a failed bet by the pension fund managers. Those managers, known as AFPs, run Chile’s mandatory private pension savings.

No source reviewed links the renewal to those contracts. Readers who see the word swap in Chilean headlines this week should treat the two stories as separate.

What the China Swap Means for Chile and China

CNN Chile called the renewal relevant because China is the main trading partner of the Chilean economy. The agreement dates from 2015, so the renewal extends an arrangement that both central banks have kept for about a decade.

Our guide Who Runs Chile’s Economy, the Key Players in 2026 explains who sets policy at the central bank and the finance ministry. Our explainer Chile in Latin America, Its Role, Weight and Alliances puts the China link in a regional frame.

What It Means for You

For US investors in Chilean bonds, New York-listed Chilean shares and copper or lithium producers, the renewal confirms that a back-up line is in place for five more years. The central bank says it does not change reserves, and nothing in the announcement points to a change in interest rates or the peso.

Importers and exporters that deal with Chilean firms in renminbi may benefit from the cheaper settlement the agreement is meant to provide, according to Diario Financiero. Dollar trade, which most US companies use, is not directly affected.

Visitors and residents see no direct change in prices or exchange rates from the announcement. Our Santiago city guide and our Chile news page cover daily costs and the latest developments.

What Is Not Known

The versions of the announcement we found give no size in yuan or pesos, no earlier size for comparison and no expiry date beyond the five-year term. The central bank’s own website blocked automated access, so the text rests on copies of its release carried by Diario Estrategia and Radio Nuevo Mundo and on reporting by three Chilean outlets.

It is not known whether the line was ever drawn between 2015 and now, and the sources reviewed do not say. They also do not say whether the new terms differ from the old ones, for example on limits or pricing.

No source reviewed says why the renewal came on 23 October or whether it relates to Chile’s trade talks with the United States. Any such link would be speculation.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Chile’s central bank announce on 23 October 2026?

It renewed its renminbi-peso currency swap agreement with the People’s Bank of China for five years. The line is worth about US$7.5 billion and has run since 2015.

What is a central bank currency swap?

It is an agreement between two central banks to exchange their currencies if one of them asks. Chile’s line is precautionary and does not change its reserves unless it is activated.

Does the China swap change Chile’s reserves?

Not while the line stays unused, according to the central bank. Reserves would change only if the line were activated.

How does the China swap compare with Chile’s IMF credit line?

The IMF flexible credit line, renewed in August 2026, is about US$11.8 billion against about US$7.5 billion for the China swap. The central bank calls the China line precautionary, and BioBioChile says the IMF line has never been used.

What does the renewal mean for US readers?

It confirms a back-up line for a key copper and lithium supplier and ties its finances to its main trading partner. It does not by itself change reserves, interest rates or the peso.

Sources: Banco Central de Chile, announcement of 23 October 2026; Diario Estrategia, 23 October 2026; Radio Nuevo Mundo, 23 October 2026; Diario Financiero, 23 October 2026; CNN Chile, 23 October 2026; BioBioChile, 23 October 2026.

World.title: Chile Lithium Price Falls to US$16,050
World.content:
Salt crust at the southern end of the Salar de Atacama, near the lithium operations, June 2005 (Photo: Bachelot Pierre J-P, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

CHILE · LITHIUM

Key Facts — The country Chile, in South America, is one of the world’s largest lithium producers, with brine operations on the Salar de Atacama run by SQM with state copper company Codelco and by Albemarle of the United States.

— Why it matters Lithium is the key metal in electric-vehicle and grid-storage batteries, and its price sets the income of producers and of Chile’s development agency Corfo.

— Why now The price fell to US$16,050 a tonne on Tuesday 20 October 2026, the lowest daily level since 20 January.

— What happened The October average to 20 October was US$17,513 a tonne of lithium carbonate equivalent, down from US$19,368 in September and US$21,674 in May.

— The numbers The 2026 average is US$19,009 a tonne, January averaged US$15,735, and one consultancy sees US$15,000 to US$21,000 for 2027.

— What it means for you Lower lithium costs should ease the bill for battery and car makers, while producers such as Albemarle and SQM earn less per tonne.

— Still open Whether prices keep sliding as Chinese electric-vehicle demand is judged and as idle mines return, or settle near US$16,000.

— Power Index Chile ranks 3rd of 14 in Chile ranks 3rd of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 63.6 points (October 2026 edition).

The Chile lithium price fell to US$16,050 a tonne on Tuesday 20 October 2026, its lowest since 20 January, according to Banco Central de Chile data that the Santiago newspaper La Tercera reported on Friday 23 October. The October average to that date was US$17,513 a tonne of lithium carbonate equivalent, the standard unit for comparing lithium products, down from US$19,368 in September.

For US readers the fall matters because Chile supplies much of the lithium that goes into electric-vehicle and grid-storage batteries, and a US company, Albemarle, produces from the same salt flat as the Chilean firm SQM. A cheaper input should help battery and car makers, while it trims the income of the producers and of the Chilean state, which collects payments from them.

We have followed the policy side of Chile’s lithium story in Chile Has 3 Lithium Deals at Audit Office and Chile Plans Five New Lithium Tenders. Those pieces ask who may produce lithium in Chile, while this one covers what the metal now sells for.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Chile ranks 3rd of 14 with 63.6 points. Strongest pillar: state capacity & security (86); weakest: diplomatic & cultural influence (38). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

How the Chile Lithium Price Fell in October

La Tercera, using central bank data through Tuesday 20 October, says the October average is returning to the levels seen in January. January averaged US$15,735 a tonne, which it describes as the lowest month of 2026.

On 20 October the daily price was US$16,050, the lowest since 20 January, when it stood at US$15,950. May was the best month of the year at US$21,674, and La Tercera describes a steady, mild decline since then, with October showing a sharper retreat.

January 2026 average: US$15,735 a tonne

May 2026 average: US$21,674 a tonne

June 2026 average: US$20,825 a tonne

September 2026 average: US$19,368 a tonne

October 2026 average to 20 October: US$17,513 a tonne

The average for 2026 so far is US$19,009 a tonne. That is still well above 2025, since Cochilco, Chile’s state copper commission, which also tracks lithium, put its August spot price 106% above the 2025 average.

Why Lithium Prices Are Sliding

Patricio Faúndez, the economics lead at the firm GEM, told La Tercera the fall reflects a downward revision of expected battery-demand growth, especially in China. He said domestic sales of electric and plug-in hybrid vehicles there fell about 17% year on year in September 2026, while exports of those vehicles keep growing.

Data from the China Passenger Car Association, relayed by the trade site CnEVPost on Monday 12 October, fit that picture. New-energy vehicle retail sales were 1.084 million in September, down 16.7% from a year earlier and the ninth straight monthly fall, while exports jumped 163.5% to 558,000 vehicles.

Lithium carbonate futures on the Guangzhou exchange fell 11.8% on Monday 12 October to their lowest since 17 December 2025, the biggest one-day drop since March, the Chilean mining outlet REDIMIN reported. It linked the move to a 9 October understanding between the European Union and China to limit exports of Chinese hybrid cars to Europe, which raised doubts about battery-material demand in 2027.

That Chinese futures price is a different series from the Chilean central bank data, so the two are not directly comparable, but they point the same way. GEM also says suspended capacity, such as the Jianxiawo mine of the Chinese battery maker CATL, could return, so the market is adjusting its supply and demand balance for 2027.

Cochilco had already described a moderate correction from mid-May. Its spot carbonate price was US$19,525 a tonne on 19 August, 12.2% below 13 May but 106% above the 2025 average, and it said upward revisions of the 2027 and 2028 surpluses limit room for a lasting rise, especially if mine restarts go ahead.

It offers potassium nitrate, sodium nitrate, specialty blends, and other specialty fertilizers under the Ultrasol, Qrop, Speedfol, Allganic, Ultrasoline, Prop, and Prohydric…

What Lower Prices Mean for Chile’s Budget

Chile’s development agency Corfo earns lithium income from quarterly payments by Novandino Litio, the joint company of SQM and Codelco, and by Albemarle, which both operate on the Salar de Atacama. Those payments reached US$791 million in the first half of 2026, up 427% from US$150 million a year earlier, La Tercera reported in August.

Novandino Litio paid US$670 million of that total, or 85%, and Albemarle paid US$121 million, up 116%. La Tercera tied the jump to the better prices earlier in the year, when the central bank series averaged US$18,733 a tonne in the first half, 114% above the same period of 2025.

In its Friday report, La Tercera says the latest Public Finance Report estimates that Corfo will receive US$1.289 billion of lithium income in 2026, a rise of 252% on 2025. The article does not say whether the lower October prices will change that projection.

What GEM Expects for 2027

Faúndez told La Tercera it is hard to foresee an immediate stabilisation because lithium remains a volatile market. He said some downward pressure could persist in the short term.

He named two possible supports for a recovery, supply restrictions in Zimbabwe and growth in energy-storage uses other than electric vehicles. GEM’s estimate for the 2027 price is about US$15,000 to US$21,000 a tonne, compared with US$17,513 so far this October.

What It Means for You

Battery makers, carmakers and energy-storage developers in the United States buy lithium products priced on these benchmarks, so a lower price should ease input costs, although retail electric-vehicle prices depend on many other factors. Investors who follow Albemarle of the United States or SQM of Chile can read the same price as pressure on revenue per tonne.

Our guides Chile Natural Resources Explained 2026 and Foreign Powers and Investors in Chile 2026 explain who holds Chile’s lithium rights and who invests there. The Lithium Triangle guide places Chile beside Argentina and Bolivia.

Travellers and residents in Santiago feel little direct effect from a lithium price move, but mining income shapes public finances, and our Santiago expat city guide covers day-to-day costs. The budget link runs through the Corfo payments, which La Tercera ties to lithium prices.

What Is Not Known

The Banco Central de Chile statistics database could not be read for this article because its site loads the series only through scripts, so the price figures rest on La Tercera’s reading of that data. Cochilco and the Guangzhou futures point the same way, but they are different price series.

It is not known whether the October low will hold or whether prices will keep falling into November. No consensus forecast for the rest of 2026 was found.

The sources do not say how much of the fall comes from weaker Chinese demand and how much from expected extra supply. The Public Finance Report behind the US$1.289 billion figure for Corfo was not opened, so that projection is attributed to La Tercera.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much did the Chile lithium price fall in October?

The October average to 20 October was US$17,513 a tonne, down from US$19,368 in September. On 20 October the daily price was US$16,050, the lowest since 20 January.

Why is the lithium price falling?

GEM’s economics lead says expectations for battery-demand growth, especially in China, have been cut. Chinese domestic electric-vehicle sales fell 16.7% in September, according to the China Passenger Car Association data relayed by CnEVPost.

Is lithium still more expensive than a year ago?

Yes, the 2026 average of US$19,009 a tonne is well above 2025. Cochilco put its August spot price 106% above the 2025 average.

How does the lithium price affect Chile?

The state agency Corfo receives payments from Novandino Litio and Albemarle, which were US$791 million in the first half of 2026. Those payments rose sharply when prices were higher.

What does the price fall mean for US readers?

It should lower input costs for US battery and car makers. It also pressures revenue per tonne for producers such as Albemarle and SQM.

Sources: La Tercera, 23 October 2026; La Tercera, 5 August 2026; Cochilco, lithium spot price note; CnEVPost on China Passenger Car Association data, 12 October 2026; REDIMIN, 12 October 2026.

World.title: Mexico Arrests Coco Ranas and 3 Others
World.content:
Downtown Culiacán, the capital of Sinaloa state, at night. File photo, 2010. (Photo: Basilio Briceño, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

MEXICO · SECURITY

Key Facts — The country Mexico is the United States’ southern neighbour, and Sinaloa state is home to the cartel that Washington lists as a terrorist organisation.

— Why it matters The Sinaloa Cartel is a main target of US fentanyl and terrorism policy, so arrests of its local commanders feed US-Mexico security cooperation.

— Why now The Security Cabinet confirmed the arrest on Thursday 22 October 2026, a day after the Defence Ministry says it took place.

— What happened Federal and state forces arrested Orlando “N”, alias El Coco Ranas, and three other men in the Lomas del Sol district of Culiacán on Wednesday 21 October.

— The numbers Officers seized four long guns, 25 magazines, 1,338 rounds, two 40 mm grenades, 50 suspected fentanyl pills and 200 suspected cocaine doses.

— What it means for you US readers see Mexican pressure on a US-designated terrorist group, while travellers to Sinaloa should expect continued heavy federal deployment.

— Still open Which charges the federal prosecutor files, and whether the 2016 ambush allegation ever reaches a court.

— Power Index Mexico ranks 2nd of 14 in Mexico ranks 2nd of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 71.4 points (October 2026 edition).

Mexico’s Security Cabinet confirmed on Thursday 22 October 2026 the arrest of Orlando “N”, known as El Coco Ranas, in Culiacán, the capital of Sinaloa state. Federal officials call him the leader of Los Ranas, a cell aligned with the Los Chapitos faction of the Sinaloa Cartel.

For US readers the arrest matters because Washington designated the Sinaloa Cartel a foreign terrorist organisation, in a notice published in the Federal Register on 20 February 2025. The sources reviewed do not link this suspect to any US case, so the US angle is the cartel, not the man.

The Defence Ministry, known as Defensa, says the arrest took place on Wednesday 21 October and links the suspect to a 2016 ambush that killed five soldiers. These are official allegations that no court has tested, and the letter N is the initial Mexican authorities use in place of a suspect’s surname.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Mexico ranks 2nd of 14 with 71.4 points. Strongest pillar: economic relationships (90); weakest: state capacity & security (46). Alignment group: Hedging. Watch21 homicides per 100,000; organised crime at 7.7 of 10. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

Our earlier reports on Sinaloa Keeps 20,000 Federal Forces Deployed and Mexico Detains Kin of US-Wanted Cartel Boss give the background. This arrest adds a named local commander to a pattern of raids in and around Culiacán.

What Mexico’s Security Cabinet Announced

The Security Cabinet, which coordinates Mexico’s federal security agencies, said military intelligence work led Defensa, the civilian Security Ministry and the National Guard to detain Orlando “N” and three more people, in coordination with Sinaloa state police. Its statement, translated here, calls him the leader of the cell “Los Ranas”, aligned with the “Los Chapitos” faction of the Pacific Cartel, a name Mexican officials use for the Sinaloa Cartel.

The statement also calls him a generator of violence in the northern zone of the Sinaloa capital. It names no charges and gives neither his full name nor his age.

Los Chapitos is one faction of the Sinaloa Cartel, and the statement describes Los Ranas as a cell aligned with it. Our reading of the sources is that the cell operates mainly in north Culiacán, where the arrest took place.

How Coco Ranas Was Arrested in Culiacán

Four men were detained in Lomas del Sol, a district in the north of Culiacán, on Wednesday 21 October, according to the Defence Ministry account carried by El Financiero and Extraoficial. The operation involved the National Guard’s special reaction and intervention force, the army and the state police’s special operations group, known as GOES.

All four detainees, the seized items and a vehicle were handed to the federal prosecutor’s office, the FGR, in Culiacán. The FGR will continue its investigation and determine the legal status of the four men.

None of the sources reviewed reported any charges as of Friday 23 October. As with any suspect in Mexico, the four are presumed innocent until a court rules.

What Officers Seized

Sinaloa’s state security ministry listed one 5.56 x 45 mm rifle, one M70 rifle in 7.62 x 39 mm and two 5.56 x 45 mm carbines, with 25 magazines for long guns. It also listed 540 rounds of 5.56 mm, 588 linked rounds of the same calibre and 210 rounds of 7.62 mm, which adds up to 1,338 rounds.

The haul included two 40 mm grenades, about 12 grams of suspected fentanyl in 50 pills and about 113 grams of suspected cocaine in 200 doses. El Economista also counted four tactical vests with ballistic plates, and officials call the drugs suspected until laboratory analysis confirms them.

The drug quantities are small, so the weapons and the suspect’s alleged rank are the weightier parts of the case. That assessment is ours and not a statement from the authorities.

The 2016 Ambush Allegation

Defensa says Orlando “N” took part in an ambush on army personnel on 30 September 2016, in which five soldiers died and ten were injured. This is an official allegation, and the sources reviewed do not say whether he faces a charge for it.

A 2016 role raises a question the sources do not answer, because El Economista, citing preliminary information, gave his age as 25, which would have made him about 15 at the time. We cannot reconcile the two figures, and the age remains unconfirmed.

Two Accounts of How the Arrest Began

Sinaloa’s state security ministry first said an anonymous tip to the 089 emergency line reported armed men at a house in Lomas del Sol. Officers arrived, saw the occupants of a vehicle try to flee and stopped them, it said.

The federal account says the arrest came from military intelligence work, and Noroeste noted that this differs from the 089 account. On Friday 23 October the head of the state security ministry, Sinhú Téllez López, said Central Military Intelligence had flagged the address as one earlier occupied by people of this kind.

The two accounts can both be true, since a tip can lead officers to an address that intelligence already knew. The sources reviewed do not settle which came first.

What It Means for You

The arrest shows Mexican forces going after a cell of a cartel that Washington has designated a terrorist organisation. It does not by itself show any change in fentanyl flows or in Sinaloa’s violence.

Travellers should read the arrest as a sign that federal forces remain active in Culiacán, where security operations can change local conditions at short notice. Our guide Mexico Security and Crime Explained 2026 covers regional risks, and our Mexico City expat guide covers daily safety in the capital.

Readers who follow US-Mexico relations can place the arrest in the wider security relationship described in Mexico Geopolitics 2026, US Tariffs and China. One arrest does not settle that picture, and the next steps by the FGR will show how far the case goes.

What Is Not Known

The suspect’s full name and age are not officially given, and outlets differ, with El Economista saying he first gave officers a different name. Other outlets print other full names, so we use only the initial that the Security Cabinet used.

El Economista says, citing preliminary information, that the man was taken to a hospital under guard, but no authority has detailed his health. The FGR has not published charges, and no link to any US case has been reported.

The sources do not say how the 2016 allegation will be pursued, or whether other members of Los Ranas remain at large. They also do not say how large the cell is or whether the arrest changes the balance inside the Sinaloa Cartel.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is El Coco Ranas?

Mexican authorities identify him as Orlando “N”, the leader of Los Ranas, a cell aligned with the Los Chapitos faction of the Sinaloa Cartel. His full name has not been officially published.

When and where was he arrested?

The Defence Ministry says he was arrested on Wednesday 21 October 2026 in the Lomas del Sol district of Culiacán. The Security Cabinet confirmed it on Thursday 22 October.

What did officers seize?

Officers seized four long guns, 25 magazines, 1,338 rounds, two 40 mm grenades, tactical gear, 50 suspected fentanyl pills and 200 suspected cocaine doses. The drugs are called suspected until laboratory analysis confirms them.

Is he wanted in the United States?

The sources reviewed do not link him to any US case. The Sinaloa Cartel itself was designated a foreign terrorist organisation in a notice published in the Federal Register on 20 February 2025.

What happens next?

The FGR decides which charges to bring after it reviews the case file. The suspect is presumed innocent until a court rules otherwise.

Sources: Ríodoce, Security Cabinet statement, 22 October 2026; Extraoficial, Defensa account; El Financiero; El Economista; Línea Directa; Noroeste; Federal Register, 20 February 2025.

World.title: El Salvador Troops Reach Haiti to Find 4
World.content:
Guatemalan and Salvadoran troops of the earlier Multinational Security Support Mission arrive at Port-au-Prince airport, 3 January 2025 (File photo: U.S. Embassy Haiti, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons)

EL SALVADOR · HAITI

Key Facts — The country El Salvador is a Central American country of about 6 million people, led by President Nayib Bukele, and it sends troops to the UN-authorised Gang Suppression Force in Haiti.

— Why it matters The United States has publicly promised to bring the four men home, and the case tests a multinational force that Washington backs on its Caribbean doorstep.

— Why now Salvadoran reinforcements reached Port-au-Prince on Thursday 22 October 2026, four days after the four aviation technicians were seized on Sunday 18 October.

— What happened The force confirmed the arrival of a contingent from El Salvador, and the first group is put at 100 or more special forces soldiers, with more expected.

— The numbers Four men are missing, the force has just over 2,000 personnel against about 5,500 planned, and no group has claimed the kidnapping.

— What it means for you Americans in Haiti are told to avoid the Santo area of Croix-des-Bouquets, and the outcome will show whether the US-backed force can protect its own troops.

— Still open Where the four are held, which gang has them, and whether Bukele’s threat of a harsher operation or a negotiated release comes first.

El Salvador troops began arriving in Haiti on Thursday 22 October 2026 to help search for four Salvadoran aviation technicians who were seized by gunmen on Sunday 18 October. The Gang Suppression Force, the UN-authorised mission the four serve in, confirmed the arrival, but no official source has said where the men are or whether they are alive.

For US readers the case matters because the United States has taken a public stake in it. US ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz told the Security Council on Monday 19 October that Washington believes the four survived and will bring them home, and the US embassy in Haiti told Americans that day to avoid the ambush area.

We covered the ambush in Salvadoran Soldiers Missing in Haiti and Bukele’s announcement of a rescue operation in El Salvador Haiti Rescue Bid for 4 Troops. This article covers what is new since then, which is the arrival of El Salvador troops on the ground and the first signs of how the search may be run.

El Salvador Troops Reach the Haitian Capital

The Gang Suppression Force said in a post on the night of Thursday that a contingent from El Salvador had arrived in Port-au-Prince to support search and security operations in the Plaine du Cul-de-Sac, the plain north-east of the capital, according to the Salvadoran daily elsalvador.com. The force gave no number and urged residents of Santo and nearby communities to stay away from the areas where operations are under way.

Le Nouvelliste, a Haitian daily, wrote that more than 100 soldiers arrived on Thursday and that more reinforcements are expected, citing two sources close to the matter. Elsalvador.com relayed a report by the Miami Herald that put the first group at 100 special forces soldiers, a figure the force has not confirmed.

Diario Libre of Santo Domingo wrote that another 100 soldiers could follow later, but said it is not officially confirmed that 200 troops are in Haiti. The Salvadoran government has not published a headcount in the sources we reviewed, so the figure of 100 or more rests on press reports.

What Happened on 18 October

The Salvadoran armed forces said the four were aviation technicians of Task Force Libertad II, a Salvadoran contingent in the force, returning to camp in an armoured vehicle in Santo, part of Croix-des-Bouquets about 12 km (7.5 miles) from the capital. Gunmen hit the vehicle with gunfire and explosives, it caught fire, the four got out, and contact was lost, Diario Libre reported on 23 October.

Bukele said the four are not combatants but aviation technicians whose main job is medical evacuation, and that they were taken while returning from buying food at a market. He and the Haitian government describe the case as a kidnapping, while the Salvadoran military statement spoke of men whose whereabouts are unknown.

Haitian police, the force and special units launched an offensive in the plain at about 5:00 local time on Wednesday 21 October, hours before Bukele spoke, Diario Libre wrote, citing Haitian media. It focused on positions of the 400 Mawozo gang in Butte Boyer and Cité Doudoune, and Diario Libre cautioned that the timing does not show every operation is a response to the abduction.

Haiti’s prime minister, Alix Didier Fils-Aimé, held a high-level security meeting on Wednesday, and his office called the release of the four an absolute priority. It said all necessary resources are being mobilised in coordination with the force.

Who Holds the Four Men

No group has claimed responsibility, and the sources we reviewed do not establish which gang holds the men. Le Nouvelliste first pointed to the Chen Mechan gang, citing government sources, while Diario Libre quoted a UN human rights expert, William O’Neill, as telling the Wall Street Journal that Chen Mechan led the ambush with support from 400 Mawozo, two gangs that both operate in Croix-des-Bouquets.

Diario Libre also relayed a Wall Street Journal report of 23 October, based on one person involved in the rescue effort, that Salvadoran officials are trying to negotiate the release before turning to a harsher military response, and that no gang has demanded a ransom. We could not confirm this at a second source, and the Salvadoran government has not commented on it in the coverage we reviewed.

That sits beside Bukele’s warning of Wednesday 21 October, in which he demanded the four be returned alive and unharmed and said that if not, what is coming would be far worse than the current operation. He added that if they are freed, everything will go back to the way it was before the kidnapping, according to the Jamaica Gleaner’s account of his statement.

On Friday 23 October Bukele answered critics on X who had warned that the mission could end in a military defeat, writing that those who call the Haitian gangs unbeatable would change their tune once God grants victory, according to elsalvador.com. His post gave no operational detail, and it does not say whether the four men are alive.

The US Role and the Force Behind the Mission

Waltz told the Security Council that gunmen fired hundreds of rounds and used explosives against the armoured vehicle, and that Washington believes the four survived but remain missing, Diario Libre reported. He told the men they are not forgotten and that the United States stands with them and will bring them home, which is a promise of support and not a confirmation that they are alive.

The Gang Suppression Force is a UN-authorised mission that replaced the earlier Kenya-led mission, and Diario Libre says it has just over 2,000 personnel against about 5,500 planned. The Jamaica Gleaner lists El Salvador, Chad, Jamaica and Guatemala among the contributors and says El Salvador passed a law in early October extending its participation by a year and widening its role beyond medical evacuations.

The Gleaner carried the story on 23 October under the headline “President launches mission to rescue four soldiers kidnapped in Haiti”, and the president in question is Bukele, not a Jamaican leader. Jamaica appears only as one of the countries with troops in the force, and our explainer Jamaica Geopolitics Explained 2026 shows how it fits into Caribbean security.

What It Means for You

Haiti lies on the United States’ Caribbean doorstep, and its gang violence feeds migration and regional security worries that reach Florida and Washington. The US embassy told Americans on Monday 19 October to avoid Santo and Croix-des-Bouquets, where roads may be blocked and clashes between gangs and security forces were continuing.

The case also tests whether a force at less than half its planned strength can protect its own troops while Haiti prepares for its first general election in more than a decade, the Jamaica Gleaner notes. If the four are freed, it would strengthen the case for the mission, and if they are not, pressure will grow on El Salvador troops and other contributors to escalate.

Our guides El Salvador Explained 2026, El Salvador Geopolitics Explained 2026 and Haiti Geopolitics Explained 2026 explain who runs the country sending the troops. They also show why Haiti sits at the centre of Caribbean security.

What Is Not Known

As of Friday 23 October, no official source had said where the four men are, whether any is wounded, or which gang holds them. Early reports spoke of five missing, but the Salvadoran military and later coverage say four, and we use four.

The size of the Salvadoran reinforcement is not officially confirmed, and the reports of a second group of 100 are unverified. We could not open the force’s own post, so its statement is quoted through elsalvador.com and Diario Libre.

Whether talks with the gangs are under way rests on one report, and it is not known whether Bukele’s threat of a larger operation will be carried out. The Jamaica Gleaner account of Wednesday 21 October said the force was still fighting gangs in the area, and no result of the search by El Salvador troops has been published.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did El Salvador send troops to Haiti?

It sent a contingent to join the search for four aviation technicians who were seized in an ambush on Sunday 18 October. The reinforcements arrived in Port-au-Prince on Thursday 22 October, the Gang Suppression Force said.

How many Salvadoran troops arrived in Haiti?

Le Nouvelliste put the number at more than 100, and a Miami Herald report relayed by elsalvador.com said 100 special forces soldiers. The force and the Salvadoran government have not confirmed a figure.

Who is holding the four Salvadorans?

No gang has claimed the kidnapping, and the sources we reviewed do not establish who holds the men. Chen Mechan and 400 Mawozo, two gangs active in Croix-des-Bouquets, have been named in coverage of the ambush.

Is Jamaica rescuing the soldiers?

No, the soldiers are Salvadoran and the president who launched the operation is El Salvador’s Nayib Bukele. Jamaica is one of the countries with troops in the Gang Suppression Force, according to the Jamaica Gleaner.

What is the United States doing about it?

US ambassador Mike Waltz told the UN Security Council on 19 October that Washington believes the four survived and will bring them home. The US embassy in Haiti also told Americans to avoid the ambush area.

Sources: elsalvador.com, 22 October 2026; Diario Libre, 23 October 2026; Diario Libre, 23 October 2026 (what is known); Diario Libre, 23 October 2026 (negotiation report); Le Nouvelliste, 22 October 2026; Diario Libre, 20 October 2026 (UN Security Council remarks); Diario Libre, 19 October 2026 (US embassy alert); Diario Libre, 22 October 2026 (offensive); Jamaica Gleaner, 23 October 2026; elsalvador.com, 23 October 2026 (Bukele reply); elsalvador.com, 22 October 2026 (what the four did).

World.title: Mexico Court Keeps 1 Charge in CIA Raid Case
World.content:
The state government palace in Chihuahua City, seat of the Chihuahua executive (File photo: Charlie MX, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

MEXICO · SECURITY

Key Facts — The country Mexico, the southern neighbour of the United States, runs criminal justice through federal prosecutors and separate state prosecutors in each state.

— Why it matters The case tests how far US agents may work with Mexican state police, while Washington talks of acting against cartels on land.

— Why now A Chihuahua judge ruled on Thursday 22 October 2026, and a federal hearing on the treason charge follows on Saturday 24 October.

— What happened In the CIA raid case, the judge kept the charge of improper exercise of public service against former Chihuahua attorney general César Jáuregui and found too little evidence for the second charge.

— The numbers Case file 3055/2026 covers the state charge, federal prosecutors say they made more than 100 investigative steps, and four people died on Sunday 19 April, two of them Americans.

— What it means for you US agencies, firms and investors with operations in Chihuahua may see closer Mexican federal scrutiny of any foreign security role.

— Still open Whether the federal court sends the treason case forward on Saturday 24 October, and whether any US ground action is under way.

— Power Index Mexico ranks 2nd of 14 in Mexico ranks 2nd of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 71.4 points (October 2026 edition).

A Mexican state judge on Thursday 22 October 2026 let prosecutors continue one charge against former Chihuahua attorney general César Jáuregui in the CIA raid case and found too little evidence for a second. The ruling comes a week after President Donald Trump said US action against cartels “on land” is “starting”.

For US readers the case shows how far Mexico will police the work of American agents on its soil. President Claudia Sheinbaum has said foreign agents may join ground operations only within the law, and said on Thursday 22 October that the two Americans had no permit for the operation and, as later became known, “were carrying weapons”, in Ámbito’s report of her remarks, translated here from Spanish.

A column in Vanguardia on Friday 23 October by Raymundo Riva Palacio argues that the April CIA presence shows Trump’s warning is already under way. That is his opinion, and the sources reviewed contain no official announcement of a US ground offensive in Mexico.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Mexico ranks 2nd of 14 with 71.4 points. Strongest pillar: economic relationships (90); weakest: state capacity & security (46). Alignment group: Hedging. Watch21 homicides per 100,000; organised crime at 7.7 of 10. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

Our earlier reports cover the arrest in “Chihuahua Ex-Prosecutor Held Over US Role”, the federal accusation in “Mexico Ex-Prosecutor Faces Up to 40 Years” and the reports in “Reports Name 2 CIA Officers Killed in Mexico”. This report covers what the state judge decided in the CIA raid case and what the sources establish about the US agents.

What the Chihuahua Judge Decided

The control judge found enough evidence to continue the charge of improper exercise of public service under case file 3055/2026, Vanguardia and El Informador reported on 22 October. The judge found no sufficient elements for the second charge, known as coalition of public servants.

The step is called vinculación a proceso, which lets prosecutors keep building a case but is not a finding of guilt. Jáuregui followed the hearing by video link from the Altiplano federal prison, where he is held on the federal case.

La Crónica de Hoy reported that the state case rests on the claim that Jáuregui allowed foreign agents to take part in dismantling a drug lab at El Pinal, work that belongs to federal authorities. His lawyer Héctor Villasana called the decision political and said the defence will appeal.

Villasana argued that nothing shows Jáuregui knew the Americans would join, beyond his post as attorney general and his meetings with the head of the state investigation agency. Jáuregui is presumed innocent on both the state and the federal case.

How the CIA Raid Case Reached This Point

State and army forces dismantled clandestine drug labs near El Pinal, in Morelos municipality in the Sierra Tarahumara, between 17 and 19 April. A vehicle returning from the operation fell into a ravine in the early hours of Sunday 19 April, Excelsior reported at the time.

Four people died: two members of the US Embassy staff, as Ambassador Ronald Johnson described them then, the director of Chihuahua’s state investigation agency and one of its officers. Mexican media later described the two Americans as CIA agents, and the column by Riva Palacio notes that the CIA has made no public statement on them.

State officers arrested Jáuregui on Saturday 17 October on Avenida La Cantera in Chihuahua City. At a state hearing on Sunday 18 October a judge let him stay free on conditions, including surrender of his migration documents, but federal agents detained him within minutes, Vanguardia reported.

Federal Attorney General Ernestina Godoy, who leads the prosecutor’s office FGR, said after the arrest that more than 100 investigative steps showed Jáuregui had allowed foreigners to take part without authorisation. She said that conflicts with the Constitution and the National Security Law, which bars states from taking powers reserved to the federal government, El Financiero reported on 18 October.

A federal judge ordered pretrial detention at the Altiplano prison on 21 October, La Silla Rota reported. A hearing set for 15:00 local time on Saturday 24 October decides whether the treason case formally proceeds.

What Is Established About US Agents

The federal case file, as described by Reforma and relayed by Vanguardia on 20 October, includes a state police officer who says he saw four English-speaking people in tactical gear, carrying weapons and wearing no insignia, at the raid site. Two videos show armed men entering the state investigation agency on 9 and 16 April, and the agency’s access log lists only one entry, for a named visitor, on 14 April.

The Defence Ministry told federal prosecutors that soldiers only provided perimeter security, yet a federal forensic report says state agents and the army found the lab together. These are allegations and findings in prosecution documents, not court rulings.

Sheinbaum has said that state prosecutors have no power to dismantle labs tied to federal crimes, Vanguardia reported on 22 October. She faulted Jáuregui not only for letting foreign agents join a ground operation against the law, but for how it was done, in her words translated from Spanish.

By contrast, the Senate approved in September the entry of 139 US soldiers of the 101st Airborne Division for joint exercises in Chihuahua from 20 to 30 September, El Financiero reported on 15 September. That vote, taken at the president’s request, shows the formal route for US troops to enter Mexico.

Trump’s Ground Warning in Context

At a White House lunch on Thursday 15 October, Trump said US forces have “not yet acted on land with full force, but that is starting”, in El Financiero’s Spanish-language account translated here. He added that cartels “govern Mexico”, that he has told Sheinbaum so, and that Mexico is not capable of acting against them right now.

He tied the remark to the US campaign against suspected drug boats at sea, which critics describe as extrajudicial killing. Mexico’s government insists that any foreign security work on its soil must be authorised and run through federal channels.

No source reviewed links the April CIA presence to a Trump order or to the land action he described. Riva Palacio draws that link in his column, and it remains his argument rather than an established fact.

The Sheinbaum and Campos Dispute

On Friday 23 October Sheinbaum said that at a private meeting on 19 September at Ciudad Juárez airport, Chihuahua Governor Maru Campos blamed the former attorney general, telling her “it was not me, it was the former prosecutor”, El Universal reported. Campos leads Chihuahua for the National Action Party (PAN), the conservative opposition party.

Campos denied that she accused him, and told Grupo Fórmula the president’s team already knew his role, El Universal reported. The two accounts conflict, and neither has been tested in court.

What It Means for You

US agencies and companies that work with Mexican state police now face a federal prosecution that treats unauthorised joint work as a possible crime against national security. Firms with plants or security contracts in Chihuahua, a border state next to Texas and New Mexico, may see closer federal scrutiny of any foreign security role.

Our guides Mexico Security and Crime Explained 2026 and Mexico Geopolitics 2026, US Tariffs and China set out how the cartel threat shapes US and Mexican policy. Readers who want to know who holds power in Mexico can read Who Dominates Mexico, Elites and Regions Explained, and our Mexico City guide covers daily life for visitors.

What Is Not Known

The federal case file has not been published, so the evidence behind the treason charge cannot be tested, and the judge’s written reasons for the state ruling were not available in the sources reviewed. The CIA has made no public statement on the two dead Americans, the column notes, and no US government comment on the Mexican prosecution appears in the sources reviewed.

It is not known whether the federal court will send the treason charge forward on Saturday 24 October, or whether the defence appeal of the state ruling will succeed. It is also not known whether any US ground operation is under way, because no official source reviewed says so.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did the Chihuahua judge decide in the CIA raid case?

On Thursday 22 October a state judge let prosecutors continue the charge of improper exercise of public service against César Jáuregui. The judge found too little evidence for the second charge, coalition of public servants.

Has César Jáuregui been convicted of treason?

Not yet. A federal judge ordered him held before trial on 21 October, and a hearing on Saturday 24 October decides whether that case formally proceeds.

Have US ground operations started in Mexico?

No official source reviewed says so. Trump said on 15 October that action on land is “starting”, and a columnist argues the April CIA case shows it has begun.

Who were the Americans who died in April?

Ambassador Ronald Johnson described the two as US Embassy staff, and Mexican media later called them CIA agents. The CIA has made no public statement on them, according to the Vanguardia column.

What happens next in the case?

The federal hearing on the treason charge is set for 15:00 local time on Saturday 24 October. The defence says it will appeal the state ruling.

Sources: Vanguardia, 22 October 2026; El Informador, 22 October 2026; La Crónica de Hoy, 22 October 2026; La Silla Rota, 21 October 2026; El Financiero, 18 October 2026; Vanguardia (Reforma), 20 October 2026; El Universal, 23 October 2026; El Universal, 23 October 2026 (Campos); El Financiero, 15 October 2026; El Financiero, 15 September 2026; Ámbito, 22 October 2026; Excelsior, 19 April 2026; Vanguardia, opinion column, 23 October 2026.

World.title: Venezuela’s 303bn Barrels Draw Expert Doubt
World.content:
A pumpjack in Lagunillas municipality, Zulia state, Venezuela, in 2012 (Photo: Rjcastillo, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

VENEZUELA · OIL

Key Facts — The country Venezuela, a South American oil exporter whose official proven reserves are the largest in the world, has been run by interim authorities since the capture of Nicolás Maduro in January 2026.

— Why it matters The United States says a deal with a Venezuelan oil company gives it majority control of more than 65 billion barrels of proven reserves, and that claim now faces independent doubt.

— Why now A wire-service report published on Thursday 22 October 2026 and carried by Venezuelan outlets on Thursday and Friday 23 October quotes about half a dozen experts who question the official reserve figures.

— What happened Analysts say the official 303 billion barrels rest on outdated data and that only 60 billion to 120 billion barrels can be produced under current conditions.

— The numbers One specialist puts the barrels that qualify as proven in the short term at 10 billion to 15 billion, against the White House figure of 65 billion.

— What it means for you US investors, refiners and drivers should treat the 65 billion barrel figure as a claim until the technical data is published.

— Still open Whether the White House or the company will publish the method behind the 65 billion barrels, and how much of it can be produced.

— Power Index Venezuela ranks 13th of 14 in Venezuela ranks 13th of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 27.0 points (October 2026 edition).

Venezuela oil reserves of 303 billion barrels, the largest on paper anywhere, are being questioned by independent analysts just as the United States builds a deal on 65 billion barrels of Venezuelan crude. A report by the Associated Press, published on Thursday 22 October 2026 and carried by Venezuelan outlets that day and on Friday 23 October, quotes about half a dozen experts who put the barrels that can realistically be produced under current conditions at 60 billion to 120 billion.

For US readers the stakes are the White House claim of 31 August 2026 that a Venezuelan company, North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP), gives the United States majority control of more than 65 billion barrels of proven reserves, against roughly 46 billion in US territory. If the true figure is far lower, the volumes, tax income and fuel-price promises built on it would shrink with it.

We covered the oil money side of this story in Venezuela Sees US$76 Billion Oil Investment and the output side in Venezuela Oil Output Holds Near 1.2 Million. This article looks only at how many barrels are really there.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Venezuela ranks 13th of 14 with 27.0 points. Strongest pillar: military means (81); weakest: economic relationships (0). Alignment group: Closer to Beijing. Some pillar data are incomplete for Venezuela; see the index notes. WatchSovereign in selective default; inflation of 252%; public debt at 309% of GDP. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

What Analysts Say About Venezuela Oil Reserves

Evanan Romero, a former Venezuelan energy official who now lives in Houston, called the plan unrealistic and said the US government did not audit the local reports before signing. He told the Associated Press that the 65 billion barrels cannot be believed, and that if officials had to testify on how they calculated the number, everyone would see it as “a funny number, an absolute lie”, in the Spanish text published by El Nacional.

Luisa Palacios, a Columbia University researcher and former president of the US refiner Citgo, said the government data probably refers to the total oil in place rather than to proven reserves. Recoverable oil would then be only 10% to 12% of the 65 billion barrels, which the Spanish reports put at about 6.5 billion; by our arithmetic 10% to 12% would be 6.5 billion to 7.8 billion, so the reports’ figure matches only the 10% end, and she said she could not tell which recovery rate the White House assumed.

Francisco Monaldi, an oil specialist at Rice University, estimated that only 10 billion to 15 billion barrels meet the criteria for proven reserves in the short term. That is about 15% to 23% of the 65 billion barrels, by our arithmetic.

Banca y Negocios, a Venezuelan business outlet, summed up the consultants’ view as roughly one third of the official 303 billion barrels, a range of 60 billion to 120 billion barrels. It said that would still be a large volume but not enough to keep Venezuela in first place worldwide.

What the White House Says About the 65 Billion Barrels

The White House fact sheet of 31 August 2026 says NABEP received 100-year concessions on 17 oil fields with proven reserves of about 65 billion barrels from Venezuela’s interim authorities. It adds that the US Department of War’s Office of Strategic Capital holds a 35% stake in the parent company, and that the State Department may buy 20% of output at production cost.

The same document says NABEP plans to invest up to US$100 billion in new oil infrastructure and expects to pay about US$200 billion in royalties and taxes over 25 years. A White House release of 2 September 2026 added that the company already produces 250,000 barrels a day, and the fact sheet says most of the additional fields were previously controlled by Russian and Chinese firms or by what it calls cronies of Maduro and Hugo Chávez.

White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers defended the terms in a written statement, calling the agreement a historic step toward stabilising Venezuela’s economy that more than doubles US oil reserves. The White House did not publish the method behind the 65 billion barrels or answer the news agency’s questions, according to El Nacional.

Proven Reserves Versus Oil in the Ground

Oil in place is everything a field is estimated to hold, while proven reserves are the part that can be produced with reasonable certainty under current technology and costs. The gap can be large for the heavy crude of the Orinoco Belt, the oil region named after the river, where El Nacional says many of the blocks in the deal are located.

Banca y Negocios, summarising the report, says many of the committed fields are close to depleted or lack the infrastructure needed to develop them, and Romero recalled that several international companies left some of the Orinoco fields because of operating difficulties. The report also notes that NABEP is not listed on a stock exchange, so it is not subject to the reserve-reporting and audit rules of the US Securities and Exchange Commission.

By our arithmetic, the 65 billion barrels in the deal equal about 21% of the official 303 billion, and the 60 billion to 120 billion range equals 20% to 40% of it. The official 303 billion figure is described by the experts as based on outdated and unreliable government data.

What It Means for You

Investors who read the 65 billion barrel figure as a measure of future US supply should wait for technical data, because the experts quoted put the near-term proven volume between about 6.5 billion and 15 billion barrels. Lower Venezuela oil reserves would not change oil already flowing, but they would reduce the long-term volumes, royalties and taxes that the White House projects.

Drivers and refiners should not expect the deal alone to move US fuel prices soon, since the White House itself says material production reaches the United States as soon as early next year. Our guides Venezuela Natural Resources Explained 2026 and Who Holds Power in Venezuela, Explained set out where the oil sits and who controls it.

Travellers and expats in Venezuela see none of this directly, since the dispute concerns long-term reserves rather than daily conditions. Our Caracas expat city guide covers day-to-day costs and conditions.

What Is Not Known

The White House has not published the technical method behind the 65 billion barrels and, according to El Nacional, did not answer the news agency’s questions; we found no statement on the method from the Venezuelan authorities or NABEP. We could not open the official reserve filings or the OPEC statistical bulletin for this article, so the 303 billion figure rests on the reports and on the experts’ description of it.

The experts’ ranges differ widely, from about 6.5 billion to 7.8 billion barrels for the 65 billion in the deal to 60 billion to 120 billion for the whole country, and they measure different things. It is also unknown whether Venezuela or NABEP will commission an independent audit that would settle the question.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many barrels of oil does Venezuela officially have?

Official figures put Venezuela’s proven reserves at about 303 billion barrels, the largest in the world on paper. Analysts quoted by the Associated Press say the volume that can be produced today is only 60 billion to 120 billion barrels.

What did the White House say about 65 billion barrels?

The White House said on 31 August 2026 that a deal with NABEP gives the United States majority control of more than 65 billion barrels of proven reserves. It compared that with roughly 46 billion barrels of proven reserves in US territory.

Who questions the Venezuelan reserve figures?

Evanan Romero, Luisa Palacios and Francisco Monaldi are among the experts quoted, and Banca y Negocios says about half a dozen were consulted. They argue that the figures rest on outdated data and may mix oil in place with proven reserves.

Is the 65 billion barrel claim confirmed?

No independent source quoted in these reports confirms it, and the White House has not published its method. Monaldi puts the short-term proven volume at 10 billion to 15 billion barrels.

What does this mean for US readers?

It means the size of the US stake and the long-term supply promised by the deal are not yet verified. Investors should wait for technical data before treating 65 billion barrels as producible oil.

Sources: El Nacional, 23 October 2026; Banca y Negocios, 22 October 2026; White House fact sheet, 31 August 2026; White House release, 2 September 2026.

World.title: Colombia Extradites Mocho Olmedo on 4 Counts
World.content:
Rooftops and green hills in El Tarra, a town in the Catatumbo region of Norte de Santander (Photo: Jusecardenas, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

COLOMBIA · EXTRADITION

Key Facts — The country Colombia, a leading cocaine producer and a long-time US security partner, is led by President Abelardo De la Espriella, who took office in August 2026.

— Why it matters A rebel commander wanted by a federal court in Florida is now in US hands, which shows how far Bogotá will go in sending armed-group leaders north.

— Why now He left La Picota prison in Bogotá and was handed to US authorities, and the transfer became public on Friday 23 October 2026.

— What happened Willinton Henao Gutiérrez, alias Mocho Olmedo, a senior commander of the FARC dissident Front 33, was extradited to face drug-trafficking and money-laundering charges.

— The numbers The US indictment dates from 15 February 2023 and lists four counts, and Colombia’s Supreme Court approved the transfer on 28 May 2025.

— What it means for you US readers see Colombia sending a cocaine-linked rebel commander to a US court, while travellers should still check the advisory for the Catatumbo border region.

— Still open When he first appears in a US court, how he pleads, and what happens to the homicide and recruitment charges filed against him in Colombia.

— Power Index Colombia ranks 6th of 14 in Colombia ranks 6th of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 51.9 points (October 2026 edition).

Colombia extradites Mocho Olmedo, a commander of a FARC dissident group, to face cocaine-trafficking charges in a Florida federal court. Colombian outlets reported on Friday 23 October 2026 that Willinton Henao Gutiérrez had left La Picota prison in Bogotá and been handed to US authorities.

For US readers the case matters because a federal court in southern Florida accuses him of moving cocaine meant for the United States and of laundering money. It also shows how far President Abelardo De la Espriella will go in sending armed-group leaders north.

El Colombiano and Infobae describe Henao as the second in command of Front 33, a dissident group in the Catatumbo region on the Venezuelan border, while the Supreme Court called him its third in command in 2025. We covered the August order to send him north in Colombia Orders Five Petro-Era Negotiators Extradited to the US.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Colombia ranks 6th of 14 with 51.9 points. Strongest pillar: military means (91); weakest: diplomatic & cultural influence (28). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. WatchRating below investment grade (BB-); 26 homicides per 100,000; organised crime at 7.8 of 10. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

Why Colombia Extradites Mocho Olmedo Now

President De la Espriella announced on Wednesday 26 August 2026 that he had signed resolutions to reactivate the extraditions of five armed-group leaders. All five had joined peace talks under his predecessor Gustavo Petro, and he said a review found no verifiable contribution to peace from any of them, El Heraldo reported.

The Supreme Court’s criminal chamber had approved the US request on 28 May 2025, and Petro’s government suspended the handover a month later by Resolution 186, Infobae reported. The suspension depended on Henao making verifiable contributions to the peace talks.

Infobae also reported that the De la Espriella government withdrew his peace-manager status before the transfer. The president said on 14 October that he had signed 131 extradition processes in his first 67 days, Semana reported.

Alias Araña, another of the five, was flown to California on Friday 25 September and pleaded not guilty on Monday 28 September, Noticias RCN reported. Henao’s handover came four weeks later.

What the Florida Indictment Alleges

El Tiempo, reading the Supreme Court file, says the case is an indictment in the US District Court for the Southern District of Florida dated 15 February 2023. The US embassy in Bogotá formalised the extradition request on 21 July 2023, the newspaper added.

The indictment lists four counts: conspiracy to distribute a controlled substance, conspiracy to import it, conspiracy to launder money and attempted money laundering. The first two concern 5 kilograms or more of a cocaine mixture between 1 September 2021 and 11 August 2022, allegedly bound for the United States.

The laundering counts allege that funds were moved out of the United States, including an attempt on 28 July 2022 in Broward County. Infobae added that one reference in the file mentions a suitcase with US$740,000 tied to a deal for 115 kilograms of cocaine.

These are allegations in an indictment, and Henao has not been convicted of any offence in the United States. The Supreme Court wrote in 2025 that he is a dissident of the peace process who never joined the post-2016 transitional justice system.

Charges Colombian Prosecutors Filed at Home

By 8 September 2026 Colombia’s Attorney General’s Office had charged Henao with conspiracy, homicide of a protected person, forced displacement and unlawful recruitment, Publimetro reported. He did not accept the charges at the hearing, which he attended by video link.

Prosecutors say he was one of the main organisers of the armed confrontation with the ELN in the Catatumbo that began on 16 January 2025. The ELN is the National Liberation Army, a guerrilla group that has fought Front 33 for control of the Catatumbo.

Among the allegations is the killing of a community leader on 17 January 2025 in the village of Guachimán, in Tibú. Prosecutors also attribute the forced displacement of 84 people from Tibú and El Tarra between 16 and 20 January 2025, and the recruitment of 31 minors, Publimetro and El Espectador reported.

These remain allegations, and no court has convicted him of the homicide, displacement or recruitment charges. Prosecutors filed them while he was held in La Picota.

From Peace Spokesman to Prisoner

Henao gave himself up in February 2025, and the Petro government then arranged a place of detention in Bogotá so he could keep taking part in the talks, Noticias RCN reported. Semana reported that his capture was announced on 12 February 2025.

Caracol News later revealed that the national intelligence directorate had hidden him for 55 days in the Chapinero district of Bogotá, Semana recounted in May 2025. The Supreme Court approved the US request on 28 May 2025, after that scandal.

Infobae places Front 33 inside the dissident network led by alias Calarcá. The FARC, the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia, demobilised under a 2016 peace deal, and the dissidents are splinter factions that kept or retook arms.

What It Means for US Readers

When Colombia extradites Mocho Olmedo after a delay tied to peace talks, its new government shows it will send an armed-group leader to a US court on drug charges. Together with Araña’s September transfer, it suggests the August order is being carried out.

The Catatumbo, around Tibú and El Tarra, is where the fighting named in the Colombian charges took place, and our guide Colombia Security 2026: Hotspots, Safer Cities, US Advisory covers the hotspots and the US advisory. Bogotá, where he was held, is covered in our Bogotá expat city guide.

Our guides Who Dominates Colombia, Elites and Regions Explained and Colombia Politics Explained, Who Holds Power in 2026 show how power is organised in Colombia. They help readers place the De la Espriella government’s extradition policy.

What Is Not Known

Reports differ on the day of the handover, with Noticias RCN and El Tiempo saying Thursday 22 October, while El Colombiano and El Espectador report the prison authority’s confirmation on Friday 23 October. They also differ on how many prisoners were extradited together, with Semana counting six in total and Infobae six others.

The sources reviewed do not say when or where he will first appear in a US court, although Infobae says he must appear before the Florida district court. No US Justice Department statement on the case was found.

It is not known what happens to the homicide, displacement and recruitment cases in Colombia. The status of the other leaders named on 26 August, aliases Muñeca, HH and Pinocho, was also not established.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is Mocho Olmedo?

Mocho Olmedo is the alias of Willinton Henao Gutiérrez, a senior commander of the FARC dissident Front 33 whom some Colombian outlets call its second in command. He served as a spokesman for the group in peace talks with the Petro government.

Why does the United States want him?

A federal court in southern Florida indicted him on 15 February 2023 on four counts tied to cocaine trafficking and money laundering. The indictment is an allegation, and he has not been convicted in the United States.

When was Mocho Olmedo extradited?

The prison authority confirmed on Friday 23 October 2026 that he left La Picota and was handed to US authorities. Two outlets say the handover itself took place on Thursday 22 October.

Why was his extradition delayed?

The Supreme Court approved it on 28 May 2025, but the Petro government suspended it on 26 June 2025, Infobae reported. President De la Espriella reactivated it on 26 August 2026.

What does it mean for US readers?

It sends a cocaine-linked rebel commander to a US court and shows Colombia’s new government carrying out its extradition order. Travellers should still check the US advisory for the Catatumbo border region before any trip.

Sources: El Tiempo, 23 October 2026; El Colombiano, 23 October 2026; Infobae, 23 October 2026; Semana, 23 October 2026; Noticias RCN, 23 October 2026; La Opinión, 23 October 2026; Publimetro, 8 September 2026; El Heraldo, 27 August 2026; Semana, 28 May 2025; Noticias RCN, 29 September 2026.
