Official banking data similarly show a broader expansion in consumer credit. Outstanding consumer loans reached P2.84 trillion in August, up 17% from a year earlier, according to the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP). Credit card receivables alone climbed 23.8%.

Play Video

More worryingly, there are signs of growing repayment difficulties. Non-performing consumer loans grew nearly 20% from a year earlier, and the share of bad debt climbed to 5.67% of all consumer loans, according to BSP data.

So what can be done?

Of course, there are big problems to fix. The study calls for holding the government accountable, addressing the economic pressures on households, and building more free public spaces where Filipinos can relax for free. But these changes will take time.

But businesses can act more immediately to help struggling consumers and earn their loyalty along the way. Asked what would make them feel a brand was genuinely on their side, 27% of respondents chose a price freeze, the most popular response. Smaller or tingi sizes followed at 16%, free shipping at 14%, and promotional bundles at 12%.

“It has to be tangible,” said Sheila Mangila, Organic Intelligence group account director for marketing intelligence. “It’s about material conditions that will really help them survive the everyday.” – Rappler.com

The study surveyed 800 Filipinos in urban areas aged 18 to 65 through an online panel in May 2026. Its findings may not fully capture perspectives of rural or digitally disconnected Filipinos.

World.title: Recall of House approved-GAB may lead to reenacted budget – senators
World.content:
Senators and officials of the Department of Agriculture (DA) review the proposed 2027 budget of the DA and its attached agencies and corporations, on October 21, 2026. Under the 2027 National Expenditure Program, the DA is set to receive ₱198.4 billion, an 8 percent decrease from its ₱215.7-billion budget in 2026.

Senators say concerns over the House-approved General Appropriations Bill can be addressed in the consolidated version of the budget bill

MANILA, Philippines – Recalling the House-approved version of the 7.2-trillion proposed 2027 national budget, as pushed by some lawmakers, may result in a reenacted budget, senators said on Friday, October 23.

Senate finance committee chairperson JV Ejercito warned of potential delays in the passage of the 2027 General Appropriations Bill (GAB) after the Makabayan bloc proposed recalling House Bill No. 10858 to correct provisions they believe could be declared unconstitutional.

“There are proposals to recall the HGAB. In my opinion, there is a great chance the proposed 2027 national budget may not be approved if that would happen,” Ejercito said in a chance interview.

“The Senate is running on a very tight schedule due to the impeachment, regular plenary sessions, and budget hearings. Right now, we are targeting to pass our version of the budget bill by second week of November,” he added

The Supreme Court (SC) declared the 2024 and 2025 General Appropriations Acts (GAA), or national budget laws, unconstitutional. Citing the court’s rulings, the Makabayan bloc called on the House to “clean its own mess,” pointing to provisions in the proposed 2027 budget involving the release of unprogrammed appropriations, cuts to foreign-assisted projects to accommodate congressional insertions, and prohibited lump-sum allocations.

ACT Teachers Representative Antonio Tinio told ANC’s Headstart: “If this were not corrected, [it] would risk many portions of the budget for 2027 as well. We don’t want yet another budget that will be declared unconstitutional.”

Senator Panfilo “Ping” Lacson, chairperson of the Senate committee on accounts, echoed Ejercito’s position, saying recalling the budget was “not the solution.”

“They can submit their proposals to the House or to the Senate finance committee for consideration. After all, the Senate version of the budget bill will be subject to the bicam so they should attest and address their concerns there,” Lacson said.

“Recalling the budget to the House is not the solution because that would result to a worse scenario — a reenacted budget,” he added.

Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian also said there was no need to recall the proposed budget, adding that the Senate could address the questioned provisions in the consolidated version of the budget bill.

“Looking at the Supreme Court decision on the 2026 budget, there are only a few provisions that will be affected. I don’t see the need to make major correction in the 2027 budget,” Gatchalian said.

Under the 1987 Constitution, if Congress fails to pass the GAB for the incoming fiscal year, the GAA for the preceding fiscal year is deemed reenacted and remains in effect until a new appropriations law is passed. – Rappler.com

World.title: Wesley So tops 2026 US Chess Championship, bags P3.55 million
World.content:
THE BEST. Wesley So beats top seed Fabiano Caruana in the rapid playoffs of the 2026 US Chess Championships.

Wesley So, a three-time Philippine champion before moving to the United States over a decade ago, rules the 2026 US Chess Championship, ending the four-year reign of Fabiano Caruana

MANILA, Philippines – Filipino-born Wesley So recovered from a hard fall in the last round to clinch the 2026 US Chess Championship on Thursday, October 22 (Friday, October 23, Philippine time).

Shrugging off a harrowing last round loss, the 33-year-old pride of Bacoor, Cavite, beat top seed Fabiano Caruana in the rapid playoffs, 1.5-0.5, to bag the $56,000 (P3.55 million) champion’s purse at the Saint Louis Chess Club in St. Louis, Missouri.

With the crown for his taking, So faltered against cellar-dweller Sam Sevian in the 11th round, allowing Caruana to catch him at 7.0 points following a victory over Awonder Liang in the 12-man, all super-Grandmaster tournament.

After a see-saw draw in the first tiebreaker, So pounced on a dubious pawn sacrifice by Caruana to win the second and secure his fourth US national title, having prevailed in 2017, 2020, and 2021.

The champions and their trophies! 🏆

Congratulations, Wesley So and Rachael Li! 🇺🇸



📸 Lennart Ootes pic.twitter.com/IYDA4WP4zC — Saint Louis Chess Club (@STLChessClub) October 23, 2026

Enjoying a strong season, So — a three-time Philippine champion before transferring to the US Chess Federation in 2014 — also ruled the Americas Cup in March and the Sinquefield Cup in August.

So bested Sam Shankland in the first round, drew with Jeffery Xiong, Liang, Levon Aronian, Grigory Oparin, Abhimanyu Mishra in succession; trounced Ray Robson and Andy Woodward; and drew with Caruana and Hans Niemann in the ninth and 10th rounds.

In the post-interview, So admitted he barely slept after that defeat to Sevian, napping only two to three hours, but willed himself to victory as Caruana wasn’t in his best form.

Caruana had ruled the annual event since 2022, but So ended his reign.

WIM (Woman International Master) Rachel Li snared the US women’s crown, where 13-year-old Fide Master Megan Paragua, born of Filipino parents in New York, shared fourth place.

Li scored 8.5 points, IM Alice Lee 8.0 points, GM Irina Krush 7.5 points, and WGM Thalia Cervantes and Paragua, niece of US-based Filipino GM Mark Paragua, 6.0 points. – Rappler.com

World.title: China Taps Myanmar’s Rare Earth Surge, Coffee Sell-Off, and More
World.content:
China’s rare earth imports swelled by Myanmar supply

China’s rare earth imports surged to 5,021 tons in September, up 23 percent from August, according to data from the Shanghai Metals Market.

Shipments of rare earth oxides from Myanmar accounted for 70 percent of the total, while arrivals from Laos fell to 1,369 tons. Together, Myanmar and Laos accounted for 97 percent of total imports. Cumulative imports for January–September reached 46,466 tons, up 14 percent year‑on‑year.

Rare earth mines along Myanmar’s northeastern border with China supply roughly half the world’s heavy rare earths, including strategically scarce dysprosium and terbium used in magnets crucial to China’s high-tech supply chain.

The surge comes as the US reengages with Myanmar’s regime, fueling speculation that global competition for rare earth resources is driving Washington’s policy recalibration. However, almost all of Myanmar’s rare earth mines are located in territory beyond regime control.

Myanmar specialty coffee faces Chinese fire sale

A Chinese fire sale beckons for Myanmar’s once-booming specialty coffee market. Once backed by USAID and American buyers, the coffee industry collapsed after the 2021 coup as Shan farmers responsible for some of the world’s finest beans were deprived of access to Western markets, transparent trade and certification. With the lucrative export path blocked, the regime and its Myanmar Coffee Association (MCA) are now aggressively pivoting to China.

MCA chairman Myo Aye told Xinhua that cooperation with Yunnan has deepened since the military takeover, with new MoUs locking in China as the top destination for Myanmar’s 3,000–4,000 tonnes of annual exports—tumbling from pre-coup levels of more than 5,000 tonnes. He said the association is looking to attract Chinese investment in value-added processing facilities, roasting plants and supply-chain logistics.

Myanmar’s coffee basket of Shan State has been ravaged by some of the fiercest fighting triggered by the 2021 coup.

Agriculture supplants industry at Myanmar-China forum

The Seventh Myanmar–China Think Tank Forum kicked off in Mangshi, Yunnan Province on Wednesday, with agricultural cooperation placed firmly at the center of discussions. Launched in 2017, the annual forum takes a different theme each year, but its underlying focus has consistently been the now stalled China–Myanmar Economic Corridor, a project designed to give Beijing direct access to the Indian Ocean.

This year’s session saw Myanmar regime officials highlight opportunities in rice and coffee. Yunnan is a major buyer of both. They urged deeper cooperation to expand exports, boost trade and investment, develop value‑added products, and facilitate technology exchange.

The forum comes as regime leader Min Aung Hlaing promotes agriculture as the key sector to revive an economy devastated by his coup and international sanctions. He has emphasized rice, cotton, oilseed crops, pulses, and rubber as priority industries to drive growth.

Earlier this month, Myanmar’s Pawsan variety won global recognition at the World Rice Conference 2026. At the 23rd China–ASEAN Expo in Nanning last month, three Myanmar rice exporters signed five MoUs with Chinese companies. According to the Myanmar Rice Federation, Myanmar earned US$ 338 million from rice exports in the first half of FY2026–27, which began in April.

Travel alert over Myanmar scams sparks Thai pushback

The Chinese Embassy in Bangkok issued a safety advisory on Oct. 16 warning its citizens of trafficking risks linked to scam compounds along the Thai–Myanmar border, prompting a scrambled response from Thailand’s foreign and tourism ministers.

The advisory cautioned Chinese nationals to be on alert for kidnapping and trafficking schemes disguised as high‑paying job offers, fraudulent investment projects, and bogus filming contracts targeting livestreamers and entertainers. It urged travelers to verify overseas employment opportunities, avoid suspicious transport arrangements, and steer clear of high‑risk areas on the Thai-Myanmar frontier where criminal networks remain active despite official crackdowns.

The warning followed recent cases that rattled public opinion in China, including the abduction of a shopping livestreamer who was lured by a bogus contract to Thailand before being trafficked to Myanmar last month. The high‑profile kidnapping of soap actor Wang Xing in Myawaddy in 2025 had already triggered a trilateral crackdown by China, Thailand, and Myanmar.

Following the latest advisory, a Chinese actress cancelled a fan meeting in Bangkok, underscoring the potential impact on Thailand’s tourism sector.

Thai Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow responded by urging the embassy to ensure its warnings are proportionate to the situation and avoid sparking unnecessary alarm. He stressed that Thailand takes visitor safety seriously and will investigate incidents, but cautioned that exaggerated advisories risk undermining confidence in Thailand as a safe destination. Chinese nationals are Thailand’s largest tourism market.

Naypyitaw eyes tourism lifeline in Kunming

Even as reports of trafficking and scam compounds along the Thai–Myanmar border dominate headlines in China, Myanmar’s regime is pressing ahead with plans to lure Chinese visitors back to Myanmar to revive a tourism industry shattered by the 2021 coup.

The regime’s Hotels and Tourism Ministry has announced it will open a tourism promotion office in Kunming, Yunnan Province. At the China–Myanmar cultural tourism exchange meeting held in Kunming from October 13–17, Tourism Ministry Secretary Maung Maung Kyaw described the proposed office as a potential “major corridor” for public‑private cooperation between the regime and Chinese tour companies. A business‑to‑business memorandum of understanding was also signed between Chinese and Myanmar tour operators.

Chinese travelers remain Myanmar’s largest foreign tourism market, but numbers have collapsed since the coup. Just over 250,000 Chinese arrivals were recorded last year—a fraction of the pre‑coup boom—despite having access to visas on arrival. In 2019, Myanmar saw 749,719 Chinese arrivals out of a total 4.4 million tourists.

Compiled by Thurein Lynn

World.title: Myanmar Rare Earth Exports Surge Amid Illusion of Regime Control
World.content:
China’s rare earth imports rose sharply in September to 5,021 tons, up 23 percent from August, according to data from the Shanghai Metals Market.

Shipments from Myanmar accounted for 70 percent of the total, while arrivals from Laos fell to 1,369 tons. Cumulative imports for January–September were up 14 percent year‑on‑year.

Meanwhile, recent U.S. reengagement with Naypyitaw has fueled speculation that rare earth competition is driving Washington’s policy recalibration.

Regime supporters are now boasting that the embattled junta has a “rare earth card” to play in its bid for international recognition, pointing to parallel interest from India.

Yet, although Myanmar is home to around 600 rare earth mines primarily feeding China’s supply chain, almost all of them lie beyond the regime’s territorial control.

Why are rare earths important?

Rare earth elements (REEs) are indispensable for high‑tech industries, serving as raw materials for magnets in electric vehicles, wind turbines, smartphones, and defense systems.

China dominates global mining and refining, producing nearly 70 percent of rare earth oxides and controlling more than 85 percent of refining capacity. Yet its domestic deposits are dominated by light REEs, leaving it reliant on Myanmar’s northern mining belt. Myanmar produces roughly half the world’s heavy rare earths (HREEs), including strategically scarce dysprosium and terbium used in powerful magnets crucial to China’s AI ambitions.

Kachin State’s riches

Kachin State, which borders China and India, hosts nearly 80 percent of over 600 rare earth mines identified by satellite imagery across northern Myanmar, with the highest concentration clustered in Chipwi and Momauk. These two townships alone contain over 370 active mining sites featuring more than 2,700 active leaching pits, according to data from the Stimson Center and Institute for Strategy and Policy-Myanmar.

Before late 2024, Kachin’s rare earth mining hubs were controlled by the New Democratic Army–Kachin (NDA-K), a junta-aligned militia turned Border Guard Force (BGF) led by warlord Zakhung Ting Ying. Under NDA-K control, rare earth extraction expanded with virtually no environmental oversight, generating tens of millions of dollars in informal taxes and dividends shared between militia leaders and top generals in Naypyitaw.

Their control collapsed in October 2024 when the Kachin Independence Army (KIA) launched a major territorial offensive. The KIA routed NDA-K forces and seized the mines in Chipwi and Pangwa, with victory placing Myanmar’s primary HREE extraction infrastructure under the direct administrative control of an armed group actively fighting the military regime.

Shan State: the new player

While Kachin State remains Myanmar’s rare-earth hub, mining in Shan State has expanded 48 percent on average over the past five years, outpacing Kachin’s 15 percent. Nearly 90 rare earth mines have been detected in territory controlled by the Ta’ang National Liberation Army (TNLA), United Wa State Army (UWSA), and National Democratic Alliance Army (NDAA).

While the UWSA and NDAA have maintained ceasefires with the Myanmar military for nearly four decades and are heavily reliant on China, the TNLA fought the regime after the 2021 coup, seizing territories beyond its self-administered zone. Today, the group operates 12 rare earth mines in Mantong, transporting the extracted minerals to China through Namhkam, opposite Ruili.

The supply chain in Mantong Township involves Chinese and Wa businesses, as well as technical and logistical support from the Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army and the UWSA, according to Stimson Center.

Myanmar’s rare earth mining boom is fueled by growing global demand, coupled with China’s tightening of its own environmental regulations in the 2010s. With domestic output restricted, China turned increasingly to Myanmar, where the concentration of mines near the border led to a thriving overland trade.

Between 2017 and 2024, Myanmar supplied at least 60 percent of China’s rare earth imports, peaking at US$1.4 billion in 2023.

Environmental Destruction

Most of Myanmar’s rare earths are extracted in situ through leaching, a process in which acid solutions are poured directly into shallow pits or boreholes to dissolve rare earths from clay deposits. Unlike China, which has tightened environmental rules, Myanmar’s border mines operate with little regulation and no post-mining restoration. Environmentalists have warned of soil destruction and water pollution in Kachin’s Chipwi Township, where untreated wastewater and chemicals from mines flow directly into the N’Mai Kha River, which feeds Myanmar’s main lifeline, the Irrawaddy River.

Geopolitical Overlay

In July 2025, Reuters reported that advisers to President Donald Trump had met with Myanmar intermediaries to explore potential access to the country’s rare earth reserves. While no formal agreements were announced, the outreach underscored how Myanmar’s heavy rare earths have become central to Washington’s strategy to counter Beijing’s dominance in high‑performance magnet manufacturing.

Earlier this month, American officials held talks with Myanmar regime representatives in Tokyo, the second such meeting since mid-September. Analysts point to two factors driving the US thaw: efforts to combat online scam operations run by junta-aligned militias that have defrauded Americans of billions of dollars, and the scramble to secure rare earth resources.

India has also joined the race for Myanmar rare earths as global supply chain competition heats up. In July, Ambassador Abhay Thakur outlined growing bilateral collaboration during a mining forum hosted by the Indian Embassy in Mandalay, where officials from both sides discussed joint ventures and investment opportunities. The talks reflected New Delhi’s growing interest in Myanmar’s mineral deposits as part of its broader “Act East” strategy and its push to divert supply chains away from China.

Myanmar military sympathizers argue that rare earths offer a crucial bargaining chip for the isolated and embattled regime. Yet as rare earth competition reshapes foreign policy, global superpowers face a glaring irony in courting the military regime: the junta controls virtually none of the mines.

World.title: A Fitting Conclusion to an Intellectual Life: James C. Scott on the Irrawaddy
World.content:
James C. Scott (2025). In Praise of Floods: The Untamed River and the Life Brings. Yale University Press. 220 pp.

In Praise of Floods, puts the Irrawaddy River itself—not generals, kings, peasants or revolutionaries—at the center of Myanmar’s history, and in doing so establishes principles for how river basins are best understood.

James C. Scott (Shwe Yoe) was one of the most important social scientists of the last 50 years. He began his international career in Burma in 1958 but was unable to return after Ne Win’s 1962 coup until 2012. His affection for Myanmar, however, did not diminish, and he then went back regularly until 2021. He was even known to give lectures in Burmese in the 2010s. He died at the age of 87 in 2024, and In Praise of Floods is his final book.

What Scott is most famous for is descriptions of how farmers resisted exploitation by feudal lords and politicians who sent armies and police to tax them. His research led to provocative books like The Moral Economy of the Peasant, Weapons of the Weak and The Art of Not Being Governed. Their creative tension was always between the cunning of the “weak” peasantries and the simplifications powerful governing elites make to squeeze surpluses from them.

In Praise of Floods is a departure in focusing instead on rivers and floods. Scott believes that they are “alive” in the sense that they are born, develop and shrink across millennia. In the Irrawaddy’s case, it created the fertile plains of central Burma at the end of the last Ice Age 12,500 years ago.

Scott’s point is that rivers emerge at particular times, support different types of life, shift channels and courses, and eventually disappear. He calls this process the river’s “pulse.” For the Irrawaddy, the low-water point is usually in February, and as the rains resume, about eight times as much water flows out of the highlands above Mandalay by September, bursting out of the meandering channels formed in previous years.

For thousands of years, perhaps from 10,000 BCE until about 5000 BCE, this meant that migratory people avoided the floods by annually moving their camps to higher ground. Life came from the rich topsoil the floodwaters laid down across the flat plains stretching from Mandalay, which is only 80 m above sea level, to the Andaman Sea some 1,000 km to the south. Early humans harvested the bounty of the river by fishing, netting birds, hunting game, collecting mussels, and gathering fruit and roots. The flood pulses determined what the people ate, and where they lived and settled.

By about 3000 BCE people began creating new ways to use the temperamental river and sought to bend the Irrawaddy’s surges to their own needs. They started by scattering seeds along the shoreline as the flood waters receded. After tending the crop of grain for a few months they could harvest more food than ever before, but this type of food needed to be processed and stored in granaries, to be eaten while waiting for the next harvest to mature.

This is also when they began managing water flows with weirs, fish traps, drainage canals and dikes, and eventually developed the engineering capacity to flatten fields with animal-drawn plows and other tools needed to harvest paddy rice. Human societies came to see the living river as a tamable resource, whose annual surges could be engineered, so people confidently settled into permanent villages near the rivers. There, the arts, markets, religion, literature, architecture and other human pursuits flourished. By about 2,200 years ago, the Pyu states began to emerge, building permanent cities, markets and worship centers.

And when the river behaved as planned, it was a great thing and populations flourished. But there were new dangers too for people living in fixed villages and cities, because the river pulses did not always rise and fall as humans intended—after all, Scott writes, the river was also alive, and perhaps even had a mind of its own. So when the monsoons arrived late or not at all, there would be a drought. Or when they arrived early and in force, there were floods.

Humans and the rest

A particularly creative touch in Scott’s book is his concluding chapters about non-human life, which includes fish, animals and plants, as well as the ubiquitous Burmese spirits, the Nats. A charismatic character, the Irrawaddy river dolphin organizes the other creatures of the river to comment on the algae, molluscs, worms, larvae, zooplankton and microbes, most of which are ignored by homo sapiens, who is only interested in the river as it applies to human endeavors.

As Scott admits, these chapters fit awkwardly with the overall tone of the book. But surely in his final book he can be given some leeway. He is correct, moreover, that social science needs to acknowledge the spiritual life that is important to the ecology of places like the Irrawaddy valley and delta.

Flooding is a catastrophe for humans, but the “infrastructure” of non-human life, including plants, fish, mammals, birds, and of course the river itself are perhaps more ambivalent, or at least have a different perspective on the river pulses. So, for that matter perhaps do the Nats.

Scott’s emphasis on these spirits reflects stories that his research associates Maung Maung Oo and Naing Tun Lin collected while travelling along the Irrawaddy seeking to understand what locals knew. They travelled from the headwaters of Kachin State through the dry zone of Magwe and Sagaing. The spirits must be placated because they are believed to cause both those disastrous floods and the good fortunes of farmers, fishers and hunters. And then there are the dangers of the surrounding forests, which are also effected by the Nats.

Scott soon segues into more modern descriptions of the Irrawaddy watershed, in which the hydrodynamics of the water surges are highlighted in the context of modern social problems like deforestation, mining, and rebellion. All such activities disturb the ecological balance, and the capacity of humans to manage the Irrawaddy.

Full circle

Scott’s lifetime of creative scholarship is impressive. He started in Burma, studied in Vietnam, went to Malaysia, and ended up studying the economics, politics and psychology of the oppressed, and how highlanders respond to attempts to control them. In Praise of Floods brings this career full circle; he is back in Burma and writing about geography. As he writes in his preface, he planned two more years of field research, following the stories of farmers, river dolphins, spirits and flooding himself, but was prevented by the 2021 coup. His own public activism supporting the Spring Revolution made a return even less likely.

But even without these field data, the book pushes social scientists yet again to consider the perspectives of beings they typically ignore. Scott spent a lifetime searching for what he once called “hidden transcripts“—the voices of people overlooked by rulers and states. In this final book he tries something still more audacious: hidden transcripts of dolphins, spirits, forests, floods and the river itself. It is an appropriately unruly ending to the provocative intellectual life of James C. Scott.

Tony Waters is a professor of sociology at Leuphana University, Germany. His most recent book is The Socio-Political Systems of Highland Burma and the Art of Governance.

World.title: Myanmar Regime Pushes on Four Fronts in Southern Chin State
World.content:
Thousands of regime troops are advancing on four fronts across southern Chin State as they push to seize the gateway to Rakhine State, according to resistance sources.

On Wednesday, the military claimed its forces had secured Hlaingdoke and nearby villages in Kanpetlet Township along the Rakhine border after clearance operations along the Laung She-Hlaingdoke-Kyindwe road.

The regime’s counteroffensive to retake Chin resistance strongholds spans from Magwe Region’s Tilin and Saw townships, across the border into Mindat, Kanpetlet and Kyindwe townships.

Intense clashes have erupted in Magwe’s border villages of Shweaungthar and Kyee as regime forces advance to cut off supply lines to Mindat, according to resistance sources.

“The regime has deployed roughly 3,000 troops across all the fronts,” Yaw Meng, spokesperson for the Chin People’s Army (CPA), told The Irrawaddy.

Regime forces began massing for a southward push five months ago after securing the northern Chin towns of Tonzang, Falam, and Thantlang. The southern Chin campaign launched in May, when around 1,500 troops advanced on Kanpetlet and Mindat from Magwe’s Saw and Kyaukhtu townships respectively, according to the CPA.

“During five months of clashes, resistance forces repelled regime troops and defended the Chin State and its people,” Yaw Meng wrote in an October 20 Facebook post.

He declined to comment on the current battlefield situation in southern Chin, where the regime’s ground offensive is accompanied by indiscriminate airstrikes.

On Sunday, a bomb struck the Paletwa jetty, killing nine civilians including a six-month-old child and injuring four others. A regime airstrike on the same site killed another person the following day, according to the Chin People’s Union, the CPA’s political wing.

World.title: Myanmar Ranks Worst in World for Internet Freedom
World.content:
Myanmar has scored just 9 out of 100 on the Internet Freedom Index for the third consecutive year in 2026, making it the world’s worst environment for internet users as the military regime continues its aggressive crackdown on media freedom and online expression, U.S.-based rights group Freedom House said.

Under the group’s rankings, Myanmar has long been categorized as “Not Free” for internet freedom, but its score dropped significantly from 36 in 2019 to 17 in 2021 after the military staged a coup, and finally to 9 from 2024 onward.

It said the military maintains control over all major service providers to enforce mass censorship, localized shutdowns and digital surveillance.

Following the coup, the Myanmar military regime stepped up suppression of internet freedom and digital rights by enforcing shutdowns, blocking social media and news platforms, and criminalizing virtual private network (VPN) use to crack down on political dissent.

As a result, Myanmar netizens have lost access to information and had their freedom of expression curtailed.

During December-January elections, authorities intensified the blocking of news platforms and the use of anti-censorship tools while arresting individuals for online expression under restrictive new laws.

“This is a very concerning situation,” Thit Nyan, a digital rights analyst from the Myanmar Internet Project, told The Irrawaddy. “This is a life-and-death matter for the public.”

He added that the people of Myanmar, whose lives are seriously affected by conflict, rely heavily on mobile and internet connections for information about airstrikes and to facilitate basic services such as health, education and money transfers.

Myanmar internet users require digital literacy for their own safety, he said.

More than 2,000 netizens have been detained as of September since the 2021 coup for sharing posts or comments criticizing the regime and supporting anti-regime movements, mostly on Facebook, according to Data for Myanmar, a monitoring group.

The regime relies mostly on the Penal Code’s Section 505A outlawing “incitement”, the counter-terrorism law, and the telecommunications law to arrest online critics, including artists and celebrities.

Data for Myanmar said, however, that in 2026 the regime has expanded its scope of action to target individuals who merely express their political views online, rather than just those who are deemed to pose a security threat.

At the same time, experts point out the regime has shut down or restricted mobile and internet networks to control information flow, in an effort to prevent military information from leaking and to conceal its human rights violations.

A total of 140 out of 358 monitored townships are facing communication shutdowns, according to Athan, a group that focuses on freedom of expression. Most of the affected townships are experiencing fighting between regime and anti-regime groups.

Meanwhile, users require VPNs, whose use the regime has criminalized, to access the most-used social platforms such as Facebook.

“I have to swallow my own feelings and control myself not to share them online,” a Yangon netizen told The Irrawaddy. He said he was using his real name for his social account and was aware of many people in major cities who had been arrested for sharing their views in favor of the anti-regime resistance.

“This is a violation of our rights to express ourselves freely and to live safely,” he said.

World.title: China’s Myanmar Policy—Consistent but Fundamentally Flawed
World.content:
Observers are often baffled by China’s outright support for Myanmar’s criminal military regime in the face of global opprobrium. But Beijing has been remarkably consistent in terms of where it believes its interests lie. During a visit to Naypyitaw in August 2024 that followed the Myanmar military’s unprecedented battlefield defeats in northern Shan, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi outlined what he called Beijing’s “three bottom lines”. Myanmar must not descend into civil strife, drift away from the ASEAN family, or be infiltrated or interfered with by external forces.

The position, in other words, was support for resolving Myanmar crisis within the ASEAN framework, with a warning that escalating civil war, state collapse, or intervention by other countries—especially of course Western countries—would directly harm Chinese interests. Stability comes before everything else.

Military first

China’s Myanmar policy has consistently centered on the Myanmar military. Since the late 1990s, Beijing has treated Myanmar military as the decisive force in stabilizing the country.

After the popular pro-democracy uprising in 1988 toppled the then-regime and the China‑backed Communist Party of Burma collapsed the following year, Myanmar’s military broke with the Western powers. With that, the assistance they had given it under the pretext of a counter‑narcotics campaign came to an end. Facing sanctions, the military turned instead to China and became Beijing’s trusted partner in assuring border security.

Beijing concluded that only the military could hold the country together. Despite its brutality, China viewed it as the sole practical guarantor of the status quo, aligning with Chinese interests and counterbalancing Western hostility.

Strategic energy interests

In 2003–2004, then President Hu Jintao highlighted the risks posed by great‑power competition over the Malacca Strait to China’s energy security. To reduce dependence on that chokepoint, Beijing proposed building oil and gas pipelines across Myanmar into Yunnan. Than Shwe’s regime obliged, and relations improved as a result.

Through these pipelines, China now imports about 22 million tons of crude oil annually—worth roughly US$16 billion—bypassing the Malacca Strait. Beijing’s recognition of Than Shwe as a trusted ally further entrenched its military‑centric policy.

The position today

China continues to prioritize the Myanmar military, treating ethnic armed groups along the border as secondary entities it must keep in check and largely ignoring forces farther afield such as the National Unity Government (NUG), People’s Defense Forces (PDF) and Spring Revolution alliances.

It was only natural, then, that when the military was on the verge of collapse after losing the northern Shan capital of Lashio in 2024, Beijing propped it up rather than let it fall.

To be sure, China’s policy on Myanmar has delivered some success, leading to the junta’s bogus elections and cosmetic transformation into a civilian government, and now ASEAN governments’ re-engagement with Myanmar. Their dealings with the putschist regime are motivated not only by trade, migration, drug trade and online scam concerns, but also by China’s political and economic influence.

It is an entirely pragmatic, interest‑driven diplomacy, prioritizing national interest over moral principles, and of course that is not unique to China. The U.S. is increasingly open about the transactional nature of its own international policies, and ASEAN has been taking note.

Drawbacks

Yet the core problems remain unresolved. The war has not abated. Myanmar is not stable. Min Aung Hlaing’s elections led to worsening airstrikes and intensified military campaigns, mass killings and war crimes.

Unlike the Thein Sein government, the rebranded regime has offered no political reforms of any kind. It rejects inclusive peace, aiming instead to divide resistance forces.

In practice, the regime remains keen on military solutions alone—retaking lost territory with Chinese backing. Since China intervened, hostilities ceased in northern Shan but the regime escalated fighting in the rest of the country, forcibly recruiting 100,000 young people under Conscription Law since 2024 for use as cannon fodder. The resulting brain drain has left the country poorer in human resources than ever.

Two years of heavy Chinese support have only allowed the regime to recapture 21 townships out of more than 100 lost. Over 80 remain under resistance control. And now its gains are slowing dramatically, with rural areas and key routes beyond its control.

China’s goal of stability in Myanmar, in other words, is further out of reach than ever. By trusting the military to deliver it, Beijing has handcuffed itself to failure. Is it too late to change course?

Thet Htar Maung is a political analyst.

World.title: Son of Aung San Suu Kyi Says He Has First Call With Her in 5 Years
World.content:
YANGON—The son of Myanmar’s Aung San Suu Kyi said he spoke Thursday to the detained former democratic leader for the first time in more than five years.

“Today, I was finally able to speak with my mother, Daw Aung San Suu Kyi, after more than five years. Hearing her voice again means more than words can express,” Kim Aris said in a post on Facebook.

Aung San Suu Kyi is detained at a “designated residence” in the capital, Naypyitaw, according to Myanmar authorities, where she has been sequestered since being unseated in a 2021 military coup.

AFP could not immediately reach Aris—who lives in the United Kingdom—and it was not clear how he spoke to his mother, who won the 1991 Nobel Peace Prize for efforts to bring democracy to Myanmar.

However, images accompanying his Facebook post appeared to show him standing outside the Myanmar Embassy in London.

“I am deeply grateful to everyone who has stood by my mother and me. I believe your voices helped make this moment possible,” Aris wrote.

“But my mother is 81 and remains unjustly detained. One conversation is not regular family access.”

Myanmar’s military held Aung San Suu Kyi in almost total seclusion for five years following the February 2021 coup, which ended a tentative decade-long experiment with democracy.

But in recent months authorities have increasingly advertised the loosening of her detention and published photographs of her taking private meetings, as supporters have demanded “proof of life” of the octogenarian.

On Monday, authorities in Myanmar said she received a package from Britain’s King Charles III, including two books about soil and a “sealed diplomatic communication” from the monarch.

Buckingham Palace did not comment on the contents of the communication.

Myanmar authorities said Aung San Suu Kyi was moved from a prison in Naypyitaw to house arrest in April, and in August they published images of her meeting the nation’s Red Cross representative.

After ruling Myanmar as military chief for five years, Min Aung Hlaing—who ousted Aung San Suu Kyi in the 2021 coup—was earlier this year installed as civilian president.

Analysts describe the election putting him in elected office as a charade, and say he may be loosening restrictions on Aung San Suu Kyi in a bid to court international legitimacy.

World.title: Japan’s Sasakawa Renews Myanmar Peace Pledge as Regime Battles Arakan Army
World.content:
Yohei Sasakawa, honorary chairman of Japan’s Nippon Foundation, met putschist president Min Aung Hlaing in Naypyitaw on Monday, pledging once again to assist Myanmar’s “internal peace process.”

Sasakawa made a similar promise during his last visit in August. This time, regime media said only that he offered to help strengthen Myanmar’s “human resources,” without elaborating on what that would entail. No details were released on what progress had been made since his earlier pledge to support peace efforts.

Sasakawa’s latest visit comes amid fierce fighting in Rakhine, where the regime is struggling to defend the state capital, Sittwe, from the ethnic Arakan Army (AA)’s attacks. Sasakawa previously mediated a ceasefire between the Myanmar military and the AA in 2021, though fighting resumed in late 2023 after Operation 1027. The regime has since lost 14 of 17 townships in Rakhine.

The regime claims to be open to peace talks with ethnic armed organizations (EAOs), but has excluded the AA from talks so far. It has demanded that the People’s Defense Force, the armed wing of the civilian National Unity Government, surrender.

Sasakawa’s latest meeting follows the regime’s self-styled “peace talks” with several EAOs that were not actively fighting the regime, having maintained earlier ceasefire deals with the Myanmar military even after the 2021 coup—an event that led other EAOs to resume fighting.

Separately, two EAOs that had been fighting the regime—the Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army and the Ta’ang National Liberation Army—agreed to ceasefires with the regime under direct pressure from China.

The regime insists that EAOs, after signing ceasefires, must transform themselves into Border Guard Forces under the Myanmar military’s command or disarm.

The Nippon Foundation on Wednesday declined to comment on the details of Sasakawa’s latest meeting with Min Aung Hlaing. The organization believes the most useful contribution it can make in Myanmar is through “quiet, practical engagement rather than public commentary,” its executive director, Takashi Arikawa, told The Irrawaddy.

“It is not helpful to discuss the substance of ongoing efforts before there are results that can be shared publicly,” he said.

Political analyst Htin Kyaw Aye noted that multiple countries and organizations are currently exploring ways to address Myanmar’s crisis, including attempts to open dialogue between the regime and resistance forces.

“Japan and Sasakawa may be among those countries and organizations. But they haven’t released details about their plans, so it is hard to gauge what measures they will take and what impacts they could have,” he said.

In recent weeks, Japanese lawmakers Hiromichi Watanabe and Shunsuke Takei visited Naypyitaw and met with Lower House Speaker Khin Yi. Meanwhile, Tokyo hosted meetings between U.S. officials and Myanmar regime representatives this month, leading to speculation that Tokyo is considering a shift in its policy toward engagement.

Japan suspended official development assistance to Myanmar after the 2021 coup. Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi reiterated in July that relations would only improve if the junta halts violence, releases detainees including jailed civilian leader Aung San Suu Kyi, and pursues genuine political dialogue.

Months ago, the regime publicly appealed for previously agreed aid to be restored.

World.title: NVIDIA CEO Proposes Kazakhstan as Global Hub for Physical AI
World.content:
ASTANA – President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev met with NVIDIA co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang in Astana on Oct. 23 to discuss cooperation in artificial intelligence (AI) and digital technologies, highlighting Kazakhstan’s ambition to become an AI-driven nation.

During the meeting at Akorda, Tokayev emphasized the importance of Huang’s visit in strengthening bilateral cooperation and expressed gratitude for his personal contribution to the development of Kazakhstan’s AI ecosystem.

“This visit is of great importance to us in terms of giving serious momentum to our cooperation with NVIDIA. I would like to personally thank you for your contribution to strengthening our partnership and for what you are doing for Kazakhstan,” Tokayev said.

President Tokayev identified AI development and digitalization as national priorities, noting that 2026 has been declared the Year of Digitalization and Artificial Intelligence in Kazakhstan.

Tokayev also welcomed NVIDIA’s partnership with Higgsfield, saying Kazakhstan was proud to see the company involved in a domestic technology project.

Huang praised Kazakhstan’s strategic ambition to become an AI nation, describing it as a goal set at the beginning of a new industrial revolution.

He also proposed positioning Kazakhstan as a global hub for physical AI, a field that combines artificial intelligence with physical systems, including robots, autonomous machines and industrial equipment.

“AI development requires, first and foremost, energy resources, as well as people with knowledge in science, mathematics and technology. Kazakhstan has significant potential to develop each of these areas,” Huang said.

The NVIDIA chief also highlighted progress in the company’s cooperation with Kazakhstan over the past year, particularly in building ties with local technology businesses.

He praised the work carried out jointly with Kazakhstan and expressed gratitude for the country’s decision to partner with NVIDIA, describing the cooperation as the beginning of a long-term journey.

Following the meeting, Tokayev awarded Huang the Order of Dostyk (Friendship) in recognition of his contribution to the development of artificial intelligence in Kazakhstan.

World.title: Republic Day Weekend: What to See and Do in Astana and Almaty
World.content:
ASTANA – As Kazakhstan prepares to celebrate Republic Day on Oct. 25, Astana and Almaty are offering a packed weekend of cultural events, from theater performances and concerts to art exhibitions. The Astana Times has rounded up some of the highlights to help readers make the most of the long holiday weekend.

Astana

Ethno Festival, Oct. 24

Spend time immersed in Kazakh traditions with horseback shows, kokpar, traditional games and local food. Visitors can also explore craft stalls and a market featuring national products, making it a great opportunity to enjoy the country’s rich cultural heritage with family and friends.

Venue: BalQaragai recreation area. Tickets are available here.

“Heritage of the Great Steppe” concert, Oct. 24

Celebrate the beauty of Kazakh dance through a program of folk choreography created by Aigul Tati. The performance brings together expressive movements, colourful costumes and traditional music, highlighting the richness of Kazakhstan’s dance heritage.

Venue: Astana Ballet; 43 Uly Dala Avenue. Tickets are available here.

“Swan Lake,” Oct. 24

Enjoy “Swan Lake,” one of the best-known works of classical ballet, set to Pyotr Tchaikovsky’s timeless music. The story of love, magic and the struggle between good and evil unfolds through graceful choreography and expressive dance.

Venue: Zhastar Palace; 34 Republic Avenue. Tickets are available here.

“Abai-Togzhan” musical drama, Oct. 25

Explore the early life of Abai through a musical drama about his first love, Togzhan, and the experiences that shaped his worldview. Inspired by Mukhtar Auezov’s work, the production brings together romance, poetry and Kazakh cultural traditions.

Venue: 47B Zhakyp Omarov Street; Musical Theater of Young Spectators. Tickets are available here.

“Living Paintings” exhibition, Oct. 24-26

Discover the famous seascapes of Ivan Aivazovsky through a multimedia exhibition that combines classic art with immersive visual technology.



Venue: Lumiere-Hall Multimedia Museum; 8 Abay Avenue. Tickets are available here.

Almaty

Almaty Open, Oct. 24-25

Tennis fans can watch top international players compete in the ATP 250 tournament. Beyond the matches, the event offers live music, entertainment and interactive activities, creating a lively atmosphere for sports fans and visitors alike.

Venue: Almaty Arena; 7 Nurkent Microdistrict. Tickets are available here.

Outlandish concert, Oct. 25

Relive the sounds of the 2000s with the Danish group behind popular hits such as “Aicha,” “Guantanamo” and “Callin’ U.” The concert offers a chance to hear familiar songs live and revisit the music that defined an era for many listeners.

Venue: Bla Bla Bar; 1A Satpayev Street. Tickets are available here.

Layla Qobyz Live concert, Oct. 25

Experience the distinctive sound of the qobyz in a live musical performance. With its rich, expressive tone and deep roots, the instrument offers a memorable way to connect with the country’s cultural heritage.

Venue: Caspian University; 85A Dostyk Avenue. Tickets are available here.

“Marc Chagall: Beyond Gravity” lecture, Oct. 24

Step into the imaginative world of Marc Chagall through a lecture exploring the artist’s life, inspirations and distinctive style. Discover the stories behind his colourful imagery, his relationship with his muse Bella and his place in 20th-century art. The program also includes a visit to the exhibition dedicated to his work.

Venue: Oylau Space; 15 Gogol Street. Tickets are available here.

Ethno-cultural tour, Oct. 24 – Nov. 30

Discover the traditions and lifestyle of the Kazakh nomads through an immersive cultural experience. The tour offers an opportunity to learn more about the country’s heritage and explore customs that have shaped life on the steppe.

Meeting place: 100 Baityrsynov Street. Tickets are available here.

World.title: World Wrestling Championships 2026: Entries Announced for Astana
World.content:
ASTANA – A total of 320 wrestlers are set to compete in wrestling at the 2026 World Wrestling Championships, which will take place at Barys Arena in Astana from Oct. 24 to Nov. 1.

The entry list features athletes from around on the world across 10 weight categories, ranging from 57 kilograms to 125 kilograms. Eight returning world champions are expected to defend their titles at the championships.

Kazakhstan will be represented by wrestlers across all 10 weight categories, including Meirambek Kartbay at 57 kg, Assyl Aitakyn and Nurdanat Aitanov at 61 kg, Ossimzhan Dastanbek at 65 kg, Sanzhar Doszhanov at 70 kg, Nurkozha Kaipanov at 74 kg, Shamsat Tair at 79 kg, Bolat Sakayev at 86 kg, Azamat Dauletbekov at 92 kg, Rizabek Aitmukhan at 97 kg and Yedige Kassimbek at 125 kg.

The entry list includes several prominent international wrestlers, among them American Spencer Lee at 57 kg, Russian Zavur Uguev at 61 kg, Iranian Amirmohammad Yazdani at 74 kg, American Kyle Dake at 86 kg, Iranian Hassan Yazdani at 97 kg and American Wyatt Hendrickson at 125 kg.

The championships will bring together competitors from established wrestling nations and countries across multiple continents, with athletes entered from Europe, Asia, the United States and Africa.

According to the organizers, entries remain subject to change until 72 hours before the draw for each wrestling style.

The championships will be held in Astana over nine days, with freestyle wrestling among the events featured at the international competition.

World.title: NVIDIA CEO Sees Kazakhstan as Emerging AI Hub During First Visit
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan has the energy resources, technological talent and growing computing infrastructure needed to develop its own artificial intelligence industry, NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang said during his first visit to the country on Oct. 23, urging Kazakhstan to turn its natural resources into a competitive advantage in the global AI economy.

“In just a very short time, frankly, you have made incredible progress,” Huang said during a fireside chat with Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development Zhaslan Madiyev.

“While the rest of the world is deciding how to engage and how to build the AI economy, here in Kazakhstan, you are doing it already,” he added.

Huang, whose company makes the advanced chips used to train and run many of the world’s leading AI systems, praised Kazakhstan’s ambition to become an AI-driven economy. His visit concluded Kazakhstan’s AI Month, a series of events bringing together technology companies, developers, investors and researchers to promote the country’s growing AI ecosystem.

“This is the first country that I have been to where the president declared the country to be an AI nation,” Huang said.

Turning energy into intelligence

Speaking at the alem.ai International AI Center, Huang said Kazakhstan could move beyond exporting energy to producing and exporting AI-powered intelligence.

“Kazakhstan has a fundamental advantage because you have so many natural resources already. You have so much energy. Instead of just exporting energy in the future, you can transform the energy into intelligence and export intelligence,” said Huang.

He pointed to the vast amounts of resources that AI development would require as it rolls out around the world.

“These AI factories require natural resources and the natural resources it needs is electricity. It needs data. And it needs offtake. The offtake is coming from the inspiration of the leadership in Kazakhstan,” said Huang,

He also emphasized the importance of sovereign AI, noting that countries should retain control over their own data and develop the capacity to operate AI systems suited to their languages, cultures and national requirements.

“I believe it to be a national security concern,” Huang said when asked whether Kazakhstan should invest in developing its own large language models.

“That data belongs to you, just as your natural resources belong to you. The data of your society is also part of your natural resources,” he added.

He welcomed the development of Kazakh-language AI models and said open-source technologies could help the country build national capabilities without having to develop every underlying technology from scratch.

“You have so many programmers, developers. You are rich with expertise here,” Huang added.

He also stressed the importance of developing and deploying AI responsibly as increasingly autonomous AI systems gain access to sensitive information and digital tools.

Robotics and the next wave of AI

Moving on, Madiyev raised the question of physical AI, which combines AI with robotics and systems that interact with the physical world.

“You want Kazakhstan to be an AI nation. AI starts with cognitive AI, cognitive intelligence, soft intelligence. But AI includes everything all the way to physical AI. Physical AI is the largest industry of all, of course, because most of the world includes interaction and understanding of the physical world,” Huang explained.

According to him, Kazakhstan could become a center for developing and training physical AI systems, particularly in sectors where the country already has substantial expertise, including mining, agriculture, logistics and energy.

He also said the technology’s applications extend beyond robots to geological exploration, seismic analysis, mapping mineral deposits and improving industrial processes.

“Now, we are at the beginning of the physical AI journey. This is the next wave,” he said, describing physical AI as an opportunity for countries to help shape an emerging industry rather than merely adopt technologies developed elsewhere.

Local AI talent

The discussion also highlighted NVIDIA’s investment in Higgsfield, an AI video-generation startup with a significant presence in Kazakhstan and a valuation of $5.4 billion.

“The first thing and the last thing is you invest in people, not companies,” Huang said.

He believes Kazakhstan’s technology ecosystem could benefit from a combination of local talent, expanding computing infrastructure and stronger international connections.

“The only thing that matters is do you have ambition? If you have ambition, then AI and robotics will lift you,” said Huang, addressing concerns that AI could displace workers.

He cited examples ranging from farmers using robots to expand agricultural operations to scientists and engineers using AI assistants to pursue more complex research and designs.

Madiyev agreed, stressing the importance of education and developing AI skills from an early age, pointing to programs at the center.

“It is our job as parents to imbue our children, instill our children with hope, ambition, aspiration, to help them dream bigger. When you dream big, then AI will lift you to achieve that. Same exact idea for children as well as for adults, for companies as well as countries and nations,” Huang explained.

‘Envy being 18-year-old’

Toward the end of the discussion, Huang was asked what he would do if he were 18 years old and living in Kazakhstan today.

“I envy being 18 years old today,” he said, reflecting on how rapidly technology is changing and the opportunities it presents for a new generation.

“I was fortunate because when I was 18 years old, the personal computer was just becoming possible. I’ve been working for 43 years, my generation was defined by the creation of the computer. All of our four decades of endeavors have led to artificial intelligence, which is a complete reset of everything that we’ve done,” Huang said.

“I would dedicate myself to be the world’s best programmer of AI,” he said, emphasizing that young people should understand how the technology works, including its strengths, weaknesses and limitations, to make the most of its capabilities.

Ongoing partnership

Huang’s visit coincided with AI infrastructure commitments in Kazakhstan. NVIDIA is set to take part in the development of the Data Center Valley project in Ekibastuz, a town in northeastern Kazakhstan.

NVIDIA reported on Oct. 23 that U.S.-based Firebird signed an investment agreement with the Kazakh government and has secured a U.S. export license for 45,000 NVIDIA Grace Blackwell GPUs (Graphics Processing Unit).

The company is developing the first phase of a facility with Kazakhtelecom, the country’s largest telecommunications company, at Data Center Valley in Ekibastuz, with commercial operations expected to begin in the third quarter of 2027.

Kazakhtelecom has already deployed 880 NVIDIA GPUs in Astana and Almaty. In 2027, it plans to deploy more than 2,000 additional GPUs, including over 1,000 NVIDIA Vera Rubin processors in Ekibastuz.

World.title: Kazakh Foreign Minister Highlights Middle Corridor Potential at Central Asia-Georgia Meeting in Batumi
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan has called for coordinated efforts to strengthen transport and transit links between Central Asia and the South Caucasus, highlighting the strategic importance of the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, also known as the Middle Corridor, during a meeting of foreign ministers from Central Asian states and Georgia on Oct. 23.

Kazakhstan’s Foreign Minister Mukhtar Tileuberdi took part in the meeting at the invitation of Georgian Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Maka Botchorishvili. During the meeting, the participants highlighted the strong potential for cooperation among the six countries, noting their similar or fully aligned approaches to key areas of cooperation and regional issues.

The ministers emphasized their shared interests in maintaining regional stability, achieving sustainable development and expanding cooperation between Central Asia and the South Caucasus. They also underlined the importance of maintaining regular dialogue to develop practical solutions and advance joint initiatives.

Strengthening the Middle Corridor

Particular attention was paid to developing the Middle Corridor, which connects Asia and Europe. The ministers discussed measures to improve its competitiveness, including modernizing transport infrastructure, digitalizing freight transportation and simplifying transit procedures.

The Kazakh side stressed the importance of coordinated action to unlock the transport and transit potential of Central Asia and the South Caucasus. According to the discussions, reliable and predictable logistics connections could create additional opportunities to increase mutual trade, attract investment and improve access to international markets.

The development of transport infrastructure and more efficient transit procedures remains an important area of regional cooperation, as the participating countries seek to strengthen connections between their economies and international markets.

Regional cooperation and potential development

The meeting provided an opportunity for the six countries to discuss shared priorities and explore ways to deepen cooperation in areas where their interests and approaches align. Participants highlighted the importance of continued dialogue and joint initiatives in supporting regional stability and sustainable development.

During the visit, Tileuberdi and his counterparts explored the potential of Batumi Sea Port in Georgia. The port is a Kazakh asset and one of the key links along the Middle Corridor. The visit offered an opportunity to examine the port’s role in regional transport and transit connections, particularly as the countries seek to improve the efficiency and competitiveness of routes linking Asia and Europe.

World.title: Tokayev: Republic Day Marks Kazakhstan’s Progress as New Priorities Set for Next Week’s Address
World.content:
ASTANA – President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev said Kazakhstan’s priority tasks and development plans would be outlined in his state-of-the-nation-address next week, speaking at an Oct. 23 ceremony marking Republic Day celebrated on Oct. 25.

Addressing the ceremony, Tokayev said Kazakhstan could not afford to rest on its achievements amid growing global challenges and intensifying competition.

“Amid current challenges and intensifying competition, we cannot afford to be satisfied with past achievements. We still have much to do. We acknowledge existing shortcomings and omissions,” he said.

President Tokayev also highlighted Kazakhstan’s economic performance and recent political reforms as the country approaches the 35th anniversary of its independence.

Economic growth and social development

Tokayev said Kazakhstan’s economy had grown by around 30% since 2019, with GDP per capita exceeding $15,000. The country’s GDP is approaching $350 billion, placing Kazakhstan second among Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) members, he said.

The share of small and medium-sized businesses in GDP has reached 40%, while nearly half of the country’s working-age population is employed in the sector.

He also highlighted social development indicators, noting that $2.5 billion had been transferred to the accounts of seven million children under the National Fund for Children program. According to him, more than 20 million square meters of housing were commissioned last year, while life expectancy has approached 76 years.

Constitutional reforms

Tokayev described the adoption of the new Constitution as a milestone in Kazakhstan’s political transformation. He highlighted the establishment of a unicameral Kurultai, the introduction of the vice president position and the launch of the Kazakhstan People’s Council, a high-level consultative body.

Tokayev also emphasized the importance of human capital, calling for the development of responsible, competitive and patriotic citizens and the promotion of hard work, mutual respect and compassion.

During the ceremony, Tokayev presented state awards to citizens who have made significant contributions to Kazakhstan’s development. The recipients included 129 labor veterans, 473 workers in industry, transport, construction, agriculture and other sectors, more than 200 small and medium-sized business representatives, over 150 teachers and scientists, and around 120 healthcare workers, among others.

World.title: News Digest: Foreign Media on Kazakhstan’s Critical Minerals, Middle Corridor and US Ties
World.content:
ASTANA — The Astana Times has selected articles from global media outlets covering Kazakhstan. This week’s foreign media digest covers a new rare-metals research center backed by South Korea, U.S.-Central Asia cooperation on trade and critical minerals, military reforms, investment opportunities, and efforts to expand the Middle Corridor’s shipping capacity.

Kazakhstan opens $15 million rare metals research center with South Korea

Kazakhstan is seeking to turn more of its mineral wealth into high-value materials for electric vehicles, electronics, and other advanced industries with the opening of a Korean-backed rare-metals research center in Almaty. The center, which opened on Oct. 21, is supported by a five-year funding program worth approximately $15 million, reported The Times of Central Asia on Oct. 22.

Based at the Institute of Metallurgy and Ore Beneficiation at Satbayev University, the center will develop technologies for processing and refining rare metals. The project is being developed under South Korea’s official development assistance program, with the participation of the Korea Institute of Industrial Technology (KITECH) and the Korea National Institute of Rare Metals (KORAM).

Rubio puts Trans-Caspian trade and critical minerals at centre of Central Asia talks

The US and five Central Asian governments backed closer transport and industrial cooperation at a C5+1 meeting in Samarkand. Rubio also held bilateral talks, while Uzbekistan signed the Artemis Accords, reported Euronews on Oct. 19.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and the foreign ministers of five Central Asian countries agreed to deepen cooperation on transport, critical minerals and security at a C5+1 meeting in Samarkand on Monday.

The talks brought together the United States, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan. In a joint statement, they backed investment in the Trans-Caspian trade route, closer industrial cooperation and simpler customs procedures.

Citibank Kazakhstan chairperson sees opportunities for US-Central Asia collaboration

Foreign investors are looking outside Kazakhstan’s oil and gas sector. But turning that interest into investment will require predictable regulations and stronger cross-border connections, according to Saule Zhakayeva, chairperson of Citibank Kazakhstan’s management board and president of the American Chamber of Commerce in Kazakhstan (AmCham).

Citi has operated in Kazakhstan since 1994, when it opened a representative office in Almaty. In an interview with The Times of Central Asia on Oct. 19, Zhakayeva discussed the country’s investment climate and its role as a regional business hub. She also addressed the future of economic relations between the United States and Kazakhstan.

Kazakhstan expands Middle Corridor fleet as Caspian Sea levels fall

Containers are piling up on Kazakhstan’s Caspian coast as they await shipment to Azerbaijan. A shortage of vessels and weather-related restrictions are delaying cargo along the Middle Corridor, a trade route connecting China and Europe while bypassing Russia, reported The Times of Central Asia on Oct. 22.

Kazakhstan plans to acquire five vessels and has ordered another six to expand maritime freight capacity. At the same time, falling Caspian Sea levels are limiting how much cargo existing ships can carry and complicating port operations.

Yerkin Nygmetov, CEO of KTZ Express Shipping, described the container backlog at the New Silk Way international transport forum, held in Astana on Oct. 15-16. According to Nygmetov, adverse weather conditions can restrict operations at Kazakhstan’s ports for a total of up to 75 days a year.

Kazakhstan military training overhauled with new drone forces planned

Less than a month after 14 service members died during military exercises in the Caspian Sea, Kazakhstan has approved plans to overhaul conscript training and introduce new safeguards against abuse in the armed forces. The reform plan was approved at a Security Council meeting on Oct. 21, with the main changes scheduled for 2027, reported The Times of Central Asia on Oct. 22.

The Sept. 24 tragedy prompted an investigation that uncovered serious failures in the planning of the exercises and measures to protect soldiers. A wider inspection of the Defense Ministry has since led to 13 criminal cases involving suspected embezzlement, abuse of authority, and other violations.

World.title: Baiterek Holding Working on $2 Billion in Projects With Foreign Investors
World.content:
ASTANA — Baiterek National Investment Holding has been developing projects involving foreign investors worth approximately $2 billion since the beginning of 2026, as the country works to attract capital for industrial production, infrastructure and technology, said Saken Olzhabayev, the holding’s managing director for international cooperation.

In an interview with Zakon.kz, Olzhabayev discussed the financing mechanisms behind Kazakhstan’s investment agenda and the challenges of converting foreign capital into domestic production. In the first nine months of 2026, Baiterek and its subsidiaries signed 79 documents with international partners, ranging from preliminary agreements to financing contracts.

Kazakhstan has set a target of attracting $150 billion in foreign direct investment by 2029. According to Olzhabayev, Baiterek’s role includes identifying industrial projects, structuring financing and connecting businesses with foreign investors.

“In 2026, the target for supporting the real economy through the holding’s instruments stands at eight trillion tenge [US$17.9 billion], with planned capitalization of one trillion tenge [US$2.24 billion]. The state capital provides a basis for attracting additional resources,” said Olzhabayev.

From investment agreements to financing

Baiterek’s database of prospective foreign investors included 163 companies from 35 countries as of the end of the third quarter of 2026. The United States accounted for the largest number of potential investors, while the holding also maintained contacts with companies and financial institutions across Europe and Asia.

South Korea accounts for one of the largest packages of agreements. During a state visit by Kazakhstan’s president in September, Baiterek and its subsidiaries worked on nine commercial documents, six of which included financing and investment commitments valued at a combined $2.45 billion.

Among them is a strategic agreement between Qazaqstan Investment Corporation (QIC) and the Korea Overseas Infrastructure and Urban Development Corporation (KIND) to establish a joint investment fund. Its initial planned volume is $200 million, with a possible increase to $1 billion. The fund would target infrastructure, logistics, energy and urban development.

Development Bank of Kazakhstan also signed a declaration with South Korea’s export credit agency, K-SURE, providing for insurance coverage of up to 200 million euros (US$224 million). The first potential project involves attracting 48 million euros (US$53.78 million) for a ferrosilicon plant in Ekibastuz, an industrial city in the Pavlodar Region.

Separately, the Development Bank of Kazakhstan signed a credit agreement of up to $200 million with Germany’s KfW development bank, backed by a guarantee from the World Bank Group’s Multilateral Investment Guarantee Agency (MIGA), to finance renewable energy projects.

A proposed investment fund involving China’s Silk Road Fund, QIC and Sturgeon Capital Kazakhstan has a target size of up to $200 million, with at least 70% intended for projects in Kazakhstan. The parties have agreed on the principal terms, with final investment agreements pending.

Olzhabayev highlighted the distinction between signing agreements and securing financing, noting that the documents involve different levels of commitment.

“A memorandum records intentions, an agreement on principal terms establishes the parameters of a future transaction, while a credit agreement or loan contract establishes specific obligations. The next stage involves fulfilling financing conditions and disbursing funds. What matters to us is not the number of intentions documented, but the quality of their implementation and the fulfillment of the commitments undertaken,” he explained.

Foreign partnerships and domestic production

Baiterek is also working with foreign companies on several industrial projects, including greenhouse complexes in Shymkent with Türkiye’s Alarko Holding, an egg-processing facility with Denmark’s Thornico Group and a hybrid power plant in the West Kazakhstan Region with Switzerland’s NovaH2. The projects are at different stages of preparation.

An existing example is Silk Road Electronics in Saran, which began manufacturing Samsung household appliances in August 2025 with support from the Industrial Development Fund. The plant has a design capacity of 1.1 million appliances annually and has created 250 jobs.

The Industrial Development Fund is one of several Baiterek subsidiaries providing financing at different stages of business development. The Damu Entrepreneurship Development Fund facilitates access to financing for small and medium-sized enterprises, while the Development Bank of Kazakhstan finances large industrial and infrastructure projects. QIC provides equity investment instruments, and the Export Credit Agency of Kazakhstan supports foreign sales.

“At the outset, a company may need a loan and a guarantee; as it expands, it needs equipment and additional capital, and when entering foreign markets, it needs export financing and insurance,” Olzhabayev said.

Baiterek has introduced a unified front-office service through Damu’s regional network to help businesses access financing instruments offered by different subsidiaries. In agriculture, financing extends from field operations and machinery purchases to processing and exports, involving the Agrarian Credit Corporation and KazAgroFinance.

Measuring investment outcomes

Despite the number of international agreements, their economic impact depends on whether projects secure financing and begin operations. Olzhabayev said the holding evaluates each initiative based on its progress from investment decisions to financing and implementation.

“We therefore assess the progress of each initiative. Has the project structure been agreed upon, have investment decisions been made, have contracts been signed, and has financing begun?” said Olzhabayev.

“Then come the production outcomes: commissioning facilities, manufacturing products, creating jobs and generating export sales. The next step is to turn concrete investor interest into projects that can be implemented,” he said.

Beyond individual project outcomes, Baiterek plans to gradually reduce its reliance on additional state funding by expanding market-based financing and reinvesting profits. According to Olzhabayev, the transition will depend on stable financial performance and returns on investments.

World.title: ‘Buying Czech aircraft is part of Armenia’s air force modernisation’ — military expert
World.content:
Expert opinion on Armenia’s Czech aircraft purchase

Armenian Defence Minister Suren Papikyan is on an official visit to the Czech Republic. He began his visit with a trip to Aero Vodochody, a Czech defence industry company. According to reports, he discussed the possibility of further cooperation with the company’s management. He also examined Aero Vodochody’s products in detail.

“These marvels will soon take to the skies over Armenia,” the defence minister wrote in a caption accompanying a video he posted shortly after visiting the company.

Papikyan also shared photographs, captioning them: “One of the landmark days in the history of the Armenian Armed Forces’ aviation.”

Experts have speculated, based on the video and photographs he posted online, that Armenia is preparing to receive Czech-made L-39 Skyfox aircraft. These are a new generation of jet trainers.

Military expert Eduard Arakelyan believes that Armenia, which has a limited fleet of aircraft, could use the L-39 Skyfox not only for training but also for certain operational tasks:

“As a result, the purchase could become a practical step towards modernising the air force. However, its scale does not yet justify claims that it would significantly change the combat capabilities of Armenian aviation. For training purposes, four aircraft could serve as the first batch in a transition to a new training system and curriculum. If the Skyfox purchase forms part of a broader restructuring of the air force, expanding the fleet further would be the logical next step.”

The L-39 Skyfox is a new-generation jet trainer designed for advanced pilot training. It features modern digital avionics, multifunction displays and an integrated virtual training system. These capabilities allow pilots to simulate various tactical scenarios during training flights. According to Defense Mirror, one Skyfox costs less than $10 million. The final price depends on the aircraft’s configuration and delivery terms. Depending on its configuration, the aircraft can carry air-launched weapons, reconnaissance equipment and additional external systems. This allows it to perform limited military and reconnaissance missions.

What we know about the defence minister’s visit

The defence minister arrived in the Czech Republic on 20 October. During his visit, Suren Papikyan attended the opening ceremony of the Future Forces Exhibition & Forum. He toured the exhibition halls and viewed the latest technologies and advanced military equipment on display.

The Armenian minister also held talks with Czech Deputy Prime Minister and Defence Minister Jaromír Zůna.

Armenia’s Defence Ministry said the two ministers discussed:

Armenian-Czech defence cooperation, including military-technical cooperation;

reforms in the Armenian Armed Forces and cooperation in military education.

“Both sides stressed the importance of cooperation in multilateral formats, including within the EU and NATO,” the statement said.

Papikyan also discussed bilateral military-technical cooperation with Czech First Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Industry and Trade Karel Havlíček.

Commentary

Military expert Eduard Arakelyan noted that a Czech defence industry source had reported a month earlier that AERO Vodochody Aerospace was producing four L-39 Skyfox aircraft for Armenia. Specialist publications had also circulated the information, but none identified the customer or disclosed the terms of the deal.

Meanwhile, Arakelyan said, the Armenian Air Force already operates Czech-made L-39 Albatros trainers. Armenia acquired these second-hand aircraft in 2004 and 2010–11. It purchased some of them from Ukraine.

“However, the exact number of aircraft that remain in service with the Armenian Air Force and can still fly regularly is unknown,” the expert said.

In Arakelyan’s view, the Skyfox purchase fits Armenia’s strategy of diversifying its arms suppliers and expanding cooperation with European defence manufacturers:

“An Armenian-Czech agreement on military-technical cooperation, which has been in force since 2023, provides an additional basis for collaboration.”

Arakelyan believes the Armenian defence minister’s statement signals that the Skyfox acquisition has reached a practical stage.
