World.title: New documentary spotlights 'silent killer' affecting First Nations people
World.content:
When Kelli Karrikarringka Owen needed a kidney transplant 10 years ago, her family members offered to donate their organs.

But the Kaurna, Narungga and Ngarrindjeri woman said the medical system "pushed back and said no".

"This is systemic racism that I’m talking about," she said.

" Basically, they were saying that because my family was Aboriginal that they couldn't donate, which is bollocks. "

Ms Owen, now a public health researcher at Adelaide University, has Alport syndrome – a genetic kidney disease which previously left her feeling lethargic, itchy and without a sense of taste.

For about three years from the age of 41, the Murray Bridge local would drive about one hour to Adelaide every second day of the week to be hooked up to a dialysis machine for five hours.

Adelaide University health researcher Kelli Owen lives with a kidney condition called Alport syndrome. (ABC News: Ben Pettitt)

"I actually had to withdraw my two youngest children from school, get in a taxi and travel down to the old RAH (Royal Adelaide Hospital) three times a week," she said.

"It was a scary time."

Eventually, Ms Owen received a kidney from a donor from New South Wales through the national donor program in 2016.

While she is now enjoying a life of "freedom" after a successful transplant, she said she felt "angry" that her family's initial requests were refused.

"I could have saved a few years being hooked up to a machine," she said.

"I could have been there for my younger children that were missing me being there for sports."

First Nations patients less likely to receive kidney transplants

Federal government data shows Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander adults are twice as likely as non-Indigenous adults to have chronic kidney disease.

But First Nations people are less likely to receive a kidney transplant.

Data from 2022, showed 16 per cent of First Nations people receiving kidney replacement therapy had a functioning kidney transplant, compared with 48 per cent of non-Indigenous Australians.

Adelaide University nurse researcher Professor Janet Kelly said kidney disease was known as a "silent killer", with some patients experiencing significant loss of kidney function without any symptoms.

Professor Janet Kelly said Aboriginal people face challenges accessing kidney transplants. (ABC News: Ben Pettitt)

Asked about Ms Owen's experience of having her family's donation requests refused, Professor Kelly said previous research suggested First Nations people could be at greater risk of kidney disease if they donated their organs.

But she said more recent studies showed different outcomes.

"Internationally, it's much more recognised that it is appropriate for First Nations people to donate kidneys," she said.

"In Australia, I think there is a change towards enabling more First Nations people to be assessed and, if there is a low risk for them, to then be donors."

Despite changing advice, First Nations people with chronic kidney disease continue to confront healthcare gaps, especially those living in rural and regional communities.

"A lot of our services are based within major cities and often half of Aboriginal people will live in cities, but half live in rural and remote places, so there is an immediate challenge to accessing equitable services," Professor Kelly said.

"There is a need for more specialist visiting rural and remote locations and providing clinics there."

Documentary highlights healthcare gaps

The Transplant Network founder Peter Crumpton, himself an organ transplant recipient, said he wanted to highlight the discrepancy in transplant rates by creating a documentary.

The Transplant Network founder Peter Crumpton before his heart transplant. (Supplied: The Transplant Network)

He travelled to remote communities across the country with Ms Owen, interviewing Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people about their experiences of receiving kidney transplants.

The documentary – titled "In Contrast" has premiered in Sydney and Adelaide.

"We spoke to about 10 different people in the documentary, from patients, to carers, to medical professionals," he said.

"My hope for the documentary is that people realise that this gap exists and that there are solutions to fix it."

Peter Crumpton filmed In Contrast to show the discrepancy faced by Indigenous Australians when accessing kidney transplants. (Supplied: The Transplant Network)

Ms Owen said she hoped the documentary raised awareness about kidney disease.

"It's a silent disease and we don't want to make it silent anymore," she said.

Planning is underway for the documentary to screen elsewhere in Australia in coming months.

World.title: Victorian victims of crime face long delays getting help from state
World.content:
Government delays in processing financial support could be having a serious impact on victim recovery, Victoria's victims of crime commissioner has warned.

Advocates say some victims of crimes are waiting more than a year for assistance, while footing counselling and medical bills themselves.

The warnings over delays come weeks from the state election, with concerns over violent crime heavily featured in the lead-up to November 28.

In 2024, the state government revamped the way support was delivered to victims of crime, with a new scheme that removed the need for victims to apply in court.

Instead, victim-survivors who have made a police report can lodge an application from home.

Applications for the revamped Financial Assistance Scheme can be made from home. (ABC News)

At the time of the changes, the state government said the expanded Financial Assistance Scheme (FAS) would be more straightforward to use.

Primary victims are entitled up to $63,401 under the scheme, which covers the costs of counselling, loss of income, medical and other expenses.

Since it was introduced, Victims of Crime Commissioner Elizabeth Langdon has fielded an increased number of complaints.

"Each of these represents a victim-survivor who has rights, who wants to be heard, and who is trying to navigate a complex and difficult justice system," she said.

"The systems established to support victims should not become another source of distress and, when delays occur, it can have serious consequences on a victim-survivor's wellbeing and recovery."

At the time of the changes, the state government said the expanded Financial Assistance Scheme (FAS) would be more straightforward to use.

Primary victims are entitled up to $63,401 under the scheme, which covers the costs of counselling, loss of income, medical and other expenses.

Victim-survivor says 'no communication' in assistance journey

Victim-survivor Elysia Roberts, who has experienced both versions of the support model, said the new scheme had "made it worse".

She said under the FAS, she had waited for more than a year for assistance.

"You're waiting hours on the phone sometimes, literally hours, just on hold to talk to somebody," she said.

Ms Roberts encountered difficulties in accessing assistance. (ABC News: Billy Draper)

The 42-year-old was awarded a music subscription service, a remedial massage, and funding for security cameras at her Melbourne home, after suffering "verbal, emotional abuse".

She said the process of applying for the FAS had impacted her recovery.

"You're not only healing from what's happened to you. You're healing physically, mentally, and emotionally. You're wanting support," Ms Roberts said.

" You can find yourself just constantly there every day checking the application. There's no communication. "

Demand for help soars

Delays and complications with the scheme have also overwhelmed some community legal services.

Azin Baghaki Jenkin, from the South-East Monash Legal Service, said the centre had stopped taking new clients as it grappled with a backlog of applications.

"We've got applications that we submitted 15 months ago, and they're still waiting for support," she said.

" We would have really loved to have seen the teething problems worked through by now. "

Ms Baghaki Jenkin said some victims had found the online portal hard to navigate, coupled with finding and uploading paperwork to submit their application.

"It can be really traumatising for victim-survivors having to wait for support," she said.

Lawyer Azin Baghaki Jenkin says clients are facing hurdles in accessing support. (Supplied)

The legal service has heard from victim-survivors who have borrowed money from family and paid out of pocket for expenses while they waited to be reimbursed.

"Many of our clients don't have that money to actually pay out of pocket," she said.

"What we would like to see from government is to deliver on that promise to put victims at the centre of the scheme."

The rate of unique victims of crime in Victoria reached an eight-year high in 2025, amid a spate of domestic violence, home invasions, and assaults.

Crime Statistics Agency data shows the rate has since fallen, sitting below the 2017 level.

Government says it's investigating ways to improve system

In a review last year, Commissioner Langdon delivered 25 recommendations to the state government to improve victims' rights, including changes to the Victims’ Charter Act.

The state government is yet to formally respond.

There have been reforms and improvements to the FAS, including changes to help process applications faster, according to its chief executive Marnie Williams.

"There is always more that can be done to better support victims of crime," Ms Williams said.

Victims of Crime Commissioner Elizabeth Langdon has called for changes. (Supplied)

Latest publicly available data shows there were 6,200 FAS applications finalised in the 2024-25 financial year, representing about 77 per cent of those lodged.

Ms Williams did not directly respond to questions about average wait times for assistance.

"Each application to the FAS is unique and needs to be assessed individually to ensure each victim receives the assistance they're entitled to," she said.

Minister for Victims Support Ros Spence said the government would continue to look at ways to improve the FAS.

"We know navigating the system can be difficult, which is why there are programs in place to connect victims with the right services and support," Ms Spence said.

Shadow Minister for Victim Support and Crime Prevention Renee Heath said the compensation scheme was falling behind with processing claims, due to the rate of crime in Victoria.

"We will stop the revolving door of bail, ensure there are consequences for actions in our justice system and strengthen the police force with 3,000 new officers," she said.

World.title: Backpackers say visa changes reduce incentive to do jobs many Aussies avoid
World.content:
Sweeping wine residue from a tank in the heat of the day is no-one's idea of a dream job, and there is only one reason Meghan Morris is doing it.

The Irish backpacker is willing to get her hands dirty in exchange for a visa.

"You're not going to do it unless you have to," she said.

Now enjoying her third year in Australia, Ms Morris has no complaints about the conditions at Griffith's De Bortoli wines in the NSW Riverina.

But she remembers some of her previous jobs in a less flattering light.

"The conditions in some of the places are pretty bad," she said.

"Some places you might not have running water in the bathroom or a lunch room.

"You're sitting outside in the field eating your lunch in the sun because you might not have shade, you kind of just deal with it."

Meghan Morris says the new ballot system for working holiday visas will only discourage other backpackers from coming to Australia. (ABC Riverina: Jostina Basta)

Backpackers often take the jobs many Australians seem unwilling to do on the basis they have a guaranteed stay in the country.

But Ms Morris said recent visa changes meant there was now much less incentive.

"It's like a lottery system … why waste the time doing it if the chance is so low?" she said.

Backpackers were previously guaranteed a second-year visa in return for 88 days of regional or rural work in their first year in Australia.

But now, they will have to enter a ballot system if they wish to stay longer than a year.

The number of visas on offer will also be significantly reduced, with second-year visas dropping from 57,000 this year to 45,000 and third-year visas declining from 31,000 to 5,000.

First-year Chilean backpacker Catalina Quiroga said with an uncertain future in Australia, regional work was no longer worth it.

First-year backpacker Catalina Quiroga says regional work is not worth it, without a guaranteed stay in the country. (ABC Riverina: Jostina Basta)

"It makes me think about whether it's worth the effort, the money, and everything we put into it," she said.

"I would go to Sydney or Melbourne and enjoy the city, versus being in the countryside."

Argentinian backpacker Javier Rodriguez has picked onions, packed produce and gardened during his time in Australia.

He said the prospect of a renewed visa and an extended stay was what made it worthwhile.

"You come here, you're far away from everything, it's a small town, it's very hot and the incentive was you get to extend your stay, but now that is all gone," he said.

"I'd rather go to the Gold Coast and just enjoy my time there instead of coming to work here under 50 degrees.

"They [locals] can't believe how we do it, how we leave our comfort zone, leave our homes and come to do that and we just kind of stand it."

Nation's food bowl 'reliant' on backpackers

In Young in southern NSW, cherry grower Tom Eastlake said backpackers were essential for the six-week spring harvest about to get underway ahead of Christmas.

"If you've got a seasonal crop that needs to come off in a very defined amount of time, and you haven't got the workers, you won't get the crop off," he said.

Mr Eastlake said the horticulture industry was heavily reliant on the seasonal workforce and losing them could be "catastrophic", amid existing pressures including rising fuel and fertiliser prices.

Tom Eastlake is a cherry grower from Young in regional NSW. (ABC Riverina: Jostina Basta)

"If we want to enjoy the best quality fruit and vegetables in the world at the highest possible food standards, we need to support that industry and make sure we're not making sudden changes," he said.

In a statement, a Department of Home Affairs spokesperson said it would work with the agriculture, tourism and hospitality sectors on how changes to how the working holiday maker (WHM) program will be implemented.

"The number of WHMs in Australia is at a historically high level. The reforms to the WHM program are designed to manage demand, support a fairer allocation of visas and ensure the long-term sustainability and integrity of the program."

Wine producer Darren De Bortoli said during the three-month vintage season, which begins in January, backpackers made up 85 per cent of his workforce.

Darren De Bortoli says backpackers make up 85 per cent of his workforce during the vintage season. (ABC Riverina: Jostina Basta)

"Without them, we wouldn't be able to function," the Griffith winemaker said.

"Backpackers are a very important part of rural Australia, as is our general immigration community."

Javier Rogriguez says he and his wife were looking to make Griffith their home but that will no longer be possible. (ABC Riverina: Jostina Basta)

Mr Rodriguez, who now works in product development at De Bortoli Wines, said backpackers brought more to regional communities than economic benefits.

"I've met a lot of people who have never left Griffith,' he said.

"They get a lot of multiculturalism from us; they get a different view of what's out there.

"We bring our home here, then we make Griffith our home."

World.title: Sydney marathon champion Jepchirchir provisionally banned over EPO finding
World.content:
Kenya's world marathon champion Peres Jepchirchir has been provisionally suspended after testing positive for the banned blood booster EPO ​in a sample taken before her Sydney Marathon victory, the Athletics Integrity Unit (AIU) said on Friday.

The AIU added that the out-of-competition sample collected in Kenya returned an adverse analytical finding for EPO (erythropoietin), which boosts the production of ​red blood cells.

"I can only ‌say that I feel terrible about what happened and I think it's only right that an athlete who uses the performance enhancing drugs should be disqualified," her agent Gianni Demadonna said in an ‌emailed statement.

The 33-year-old is one of the most decorated women in the sport, having ⁠won gold at the Tokyo Games in 2021 and having claimed ‌major marathon victories in New York (2021), ​Boston (2022), London (2024) and Sydney (2026). She ‌previously held the half marathon world record.

Jepchirchir is the latest in a long string of Kenyan athletes to fall foul of doping rules. More than 140 Kenyan athletes have been sanctioned since the AIU was established in 2017.

"So much of what I see ​when ‌I'm on a broadcast call I do not believe. I'm not surprised by this," said Olympic 10,000 metres silver medallist and broadcaster Kara Goucher, who was a whistleblower ⁠in the Nike Oregon Project case.

"I am, however, ‌sad for all the athletes ‌who finished behind her and were screwed out of a podium."

Jepchirchir dominated the women's race in ‌Sydney in August, pulling clear of the field to finish in 2:18:31, more than 3 minutes ahead of second-placed compatriot Irine Cheptai.

The Sydney Marathon, which ‌was added ​to the list of ⁠world majors beginning in 2025, said it was "extremely disappointed" by the news.

"Our commitment to clean sport is unwavering. Every athlete who lines up in Sydney deserves to race on a level playing field," it said in a statement.

Last year, Kenya's ⁠women's marathon world record holder Ruth Chepngetich was banned for three years after admitting anti-doping rule violations involving hydrochlorothiazide (HCTZ), a ‌prohibited diuretic, though ‌her world record of 2:09:56 remained on the books because it ​was set before her positive test.

Reuters

World.title: How Brendan Nugent went from plant scientist to alleged attacker
World.content:
Ten years ago, a researcher named Brendan Nugent was slogging through the bush in western Victoria, searching for a critically endangered shrub.

Navigating steep terrain and camping in national parks, he documented the places where he found the Grampians Bitter Pea, according to a local newspaper article.

Brendan Nugent spent many of his adult years researching the Grampians Bitter Pea and took this photo of the endangered shrub. (Victoria National Parks Association/Brendan Nugent)

"He is a terrific scientist and has drawn many people into helping with this research," a park ranger who worked with him told the Ararat Advertiser.

Mr Nugent, who held a masters degree in forest ecosystem science, dedicated more than eight years of his life to that little flower — coordinating citizen science projects, writing in nature newsletters and giving talks to wildlife groups.

People who knew him then described him as a passionate environmentalist who got along well with people.

Mr Nugent took part an environmental campaign in 2019 to ban logging in native timber forests. (X: Lily D'Ambrosio)

But over the course of the last few years, he had reportedly cut off his family, become isolated and threatened neighbours.

One said he'd been talking "gobbledegook" and could be heard screaming from his property.

On Monday afternoon, when he was driving along Wangaratta's main street, he allegedly did a U-turn to deliberately target the local MP Helen Haines outside her electorate office as she was getting items from her boot.

Witnesses said the 43-year-old's car rammed her repeatedly.

Loading...

The politician has had her legs amputated and remains in a critical condition in hospital.

Mr Nugent is now facing charges including intentionally causing serious injury, causing harm to a Commonwealth public official and possessing and cultivating cannabis.

Hours of news coverage since then has tried to answer the question — how did that man searching for delicate flowers in the bush go on to allegedly commit such an act?

Brendan Nugent faces potentially decades behind bars after being charged over the attack. (ABC News: Anita Lester)

A 'pacifist' vegan with a history of mental health struggles

Mr Nugent had struggled with mental health issues from a young age, according to a family member who spoke to the ABC.

He channelled his energy into the environment, his commitment to veganism and greening.

"But he was a pacifist. That's why this is completely out of the blue," the family member said.

Brendan cut off ties with that family member more than 10 years ago, they said.

He moved into a property in Tarrawingee, a short drive east of Wangaratta.

Neighbours living near Brendan Nugent's Tarrawingee home say his behaviour became more erratic in recent years. (ABC News: Erin Somerville)

He has been an avid social media poster, with more than 10,000 posts on the platform X across more than 12 years.

In 2019, they show he was engaging with people across the world about environmental research and current issues, tagging politicians and media in his posts.

In one post, he reflected on the beauty of the sounds of nature in his local area, and invited a fellow poster to come and stay.

But he also expressed disappointment in the Australian government and the mainstream media.

He also wrote about living with transverse myelitis, which causes spinal inflammation and left him in chronic pain.

In 2022, he complained that he wanted to get off the Disability Support Pension to go back to work. Earlier, he'd posted he was being stymied by Centrelink miscalculating his income.

He seemed agitated about the system.

"I have a masters degree, H1 average, still … [can't] get the basic assistance I need to work. Tried many times. Disability pension not enough to manage it so I'm constantly broke spending on health, NDIS is unavailable. We are left to sit in pain 24/7," his account posted.

The ABC has been told Mr Nugent — who police have charged with growing cannabis — had been consuming the drug for some time.

In 2022, he was charged with breaching an interim personal safety intervention order in Tarrawingee.

A now-deleted post from his X account in 2024, which was unearthed by the ABC NEWS Verify team, appears to show cracks in his mental health.

"Im just at home … Tarrawingee, being peaceful, and it feels like they are going to kill me," his caption reads.

A now-deleted tweet made by Brendan Nugent in July 2024. (Wayback Machine/X:NotLaoTzu)

He was seen by mental health teams at the Kerferd Clinic a few years ago, a mental health facility in Wangaratta.

His former teacher Jacquie, who went to his court appearance on Thursday, said she had helped him through that period, so he could "interact with the world again".

"He was quite confused about being in an institution … and needed support and I felt that I could do that," she told reporters.

This week, the property where it seems he became increasingly isolated had dozens of beer and spirits bottles, along with empty vegetable tins and juice bottles outside.

Empty beer bottles and boxes of rubbish line the side of Brendan Nugent's home in Tarrawingee. (ABC News: Erin Somerville)

The ABC has confirmed he was connected to community mental health teams, although it is not known how often they had been seeing him.

No promotion of violence found in Brendan Nugent's posts

Independent of Mr Nugent's health issues, he existed within a swirling hothouse of political anger and discontent — both online and in Victoria's High Country, a stronghold of the sovereign citizen movement.

Roughly 50 kilometres down the road from Mr Nugent's home was where self-declared sovereign citizen Dezi Freeman shot dead two police officers in August last year.

While this will form part of police investigations, no evidence has emerged that Mr Nugent himself was espousing violence online or mixing with sovereign citizens.

An ABC analysis of a sample of 1,800 of his tweets has found nothing promoting violence.

Brendan Nugent was a frequent Twitter user, posting on average nearly three times a day for more than of a decade. (X: NotLaoTzu)

Police are gathering evidence — and will have access to much more material — but Mr Nugent's former teacher Jacquie did not believe the man she knew was any kind of extremist.

"He does not threaten violence. He does not speak about terror," she said.

Mr Nugent's public postings on the platform X do show that he held firm political views.

He was against the war in Gaza, highly critical of Israel and was angry with the Australian government's actions.

He took aim at senior Labor MPs Richard Marles, Mark Dreyfus and Penny Wong, as well as commentators at the ABC and the Guardian.

"What a disgusting offical [sic] response to the killing of our citizens by israel" he posted to then-attorney-general Mr Dreyfus, after two Australians were killed in Southern Lebanon in an Israeli airstrike in 2023.

"You don't even call on israel to stop".

He railed against fossil fuels and in his earlier years he tweeted against logging, which was banned in public forests in Victoria in 2024.

The issues he was concerned about were also issues important to Helen Haines, who he allegedly went on to attack.

On her website, Ms Haines states she is "appalled" at the Gaza conflict and has called on the federal government "to do more to put pressure on the Netanyahu Government to end this conflict".

She spoke in support of ending native forest logging in parliament.

In the handful of tweets aimed at her, which seemed to end five years ago, Mr Nugent was pleasant and supportive.

But Josh Roose, who researches political and religious violent extremism at Deakin University, believes his public postings seemed increasingly frantic this year.

"He starts to engage with more conspiratorial material, but also a lot of anti-Zionist material and Israel content, and he is becoming more hardline," Dr Roose said.

After silence for a month, he made three posts on Sunday, the day before he allegedly attacked Haines.

The intersection of 'thin' ideology and poor mental health

Commenting more generally, Dr Roose said increasingly people were driven by "thin ideologies" — fuelled by personal grievances more than strong alignment with a religious or political cause.

He said the 2022 Wieambilla attack in Queensland, in which two police officers were killed, and last year's Porepunkah attack, had things in common with the alleged attack on Ms Haines.

Deakin University extremism researcher Josh Roose. (ABC News: Kyle Harley)

"There are clear similarities, including living, if not off grid, then living in isolation," he said.

"Living in rural poverty. Strongly held beliefs intersecting with mental illness. Raw political emotion.

"It is no coincidence to me that we have had Wieambilla, Porepunkah, and now this, in regional Australia — where there is a significant undercurrent of rural poverty and the stripping of support networks."

Just five days before she was attacked, Ms Haines had lobbied the prime minister for more funding for rural health services.

Mental health experts say violent incidents becoming more common

Former Australian of the Year, psychiatrist Patrick McGorry, said the mental health of Mr Nugent must be considered before any considerations of motive.

"[Mental health] may or may not have been a factor in the tragedy, but it wouldn't be surprising if it was," Professor McGorry said.

He said the mental health system in Victoria was in a worse state than before the 2019 royal commission into the sector.

Patrick McGorry says he believes violence is becoming more common among Victorians who suffer from mental health issues. (Supplied)

And while it was very rare for someone with a severe mental health condition to commit violence, he believed it was increasing — a position backed by the union that represents mental health workers.

Earlier this month, a woman was allegedly stabbed in the neck on a tram in Melbourne by a stranger who had schizophrenia.

In August, a 10-year-old child with cancer was punched in the head, and his mother was stabbed with scissors, by a man who told court he was in a "mental state of mind".

In October last year, CCTV captured a woman stabbing another woman as she walked through Melbourne's CBD. A court said she had "complex psychiatric illnesses".

"I wake up every morning half expecting to see another Bondi Junction on the front pages of the paper, " Mr McGorry said, referring to the 2024 attack where six people were killed in a mall by a man who a coroner found was in psychosis.

"Because I know that there are many untreated patients out there, some of whom, a small percentage of whom, when they're not well, can be quite dangerous."

World.title: Indian citizen trying to settle brother's estate slams 'humiliating' visa process
World.content:
Shipra Saini does not want to stay in Australia a second longer than she needs to.

The Indian citizen loved her life in Delhi but came to Australia in 2025 to care for her brother, who was battling a long illness.

On November 1 last year, he died from a brain haemorrhage, leaving Ms Saini in charge of his affairs.

Now she is living in Ballarat while she tries to settle her brother's estate, a process she has found complicated, emotional and difficult.

She has to apply for a death certificate, get a grant of probate, sell his Ballarat home and belongings, ship things back to India, open an estate bank account and pay off any expenses, then distribute the remaining assets.

But Ms Saini has had to jump over an extra hurdle; she is in a race to settle the estate before her visa expires and says she is battling a system that lacks compassion and empathy.

Shipra Saini says she will have to leave Australia with matters regarding her brother's estate outstanding. (ABC News: Charlotte Wilkes)

'Humiliating' visa processes

Due to the conditions of her visa, Ms Saini has a limited ability to work in Australia, so has had to rely on a loan to survive.

Each visa application can be expensive, and she estimated she had spent more than $40,000 while trying to settle her brother's estate and cover her living expenses.

She said the sooner she could get back to work in India, the better.

"Until my brother was here, [Australia] was a beautiful country," Ms Saini said.

But after the "humiliating" visa process she went through, she said she has "lost the charm of this country".

Shipra Saini says her brother, who was an Australian citizen, loved living in Ballarat in regional Victoria. (Supplied: City of Ballarat)

In August 2026, Ms Saini applied for another visa, supported by a letter from her solicitor, citing that settling the estate would take at least a further six months.

It was declined and her original visa, which has condition 8503 attached, was upheld with an end date of October 30.

According to the Department of Home Affairs, a person who holds, or has held, a visa with condition 8503 attached is prevented from validly applying in Australia for most visas unless they are granted a waiver of the condition.

"Before Condition 8503 is waived, the person will need to demonstrate that, since the time they were granted the visa to which Condition 8503 is subject, compelling and compassionate circumstances have developed over which they had no control and that resulted in a major change in their circumstances," the Department of Home Affairs said.

Ms Saini said despite requesting a waiver under compassionate grounds, the department rejected her application.

She said despite doing everything in her power to get things organised, Australia's processes were slow and out of her control, something she thought the department would have taken into account.

"Things which were not in my hands, such as the wait getting the probate and selling the house, it takes time," she said.

"It's not overnight that you expect a person to sell a house within a jiffy.

"It's a panic state."

Shipra Saini says she had to take the first offer on her brother's home. (ABC News: Charlotte Wilkes)

Ms Saini said because of the visa issue, she had to take the first offer on the home, when she would have preferred to wait for a better one.

She said the department's lack of compassion had already made a difficult situation worse.

"I'm on the brink of breaking down," she said.

"I'm in a situation stuck here because of somebody's death in the family.

"We are already grieving. It's adding on to the grief."

Shipra Saini says the Department of Home Affairs lacks compassion. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Ms Saini now plans to return to India later this month with matters regarding her deceased brother still outstanding.

She will not be able to attend a memorial service for her brother in November, be present for his property settlement, or finish settling her brother's employment-related entitlements such as superannuation while in Australia with the help of her solicitor.

The Department of Home Affairs said in a statement it could not comment on individual cases because of privacy reasons.

'A very difficult position'

Accredited specialist in immigration law Jordan Tew said there needed to be more "flexibility" for compelling and compassionate circumstances such as settling an estate.

"Someone trying to settle a deceased family member's estate is in a very different position to someone wanting more time in Australia for leisure or work, and administering an estate, particularly selling a property, often takes far longer than anyone anticipates," Mr Tew said.

"Where a waiver isn't available, a person will generally need to leave Australia and apply for a new visa from overseas, which can be costly and time-consuming.

"With the [federal] government announcing that it will introduce the 'no further stay' condition 8503 on all visitor visas, we expect many more people will be subject to the condition, and will need to rely on a waiver if their circumstances change while they're in Australia."

Mr Tew said situations like Ms Saini's could become more common with major political parties vowing to decrease migration.

"The level of migration is a legitimate matter for the government and the community to debate," he said.

"Our concern is less about the targets themselves, and more about how they're implemented.

"The political focus on net overseas migration is translating into policies that make it harder for people to come to, or remain in, Australia, and the risk is that genuine applicants get caught up in that as well."

With migration set to decrease, Ms Saini said she was a real-life example of the consequences.

"How could they be treating the immigrants this way?" she said.

"Unfortunately, we are stuck in election times, so people are not ready to help us.

"Politicians, they just go with the wave of whatever is going on."

World.title: A flight leaving Sydney tomorrow was 80 years in the making
World.content:
For Matthew Hayes, the first passenger flight taking off tomorrow from the newly built Western Sydney International Airport (WSI) is a dream come true.

The 20-year-old transport enthusiast has been looking forward to a second major airport in Sydney since he was a child.

Matthew Hayes is excited for WSI's opening. (Supplied)

"I used to go with my mother down to the site of the [Badgerys Creek] airport. Back then it was just paddocks and hills, and livestock grazing along the way," he said.

"My mum would tell me, 'One day, when you're older, this is going to be a whole airport.'"

Now it is.

Mr Hayes was one of the trial passengers who tested the airport's new systems two months ago, alongside 80-year-old Kevin Appleby.

The Mount Druitt resident was a teenager when he first heard about the possibility of a second Sydney airport.

Mr Appleby was one of the trial passengers breaking in the airport's new systems two months ago. (ABC News: Nabil Al-Nashar)

Separated by more than half a century, both men share the same excitement about the historic milestone.

The first flight from WSI to Gold Coast may take an hour and 20 minutes, but passengers embarking on that voyage will be completing a journey that began 80 years ago.

Where to put a second airport?

In the wake of World War II as aviation boomed, the question was already being asked; where should a second Sydney airport be built?

Federal and state governments have tried, failed and tried again to answer it since 1946.

The new Western Sydney International Airport has been 80 years in the making. (Supplied)

Potential locations ranged from as far north as Wyong to as far south as Goulburn.

In 1964, a NSW government study recommended Towra Point in Botany Bay.

For the following decade, federal and state bodies, both jointly and separately, considered this location and others, including Richmond, Somersby and Duffy's Forest.

Within a year of Gough Whitlam's rise to power in 1973, his government selected Galston in north-west Sydney as the second airport's location.

Gough Whitlam wanted to build a new airport at Galston. (ABC News) Protesters rallied against plans to build an airport in north-west Sydney. (ABC News)

The Galston airport proposal attracted community opposition. (ABC News)

Nearly 2,000 people travelled to Canberra to protest against the decision.

Back in Sydney, Whitlam faced a crowd of protesters in Baulkham Hills carrying placards reading "Don't pave paradise" and "No airport".

Protesters debated then prime minster Gough Whitlam. (ABC News)

Less than a year later, the government reversed its decision, citing financial and environmental feasibility concerns, as well as the site's proximity to the Richmond RAAF base.

When an International Air Transport Association (IATA) report in 1976 concluded a second airport was unnecessary, attention shifted to expanding Kingsford Smith Airport in Mascot.

Three years later, a federal and state government group called Major Airport Needs Of Sydney (MANS) recommended a third runway be constructed at Kingsford Smith and advised that should a future need for a second airport arise, Badgerys Creek should be its location.

Over the years, committee after committee and study after study made conflicting recommendations as politicians played political football with the issue, without a shovel ever touching dirt.

Almost 20 locations have been suggested as sites of Sydney's second airport over the decades. (ABC News)

In the end, 19 different sites across the state were considered before the Hawke government selected Badgerys Creek in 1986.

The government started buying up land in the Western Sydney suburb, which was mostly grasslands and cow paddocks at the time.

Protests over new airport

Regular protests against the project continued over the years, fuelled by noise and environmental concerns.

Several community groups organised campaigns, protests and events to agitate against a new airport.

Western Sydney locals Carolyn Wong and Katherine Wong oppose the new airport. (ABC News: Floss Adams)

Carolyn Wong's family has lived in Luddenham for 70 years and has been protesting against the airport for the majority of that time.

Locals asleep at school, 'walking around like zombies' due to new 24/7 airport Locals living near the new Western Sydney airport say they are only managing a few hours' sleep a night since operations began.

"I was allowed to take the day off school to go down to Canberra and protest, that was over 50 years ago," she said.

"We had a big protest at the Old Hubertus Club one day; the media came but it was the day Mrs Gandhi was assassinated so we didn't make it to the news."

A No Aircraft Noise Party was founded and contested the 1995 NSW state election, which was won by Labor's Bob Carr.

When John Howard's government took control in Canberra the following year, the location was back on the table, with an investigation launched into whether Holsworthy could be an alternative to Badgerys Creek.

By 1998, federal and state Labor MPs had formed a bloc called Labor Against Badgerys to oppose the construction of the airport.

A plan to build an airport at Badgerys Creek was opposed, (ABC News)

Demonstrators against a second Sydney airport at Badgerys Creek outside the Liberal Party election launch in 1998. (Reuters)

They were joined by the Western Sydney Alliance of Councils, which vowed to fight the airport.

Subsequent governments would continue the painful back-and-forth until Tony Abbott's Coalition government in 2014 locked in Badgerys Creek as the site of the city's future second airport.

In 2014, the second Sydney airport at Badgerys Creek was finally approved. (ABC News)

Funding and approvals took four years and construction began in 2018.

The greenfield site was transformed into Australia's largest civil earthmoving project outside of the mining sector.

Over the next eight years, the rolling green pastures of Badgerys Creek slowly disappeared and were replaced by a cargo precinct, passenger terminal and a 3.7-kilometre runway.

Residents protest against potential aircraft noise in 2020. (ABC News: Luke Rosen) A house earmarked for demolition as part of the airport project. (ABC News: Jessica Kidd)

Construction of the new airport pictured from a farm at Badgerys Creek in 2021. (ABC News: Jack Fisher )

It took 10,000 workers to make the $5.6 billion airport a reality.

It has the capacity to move 1.8 million tonnes of cargo and 10 million passengers annually.

The WSI runaway being constructed. (Facebook: Western Sydney International Airport)

'Kick in the guts'

Cargo flights have been taking to the skies since July, confirming decades of angst and some local residents' worst fears about the project.

The round-the-clock freight flights have already caused many a sleepless night for residents living close to the airport.

Weighing up if a trip from Sydney's new airport is for you The doors to Western Sydney International Airport are set to soon welcome commercial passengers.

Ms Wong and her daughter Katherine were considering moving away from the area due to the noise from overnight flights.

"It makes me sad that the airport is about to fully open; it really is the end of an era and our lives as we know it," she said.

"We still don't have access to the new buses, the rail isn't ready, the houses that need [sound] insulation haven't got it, the Luddenham Village Plan and zoning haven't been sorted.

"It's such a kick in the guts that they are opening it without addressing any of the community's concerns."

The new airport is ready to take passengers. (ABC News: Digby Werthmuller)

Some locals still oppose the new airport. (ABC News: Liam Patrick)

Seven passenger-carrying airlines have already signed up with WSI including Qantas, Jetstar, Air New Zealand and Qatar Airways, with flights to Doha, Singapore and Ho Chi Minh City already scheduled.

Their jet trails will mark the end of a long and arduous chapter in the airport's development.

World.title: Gone in less than six minutes: Watch as floodwaters swallow 4WD
World.content:
For the first few seconds, it doesn't look like a life-and-death situation.

A grey four-wheel drive ute enters floodwater covering a road in Morayfield, north of Brisbane.

The water appears mostly calm. There is no raging torrent, no dramatic wall of water.

But within minutes, the vehicle is gone.

It's a stark demonstration of a message flood safety experts repeat year after year: "If it's flooded, forget it."

While ABC reporter Will Murray and bystander Daniel Hainey pulled the driver free, the footage shows just how little time there is to escape a sinking car.

Loading...

10:04am Thursday



A car drives past a "road flooded" warning sign on Buchanan Road.

Mr Murray and ABC camera operator Liz Pickering are on the scene to report on flash flooding in south-east Queensland. Almost instantly, they start running toward the scene, aware of the danger.



But for the driver, there is little indication of how deep the water is.

According to UNSW senior research fellow in the School of Population Health Amy Peden, that uncertainty is precisely what makes floodwaters so dangerous.



"You can never know the velocity and the depth of the water," Dr Peden said.

The 4WD quickly became stuck after it drove towards the flooded road.

Approx 30 seconds



The ute is stranded and starts to float after making it about halfway across the flooded road.

On her own camera tape, Ms Pickering is heard saying: "How can we help him? Jesus Christ."

Air trapped inside the cabin initially gives the vehicle some buoyancy. But water is already starting to infiltrate the vehicle's systems.



"As the water gets into the workings of the car, it will start to sink," Dr Peden says.

Mr Murray immediately calls Triple Zero (000), trying to pinpoint their exact location for emergency services.



What began as a vehicle crossing a flooded road has become a race against time.

The ABC reporter was quickly on the phone to Triple Zero.

Approx 1 minute



The car begins to spin. The bonnet is under water.



The driver is trying to reverse out, with no luck. His window line is edging closer to the water's surface.

For anyone trapped inside, every passing second is reducing escape options.



"You need to try and get out of the vehicle quickly," Dr Peden says.

Loading...

Approx 2 minutes



The rear wheel is fully submerged; the ute's snorkel is soon underwater.

Loading...

Approx 3 minutes



The situation hits a tipping point. The car is sinking, and quickly.



The driver is trapped inside what's rapidly become an underwater chamber.



In the distance, bystanders are shouting.

What comes next is an extraordinary act of bravery. But Dr Peden warns such rescues can come at a devastating cost, with would-be rescuers sometimes drowning while trying to help.



Her advice is simple: don't put yourself at risk, and call for help as quickly as possible.

Loading...

Approx 3 minutes 30 seconds



Passing the phone to Ms Pickering while still talking to Triple Zero, Mr Murray decides to act. He starts swimming towards the sinking car.



Mr Hainey follows.

"When we got to the car we tried to open the closest door, no luck, then got on the back of the car with the thought to break the back window," Mr Murray said.



"I thought to try the passenger side rear door first and put my feet against the car and pulled as hard as I could, and with some luck the door swung open."



As soon as the door opens and the driver comes out, the vehicle sinks completely.

It is only 90 seconds from the moment Mr Murray and Mr Hainey get into the water to attempt the rescue until the four-wheel drive's roof is submerged.



"I think what this vision very clearly shows is that you will not have a lot of time," Dr Peden says.

The driver, Mr Murray and Mr Hainey emerge safely.

The car disappears underwater.

The three men swam to safety after the rescue.

Within seconds, the man was freed.

Every second counts

For both flood researchers and emergency responders, the rescue demonstrates a simple reality: people often have far less time to escape than they realise.

Queensland Fire and Rescue swift water instructor Matt Kelemen says the first thing people should do if caught in this situation is take off their seatbelts and try to wind their windows down.

Even if the car's windows are electric, they should work for at least 10 to 60 seconds.

"Before the water comes up too much and shorts out the car's circuits, let the windows down so you've got an egress area out of the vehicle," Mr Kelemen says.

How to plan for flooding If you could be cut off by floodwaters, make preparations. ABC Emergency has put together a list of things you should do if you are affected.

If that's not possible, experts say to try to find something inside the car to smash the window. But not just any window.

"Your front windscreen and your rear dash window are both laminates, so they're not the best to break because they'll just crack and they'll stay in place," Mr Kelemen says.

"But nearly every side window on all cars now is just tempered glass, so you should be able to hit it, and it should shatter."

You may be thinking, why not try to just open the door?

Well, opening a door against floodwater can be difficult because of water pressure acting on the outside of the vehicle.

Mr Keleman says occupants may effectively be trying to push against hundreds of kilograms of water, which is why emergency services encourage people to use windows as their primary means of escape.

No safety tools can remove floodwater risks

A 4WD became unstable in 45 cm of water, and floated in water 95 cm deep. ( )

Research from the University of NSW Water Research Laboratory shows even relatively shallow water can cause vehicles to begin floating.

A small car like a Toyota Yaris can be moved by water just 15 centimetres deep with a flow speed of 3.6 km/h. It can be carried away in 60cm of water.

A larger four-wheel drive can be moved by 45cm of water and begin floating in 95cm of water, able to be pushed along by just a finger.

"Don't think because you've got a bigger vehicle, a more powerful vehicle, that you're going to be OK," Dr Peden says.

"The safest car in floodwater is the one that never enters it."

The Morayfield rescue ended with handshakes, hugs and relief. But the footage leaves a sobering lesson.

The driver entered the water in a functioning vehicle. About six minutes later, it had disappeared beneath the surface.

And without two brave bystanders, the outcome may have been very different.

World.content:
WorldEuropeCrime Deadly shooting outside Paris a ‘terrorist attack’, say police David Crowe October 24, 2026 — 6:34am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. A gunman has killed one victim and wounded five others in an outer suburb of Paris known for its migrant communities, prompting public warnings of a terror attack in the wake of violent protests. Police arrested the alleged killer after a frenzy of drive-by shootings that left one 12-year-old girl fighting for her life. Forensic investigators search for evidence after a shooting in Trappes, outside Paris. AP French President Emmanuel Macron described the shootings as a “racist terrorist attack” in the areas of Trappes and Yvelines, south-west of the Paris city centre, and warned of the pressure on the nation from weeks of unrest. Police said they were treating the attack as terrorism and were aware of reports that the killer had set traps in his home to kill visitors that he expected to investigate him after the shootings. Police also detained one of his family members.



The shootings on Friday (France time) came on the eve of another series of protests and rallies due to be held on Saturday in Paris and other cities over the cost of living and school funding. Worried about another outbreak of violence and looting, the French government has mobilised 70,000 police to guard against rioting, while authorities in Lyon and Marseilles have banned the marches. French President Emmanuel Macron meets community members at the town hall in Trappes after the shooting. Reuters Authorities did not draw a direct link between the riots and the shootings, but the attack in the Paris suburbs came after a week of debate about whether migrants were among the looters who smashed stores last weekend. Macron spoke of a “turning point in our republic and our nation” as a result of the terror attack.



Mayor Nicolas Dainville, whose local government of La Verrière includes Yvelines, said the attack was another sign of the pressure on French unity after the protests. Related Article Protests Just what do France’s angry youth want? It’s complicated “A racist motive seems clear, given that here in La Verrière three individuals of African descent were targeted,” he told Franceinfo. “This points to a very serious situation in France, a country that is fractured and divided. “The atmosphere we are currently living in – in which the mayors, in their own modest way, are trying to address – is truly critical.”



National police union spokesman Rudy Manna told Franceinfo the gunman fired multiple times at people walking on the street who had done nothing to provoke him. Manna said the evidence suggested the gunman also intended to kill a police officer. Interior Minister Laurent Nunez warned on Friday about the risk of further violence in protests on Saturday, accusing ultra-left groups of encouraging violence and looting. More than 3000 stores were damaged or looted last weekend after protests turned violent across the country. Police arrested 2700 people, about 70 per cent of them adults.



Related Article Analysis

Paris protests The violence of the streets of Paris looked like rage. It revealed a society that will take years to heal “We will be uncompromising with rioters, looters and all those who commit acts of violence,” Nunez told reporters on Friday after meetings with Macron and other government leaders. Nunez said authorities had identified online calls from hard-left groups that encouraged activists to target public buildings. “We are not ​talking about a nice, friendly demonstration,” he said. “We will be extremely vigilant, extremely firm, and ⁠we will let absolutely nothing pass.”



Police have authorised ​a union demonstration in Paris on Saturday but have insisted it take place away from the Place de la Republique, an area that was a focal point of the riots last weekend and has been under curfew since then. Authorities rejected requests for rallies in Paris by the main student union, UNEF, and the Yellow Vest movement, an anti-establishment force that first emerged in 2018. Many French cities beyond Paris have also banned protests, including France’s second- and third-largest cities, Marseille and Lyon. Nunez ‌said 10,000 more ⁠police would be on the streets than a week ago. With Reuters

World.title: Crisafulli hopes he’s shed the ‘new’ government tag. That has its own risk
World.content:
Perspective PoliticsQueenslandQueensland government Crisafulli hopes he’s shed the ‘new’ government tag. That has its own risk Matt Dennien October 24, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Approaching the halfway milestone of Queensland’s four-year electoral cycle, Premier David Crisafulli has spent the past week doing plenty of talking – in speech after set-piece speech. He has spent it talking about what his government has done, and what it’s yet to do. The latter involves fixing the more nebulous “crises” he rode to power vowing to address. “The big four issues that I spoke about before the election remain the big four issues and the big four challenges,” Crisafulli said at his 2026 CEDA State of the State address on Monday. Over a week of speeches, Premier David Crisafulli stayed resolutely on message. AAPIMAGE “And on all of them [health, housing, crime and cost of living], we are making progress after a long period of time where the numbers went in the wrong direction.”



While Crisafulli can cite numbers heading in a better direction – and did, across several other major speeches this week, including to the property and local government sectors – more than anyone else, he should know the limits of relying on statistics. During a Queensland Media Club appearance on Wednesday billed as featuring a “significant policy announcement” in the law and order space, no such thing came, beyond confirmation the parliament will pass a government bill next week. Nor was there anything new in any other area. ‘I want to talk today about what I call a trio of opportunities: fuel, critical minerals, and data centres. All three have challenges. All three have opportunities.’ Crisafulli in his Monday State of the State speech This is the bind in which the government now finds itself: a list of concrete election platform items already all-but ticked off, leaving them either pushing ahead with new policy efforts in areas plaguing governments across the country and globe, or hoping its “let us cook” line finds sympathy. s are still running for the work of the “new Queensland government”, but frustrations over this positioning are beginning to emerge – particularly on crime, where the LNP set the terms of the debate while in opposition, yet admits that public dissatisfaction remains, two years on.





Crisafulli and his strategists seem to believe these glimpses beyond the pre-election picture they painted are too minor to spook a wider population wary of action that’s too swift or extreme. The Labor opposition, led for now by Steven Miles, seems stuck on a small-target strategy, hoping that something – or an accumulation of things – will suddenly become too much for people to bear. The resignation from cabinet of Child Safety Minister Amanda Camm may be the first bit of bark taken from Crisafulli that Labor would view as a win. While Crisafulli’s LNP remain the clear favourites in this masthead’s regular Resolve Political Monitor, that polling also shows the broader mood has soured across a year that has thrown no shortage of extra problems at households and governments.



After significant improvement following the 2024 vote, the outlook for the next year or so among those surveyed for both their personal lives, and the state more broadly, has since returned to pre-election levels. Related Article Exclusive

Resolve Political Monitor ‘Not landing many blows’: New polling to heap pressure on Miles’ leadership Almost more people think things will get worse in their lives than not change, and both cohorts are double the size of those who think it will get better. Compared to before the election, their view of the state’s future is now more pessimistic. The tectonic plates long holding the two-party system in place appear their shakiest since Queensland saw Pauline Hanson’s best yet showing in an Australian parliament three decades ago. So two years could be a long time – for all involved. How do you act, or give the appearance of acting, on fundamental social and economic problems in a way that makes people feel things have changed for the better, when you are also cautious of moving too fast or too far, let alone actually change things for the long-term good?



The Crisafulli government may have a swathe of state and national elections across the country to learn from before it has to face voters for the first time from office, but a bet on people’s willingness to wait to feel change while being told it is happening is no longer such a sure thing. World.title: We’re all excited about the new Powerhouse Parramatta, but I have a better idea
World.content:
CultureArt & designVisual art Opinion We’re all excited about the new Powerhouse Parramatta, but I have a better idea Richard Glover Broadcaster and columnist October 24, 2026 — 5:30am

October 24, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Sydney’s new Powerhouse Museum opens in a fortnight, with displays of cutting-edge food, design and music. Fair enough, but I thought museums were supposed to be a snapshot of the past. Herewith, my pitch for a Museum of Forgotten Places. Come, let me be your guide. The new Powerhouse Museum in Parramatta will be a “cutting-edge” marvel. My museum, on the other hand, will take you back to the old days. Steven Siewert First, we enter a barber shop, a replica of the establishment found in every Australian suburb until about 1983. There are two barbers cutting hair, both chain-smoking as they snip. You can hardly see yourself in the mirror for all the smoke. The radio is tuned to the races and a wide range of reading material is available, but only if you count 20 flyblown copies of The Australasian Post as a “wide range”. Each issue of The Post is missing the Ettamogah Pub cartoon, these having been removed in order to decorate the walls.



The whole place stinks of flammable hair oil, a substance which will occasionally form a dangerous partnership with the cigarette dangling from the barber’s lips. One drop of ash and it’s a conflagration. The barber rarely confesses his previous life as a shearer, although you may notice the pot of tar, sitting there on the counter, employed whenever he nicks his customer’s ear. A classic Australian barbershop in 1956. Add some carcinogenic fumes, and voila! In the next room, we spot a Holden car, dating from the mid-1960s. There are bench seats front and back – 100 per cent vinyl – and no seatbelts. Four children are on the back bench, standing, untethered, like little missiles waiting to be launched through the front window whenever dad touches the brakes. The windows are closed, except for the driver’s window, which is open just a crack, through which cigarette smoke bellows as if from Vesuvius. Mum is the navigator, reading directions from a Gregory’s Street Directory, but only to the extent she can see the map through all the smoke.



Given the secondhand smoke, you’ll probably want to move to the next room. In Room Three, you’ll find a replica of a traditional Australian motel room. Once inside, you’ll discover the carpet is covered with suspicious stains, but of a greying hue, so it’s unclear when the murder took place and how many were killed. The toilet features a sash, rather like those awarded at the Royal Easter Show. Hurrah! On this occasion, they’ve cleaned the toilet! Good on ’em! Enjoy all the greatest recipes from the ’50s, ‘60s and ’70s. There’s also a hatch through which breakfast will be delivered. This will consist of two pieces of rubbery toast destined to be ripped to shreds by the rock-hard pat of butter on offer. The four kids, featured in our earlier display, will jump up and down on the bed until every spring is busted. Let’s move on to Room Four. Aware that visitors have a taste for gore, as seen in Europe’s proliferating torture museums, we feature a typical 1970s Australian classroom. In a scene reminiscent of Old Sydney Town, students are continuously thrashed by the deputy principal, their indignant screams echoing against the walls.



Also, in a postmodern flourish, all the clocks in this room are designed to go backwards, reflecting the experience of all those from the 1970s who studied geography. And inside every desk, you can find copies of Go-Set or Dolly, a surreptitious peek at which was the only upside of an Australian schooling. Related Article Opinion

Money & relationships You don’t need to see my bank account to know I’m truly middle class Richard Glover Broadcaster and columnist Be sure to time your visit to Room Four for 11am. At this point, every day, staff will serve everyone a small bottle of milk, left in the sun until it is warm and curdled. A replica school dunny is located nearby for when you need to chunder. Room Five celebrates the world of food: not the fancy stuff featured in the new Powerhouse, but the food of Australia’s recent past. To bring alive the ’50s, ‘60s and ’70s, our curators have created a “smell-scape” in which visitors entering the room will be immediately struck by the stench of overcooked cabbage and boiled-to-death beans. A BBQ station, located on one side of the room, will see T-bone steaks being incinerated until the meat pleads for mercy. On the other side of the room, small cans of tuna will be ladled into large buckets of wallpaper paste in order to produce “Tuna Mornay”. Do get in quick before it sets.



In Room Six – we’re reaching the climax here – there’s a perfect replica of a traditional Australian pub. Every surface is covered in tiles, with not a scrap of fabric to be seen. There are two beers on offer: New and Old. If you want a red wine, there’s a half-empty bottle in the fridge. Women are not allowed in here – are you crazy? – and the smell is terrible. At least it gets you limbered up for the smell of the latrine. Try to be in the museum at 6pm to see the traditional hose-out! Edwardian tiling, you’ll discover, was more than an aesthetic choice. After all that excitement, you’ll be forced to exit via the gift shop. Why not pick up a pair of desert boots, some Bogart jeans and a 10-pack of cigarettes (perfect for the underage smoker)? Or you may prefer a tin of hair oil, a copy of The Australasian Post, and an authentic, blood-stained teacher’s cane? What a day! What memories! Let’s wait a fortnight and see if the new Powerhouse can offer anything better.

World.title: Why your home now costs you twice as much – and how to fix it
World.content:
MoneyBorrowingHome loans Opinion Why your home now costs you twice as much – and how to fix it Nicole Pedersen-McKinnon Money contributor October 24, 2026 — 5:01am

October 24, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

It’s at 6.36 per cent interest – where most mortgages are now – that the price you initially paid for your home, doubles. Yes, the interest you outlay on a typical $400,000 mortgage is almost exactly $400,000, on $700,000 borrowed it’s $700,000 and on $1.5 million – you get it. That’s over a 25-year loan term. And, crucially, it’s only if you let your loan term run for 25 years. So, let’s look at your shortening strategies, at all the ways you can bring your mortgage-freedom date forward. Some of them are cheaper and easier than you think. We will start with the cheapest. Struggling under the weight of your mortgage? Here’s how to break free. Simon Letch Use the offset potential properly: Very few people operate offset accounts to their full benefit. But let’s make sure you have a proper one first – because ASIC has lenders in its sights about this.



To take maximum advantage of an offset account attached to a mortgage, money you hold in the offset must reduce the loan balance by an equal amount. In other words, dollar for dollar. Editor's pick Opinion

Home loans Why your bank might be overcharging you interest – and how to check Bec Wilson Money contributor Watch out, too, for offset accounts that don’t give you the same interest rate saving as your home loan. Many offsets attached to fixed-rate loans do not. But a quality offset account is a powerful thing. Let’s say you scrounge every dollar you have to your name and put them in an offset account or accounts – note that housing money here will save you more than you will earn in a deposit account and those “returns” will be tax-free. You hold $30,000 – your savings for everything, as well as your emergency fund – in an offset account against a $700,000 loan.



By simply redeploying money thus, you won’t pay $700,000 in interest but only $594,133 – so save more than $105,000 – and you will slash nearly two years off your time in debt. If it helps with motivation, realise that at a higher interest rate, those interest and time savings are bigger. Up-level your offset Part of the reason I like credit cards – apart from an insatiable appetite for frequent flyer points! – is this strategy. But let me begin by saying you should use credit cards only if you can 100 per cent trust yourself with debt. Just by shaving 36 basis points off your interest rate, you’ll go from paying $700,000 in loan interest to $653,033. A credit card lets you get your salary paid into an offset account and sit there for an entire month. You take full advantage of the interest-free days on the credit card by paying off the balance in full on the statement due date. What it means is that you use the bank’s money to save you mortgage interest.



How much difference could it make to the bottom line of a loan? Say your household makes $10,000 a month and you offset that as well as your $30,000 in savings against your $700,000 loan. This will get you out of debt two years and five months early and boost your interest savings to $136,875. Your bill drops from $700,000 to $563,125. Again, that’s just by simply re-organising your finances. Try the mortgage mind-tricks: You might have heard this strategy before but it works thanks to our Gregorian calendar. Think about it – there are 12 months in a year but 26 fortnights. And that means a beautiful thing: if you simply halve your monthly required minimum mortgage payment and pay that amount fortnightly, you will come out a whole month ahead. It will only cost you a few dollars extra each fortnight but will get you ahead a massive amount. On our model $700,000 mortgage, you go from paying $700,000 in interest to $564,546, a saving of $134,262. You will be paying $2333 instead of each fortnight $2152, but the impact – wow!



And is your minimum repayment a weird number? It’s usually so. Consider making it a nice neat one on the higher side. The effect of a round-up will be similar to the above. But this next technique is the mic-drop mortgage-busting moment … all it requires is a renegotiation or refinancing. Editor's pick Opinion

Money psychology The one mistake that turns sensible investors into panic buyers Paridhi Jain Money contributor Up stumps but still stump up: While an average mortgage is now in that 6.36 per cent “double-trouble” zone, the best are still down around 6 per cent. And as always, we are talking about quality, comparable loans to the big four banks – ones that are backed by authorised deposit-taking institutions so can both offer real offset accounts and also have the protection of the government’s $250,000 deposit guarantee if an institution goes bust. What are we talking in savings here? Just by shaving 36 basis points off your interest rate, you’ll go from paying $700,000 in loan interest to $653,033.



Don’t miss that this hasn’t cost you even a dollar extra – but if you “up stumps but still stump up”, as I call it, your savings go stratospheric. Move mortgage (or negotiate a discount) and simply keep your repayments the same, and you’ll save $102,480 and shave 1½ years off your time in debt. That total outlay is just $597,520. Given you are used to paying that amount already, all that early repayment power is no extra pain to your pocket (in reality you will be suddenly overpaying by $155). Editor's pick Good Weekend The funeral where the worlds of power, politics and organised crime came together And just imagine if did all of the above. You’d stack savings upon savings and entirely avoid the horrible possibility we’ve just hit: mortgage price doubling. Nicole Pedersen-McKinnon is author of How to Get Mortgage-Free Like Me, available at nicolessmartmoney.com. Follow her on Facebook, X and Instagram.

They should always seek their own professional advice that takes into account their own personal circumstances before making any financial decisions. World.title: The women who kill and the desperation that drives them
World.content:
NationalNSWCrime The women who kill and the desperation that drives them Perry Duffin October 24, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

At the end of a horror winter for domestic violence in NSW – in which three women were allegedly murdered in just one day, a mother was accused of stabbing her children to death, and a caustic debate erupted over a politician’s comments – new research quietly revealed an ugly truth. Women who kill their partners are almost always killing their abuser. Jessica Silva, Cathrina Ann Cahill and Nirmeen Noufl all endured abuse. New data shows women who kill male partners are usually killing their abuser. Artwork: Matthew Absalom-Wong Three women – a 23-year-old in Wagga Wagga, a woman in her 90s in Bondi and a 70-year-old near Tenterfield – were allegedly murdered in separate domestic violence incidents across NSW within hours on September 19. Three men were charged with murder, including the Wagga woman’s partner and the Tenterfield woman’s son. Two days earlier, Nirmeen Noufl was sentenced to a minimum three years behind bars after she stabbed her husband Mamdouh to death following a fight at their Greenacre home in October 2024.



The seemingly light manslaughter sentence shocked Mamdouh’s family. It also reignited a debate simmering since Senator Pauline Hanson in July declared domestic violence a “two-way street”. Noufl used a saw to cut up her husband’s body and disposed of the remains in bins around Sydney’s south-west. His body parts were never recovered. An appeal for Mamdouh “Emad” Noufl’s disappearance was issued in 2023. NSW Police Noufl pleaded guilty to manslaughter, which prosecutors accepted in lieu of the original charge of murder, because of Mamdouh’s lengthy history of abuse. “[Mamdouh] was controlling of his wife and daughters. He held conservative Islamic views with respect to the role of women in the home and community and was strict in the application of these views to his female relatives,” the agreed fact sheet released by the court reads.



“How does this woman get away with killing and dismembering her husband and then pleading manslaughter? Oh yes, she claims he abused her. The usual story,” one commentator posted. The sentence divided the community. However, new research suggested it was part of a well-established pattern. The NSW Coroner’s Domestic Violence Death Dashboard was launched in June and covers deaths between 2000 and 2026, and looked at 2234 homicide victims. A subset of 336 are intimate-partner homicides, which are distinct from other forms of fatal domestic violence including children, parents, grandparents and siblings. Of the 336 victims, four in five (293) were women and almost all women (99 per cent) were killed by their abuser.



Related Article Graphic content

Crime ‘I had enough’: Mum dismembers abusive husband, escapes murder conviction The men killed in domestic violence (75 in total) were killed mostly by women (65) and rarely by male partners (10). But the data also showed that 73 per cent of men killed by their partner were like Mamdouh Noufl – the primary abuser in the relationship. The youngest female victim of an intimate partner homicide was aged just 15 years old, the oldest was 82, the data shows. “These are lives cut short, children left without a mother, and families and communities shattered. This dashboard honours the victims, their families and communities,” NSW Women’s Safety Commissioner Hannah Tonkin said.



“Sadly, we know that for every death, there are thousands more women and children experiencing violence across the country every single day.” Noufl was given six years and nine months in prison with a non-parole period of three years. She has spent two years in prison already, which means she will be eligible for parole in October 2027. ‘[Noufl] was in a violent and abusive relationship for many years, which satisfied the subjective limb of self-defence.’ Robert Candelori, solicitor The sentence, handed down by Justice Peter Hamill on September 18, shocked Mamdouh’s family. His nephew flew into a rage outside court, saying Noufl should be doing “25 to life”. Sydney solicitor Robert Candelori said Noufl’s sentence actually fell towards the higher end for manslaughter cases where women kill abusers.



“This is an unenviable sentencing exercise for any judge given the macabre manner of disposal of the victim’s body, however, that clouds the basis of the plea,” said Candelori, who has defended women who kill. “There was evidence, corroborated by her children and other sources, indicating she was in a violent and abusive relationship for many years, which satisfied the subjective limb of self-defence.” Prosecutors were obliged to prove Noufl had intentionally killed Mamdouh but couldn’t, in part because his body was never recovered. It forced them to accept a plea to manslaughter instead of murder. Noufl’s case, as with many abused women who kill, was replete with evidence she had suffered extensively at the hands of people who should have cared for them, Candelori said. “This is a woman who on all the evidence, including two expert psychiatrists, had serious mental health issues not just from the violent trauma she suffered at the hands of her husband but also in her abusive upbringing, including being subjected to female genital mutilation at the direction of her mother,” he said.



“In my opinion, her sentence was not lenient in the circumstances. But for the 25 per cent statutory plea discount, she would have received a head sentence of nine years which is towards the higher end for manslaughter sentences.” There are notable other case studies in which women have killed their abuser, long before Noufl. Bankstown mother Thi Bich Huynh, 37, stabbed her husband, Quo Dung Bui, 49, through the neck as he slept in 2021. Bui had been physically and verbally abusive for years against his family, a court heard. Huynh was found not criminally responsible and dealt with under mental health laws in 2023. Cathrina Ann Cahill and her fiance David Walsh in October 2016. Facebook



Sydney’s Irish diaspora were shocked in 2017 when Cathrina Ann Cahill killed David Walsh in a drunken fight involving friends at their Padstow home. Jessica Silva pictured in 2012 after being sentenced for the manslaughter of her ex-partner James Polkinghorne. Peter Rae Walsh had used “controlling conduct, verbal abuse and demeaning language” against Cahill throughout their relationship, and she would also respond with violence. Cahill was sentenced to eight years in prison after pleading guilty to manslaughter. Jessica Silva, similarly, stabbed James Polkinghorne to death in 2012 outside her Marrickville home and received just 18 months for manslaughter which was entirely suspended. She was then acquitted entirely on appeal.



A judge noted “the circumstances faced by Ms Silva were horrendous” – Polkinghorne had attacked Silva, her father and brother in a rage. Silva stabbed Polkinghorne in the back, killing him, in self-defence. Noufl told confidants she “had enough” of the abuse, before she killed her husband. “All my life I have dedicated to the kids and him, and he just treated me like shit. Spat at me,” she said. Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.content:
LifestyleFashionStyle How this ‘grandma’ accessory became the coolest celebrity must-have Lauren Ironmonger October 24, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.
