World.title: What should I do about a cat foster carer who can’t follow the rules?
World.content:
You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.

Q: I am a cat foster carer and I’ve noticed that some of the other foster carers don’t follow the strict “rescue rules”. One lets her foster cat go outdoors, which is strictly forbidden. Another feeds her foster cats on the kitchen benchtop. Should I say something? S.B., Waverley, NSW

Photo: Illustration by Drew Aitken

A: We got our dog through a foster carer, so I know what great work you guys do, taking in rescued pets, then matching them with suitable owners, like some kind of animal-human dating service: OkCute-pet or Rin Tin Tinder. Even more amazingly, you do all this for no financial reward, just the joy of helping a sad, unloved little critter embark on a happier life with a rescued pet in their home.

So because foster caring is an unpaid, thankless, time-consuming job, I’m sure most of us would forgive a few tiny lapses of judgment, like letting a cat go outdoors now and then. I mean, sure the cat could do a runner, then go feral in bushland and eat all the remaining endangered numbats – but still, a cat strutting around outside enjoying the sunshine?

World.title: Mel C was young, rich and famous. This is the advice Lionel Richie gave her
World.content:
NationalGood Weekend Mel C was young, rich and famous. This is the advice Lionel Richie gave her Benjamin Law October 24, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Each week, Benjamin Law asks public figures to discuss the subjects we’re told to keep private by getting them to roll a die. The numbers they land on are the topics they’re given. This week, he talks to Melanie C. The singer, songwriter and performer, 52, is also known as former Spice Girl Mel C, aka Sporty Spice. Her latest release, Sweat, is the highest-charting solo album by any member of the band. Melanie C on finding success: “I felt guilty … I was earning money that my relatives wouldn’t earn in a lifetime. Some were doing very hard manual labour.” Conor Clinch MONEY What was money like, growing up? My family’s from Liverpool and I grew up in a place called Whiston, in between Liverpool and Manchester, a working-class area. There wasn’t much money around, and people worked really hard to just put food on the table and pay the bills. But we’re proud to be working-class: of our work ethic, of our community, of the way we stick together. What did you always have and what did you go without? We went without anything that was surplus to requirements. As a young kid, I went to dance class, but my mum and dad got divorced when I was, like, four, and finances changed a lot. Dance classes weren’t something my mum could afford, though they were something I went on and on about. Eventually, she found the money to get me there, which led to … this. Gosh, how different life is now.



Do you remember there being a point in your career where you thought, “Oh, I’m rich now”? When I got my first cheque from Virgin Records for £10,000 [in the mid-1990s]. I could go to JD Sports and buy whatever trainers I wanted that day. Becoming rich so young can be a curse, too … Actually, it was very difficult. Being where I’m from, I didn’t know anybody with money. The Spice Girls became very successful, money started coming in very quickly, and I felt guilty. Related Article Sunday Life Melanie Chisholm: 'I was really lonely while I was in the Spice Girls' Guilty. Why? I had this career – which was my ultimate dream – and I was being rewarded financially very well for it. I was earning money that my relatives wouldn’t earn in a lifetime. Some of them were doing very hard manual labour, and I was getting up on stage and singing. Getting up on stage and singing doesn’t feel like work to me. It’s not work: it’s joy. It took me a long, long time before I didn’t feel guilty about the money I was earning. What changed? Fame brings other things with it. I’ve had some very difficult times – personally, emotionally, psychologically – and there can be hardships in this industry. It’s not all happiness and light. So that makes me feel less guilty.



What advice would you give to young pop stars on the rise? We were at an awards show, and Lionel Richie said to us, “Earn here [raises one hand] and spend here [lowers the other hand].” In other words, “Live within your means.” It stuck with all of us. SEX When I say “sex”, what’s the first thing that comes to mind? That I didn’t want to land on this topic [laughs]. I think I’m a bit of prude at heart. And yet the video clip for Sweat – the lead single on your new album – is pretty steamy. Thank you for saying that! [Beams] What’s interesting about that is: I’ve never felt comfortable, as an artist and performer, being sexual. I was very comfortable being Sporty Spice; I didn’t have to be an overtly sexual performer. The most sexual I’ve ever been in my career is this video – which is interesting, given I’m now in my 50s. Has it unlocked something? I think the older you get, the more comfortable you become in your own skin, and the fewer f---s you give. It’s a beautiful thing. We often talk about the negatives of ageing, and there are shit things. Physically, it’s harder to recover; things kinda fall apart. But the beauty of ageing is you do feel more courageous, and you care less about what people think. I don’t think I ever would’ve felt comfortable doing that video before now.



What first attracted you to your new husband, model Chris Dingwall? I mean, I can guess … I met him on [celebrity dating app] Raya, so of course it’s all about appearances! [Laughs] However, I was in the UK and he lived in Sydney, and I was like, “What’s the point? He lives on the other side of the world … but he is really hot.” Two-and-a-half years later, we’re married. Sometimes, it works. And he is beautiful to look at! But he’s a beautiful person as well. I hit the jackpot. Related Article Good Weekend ‘Should have done that in your 20s, dude’: A middle-aged rock star’s big regret POLITICS You once publicly disagreed with Geri Halliwell’s assertion that “Thatcher was the first Spice Girl.” Why was it so important to you to set the record straight? It was really difficult for me when she made that statement. Liverpool was affected very negatively by Margaret Thatcher being in power. Generations of my family had worked on the docks and the city was decimated, through the ’80s, by decisions she made. It was very hard for me to be tarred with that brush, but that’s one of the problems of being in a band. Did that lead to a moment where you had to hold Geri’s hand and say, “I love you, but we’re going to have to disagree on this”? [Nods, laughs] “I love you, but don’t ever say that again.”



How do you feel the UK is going generally right now? Well, I’m very happy that we have a new prime minister in Andy Burnham. He’s got charisma and he’s a human. I’ve been lucky enough to do some charity work with Andy. He’s from Liverpool and we’ve done lots of fundraising for Hillsborough [after the 1989 soccer stadium tragedy in which 96 people were killed]. Andy just feels like a human who cares about other humans. I think people like him are the kind we need in power. Have you ever been approached to run for office, Melanie? Only the Office of Girl Power. Melanie C will perform in Perth, Melbourne, Brisbane and Sydney, November 11–15. diceytopics@goodweekend.com.au Get the best of Good Weekend delivered to your inbox every Saturday morning.

World.title: At least five schools impacted by tutor under investigation
World.content:
Police say students at at least five schools interacted with a tutor they are investigating after alleged inappropriate behaviour.

Police and Oranga Tamariki announced on Friday they were jointly investigating a tutor who previously taught at several schools and community organisations in the Waikato and Bay of Plenty regions.

Waikato Police Detective Inspector Kevin McNaughton told RNZ they were in the early stages of determining whether criminal activity had occurred after receiving a report from a single school about the tutor in the past couple of weeks.

"This person provides tutoring services via a professional provider who has full records of any schools or children with whom this person comes into contact through their work."

He said a number of students at five to six schools engaged with the tutor.

"We've quickly gone out to identify parents who may have children who had contact with this person, to contact them and invite them to meetings so we can talk them through the screening process, how the investigation runs, and to provide support to them."

He said the tutoring provider had been fully cooperative in handing over their records.

McNaughton said no charges had been laid, but Police would prosecute if they found evidence of criminal activity.

"Whilst investigations of this type take some time, it's not a matter where we would wait until the end of the investigation to take action. Should any single criminal offence be identified to an evidential standard, then action would be taken with respect to that offence immediately."

He said the tutor was no longer working with the schools when Police began their investigation.

He urged the community to let Police complete their investigation and avoid speculation online.

"I'm aware there's some social media commentary with respect to this matter, and that comes as a result of our contact with parents. Some of that social media content is inaccurate and unhelpful.

World.title: Country Life: Riding along with the truckies moving cattle
World.content:
I'm wide-eyed with apprehension, my face creased in concern and fist curled tight around the microphone handle.

To my right, truckie John Robson is expertly reversing a Freightliner Argosy through a narrow gate and up a steep, rugged farm track near the back of Tūtira, in northern Hawke's Bay.

With no reversing camera, it's all skill, experience and my nervous no, no, yups that are helping him manoeuvre this massive truck - rated for up to 54-tonnes - into the paddock on our way to the yards where we're picking up a load of in-calf cows.

I'm comforted knowing he's one of Stephenson Transport Ltd's most experienced drivers and has been doing the job so for almost 30 years.

Audio player for " Ride along: Ninety years helping drive Hawke's Bay's economy " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/country/2118905%2Fcountry-life-riding-along-with-the-truckies-moving-cattle

Ride along: Ninety years helping drive Hawke's Bay's economy Country Life Download MP3 17m

Follow Country Life on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, iHeart or wherever you get your podcasts.

The Hawke's Bay-based family business, was established in 1936 by Sep Stephenson - with just one truck. Today Sep's son Bruce Stephenson, and grandchildren Todd Stephenson and Kim McRae are driving the business forward.

"A lot came before us, but not with the two decks and that sort of thing," Bruce told Country Life. "It started off logging, and that's how it all come about, then got into the livestock after that."

John Robson is one of Stephenson Transport's longest serving drivers. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

The truck we're in today is a Freightliner Argosy, permitted for up to 54 tonne. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

The business now has 50 trucks and trailers and does a bit of everything related to agriculture - whether that's ground spreading, carting bulk fertiliser, wool or apples, and transporting livestock, which makes up the majority of the work.

It employs between 70 to 80 people at peak, with drivers that service most of the North Island and travel over 2.58 million kilometres per annum.

Its busiest time is from October to March which includes the apple harvesting season in Hawke's Bay.

During an average 12-month period, the company carries well over 1 million lambs, 600,000 sheep and around 160,000 head of cattle.

The farm track is too steep and too rough for both the truck and trailer, so we're transhipping today. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

First we have to drop the trailer off on the roadside. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

Todd, who started as a mechanic, says he was "always going to be involved with trucks", having been born into the industry.

Looking over old photos he noted the way in which the business had changed - from single trucks to drivers having to bring their own races and ramps for stock to climb in.

"The roads haven't changed much. Neither have the yards. But yeah, technology certainly has."

Ever the gentleman, John's getting the gets - the job normally reserved for passengers. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

The new technology makes things easier and more comfortable - for both the livestock and drivers - but has added to costs. High fuel prices this year have also been a significant cost for the business, though Stephenson said it has managed this. He just hoped it would ease soon.

"Our gear is all fairly modern. We like to keep everything up to spec there. You've got to keep up with it, keep moving with the times."

It's still a job that requires a good level of skill and experience.

"[The] driving skills, I believe, are far greater than any other. For a start, you've got to reverse up to every load. And as I said, not many of the facilities have changed over the last 50 odd years. A lot of it was only designed for truck-only before the trailers were even invented."

As the driver, John is responsible for ensuring the welfare of every animal he transports. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

This means drivers are somewhat limited in terms of how many animals can be transported as most units are "maxxed out" in terms of length and weight.

"It's also an incredibly physical job, with animal handling a big part of the role," Todd said.

"It's like going to the gym half a dozen times a day."

John's certainly demonstrating that up at the yards, as he jumps up to adjust the ramp levels and open and close the door.

Keeping weight distribution in mind, as well as each animal's welfare, he directs the others which stock to load first and helps push them up the ramp into the truck.

There are rules around transporting livestock and as the driver, it's up to John to ensure the animals are fit to travel and looked after during transit.

Today we're shifting a mob of expectant cows, moving them further inland to more gentle country where they'll calve. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

The stock are loaded into the back of the truck. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

As it was for the others, it was through a family connection that John started driving, almost 30 years ago.

He'd worked in farming doing a bit of fencing, shearing and working with stock before his brother-in-law - a livestock truck driver - gave him a lesson in a paddock. The next week John headed down to Wellington to do a run after qualifying with his full Class 5 licence.

" did a little bit of freight beforehand, but nah, this is my forté."

He enjoys working with the stock as well as the people.

"Every day is different, which is good about this job. So you might have a sale run Monday, unload, do a load into the works, have a cup of tea, do one to Wairoa, come home.

"It's not just driving, it's all the people as well too. Cockies, drivers, and the livestock, there's a good camaraderie, so I really enjoy that."

From the top of the farm you can see the trailer way off in the distance, back where we left it on the roadside. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

The Stephensons are proud to be carrying on the family business and have hopes it will pass on to the next generation eventually - Todd's three children have all got their Class 5 licence, while Kim's boys are getting more into the business too.

"It's very exciting and it's a privilege to be in the business that's been going for such a long time," Kim told Country Life.

She praised the staff as the "backbone" of the firm.

"We ask a lot of them in the livestock industry because of the crazy hours they have to start in the morning. Rain, hail or sun, sometimes those guys are starting at like three in the morning.

World.title: Country Life: NZ's biggest wool scouring factory rises from the flood
World.content:
Audio player for " Fleeces fly again at Napier's WoolWorks " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/country/2118904%2Fcountry-life-nz-s-biggest-wool-scouring-factory-rises-from-the-flood

Fleeces fly again at Napier's WoolWorks Country Life Download MP3 7m

When shearing reaches its busiest period on farms around the North Island from December through to March, the WoolWorks scouring plant in Hawke's Bay will process around 165,000 kilograms of wool each day.

It's critical infrastructure for the farming sector, transforming fleece from hill country shearing sheds into the clean, dry, pressed, product ready for manufactures to make into carpets and building products.

The factory just south of Napier at Awatoto transforms greasy wool, neatly packing it into bales using an impressive new German wool press that exerts 600 tonnes of pressure. The bales then start a long journey on shipping containers to manufacturers around the world.

"To put that back to sheep numbers, that's around about 50,000 sheep. So that's every day. It's a lot of farms, so it's big numbers," WoolWorks chief executive Rosstan Mazey told Country Life.

The bright scoured wool reaches the end of the production line before it's packed tightly into bales. WoolWorks chief executive Rosstan Mazey handles the scoured fleece at the factory near Napier. Penny Miles

Follow Country Life on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, iHeart or wherever you get your podcasts.

Think about doing your laundry 10 times over - that's roughly what happens to wool from thousands of sheep every day at the busy plant. You can hear forklifts buzzing and beeping as they carry heavy bales around the floor. Wash basins bubble, dryers rumble, and the wool press thumps.

Despite some rough times for the sector, Mazey believes there's a bright future for the country's wool exports.

He points to one innovative customer, Ngamatea Station, which sends its scoured wool to be made into tennis-ball felt, used on the courts of the world's biggest Grand Slam tournaments.

"We've had a tricky last year with the amount of greasy wool that's been taken out of New Zealand, primarily to China," Mazey said.

"We're seeing the situation change quite quickly over there just in the last couple of months.Their appetite for greasy wool from New Zealand is starting to reduce.

"We're also seeing renewed interest for other scoured wool markets, particularly from Europe and India."

Rosstan Mazey stands by a craft wool tapestry of a Drysdale sheep. The breed was developed in New Zealand for its coarse, hairy wool, particularly suited to making carpets and other hard-wearing products. Penny Miles

Industry leaders are also hopeful that the India Free Trade Deal will strengthen ties with Indian manufacturers and, in turn, boost demand for New Zealand wool.

The vast majority of the wool scoured at WoolWorks - about 85 percent - goes to China, India, the United States and Europe, where it's made into rugs, bedding, carpets and building materials.

About 15 percent stays in New Zealand. Carpet and rug manufacturers Bremworth and Godfrey Hirst continue to manufacture fine wool carpets here.

Wool is also becoming more popular in building design, with Auckland-based Autex making insulation and acoustic panels. Another Kiwi company based in the South Island, Terra Lana, also makes insulation, acoustic control and landscaping products using scoured wool.

A factory that went under

You wouldn't know it now, but three-and-a-half years ago, the WoolWorks factory was inundated when stopbanks along the Ngaruroro River gave way during Cyclone Gabrielle.

During the cyclone the water rose to around two metres. Processing equipment was submerged and thick, silt-laden mud was left across the factory floor. It was months before the water subsided and the rebuild lasted more than a year.

Romney sheep dominate hill country flocks across the North Island. RNZ/Susan Murray

WoolWorks Group Assurance Manager Tony Cunningham said the rebuild was significant. There was a full rewiring of the plant. New electronic monitoring equipment was installed, while damaged machines were pieced back together by engineers.

Cunningham said it's crucial that New Zealand maintains its wool-scouring capacity, despite some companies sending greasy wool offshore. He said most of Australia's wool is now scoured in China. The manufacturer is also grappling with high energy costs and declining sheep numbers.

World.title: Country Life: Indigenous knowledge fuels 'food forest' trial
World.content:
It may not look like much now - but this small plot of land will soon bear blueberries, apricots, mandarins and more.

A team of Lincoln University researchers are trying their hand at growing a ngahere kai, or food forest - a food system used by indigenous communities around the globe.

"If you think of the Amazon - that would be one of the oldest living examples, that Mayan have cultivated for between 2000 to 3000 years," Dr Chystal O'Connor told Country Life at a planting day.

Dr Chrystal O'Connor, standing amongst weeds in what will become a food forest, depots a sapling. RNZ/Anisha Satya

Audio player for " Future-focussed food forests " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/country/2118903%2Fcountry-life-indigenous-knowledge-fuels-food-forest-trial

Follow Country Life on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, iHeart or wherever you get your podcasts.

It is what it says on the tin: edible bushes, tubers and trees are planted in a layout which mimics a natural forest.

The forest-like layers mean multiple plants can grow in one area, she said.

"There're usually up to seven layers, and a food forest creates the climate of a natural forest, so it increases the humidity and helps everything else to grow."

Food forest project leaders (from left) Chrystal O'Connor, Jorie Knook, and Hiraina Tangiora. RNZ/Anisha Satya

A food biochemist and former Whanake Ake appointee, O'Connor is one of three Lincoln lecturers heading the food forest trial.

Fellow project leads Dr Jorie Knook and Hiraina Tangiroa, of the Agribusiness and Commerce faculty, share an interest in finding new ways to grow food.

"There's a real lack of information on how food forests are established in Aotearoa, New Zealand, and then what that production could look like," O'Connor said.

Applying a local, te ao Māori lens to this system means finding ways it can benefit people and the environment, she added.

"A big part of our vision is to connect people back to their food and connect communities back to growing food.

Lunch break at the Lincoln University food forest - currently covered in cow parsley, but soon to host a vast array of edible trees and nitrate distributors. RNZ/Anisha Satya

"And we really see a food forest that is not only for food production but for biodiversity, attracting the insects, the birds.

"So setting this up is [not] only a proof of concept, but you can see everyone out here planting today, just the connections and relationships that it builds with it as well."

Accompanying the edible plants are native nitrogen distributors - like matagouri and kākābeak- and purely aesthetic plants, like a circle of willows which will be bent into a dome shape.

The trial is being carried out at the Biological Husbandry Unit's (BHU) organic farm - and it's one of three food forests to come.

"We have another two sections, also 20 by 50 metres. One, we want to design what [this] could look like on farming systems, so easier for harvesting.

"And the last section is how it could be implemented into communities, both for papakāinga - our Māori housing communities - but also within urban areas and cities, park-type systems."

BHU manager Harry Baitz said the charity had spent the last half-century supporting such projects.

The remnants of an apple orchard and cow parsley experiment from 40 years ago are still growing strong on the site.

Biological Husbandry Unit manager Harry Baitz. RNZ/Anisha Satya

"The Granny Smith orchard was a rootstock trial, back when Granny Smiths weren't a big commercial crop.

"They were wanting to see if it was a viable commercial enterprise ... and now, of course, you see Granny Smiths everywhere."

"That's kind of cool," O'Connor said.

"The Granny Smith orchard was implemented before it became commercial. Now we have the food forest, so hopefully in 20 to 40 years' time, this will become a normal thing that you see too.

World.title: More than a dozen flights cancelled in Auckland due to fog
World.content:
More than a dozen flights have been cancelled and several others delayed in Auckland due to fog.

Auckland Airport said fog restrictions were put in place from 6:33am on Saturday morning.

It said 15 domestic flights had been cancelled and a another six had been delayed.

International flights were not cancelled or delayed because of the fog.

World.title: Tonga secures its second win at Rugby League World Cup
World.content:
Tonga recorded its second win at the Rugby League World Cup on Friday night, beating Lebanon 36-0 in Sydney.

With over 10,000 fans in the 'Sea of Red', the side kept their hopes of securing a semi-final spot alive with the win.

That came on the back of their first round victory over England in the first round.

Three first half tries gave them a 14-0 lead at half-time, before they added to that in the second half.

They ended the game with seven tries to their name.

But it was not their way all the time, with Lebanon showing strong resistance in the game, denying the Tongans early in the first half with some good defensive work.

The Cedars were also unlucky not to have scored any point in the first 40, with some close saves by Tonga off their line.

Co-captains Jason Taumalolo and Addin Fonua-Blake led the forward drives for Tonga, supported well by Salesi Foketi, Stefano Utoikamanu, Haumole Olakau'atu and Kulikefu Finefeuiaki.

Their backline of Lehi Hopoate, Sione Katoa, Tolutau Koula, Paul Alamoti, Jojo Fifita, Tuimoala Lolohea and Latu Fainu ran the ball at every opportunity they had.

Lebanon's attacks were led by winger Jason Saab, Khaled Rajab and Alex Conti at the back, while the forwards of Jaxson Rahme, Moustafa Dirani, James Roumanos, Tony Sukkar, Mikael Ibrahim and captain Alex Twal tried their best to gain territory with their runs.

Tonga's defence, which stood out against England last weekend, proved to the difference again against Lebanon in the end.

That told in the fact that they managed to stop Lebanon from crossing for tries.

Reaction by captains

Tonga's Jason Taumalolo and Lebanon's Alex Twal Rugby League World Cup

Tongan co-captain Taumalolo said the win and the overall performance was great, especially with their fans backing them.

"To both Lebanese and Tongan fans tonight, despite the results, it's great to see two countries who love where they come from and what they are about come out here and celebrate tonight in rugby league," Taumalolo said.

"Obviously a lot to like about the performance.

"We still had our defence, obviously carrying on from last week. It's good to see the guys putting that on the line.

"Obviously abit slow out there at the start but finally picked up towards the back end .

"Thank you to our Tongan fans who turned up in numbers tonight."

He said the players love playing in front of the red flags and said they will rest and move their focus to Samoa, who they play next week.

Lebanon captain Alex Twal said he was proud of his players, adding that the Tongan team was an all-star team who deserved the win.

"Couldn't be more proud of the boys," he said post-match.

"Our boys are all hard workers, boys who just wanna play for the jersey.

"I don't think the scoreline reflects how the game really went. I couldn't be prouder to be Lebanese tonight and I couldn't be prouder of my Cedar brothers."

Twal said he will back Tonga all the way now.

"Individually they are probably some of the best players in their clubs you know," he said.

"We came here with a lot of respect and the way you show respect to them is you play hard and play tough.

"I will be supporting Tonga all the way , they are a proud nation and I think we see here today how the people get behind them, it's an amazing spectacle."

How the game went

Tonga started scoring with winger Katoa in the 13th minute, finishing off in the corner after he received a cut out pass from fullback Hopoate.

Alamoti finished off another Tongan attack eight minutes later, with the ball travelling from left to right, before Lolohea drew the defence to him and letting the ball go wide. Alamoti jogged to the line with the ball in hand to claim Tonga's second try for the half.

Koula then sprinted the full length of the field after he got the ball from Lebanese winger Saab, who had knocked it back after he climbed high on the Tongan line to collect Conti's high kick.

Alamoti's conversion saw Tonga lead 14-0 at halftime.

The second half started with Jojo Fifita claiming Tonga's fourth try in the 43rd minute.

But Lebanon managed to get themselves back into the game and defended Tonga's attacks successfully, holding the island kingdom warriors at bay until the 70th minute when Lolohea's flat pass found replacement Leka Halasima, who beat the defensive line to touch down.

Tonga led 24-0 heading into the last 10minutes with Lolohea's goal kick.

In the 74th minute Hopoate claimed a high ball on the Tonga 10 metre and sliced his way through the Lebanese line, before he was taken in Conti's tackle.

The ball went right and an overlap saw Fifita finishing off with his second try, which Lolohea converted for a 28-0 lead.

Katoa got his name on the scoresheet for the second time with a minute to go, running on to a Lolohea grubber for the corner, catching the ball on the bounce and running in unchallenged for Tonga seventh try.

Lolohea had the last say with his conversion, to take the 36-0 lead.

Tonga made nine line-breaks against Lebanon's one in the game, while possession was almost equally shared.

Tonga controlled the open play with 10 dummy passes

World.title: Australia rugby league head stands firm by PNG Chiefs name
World.content:
The head of the Australian Rugby League Commission (ARLC) has doubled down on its defiant stand over the name of the PNG Chiefs franchise.

Commissioner Peter Beattie said they will not compromise in the face of attempts by New Zealand Rugby to prevent use of the name of the NR's incoming PNG Chiefs franchise.

NZ Rugby has taken court action in New Zealand as it claims its trademarked brand for the Chiefs Super Rugby franchise is under threat from the new NRL team.

While the High Court last week declined NZ Rugby's bid for an interim injunction on use of the PNG Chiefs name, the dispute is expected to go to a full hearing in February or March next year.

Beattie made his comments as the PNG Chiefs this week officially launched their logo and jersey in Port Moresby.

PNG news outlet The National reports Beattie saying the ARLC stands firm that the NRL will continue to use the name.

He said the name of the franchise was decided by PNG in a competition that sought public input, and that it will remain the name.

Legal wrestle

Justice Karen Grau, the judge who declined NZ Rugby's bid for an interim injunction on the ARLC's use of the name, said her court could not prevent this week's launch because it was in a different jurisdiction.

She said it would be "next to impossible" to rebrand the team at this stage, noting the critical juncture that the PNG Chiefs are at as they try and recruit players to build a good squad for their inaugural NRL season in 2028.

Justice Grau also noted that it was clear the ALRC was "never going to back down and change the name of its new team in response to the NZRU's concerns".

NZ Rugby indicated to the court that it was "taking active steps to monitor and, if necessary, oppose ARLC's application to register and use the PNG Chiefs mark in Australia".

The CEO of the rugby Chiefs, Simon Graafhuis RNZ Pacific last week that since NZ Rugby holds the trademark for the Chiefs brand in Australia, legal action in Australia remained a possibility.

Meanwhile, the judge also said that in order to avoid brand confusion, the ARLC and PNG Chiefs had undertaken to make efforts to ensure the team's full name is used.

World.title: Auckland’s Cornwall Park to introduce carpark fees
World.content:
One of Auckland's most popular parks is planning to implement paid parking to manage overwhelming crowds, RNZ can exclusively reveal.

The independent trust that manages Cornwall Park confirmed to RNZ that, from 1 December 2026, it would charge between $2.50 and $5 an hour to park in some areas of the Epsom parkland and along Pūriri Drive.

On weekdays, parking would be $5 an hour after an initial two-hour free period and capped at $35 a day.

Weekend and public holiday parking would be $2.50 an hour after the initial free period and capped at $20 a day.

Cornwall Park Trust chief executive Murray Reade said the park had become increasingly busy over the years and many people who came to the park struggled to find a parking spot.

"Parking demand at Cornwall Park continues to grow, particularly during weekends, major events, and peak seasonal periods.

"Finding a park can be challenging during busy times, and visitors regularly tell us that parking availability is becoming more difficult. During peak periods, high-demand parking areas can become heavily occupied, making it harder for visitors to find a space."

Reade said it had struck a balance by keeping parking for the first two hours free and providing 300 free all-day parking spaces on Grand Drive and Bollard Avenue.

"We've deliberately structured the pricing to support the way people use Cornwall Park. Most recreational visits remain free, while reduced weekend and public holiday rates support families, groups, and recreational visitors.

"Paid parking is one tool that will help improve parking turnover, support fair access, and make parking more readily available for visitors."

He said about 70 percent of the two million visits to the park each year lasted less than two hours.

He said the revenue generated through paid parking would go towards the park's ongoing maintenance and preservation and improving the visitor experience.

World.title: In the wreckage of World Cup blowouts, hope is where you find it
World.content:
As it enters its second round of matches, just about every game of the Rugby League World Cup has become a battleground between true believers and sceptics.

The former point to the games of the opening week that attracted bumper ratings and healthy crowds for blockbuster contests like Australia against New Zealand or Tonga's clash with England.

Test football is better than ever, they cry, and these numbers prove it.

The latter scoff at the blowouts, feeling ever more justified in their derision as the scorelines mount when powerhouses old or new collide with teams who have been left behind.

Test football is a waste of time, they sneer, and these numbers prove it.

With the tournament entering a weekend where a close game will be hard to come by, the truth is firmly in the middle but hope is always where you find it, even among the wreckage of a smash-up.

For proof, look no further than Tonga's match against Lebanon in Parramatta last night.

The Cedars were 23-1 to win, making them the second-shortest-priced underdogs of a round when Australia will play Fiji, England take on France, Papua New Guinea host Samoa and Cook Islands do their best against New Zealand.

It will rain tries and apart from perhaps PNG-Samoa it will be a surprise if any match is closer than Tonga's 36-0 win over the spirited Cedars.

But you'd be hard-pressed to find a single one of the 25,605 strong crowd — the third highest of any match in history between two second tier nations — who'd call it a waste of time.

If you can pack that many people into a stadium for a result that was never really in doubt you've got something worth having.

Tonga's superior athleticism and cohesion across the field won them the day, with veteran halfback Tui Lolohea and rising fullback Lehi Hopoate both enjoying fine nights amid the rowdy atmosphere.

Western Sydney is a stronghold of both communities and Parramatta Stadium was awash in red, white and green, as it was drowned in cheers and buried in flags.

The only part of the ground that wasn't awash in colour and noise was the empty corporate sections which was fitting because this was not a game for the suits.

All through the 80 minutes beating of the Lebanese drums were answered by a chorus of Tongan voices, many of whom stayed well after fulltime to revel in their victory.

They have confirmed their place in the semi-finals but first must face their ancient rivals Samoa next week.

Tonga have established themselves as one of Test rugby league's new superpowers. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer )

It will be a highlight of the tournament no matter who wins or what happens next, a meeting of the two new powers in these waters and it was not so long ago that they were copping the beatings rather than handing them out.

Back in 1999, Tonga lost to New Zealand 74-0 and nine years later, boasting a full team of NRL and Super League players, the Kiwis repeated the dose 56-8.

If those big losses killed Tonga off they never would never have transformed into what they are now, which is one of Test rugby league's apex predators.

Sticking with it despite heavy losses meant there was something for Tonga and Samoa's star players to come back to when they decided to choose their heritage and the result is what we have now — two extra high quality teams in Test football, making a gang of five where for years there was only three.

If you're outside that five, life can be much harder. With the streamlined World Cup format there will be fewer meetings of the high and the low, but some of them are unavoidable.

Lebanon fought hard despite a lack of star power. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer )

A team like Lebanon is trapped in a land of wolves and asking for them to undergo a Tongan style transformation into a heavyweight is not realistic.

They are at the mercy of what talent they can gleam from Australia's Lebanese communities and getting them all together for matches is difficult amid an already packed rugby league schedule, but they have found a way to make the most of it.

Young Canterbury halfback Alex Conti lost no admirers, nor did Tigers lock Alex Twal and some strong scrambling defence stopped the scoreline from getting to embarrassing territory.

What they wouldn't have given for a half like Mitchell Moses, who instead represented Australia, or Adam Doueihi, who is injured, given they only had one fewer tackle inside the 20 than Tonga but could not find a point to show for it.

It might be Lebanon's last big dance for a while. Since the last World Cup they were demoted to affiliate status by the International Rugby League and only qualified this time around because they were quarter finalists in 2022.

Major infrastructure changes will need to be made at a domestic level if Lebanon are even to be given a chance to qualify for 2030.

Their diaspora talent, which is considerable, will not be enough to shepherd them through and their tournament finale next week against France could be their last World Cup game for many years.

Lebanon could be in their last World Cup for some time. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer )

If that's so the tournament will be poorer for their absence but they could finish with a flourish.

Next week's game against les Chanticleers is winnable for them and will be played in a double-header with Samoa-Tonga.

It will give Sydney's vast Lebanese community one more opportunity to show their pride and love through their national side in a major sport, which is a chance they are rarely offered and one they made the most of on Friday night against long odds.

That still means something, which means the game is worth something, as sure as the Pasifika blockbuster will be and as sure as this game was.

Scorelines always matter and not every blow-out is created equal. Sometimes you can squint so hard looking for a silver-lining you may as well be blind.

But other times it's right in front of you, so clear you cannot miss it, as loud as the drums that hammered out into the night and as striking as the sea of red in the stands.

World.title: How the Western Bulldogs engineered a return to AFLW finals
World.content:
It's a story that's been told countless times. The Western Bulldogs hit rock bottom in 2023, opted to undertake a review into their program, and made wholesale change. Since then, they've made steady improvement, but that hasn't been without some rocky moments along the way.

Now, the Bulldogs are locked into finals for the first time since 2022 and present as a genuine threat in the post-season, rather than simply making up the numbers.

And while their off-field changes have been immense, and an easy starting point when it comes to analysing their improvement, what has happened on field is even more interesting.

Rock bottom

The Bulldogs finished 2023 as wooden spooners, winning one game from 10 rounds of footy just a year after reaching its second ever final. Across that season they gave up control in-game easily, and relied heavily on a small handful of players to carry the load.

This required a personnel change to start the improvement spike. A new head coach, head of footy and list manager were certainly key to the shift, but change on field was also essential.

From the playing list that reached a final in 2022 just 12 players remain, and while the club has largely focused on careful draft selections, it has also engaged in trades to add experience on top of the youth.

Listed in 2022 S7 Added since Elle Bennetts Deanna Berry Ellie Blackburn Alice Edmonds Jess Fitzgerald Elisabeth Georgostathis Isabella Grant Britney Gutknecht Sarah Hartwig Isabelle Pritchard Rylie Wilcox

Heidi Woodley Lauren Ahrens (trade) Brooke Barwick (draft) Mizuki Brothwell (draft) Cleo Buttifant (draft) Mikala Cann (trade) Dom Carruthers (draft) Ellie Gavalas (trade) Maggie Gorham (free agent) Elaine Grigg (draft) Keeley Hardingham (draft) Kaylee Kimber (replacement) Vaomua Laloifi (trade) Emma McDonald (draft) Analea McKee (trade) Charlie O'Connor Moreira (draft) Sarah Poustie (draft) Jasmyn Smith (trade) Lou Stephenson (trade) Amaia Wain (draft)

This list build has happened quietly. There are no boom recruits among the incoming trades, no premiership players or All-Australians in the mix as other clubs have targeted, but they have been specific choices to work toward the game plan.

Mikala Cann has been one of those players. Little more than a role player at Collingwood, albeit a very good one, Cann has been exactly the kind of midfielder/forward required at the Dogs to elevate the team as a whole.

The stat changing Geelong in 2026 When Geelong made the move to bring Mick Stinear to the cattery, it made a bigger difference to their 2026 season than any player movement could.

Outside of this, the club's capacity to improve some down-and-out senior players has also been important.

Mua Laloifi has emerged on the other side of an ACL injury in close to her best career form, offering important intercepting strength behind the ball, and Ellie Gavalas has spent a couple of years in the wilderness but now adds some leadership and ground-level speed in the forward half.

And the draftees have been carefully selected. Although some choices haven't quite come on in the way the club would have hoped — every club has been burned by a speculative pick here or there — others have been the ideal slow burn.

Emma McDonald and Elaine Grigg were arguably the Dogs' biggest-name draftees across this period, but others like Cleo Buttifant and Dom Carruthers have complemented the growth of the list.

The Bulldogs are becoming a team that is clearly greater than simply the sum of its parts. The puzzle as a whole works well together.

Build defence

The traditional route for a club's rebuild is to start with defence, then add attack, and that's exactly the direction the Bulldogs went once Tam Hyett was appointed coach in 2024.

They were coming off a base that was easy to win the ball against, easy to maintain momentum against, and ultimately far too easy to score against.

Taking back control

Avg disposals conceded Avg uncontested possessions conceded Avg disposal efficiency conceded (%) Avg marks conceded 2026 236.4 120.6 61.8 51.2 2025 241.1 124.9 62.0 44.4 2024 241.9 128.5 63.0 50.2 2023 269.4 155.9 66.6 56.2

Finding that defensive mindset isn't simply about establishing a strong backline, rather as the numbers above suggest, it is about making the game scrappy at times to prevent the opposition from clean access at the footy.

No longer are the Bulldogs walkovers around the footy, or easy to maintain possession against around the ground. When a team plays the Bulldogs, they are to expect a battle around the contest and pressure on the outside.

This, then, leant into tightening up on the scoreboard.

Becoming harder to score against

Avg points against Avg I50s conceded Avg marks I50 conceded Avg shots per I50 conceded (%) Avg shots on goal conceded 2026 32.3 32.5 7.7 36.9 12.0 2025 32.1 28.1 4.8 38.6 10.8 2024 41.9 31.5 7.4 43.1 13.6 2023 59.5 37.5 11.3 52.3 19.6

To get here they played some admittedly ugly footy (everyone remembers that 2024 game against the Bombers), but the first step in the plan has been the foundation upon which everything else has been built. And although some of those numbers have swung slightly back up (specifically inside 50s and marks inside 50 conceded), this has been a result of now working to find the balance between defence and attack.

Learn to attack

In Hyett's first year at the helm, the Bulldogs had their worst year in attack since the AFLW began, averaging just 26.5 points per game. Things seemed bleak and the end of the tunnel felt a long way away. But steadily, on top of that tightening defence, they have also found their own confidence to attack.

As with the defensive tightening, the first part is establishing more control through the middle of the ground, then the next layer is engaging those forwards close to goal to actually get scores on the board.

Winning the footy

Avg handballs Avg kick rate (%) Avg uncontested possessions 2026 120.3 55.5 148.4 2025 99.8 59.6 122.8 2024 70.7 64.4 95.2 2023 93.1 61.8 135.3

Getting their hands on the footy has been a key part to winning back control throughout games, but part of that has also been a shift in how they want to use the ball.

Instead of dump kicking the ball long to escape danger or opting for long down-the-line kicks to a contest where they can compete again, the Dogs are now establishing a clear handball game; moving neatly from layers around the contest via hand and looking for the running handball receive option to add speed on the ball.

That outside ball has been a huge growth area as they develop more confidence in their game style, and for the first time since 2022 the club is averaging a positive uncontested possession differential.

Kicking a winning score

Avg points for Avg I50s Avg shots on goal Avg shots per I50 (%) 2026 45.5 32.9 14.8 20.1 2025 40.6 34.3 14.6 16.1 2024 26.5 27.0 9.3 13.5 2023 32.0 27.4 10.8 16.4

A whole new forward line has been built, with Sarah Hartwig becoming the club's all-time leading goalkicker back in round nine, and Emma McDonald posting the most goals of any Dog in 2025, her debut season.

It has been a calm, steady club-wide build that has flown under the radar in the context of the wild swings that occur in the AFLW, but it has been done for the long haul.

And in a fortnight, the Dogs will get a chance to show their wares in finals, and are a good chance of winning their first final since their flag in 2018.

World.title: Man United legend lashes current players for behaving 'like babies'
World.content:
Manchester United's all-time leading scorer Wayne Rooney has labelled the club's current players selfish, lashing them for behaving "like babies" after captain Bruno Fernandes questioned the coaching staff's tactics following their Champions League thrashing by Como.

Fernandes said United failed to apply enough pressure and adopted a "mood of defeat" after conceding in the second minute, as Thursday morning's 4-1 loss intensified scrutiny of manager Michael Carrick.

United's collapse at Como left them staring at another damaging result, with only a stoppage-time goal from Joshua Zirkzee reducing the margin of defeat.

Man United captain branded 'disgrace' for comments following latest loss Bruno Fernandes takes aim at Michael Carrick as Manchester United's horrible start to the season goes from bad to worse in the Champions League.

The criticism follows signs of growing frustration within the squad. Earlier this month, defender Lisandro Martinez criticised the club's hierarchy after a 2-0 Champions League defeat by Atletico Madrid, saying he expected greater investment to help the team compete at the highest level.

"When Martinez came out, I said this is an absolute nightmare because it will rip the dressing room apart," Rooney told the United Stand podcast on Thursday.

"That was the start. We've seen it now with Bruno, and you're going to see it with more players because they don't want to take responsibility.

"You can say whether Bruno was right or wrong in what he said, but you have to take responsibility on the pitch. You have to take responsibility as a group of players.

Wayne Rooney (right) was a long-time teammate of current United boss Michael Carrick (left). (Getty Images)

"These players, they're selfish. They don't care about their teammates, don't care about the manager, the staff or the fans, they care about themselves.

"If they're not getting what's right for them, they're like babies and just throw their toys out of the pram and go and deflect the blame on to anyone else but themselves."

Carrick, a former United midfielder who played alongside Rooney at Old Trafford, was appointed on an interim basis following Ruben Amorim's dismissal in January before earning a contract through 2028 after overseeing a dramatic improvement in results.

Carrick is under growing pressure with United winless in seven matches across all competitions. They are 20th in the Champions League standings and 13th in the Premier League.

Reuters

World.title: Trump calls LeBron 'total disgrace' over perceived anthem disrespect
World.content:
US President Donald Trump has accused LeBron James of disrespecting the United States after the NBA star appeared to continue his warm-ups while the national anthem was performed before Philadelphia's season opener on Wednesday AEDT.

"I said right from the beginning that he's no good, a TOTAL DISGRACE," Trump said of James in a social media post sharing the video.

"LeBron James should apologise to all of those Great American Warriors and Heroes who died for the American Flag, and all that our Country stands for!"

James appeared to practice a golf swing and jump shot as The Star-Spangled Banner was performed at New York's Madison Square Garden.

James, starting his first season with Philadelphia, was lined up alongside teammates who mostly stood still during the anthem.

Trump and James have been critical of each other for years, occasionally trading public swipes.

James offered a short response to Trump's comments when questioned, declaring it was a "slow news day in the office".

Coach Nick Nurse had talked at length since training camp opened about the Sixers' need to tune out outside distractions. Hours before their home opener, the Sixers had to deal with one from the president.

"I think that goes right in with other outside noise we've already had," Nurse said before Friday's game against the Cleveland Cavaliers.

"I keep saying the same thing. All I really care about is getting to the practice floor, getting them in the film room, getting them to the game floor. The focus that they've had and the intent and all the stuff like that has been outstanding."

AP

World.title: Awkward questions linger as creaky Australia receives South African hiding
World.content:
That Australia slowly folded and lost the Gqeberha Test by an innings and 31 runs late on day five was hardly surprising in light of its batting calamities of 24 hours earlier. That Kagiso Rabada and Marco Jansen ran through the tail to finish things off even less so.

But it remains startling to consider the reversal of fortunes this quite disastrous loss represented for Australia. On day two, they were 1-0 up in the series, had South Africa on the ropes at 5-97, on a greenish pitch, and fancied a rout of their own.

Bavuma hides from Smith catch as Boland outdoes batters in loss Temba Bavuma turns his back as Steve Smith throws his wicket away, while Scott Boland shows the batters how it's done as the Aussies go down in Gqeberha. Here are the quick hits from the final day of the second Test.

Instead, in a game that lost 145 overs to rain and associated delays, the annihilation took place in reverse and a series some considered Australia's stepping stone to more difficult engagements ahead is now set for an enticing decider. For Australia, the task ahead is now daunting on multiple levels — not just to find form and the right combination of players to defeat an ascendant and cohesive opponent, but how to do so in Cape Town, with all the extra heat that will entail.

First the few positives. Travis Head, whose role as opener will continue to be endlessly scrutinised, laboured unselfishly for five hours to make 121. Nightwatchman Scott Boland, who was Australia's best all-round performer of the game, absorbed 187 deliveries for his rearguard 40.

Scott Boland's vigil at the crease on day five was one of the few positives for Australia. (Getty Images: Richard Huggard/Gallo Images)

The negatives? Australia's next-best batsman was Mother Nature, who wiped out the first session of play and briefly raised hopes that Australia would force a draw. It didn't, for neither did Boland's patient hand inspire his better credentialed batting partners to hang around and save the day.

It is pointless to analyse the tail. Most culpable this time was Steve Smith, who in his short and strange stay at the crease was given a reprieve by Proteas keeper Ryan Rickelton but failed to make South Africa pay, falling soon after to an objectionably unserious dismissal in a game that was, from Australia's perspective, a little too full of them.

Australia was 5-219 at the time of this pivot point, not entirely written off. Rabada had just taken the second new ball. Boland, batting steadily, had just driven him to the long-off boundary with a beautifully straight bat. Smith? Convention be damned. Rabada sent down a length ball on a fourth-stump line. Smith, for reasons known only to him, decided he should launch over the fence at deep mid-wicket. Instead he skied it and Matthew Breetzke juggled a catch. Therein lay the death of the contest.

Steve Smith's nightmare shot in the second session opened the door to a South African win. (AP Photo: Themba Hadebe)

Much has been made of Marnus Labuschagne's battle against his cricketing mortality, but Smith is now a fairly pressing problem too. For a long time, he has been Australia's Mr Dependable — not simply a better batsmen than younger alternatives, but an undroppable ornament, encouraged to play how he likes, to bat where he wants and indulge his obsessions however he sees fit.

Yet that greatness is suddenly fading fast, the numbers dwindling, Smith's insularity intensifying into less pardonable distractions. It is hard to shake the feeling that he and Labuschagne's overall effect on Australia's flaky batting group is a net negative on a psychological level as much as a statistical one.

A subtle but remarkable insight into this dynamic — ignored at the time — was glimpsed during the Bangladesh series in August, when Cameron Green used a post-match interview to explain the genesis of his own breakthrough first Test century on home soil.

South Africa has the momentum going into the final Test, something that seemed inconceivable two days into this match. (Getty Images: Richard Huggard/Gallo Images)

"I was able to go back to Shield cricket … kind of a good little reminder about how I want to go about it," Green told ABC Sport at the time. "I think when you're playing in a pretty good Australian Test team, you bat behind some pretty good players in front of you and I think I probably got caught up in how they go about it. So, I think the beautiful thing about going back to state cricket is to remind myself how I want to go about it."

In other words, Australia's most gifted player of the generation to come was admitting that in order to get himself firing as a middle-order batsmen in this Test side, first he had to get himself far away from the influence of his teammates.

Green, of course, will be pushing his case for selection in Cape Town after injury ruled him out of the first two Tests. Should he be declared fit, the Beau Webster dilemma need not be as emotive as Australian coach Andrew McDonald made it in his press conference on day four.

Beau Webster (right) is likely to make way for Cam Green for the series finale, provided Green is fit to play. (AP Photo: Themba Hadebe)

But it is puzzling to consider the reasoning for even selecting Webster in this match, in which he was never likely to bowl many of his seamers in an attack featuring four frontline quicks, was not asked for his off-spin, nor deemed top-six material with the bat.

McDonald was right to say the issue is not as straightforward as armchair selectors would have it. Like Mitch Marsh before him, Webster is clearly a much-loved team man. Over the English summer just gone, Warwickshire teammate Sam Hain spoke with genuine emotion of the mutual respect and pride Webster had created from the minute he arrived. Warwickshire duly won the championship trophy. But Webster's numbers told a less compelling story: 403 runs at 33, 12 wickets at 40. At Test level, same goes.

The most sensible scenario at the top of the order is that Nic Maddinson, a walking wicket against Rabada, will drop out and Matt Renshaw slide up. Cooper Connolly, who at ODI level recently justified the hype around him, must surely be in line to enter a team crying out for fresh blood.

Australia selector George Bailey's refusal to infuse the Test side with youth is providing diminishing results. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Looking beyond this result and this series, one wonders whether Australian cricket can find a clarity of purpose and be as ruthless as it needs to be to avoid toppling over a cliff when Smith, Pat Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon are finally gone.

On that note, here is a quote to consider, from Australia's chairman of selectors: "Part of our charter is obviously to provide for the future," he said. "We are very aware that some of these blokes are getting on in age, and that's why it's very, very important for them to continue to perform."

Unfortunately, that was not George Bailey referring to this current Australian team, average age 34, which in Durban was the oldest XI since the 1920s and the first in Test history to not feature a single player under the age of 30.

No, it was Trevor Hohns, late in 2000, referring to arguably Australia's greatest combination ever. Its average age? Erm, 30.

Time, perhaps, for a new charter.

World.title: England stunned as Sri Lanka chases 430 after Brook's record ODI knock
World.content:
Sri Lanka has chased down 430 in a thrilling one-day clash against England despite Harry Brook scoring the fastest double-century in ODI history.

Brook's double-century helped England post a mammoth score of 4-429 before Sri Lanka chased down the target with two wickets and one ball to spare.

Sri Lanka's chase is the second-highest of all time in ODI cricket, trailing only South Africa's chase of 435 against Australia in 2006.

The 27-year-old captain rewrote the record books by racing to his double hundred in 114 balls, surpassing the previous mark of 117 deliveries set by India's Shubman Gill.

Brook's double-century was the fastest of all time and he also eclipsed England's highest individual ODI score of 182, previously held by Ben Stokes.

He made 202 from 116 deliveries, peppering the Sri Lanka attack with 21 fours and 10 sixes before departing to warm applause from the crowd.

The defeat leaves England bottom of the standings after losing both their matches, with Brook saying they need to win their next two games to reach the final in Lahore.

Harry Brook's record-breaking double-century was ultimately in vain as Sri Lanka chased down the target of 430 with a ball to spare. (Getty Images: Sameer Ali)

"Unfortunately, it [the record] doesn't matter now. I thought we were going to be in a good position but, unfortunately, it doesn't even count," Brook said after the game.

"Heartbreaking. I think you've hit the nail on the head there. It's very disappointing that we haven't been able to defend 430, but that's life, that's cricket," he added.

"You don't see many teams chase down 430 and hats off to Sri Lanka. They've played exceptionally well. We couldn't execute our skills enough with the ball and, again, they've just played an absolute blinder there.

"We'll have a good chat about it now and over the next couple of days. We've got a good opportunity in the next couple of games to really try and get to that final in Lahore."

Pavan Rathnayake top-scored for Sri Lanka with 130 from 106 deliveries, while opener Avishka Fernando and Dasun Shanaka both fell three runs short of centuries.

Needing six runs from the final two deliveries, Sri Lanka sealed victory when Janith Liyanage launched Josh Tongue over long-off for six, leaving Brook's record-breaking innings all in vain.

Tongue was England's most successful bowler with 3-79.

England lost by 87 runs at the same venue in Rawalpindi on Tuesday to Pakistan, who lead the table with two wins from two.

Reuters

World.title: Wallaroos great inspired by mantra 'you can't be what you can't see'
World.content:
As Emily Chancellor runs out for her final Test, she will know she has fulfilled one of her ambitions as a Wallaroos representative.

Upon making her Test debut in 2018, Chancellor wanted to help increase the visibility of the Wallaroos among young fans.

Even though she followed rugby growing up, the Wallaroos were not on her radar as the women's game lacked adequate support and promotion.

Chancellor only began playing as a 21-year-old university student, admitting earlier this week "rugby wasn't an option" during her childhood.

At Canberra Stadium this evening, there will be young girls among the spectators eagerly watching the Wallaroos play Scotland.

They will be cheering on their heroes and dreaming of playing for the national women's rugby team, proving Chancellor has taken giant steps in accomplishing her mission.

Inspiring young fans has been at the forefront of Emily Chancellor's mind. (Getty Images: Robbie Stephenson)

"You can't be what you can't see," Chancellor told ABC Sport on the eve of her Test farewell.

"I feel like that is something that has driven me so hard; to want to keep playing and pushing the image of the Wallaroos to a wider audience.

"I feel like I've had a positive impact on that over the last eight years. I love seeing the kids in the crowd, with their parents, excited.

"What excites me is that there has been so much growth when I look back over the last eight years, considering where I was when I was a kid and the visibility of the game in the women's world [at the time].

"It's come so far. I'm really proud of where we've got to and how many young girls are turning up to games."

Tight bond

After 42 Tests, Chancellor will leave the game as a Wallaroos great.

The 35-year-old appeared in two World Cups and captained the team during the 2025 season.

A stellar domestic career with the NSW Waratahs and stints playing club rugby in the UK and Japan are also among her most cherished experiences.

Emily Chancellor captained the Wallaroos in 2025. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

Aside from her on-field achievements, nothing means more to Chancellor than the tight bond she enjoys with her Wallaroos teammates.

She describes the close-knit squad as a "sisterhood".

"We're all struggling or thriving with the challenges rugby faces, particularly in the women's space," said Chancellor, who will start at openside flanker against Scotland.

"Be it pay, the lack of professionalism, or the striving for both of those things, I think that bonds you together massively."

'Limitless' future

The Wallaroos's semi-professional status has made it difficult for the squad to compete with the likes of England and New Zealand, both of which benefit from having full-time programs.

The Wallaroos are in the process of becoming full-time in the build-up to the 2029 World Cup, which will be hosted by Australia.

Emily Chancellor made her Test debut against New Zealand in 2018. (Getty Images)

Chancellor believes the team's opportunities will be "limitless" when this is finally achieved.

"You see how much natural ability the girls have, how much we do with so little in terms of game time at the moment," she said.

"I get excited by what Rugby Australia did with the Aussie women's sevens team when they went full-time.

"A bit more hard work and time together … wow, I think it will be exciting."

Chancellor will be enjoying retirement once the next World Cup rolls around, but her commitment to the Wallaroos's cause shows no signs of diminishing.

The drive to increase visibility of the Wallaroos and women's rugby will remain.

"We've still got a long way to go, and I don't plan on letting up on that goal of making it as visible as possible when I step away from playing," she said.

World.title: Quick hits: Bavuma hides from Smith implosion as Boland outdoes batters
World.content:
Temba Bavuma turns his back as Steve Smith throws his wicket away, while nightwatchman Scott Boland shows the batters how it's done as the Aussies go down in Gqeberha.

Here are the quick hits from the final day of the second Test between Australia and South Africa.

1. Head passes 100 but can't go on

Travis Head began day five needing 13 runs for a gritty, fighting century.

And after a two-hour rain delay, the punchy southpaw reached three figures with relative ease, bringing up the milestone with two leg-side boundaries against South African destroyer Marco Jansen in the sixth over of the day.

Travis Head scored his 13th Test century. (AP Photo: Themba Hadebe)

His celebrations were understandably muted given the state of the game, with his helmet staying in place as he raised his bat and a grin not even threatening to peek through his grill.

It was just Head's second overseas ton after his effort in the 2023 World Test Championship final at the Oval against India, and first against a team on its home patch.

But Head was unable to set up for the long haul his team so craved, with the Australian departing just after the first drinks break, chopping on while attempting a cut shot that was never there.

Head was out for 121 and Australia was 5-209.

2. Boland shows batters how it's done

By now, Australian cricket fans should know better than to doubt Scott Boland.

But even the most optimistic of those watching back home surely wouldn't have expected the nightwatchman to outlast both Head and Steve Smith, take his innings deep into the day and soak up a staggering 166 deliveries.

Boland found the middle of the bat more often than not during his heroic vigil. (Getty Images: Richard Huggard/Gallo Images)

There were a couple of streaky moments, sure, but Boland made his luck more than he rode it, defending with the kind of authority and simplicity his more celebrated batting teammates were so desperately lacking throughout the Test.

He even played a few memorable shots, including an immaculate straight drive back past South Africa spearhead Kagiso Rabada.

But finally, in the second over after tea, Boland's marathon vigil was over, with Wiaan Mulder producing a jagging peach to have the brave nightwatchman bowled through the gate for a new Test best of 40.

3. Bavuma can't watch as Smith throws it away

It was the moment — and didn't Temba Bavuma know it.

The South Africa captain just couldn't watch as Steve Smith top-edged a Kagiso Rabada bouncer high into the blue Gqeberha sky, turning his back completely as Matthew Breetzke raced back and settled under the ball.

Bavuma couldn't watch as Breetzke took a dramatic juggling catch. (Fox Cricket)

It was a rash, ugly shot from Smith, and certainly not one befitting of a man tasked with saving a Test match.

But for a moment, it looked like he was going to get away with it.

Having just-about settled underneath the ball, Breetzke juggled once and then twice before securing the wicket that was destined to end the Australian resistance.

Smith, perhaps still struggling with his neck issue from day four, was out for 3 and Australia was 6-255.

4. Mulder does damage after tea

With four wickets still in reserve, Australia reached tea still with a sniff of pulling off one of the great escapes.

But in removing Australia's best two batters, the Proteas had already done the hard part, and there would have been no panic as they readied themselves for the game's final stanza.

And in the opening exchanges of what was being sold as a marathon, 44-over evening session, all-rounder Mulder struck not once, but twice.

First, he ended Boland with that divine off-cutter; then he produced something similarly inspired to send the newly-arrived Pat Cummins packing for 4.

At 8-262, it was all beginning to unravel.

There was only one thing that could save the Aussies now ...

5. South Africa beats descending gloom

All of a sudden, things were beginning to darken in Gqeberha.

With ominous clouds gathering on the outskirts of the oval and ground staff poised to pounce at the boundary rope, the South Africans were in a race with the elements.

Clouds were gathering ominously with the Proteas in search of their final two wickets. (Fox Cricket)

Two wickets were needed.

Well aware of the descending gloom, Bavuma threw the ball to his premier spearhead.

And Rabada delivered in the first over of his spell, bowling Mitchell Starc with the tailender attempting an ugly and wholly unnecessary slog.

But with the skies continuing to intimidate, we were treated to surely one of the most farcical drinks breaks in Test history.

Those five lost minutes, however, were not enough to save the Australians.

The heavens never did open, and number 11 Josh Hazlewood was promptly caught behind the wicket, confirming a chastening innings and 31-run defeat for Australia and a richly deserved series-levelling triumph for the South Africans.

Tech.title: Abandoned Popcorn Time apps had to be disabled to prevent a zombie army
Tech.content:
Remember Popcorn Time, the app that served as an easy-to-use front end for streaming torrents of movies and TV shows? Development of the MPAA’s least-favorite app of the 2010s has been abandoned for years, but the “Netflix of Piracy” software is still installed on millions of devices that are just waiting to join a bot army. Researchers at Eye Security found the updater for a Popcorn Time fork called “Time4Popcorn” still running on tons of Windows, macOS, and Android devices located around the world, phoning home to now-abandoned web domains over unencrypted HTTP and running an outdated, insecure version of Chrome.

Eye Security’s Niels Teusink says the updater could have been used to install and run basically any kind of software with full privileges, easily enabling someone to create a botnet just by taking over one of the domains, using a man-in-the-middle attack to target specific devices, or perform surveillance by identifying the machines running the software.

Their solution was to register one of the domains and use it to send their own update that instructed the updater to disable itself. Despite ethical concerns about the fix, the researchers say their only alternative “was to do nothing,” pointing out, “The update process wasn’t doing anything functional anyway, it was only creating risk for users.”

Eye Security said on Windows devices, their update “simply stops and disables the service via the Service Control Manager” without deleting any files or anything else. On macOS, it uses a shell script to execute a command that blocks the update process from starting. They didn’t address the software on Android devices, where installing the update would still require actual user interaction first.

They had to tweak their update after it was uploaded to VirusTotal, causing security programs to flag it as malware and block it while leaving the vulnerable updater running. It’s unclear exactly how many devices were at risk, but Eye Security says it “sent out over 2 million update downloads” by March, when they stopped sending the update and transferred the domains they used to the Shadowserver Foundation, a web security non-profit.

Tech.title: Jack Dorsey’s Block made an AI model that talks to you like an awkward new friend
Tech.content:
Babies learn to talk without ever seeing a word written down. We wanted to see if a model could too. It can. It’s just very hard.

Speech is the most natural interface to any intelligence, super or otherwise, and today’s voice AI wastes it. It flattens what we say into text and can’t keep up with human timing.

AI keeps gaining power and independence, and it’s still nearly deaf to the emotion in our voices. Imagine being in serious pain while a voice AI has no idea and just keeps going. That’s the safety problem. Dessa is a step toward fixing it.

Tech.title: Soundcore’s latest noise-crushing headphones are on sale for a new low price
Tech.content:
My colleague John Higgins considered Soundcore’s Space One some of the best budget noise-canceling headphones you could buy when they launched in 2023 — and their successor has only improved upon their winning formula, albeit with a $30 price increase. Thankfully, the Soundcore Space 2 are currently on sale at Amazon, Best Buy, and Walmart in all three colors for an all-time low of $106.49 ($23 off), making them even easier to recommend.

The Space 2 builds on the original with improved active noise cancellation, particularly when it comes to the low-frequency sounds associated with trains and airplane engines. They also deliver more accurate sound performance thanks to various design upgrades, while retaining many of the same features that made the Sound One sound so good for the price, including support for high-resolution LDAC audio. You also still get access to HearID 3.0, which lets you personalize the sound by listening to a series of samples and adjusting accordingly.

Battery life is another welcome improvement. The Space 2 can last up to 50 hours with ANC enabled or 70 hours with it switched off, up from 40 and 55 hours, respectively, on the original. And when your battery dies, you can still use the equipped 3.5mm jack for wired listening. They’ll also automatically pause playback when you take them off, which is handy when you need to step away without losing your place in a song or podcast.
