Tech.title: Elon Musk Just Dumped Another $76 Million Into the Midterms
Tech.content:
Elon Musk gave his personal political committee, America PAC, more than $76 million in the first two weeks of October to boost Republicans in the final stretch of the midterms, according to a pre-election report the PAC filed Thursday evening with the Federal Election Commission.

The group spent nearly $43 million in the first two weeks of October, and entered the campaign’s last leg holding nearly $47 million in cash.

The Texas Senate race dominated the new spending. It drew $15.2 million, double what the PAC spent there all summer. That spending included $12.4 million to attack Democratic candidate James Talarico and $2.8 million to promote Republican Ken Paxton.

Daily filings since then show $9.1 million more against Talarico, bringing the PAC’s spending against him this cycle to nearly $28 million, about 40 percent of everything it has spent supporting or opposing candidates. The PAC also shifted toward online ads, spending $11.4 million on digital ads in the same two weeks, which is close to what it spent on mail and texting combined.

All told, Musk has given more than $445 million to Republican political groups this election cycle, according to WIRED’s analysis of FEC filings, making him the biggest known individual donor in the midterms. More than $165 million of that has gone to America PAC since July alone.

Tech.title: How Many Billions Would It Take to Hold Meta Accountable?
Tech.content:
Earlier this week, a New Mexico judge ordered Meta to pay a $25 billion fine for violating consumer protection laws dating back to the Cambridge Analytica scandal. $25 billion is a massive fine, the largest Meta has ever faced, but it still had us folks at WIRED wondering: Would Meta even feel the pain?

A quick recap of the case: Filed in 2021, the suit alleged that the company violated the state’s Unfair Practices Act by lying to Meta users about the way it handled their data. (Later, New Mexico’s attorney general also made claims against Meta’s content moderation policies.) In September, a jury ruled in favor of the state. Then came the multibillion-dollar penalty.

“This ruling, and the Attorney General's approach to enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico,” C.J. Mahoney, Meta’s chief legal officer, said in a statement. “At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online. We are confident we will prevail on appeal.”

Meta’s legal troubles have proliferated so much this year that it’s hard to keep track of them. Earlier this year in New Mexico, a jury ruled that the social media company should pay $375 million for violating the state’s Unfair Practices Act. That trial was related to child safety. A second phase of the case resulted in Meta being ordered to pay $567 million.

Meanwhile, a Los Angeles County superior court found Meta—and Google-owned YouTube—liable for harming a user’s mental health with the addictive design features of their apps. The plaintiff, a young woman, was awarded $6 million; Meta is on the hook for the bulk of that payment. Then in August, Meta settled a landmark federal case brought against the company by the majority of US states. This suit, once again, centered on addictive features in its apps that were alleged to be harmful to kids. As part of that settlement, Meta will pay the states between $17 and $18 billion over 10 years.

Tech.title: Samsung Galaxy Z Flip8 Review: The Littlest Smartphone That Could
Tech.content:
If you crave a compact phone that doesn’t feel like a brick in your pocket and slips easily into a small bag, the flip style is for you. Samsung’s eighth-generation clamshell is seriously refined, and as svelte and slick as it comes. It may not offer a tablet-sized screen or the fashionable new passport shape, but it is arguably the most practical type of folding phone.

Like almost every other phone this year, the Z Flip8 offers tiny improvements over its predecessor and costs $100 more. If you’re wondering whether it’s worth updating from last year’s Z Flip7, it’s not. The Flip8 is a teeny bit lighter and slimmer with a newer processor, and that’s about it. But if you’re looking to dip a toe in folding-phone waters or just want something small, the Z Flip8 should be in the conversation.

Slimmer and More Foldable

Photograph: Simon Hill

Everyone is excited about the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold8’s sexy new form factor, but Samsung continues to iterate on the flip phone format for folks who prize compact devices. The Z Flip8 shaves off 0.02 inches (0.55 millimeters) and a third of an ounce (8 grams) compared to its predecessor, making it the slimmest and lightest option in this category. The improved hinge makes the crease slightly less noticeable and a little easier to open. I still found it a bit tricky to open one-handed, but you get the knack after a while. The new hinge is also supposed to be more durable.

Tech.title: Split Tunneling Is Your VPN’s Best Feature. Here’s How to Make the Most of It
Tech.content:
While you may well be familiar with virtual private network apps, you might not have come across one of the best features available inside these privacy protectors: a feature called split tunneling.

In simple terms, split tunneling lets you choose which apps or sites use the protection of a VPN and which don't. While VPNs are worth using for extra security and privacy online—foiling trackers, spoofing your location, and stopping your internet provider from seeing your browsing—they do by their nature come with some compromises in speed.

If, for example, you want to get the fastest possible speeds with your online games, you might want to leave your games outside of the VPN's remit. Likewise, since VPNs typically obfuscate your actual location, if you want to make sure you can always check movie showtimes in your local area, you can use split tunneling to keep those ticketing apps outside your VPN. Putting a VPN in place can also interfere with access to other devices on your local network, like smart home gadgets and printers.

For all these reasons, you might want the extra control that split tunneling gives you, and it's available in a lot of VPN packages. Here's what you need to know about it.

How VPN Split Tunneling Works

Split tunneling on Android. Courtesy of David Nield

VPNs work by offering an encrypted bridge for data going to and coming from the web. This bridge means your internet provider, law enforcement agencies, and people connected to the same Wi-Fi can't see what you're doing online. Split tunneling lets you route some online traffic away from that bridge, without you having to constantly turn your VPN on and off.

Tech.title: Turtle Beach Vulcan II XP Review: Clicky Compromise
Tech.content:
Unfortunately, unlike Turtle Beach’s earlier Vulcan II TKL Pro, the keys here aren’t Hall effect, but they are hot-swappable—another trade-off, exchanging long-term reliability and accuracy for the ability to replace or upgrade keys easily. The board supports three-pin or five-pin mechanical switch keys and makes swapping them easy. The flat keycaps also pop off without trouble, which makes cleaning simple. Turtle Beach claims the switches last 50 million keystrokes, which should be plenty, but only a third of the TKL Pro's 150 million.

In gaming, the Vulcan II XP offers a 1,000-Hz polling rate for a 1-millisecond response time, which is competition-grade but falls short of the higher-end 8,000-Hz keyboards on the market. Hopping back to Swarm II, you can activate its more advanced features, like Easy-Shift, allowing for key duplication—basically putting commonly used features within easier reach—and ReacTap, assigning two commands to the same key, useful for games that require very swift inputs. (This might be banned in some competitive scenes under automation rules, though.)

These features can be a little fiddly to set up and map, but with a little experimentation, you can build layouts and input fields that work exactly as you want or need. I tailored a bunch of controls for Borderlands 3 and was dropping Psychos like never before. A minor annoyance, though: Reverting a specific input while trying to create a custom setup would sometimes revert the entire profile, which meant I had to redo everything.

Back to the Drawing Board

Photograph: Matt Kamen

While the Vulcan II XP offers great performance for the price, I do have concerns about the overall build quality. On the unit I received, the media wheel was inverted by default—turning it counter-clockwise toward the minus symbol turned the volume up. This was even after I updated the board’s firmware through the Swarm II app, and I had to remap the inputs for it to work as intended. It’s good that the Vulcan II XP’s customization is specific and nuanced enough to remap even the dial direction, but I shouldn’t have had to.

I also found that the LEDs below the “0” and “.” keys on the NumPad don’t seem to work properly, glowing a stubborn, glaring white no matter what color or pattern is assigned. I even tried turning off every other key’s light and manually assigning colors to just those—to no avail.

It’s another reason the board feels middle-of-the-road. Like the shiny metallic top plate hiding the cheaper plastic base, the Vulcan II XP dazzles at a glance, but the closer you look, the more flaws and small annoyances are revealed.

For the price, some of those annoyances are forgivable. For anyone who hasn't upgraded to a mechanical keyboard, this is a decent entry without breaking the bank, delivering a lovely typing experience backed up by enough pro-tier gaming features to feel like a real upgrade—but more demanding or professional players will want to aim higher.

Tech.title: TDM Neo Hybrid Headphones Review: Two-in-One Woes
Tech.content:
Unveiled at CES 2026, the TDM Neo is a pair of on-ear headphones that transform into a Bluetooth speaker. It caught the imagination of the attending media, won a handful of awards, and inspired countless column inches.

Given the current state of the portable audio industry, it's easy to understand why. Most designs seem to revolve around incremental updates and new colorways rather than genuine technical innovation. Neo is an exciting alternative, and it’s little wonder the startup brand went on to smash its Kickstarter targets.

I’ve spent the past couple of weeks listening to the headphones and Bluetooth speaker, and have lost count of the number of times I’ve showed off the clever twist-and-fold mechanism to friends. But has TDM managed to produce a genuine tech twofer, or designed a novelty product that gives you the worst of both worlds?

Twist and Shout

Video: Chris Haslam

The twist-and-fold mechanism on the Neo is clever and addictive. Rotate the ear cups around the cushioned but flexible headband, bring them together, and strong magnets snap everything firmly in place. Once connected, the headphone drivers disable, and the outward-facing Bluetooth speakers kick in. Twist them apart and you've got your headphones back.

It’s innovative, and the engineering is impressive. Once in speaker mode, the two rubber TDM logos sit closely together and form a protective base, while the asymmetrical twisted headband cocoons the ear cups together. It works well—it never once popped open accidentally. The action is smooth, the connection reassuringly solid, and switching between modes works exactly as intended.

The Neo has four 40-mm drivers—two for the headphones and two for the speakers. The outward-facing speakers are each rated at 5 watts (for a total of 10). Ten watts is not a lot for a modern Bluetooth speaker, but wattage doesn't automatically tell you how loud or good a speaker will sound, especially in the current age of digital signal processing. The highly regarded $55 JBL Go 5 has just 4.5 watts of output, for instance.

Tech.title: 7 iPhone Duo Apps That Take Full Advantage of the New Foldable Phone
Tech.content:
The iPhone Duo is easily the most experimental iPhone that Apple has released. That’s both good news and bad news.

On one hand, the shape-shifting design, like on existing foldable Android phones I’ve tested, lends itself to creative use cases, such as hands-free entertainment and self-mounting for long-exposure photos.

On the other hand, the device is so new to iOS that some of your most frequently used apps may not yet be optimized to take advantage of the added screen space. There’s even a “does it work on iPhone Duo?” web tracker.

Needless to say, the next few weeks and months will be very telling about the future of apps on the iPhone Duo. Dozens, if not hundreds, of the App Store’s popular picks are already being worked on to take advantage of the flexible iPhone Duo screen. They’ll be labeled with a “Made for iPhone Duo” badge on their product page.

If you’re one of the lucky few who’s getting an iPhone Duo today (or soon), I’ve listed below some of the standouts that have already been optimized for the iPhone Duo and that I’ve personally tested.

1. Netflix

Netflix on the iPhone Duo. Kerry Wan/CNET

One of the primary iPhone Duo use cases is multimedia consumption, whether it’s streaming live sports and keeping tabs on player stats or docking the phone to catch up on the latest episode of Below hands-free.

Of all the streaming services I’ve used on my iPhone Duo thus far, Netflix is the most polished, with seven (from what I’ve tallied) different orientations for watching movies and shows. There’s the standard widescreen layout when the iPhone Duo is unfolded, as well as the ability to fold it and set it down like a tent.

For something more creative, you can rotate the iPhone Duo to portrait orientation and have the video play in the upper third of the screen while you use a different app in the bottom half.

2. NYT Cooking

NYT Cooking on the iPhone Duo. Kerry Wan/CNET

I’m no Michelin-star chef, but thanks to the dishes I’ve been able to make with the NYT Cooking app, at least my wife hasn’t completely banned me from the kitchen.

Previously, I’d look through and follow recipes on an iPad Air that’s docked on the countertop. With the iPhone Duo, I’ve been setting it down so that one half of the inner screen is lifted, toggling on Cook mode, and increasing the text size so I can comfortably scan the instructions from afar.

There’s nothing more satisfying than shutting the phone closed at the end of cooking and seeing a countertop that’s a little more tidy than before.

3. Fantasical

Fantastical on the iPhone Duo. Kerry Wan/CNET

I’ve never been a big to-do list guy; I’m the type who just waits for a calendar event to notify me, and I prepare then and there for what’s to come. Fantastical may keep me in better order.

It’s a calendar app that doubles as a task manager and weather tracker, which just makes sense. With the iPhone Duo unfolded, you get a clear view of your day’s tasks and appointments, what the week, month, quarter or even year looks like, and the latest weather forecast. It can easily be an information overload for some people, but I’m a fan of how everything’s color-coded and organized.

Fantastical also supports enhanced Siri AI interactions, so you can add calendar events, to-dos and other happenings through voice or text prompts.

4. Edits by Instagram

Edits on the iPhone Duo. Kerry Wan/CNET

For content creators, the Edits app is one of the most popular video editing tools. It’s the one I’ve been using over the past year to produce reels and other short-form videos, and the latest update for the iPhone Duo makes my job easier.

Edits can now show a preview monitor of what you’re editing on one half of the inner screen, while the other half shows your timeline. That means you can comfortably add effects or text, set keyframes, and scrub through the timeline without having to minimize and expand the preview to see how the changes look.

5 and 6. TikTok and Instagram

Instagram on the iPhone Duo. Kerry Wan/CNET

That’s also my segue to give flowers to two apps I’ve spent an unreasonable amount of time on: TikTok and Instagram. In line with the iPhone Duo launch, both social media apps have been optimized for the foldable iPhone’s larger screen. You can now watch videos on the left side while reading and interacting with comments on the right.

Safe to say, it’s my new favorite way to doomscroll at night.

7. Toastie

Toastie on the iPhone Duo. Kerry Wan/CNET

Toastie is easily the most whimsical “for iPhone Duo” app I’ve used, and it reminds me a lot of the early iPhone days, when chugging digital beer and swiping a paper ball based on the aerodynamics of an office cubicle were the greatest things ever.

The goal of this game is to prepare sandwiches as perfectly as possible, from the way slices of cheese are placed to how evenly spread out the butter is, to the amount of time they’re pressed in the toaster.

Oh, and you do that last step by folding the iPhone Duo shut, just like how you would with a panini press. There are even haptic effects that mimic the sizzling of the toast. It’s silly, fancy, and very charming.

There are many ways to pair up apps on the iPhone Duo for your convenience. Celso Bulgatti/CNET

Bonus: Your duo of choice

During my days testing the iPhone Duo, there was one configuration I kept going back to: running split-screen mode with two apps. To me, this is what using a foldable phone is all about, and it’s the reason why I’ve stuck with Samsung and Google’s foldable phones for the last several years.

Running split screen effectively makes apps that aren’t optimized for the multidimensional screens of a foldable phone work better by splitting the wider, tablet-like inner screen into two traditional-sized phone screens.

For my work commutes, I usually keep both Google Maps (the superior navigation app, in my opinion) and Spotify open for quick adjustments. During a recent telehealth appointment, I had my video call set up on one half of the screen and my note-taking app on the other.

And during the Lakers’ home opener the other night, I had my fantasy league and group chat open so I could throw shade throughout the game, only to come up short in points for the week because Luka Dončić decided to chuck extra shots during garbage time.

That’s why I highly encourage you to head to your local Apple store, experiment with app pairings on the iPhone Duo, and decide whether the two screens actually make you more productive.

Tech.title: The iPhone Duo Is Here, and Only That Device Will Run iOS 27.1
Tech.content:
Apple released the iPhone Duo on Friday, Oct. 23, and the tech giant released iOS 27.1 alongside the device. However, only the foldable iPhone will run that iOS version.

“This version of iOS builds on the foundation of iOS 27 but introduces features that were purpose-built for the new foldable design,” Apple told CNET in an email in September.

So unless you preordered the iPhone Duo, or were able to buy one in stores, you won’t see iOS 27.1 on your device.

The Duo is Apple’s first foldable phone, a long-anticipated move into a device category that’s still pretty niche. Launching it alongside a version of iOS tailored to that foldable design could help smooth out the debut of what is likely to be many buyers’ first foldable phone.

However, Apple did say all devices, including the iPhone Duo, will be able to update to iOS 27.2 later this year. So Apple likely won’t stagger iOS releases in the future in this way. And since Apple released the iOS 27.2 release candidate on Monday, Oct. 19, folks likely won’t have to wait long for that update to land on their foldable and nonfoldable iPhones.

For more on Apple, here’s what you should know about the iPhone Duo as well as iOS 27. You can also check out what iOS 27.2 might bring to your iPhone soon.

Tech.title: Time Is Ticking By to Claim Your Part of Apple’s $250M Siri iPhone Settlement. See if You Qualify
Tech.content:
For people who bought the newest iPhone models in 2024 expecting advanced AI features that didn’t materialize, the online form is now open to register a claim in Apple’s $250 million class-action settlement.

The iPhone 16 went on sale in September 2024 with Apple Intelligence at the center of its marketing. However, the first AI features didn’t arrive until iOS 18.1, several weeks later, and the most heavily promoted one, a Siri that could pull personal context from your apps, was further delayed in March 2025.

Now you can turn that initial dismay into a payment in Apple’s $250 million legal settlement by signing up at a live website. The opt-in form is available only for a limited time, so get your name in the pool before it closes. Eligible buyers have until Dec. 21 to file, and each qualifying iPhone gets its own claim.

The steps leading to the settlement

Apple settled a false advertising lawsuit brought by Clarkson Law Firm in May, agreeing to pay $250 million to customers who bought some iPhone models during a specified period. The lawsuit alleged that Apple misled customers by promising AI features that didn’t ship with the new devices. Apple denies all of the lawsuit’s allegations and denies that it did anything unlawful or improper.

If you purchased an iPhone 16 or iPhone 15 at launch, you may be entitled to receive a portion of the quarter-billion-dollar settlement. Payouts between $25 and $95 per eligible device are expected.

“Apple has reached a settlement to resolve claims related to the availability of two additional features. We resolved this matter to stay focused on doing what we do best, delivering the most innovative products and services to our users,” an Apple spokesperson said in an earlier statement to CNET.

The court granted preliminary approval of the settlement on July 17. Then an Aug. 13 order moved up the final approval date by seven months.

“False advertising settlements aim to raise the floor of truth-telling, protect fair competition and increase consumer choice,” said Ryan Clarkson, co-lead counsel on the case and founder and managing partner of Clarkson Law Firm, in a statement to CNET. He claimed it’s the largest false-advertising settlement in history.

Apple lit up its flagship New York City store to resemble Siri’s new color scheme. Bridget Carey/CNET

How to claim your portion of the settlement

As of Sept. 21, you can go to SmartphoneAISettlement.com and enter your information to confirm your eligibility for monetary relief. People whom Apple and the settlement administrator determined would be eligible will also receive email or postal notices from the company Verita directing them to the website.

The claims window closes on Dec. 21, 2026, so you have three months to act.

Who is eligible for the $250 million settlement?

If you bought one of the following devices between June 10, 2024, and March 29, 2025, you could be eligible to receive a settlement payment:

iPhone 16

iPhone 16E

iPhone 16 Plus

iPhone 16 Pro

iPhone 16 Pro Max

iPhone 15 Pro

iPhone 15 Pro Max

The iPhone 15 Pro and iPhone 15 Pro Max are included because they have the processor and memory to run Apple Intelligence features.

It’s estimated that approximately 36 million customers are eligible for this settlement.

Why is there a lawsuit over Apple Intelligence?

When Apple advertised its new iPhone 16 lineup in 2024, it emphasized how the models were optimized for AI features such as an enhanced Siri that could act as an intelligent agent. When the phones did arrive, Apple Intelligence wasn’t yet ready; its first features didn’t arrive until iOS 18.1, five weeks later.

According to the proposed settlement, “Apple allegedly saturated the market with deceptive ads, inducing consumers to purchase iPhones based on the promise of certain enhanced Siri features.”

Some features of Apple Intelligence did ship soon after the introduction of the iPhone 16 and iOS 18, including Visual Intelligence, Live Translation, Writing Tools, Genmoji and Clean Up. But those weren’t the advanced features Apple highlighted. In fact, the type of intelligent interactions Apple advertised is only starting to show up in Siri AI, which is part of iOS 27, which was released in early September.

When can you expect to receive a settlement payment?

According to the settlement, Apple needed to provide the information about affected customers within five days of the settlement approval. As of late July, preliminary approval has been granted by the court.

After the data is provided and verified, a 45-day notice period begins to inform potential consumers that they’re eligible for a payment.

On Aug. 13, US District Court Judge Noël Wise granted approval to push forward the date from Sept. 29, 2027, to Feb. 24, 2027.

Provided approval is granted, the first checks or deposits will arrive sometime within a 60-day window after February next year, depending on court dates and possible extensions.

Tech.title: The iPhone Duo Hit Stores Friday. Next Came Long Lines, Sellouts and Resellers
Tech.content:
Apple’s causing a commotion with its new iPhone Duo.

The tech giant’s first foldable phone hit shelves Friday, and lines were forming (and selling out) well before Apple stores even opened. Many preordered the phone, but that didn’t stop people from trying their luck to buy one without an order number. CNET editors and reporters were on the ground to bring you all of the uproar, so you can save yourself the trip if you were trying to buy one over the weekend.

At Apple’s flagship 5th Avenue location in New York, the line started forming on Wednesday by 9 a.m. ET — two days before the launch. Over 50 people were waiting in line by Thursday at 7 p.m. ET, sometimes with buckets serving as placeholders. In the first minutes after the store opened, there was no word that the iPhone Duo had sold out yet, but other stores were sold out before their doors opened.

The Oxmoor Center opened at 6 a.m. ET for Apple fans planning to buy the iPhone Duo on launch day. Faith Chihil/CNET

At the Oxmoor Center in Louisville, Kentucky, the Apple store opened at 8 a.m. EDT, and CNET’s Faith Chihil saw a line of more than 40 people three hours earlier. At about 7:27 a.m. ET, Apple store employees started taking orders for the phone. But the 256GB iPhone Duo was already sold out.

Lines gather outside of Walt Whitman Shops in Huntington, New York, where the iPhone Duo sold out before 7:30 a.m. ET. David Katzmaier / CNET

CNET Editor in Chief David Katzmaier reported that the first person was in line at Walt Whitman Shops in Huntington, New York, on Thursday at 10 a.m. ET, and was able to preorder the phone. Apple store employees started taking orders to pick up the phone at 7 a.m. ET. But by 7:30 a.m. ET, the rest of the line was dismissed after an announcement that the store had sold out before doors opened.

CNET’s Patrick Holland reported from Apple’s Union Square store in San Francisco. The first people started forming a line at 9:30 p.m. ET on Thursday. As of 11 a.m. ET, lines were down the block and around the building. There were also some sightings of people reselling the iPhone Duo just moments after waiting in line to buy one.

The line for the iPhone Duo started at 9:30 p.m. ET on Thursday at Apple’s Union Square store in San Francisco. Patrick Holland / CNET

Meanwhile, at the Apple store at University Village in Seattle, about 180 people were waiting in line who didn’t preorder the iPhone Duo. It sold out within 15 minutes of the store opening.

While many may have expected new Apple CEO John Ternus to be at the New York flagship store, he debuted the iPhone Duo launch at the Apple store in Austin, Texas. He might have been there because of this weekend’s Formula 1 race in the city — streaming on Apple TV.

iPhone Duo buyers had ‘one more thing’ waiting at pickup

Apple is full of surprises. In line with the company’s “one more thing” tagline, those who preordered the iPhone Duo had a surprise awaiting them at unboxing.

Apple’s usual “Hello” welcome screen included their name when they first turned on the phone. It’s clearly a special detail the company thought of before today, and it’s the first time it has customized its usual welcome screen for customers.

Jean Vasquez, founder of True Skies, shows off his iPhone Duo with his name on the opening screen. Bridget Carey / CNET

The iPhone Duo, Apple’s long-awaited first foldable iPhone, debuted earlier this month alongside the iPhone 18 Pro Max. It features split-screen capabilities, a photo preview display, Touch ID instead of Face ID and Apple Pencil support. The iPhone Duo’s preorders opened on Oct. 16, but quickly turned into a backlog that stretches into early next year. Pricing starts at $1,999.

“Details like the matte inner display, under-display inner camera and smooth transitions between screens give the Duo a premium feel that helps to justify its high price tag, at least to some extent,” CNET’s Abrar Al-Heeti said in her review of the iPhone Duo.

The Duo, Al-Heeti said, “is a foldable experience that feels cohesive, intuitive and genuinely useful, which could help win over more people to foldables in general. But I think that broader appeal is still a ways off.”

We don’t know how many iPhone Duos are available at each store or when Apple will restock its physical locations. But there’s a limit of two iPhone Duos per person, per day, which marks the first time in a long time that Apple’s put a cap on how many you can buy.

If you’re set on getting the phone, try ordering on Apple’s website and picking it up at a nearby store to get the phone sooner, but you’ll need to check availability on Oct. 24. It could be sooner than its estimated shipping times that say the phone won’t arrive until Jan. 29 in some areas.

Tech.title: New iPhone Duo? Here are 4 Features You Should Check Out Now
Tech.content:
If you’ve managed to snag a shiny new iPhone Duo, congratulations on surviving the scramble to get one. Now the fun begins.

I’ve spent a little over a week with Apple’s first foldable phone, and it has several features that make it feel like a genuinely practical and intuitive device — and with a $1,999 starting price, I’d sure hope so.

What stands out about the Duo is its versatility. Similar to other passport-size folding phones like the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 and the Xiaomi 18 Fold, you can hop between a more compact, 5.4-inch cover screen when sending a text or checking a notification and a wider, 7.6-inch inner display when watching videos, multitasking or scrolling through social media. It’s like a phone-tablet hybrid that fits neatly into a pocket or the palm of your hand.

Details like the matte inner display, which minimizes glare and makes the crease less noticeable, along with seamless software integration across screens give the Duo a distinct character of its own.

Here are four features worth checking out to get the most of your new iPhone Duo. And if you’re still in the market for one, it’s worth checking out carrier and trade-in deals to help bring down the cost (and maybe get the phone earlier than January).

Use Duo Preview and Smart Take for photos

Smart Take and Duo Preview can make taking photos a little easier. Abrar Al-Heeti/CNET

The iPhone Duo’s foldable design and dual screens open up more ways to take pictures. A few handy features let you easily use the 48-megapixel rear cameras for better shots than you’d get with the 12-megapixel cover-screen selfie camera.

If someone is taking a picture of you or you want to snap a selfie with the rear camera, use Duo Preview to get a glimpse of what the shot will look like. With the phone open, you’ll see an image preview on the cover screen as you or your photographer snaps away, so you can ensure the framing and poses look exactly how you want.

To turn on Duo Preview, unfold the Duo and open the Camera app. Then tap the control in the top left corner (when the phone is in landscape) that looks like a mini Duo. Tap Duo Preview and snap away.

If you’re trying to take a group photo and there’s no one around to snap it for you, you no longer have to awkwardly prop your phone against a surface and then race against a timer — or make do with a lackluster selfie. Place your Duo on a flat surface when it’s half-folded and point the camera at your subjects. A feature called Smart Take will use AI to detect when everyone is in-frame and ready, and then automatically take a photo. As people change their poses, Smart Take will register that there’s a fresh scene to snap. You can also use Duo Preview to check framing via the cover screen.

To enable Smart Take, open the camera app while the Duo is either opened or closed. Then tap the photo options in the corner (six little dots), and tap Smart Take. A button with a yellow circle will then appear to the right of the shutter; tap that to start the process.

Smart Take will keep snapping pictures for around two minutes or until it captures about 20 images as people readjust their poses. You’ll then be able to sift through the options in Photos.

Lastly, Kid Cue can make it easier to hold a child’s attention when snapping photos. With the Duo open, a Snoopy animation will play on the cover screen to draw attention toward the camera. To turn on Kid Cue, unfold the Duo, open the Camera app and tap the Duo icon in the upper left corner. There, you’ll see the option to turn on Kid Cue.

StandBy mode gets more handy

StandBy on the iPhone Duo works even when the phone isn’t charging. Abrar Al-Heeti/CNET

Apple launched StandBy in 2023, which turns the iPhone into a smart display of sorts, with access to widgets like the clock, calendar and weather. But unlike other iPhones, the Duo doesn’t have to be charging to launch into StandBy.

Just set the Duo down while it’s locked, either slightly unfolded and on its side in tent mode, or while standing upright. Then you’ll see your favorite widgets, as well as Live Activities. That way, you can track the status of a food delivery, sports score or approaching rideshare at a glance.

To ensure StandBy is enabled, go to your iPhone’s Settings, then tap StandBy and check that the toggle is on.

Marathon watch as you like

Netflix is optimized for the Duo’s displays — from the cover screen to the main display to this half-open configuration with controls on the bottom half. Celso Bulgatti/CNET

Streaming video really shines with the iPhone Duo’s dynamic design. Open the phone to watch on the tablet-like, 7.6-inch display. Minimal black bars at the top and bottom of the screen allow for more immersive viewing.

You can also fold the Duo halfway and set it down, essentially making it look like a mini laptop. With apps like Netflix and Apple TV, your movie or TV show will play on the top half, while controls appear on the bottom for skipping forward, rewinding, pausing, playing and turning on closed captions. Netflix also has an added flair: You’ll see what appears to be a reflection of the upper-screen’s content playing down by the controls, as if it’s subtly mirroring that footage. It makes for a nifty immersive effect.

You can also prop your iPhone Duo into tent mode and watch content on the 5.4-inch cover screen. I do this when I’m moving around my apartment tidying up. That way, I can easily see what’s happening without needing a phone stand. Even though the Duo’s cover screen is significantly smaller than the main display, it’s just big enough to still comfortably watch most content (perhaps not as Christopher Nolan intended, but it’ll do).

Lock a pair of apps when multitasking

You can lock an app pair when multitasking. Celso Bulgatti/CNET

The iPhone Duo can run up to two apps simultaneously in its open horizontal orientation, so you can watch a YouTube video on one half of your screen while texting your friends on the other, for example. Some other foldable phones support running three apps side-by-side, but I find that feels too crowded.

On the iPhone Duo, you can save an app pair, so that if you swipe away, you can quickly pull up that same combination without having to drag the apps side by side again. It’s a quick time-saver that lends itself to the intuitive nature of iOS 27 on the iPhone Duo.

To create an app pair, tap the divider between two apps that you’ve already dragged side by side. This will lock in that combination, so you can easily restore that dual-window card when you’re scrolling through the App Switcher. Just select the still-paired window and carry on with your multitasking (or doomscrolling).

Tech.title: Beyond the Review: Inside the Onyx RCR 80V E-Bike
Tech.content:
The first thing people ask about the Onyx RCR 80V is how fast it goes. After hundreds of miles around New York, I’m more interested in what this electric bike is like to live with.

The acceleration certainly gets your attention. But so do the compact proportions, CarPlay, cruise control and little design decisions that become more noticeable the longer you ride. Then there are the bigger questions: Can you repair it? Will parts still be available? What happens when the technology gets old?

My impression is that Onyx is trying to build a compact electric motorbike with BMX-inspired maneuverability and modern electronics, while leaving owners room to customize it and keep it running. Riding the RCR and talking with Onyx founder Tim Seward helped me understand that approach. Whether it holds up over years of ownership is a question a few hundred miles can’t answer.

More from CNET

Joseph Kaminski

Onyx RCR 80V GeekBox

Manufacturer figures below are advertised specifications, not independently measured performance results. Prices as of Oct. 14.

Specification Onyx RCR 80V Starting price $4,699 Street / $4,899 Dual Sport Motor Rear hub; advertised 8kW nominal Battery Removable 80V, 45Ah / 3.6kWh Claimed top speed 65–75 mph, depending on configuration; advertised for off-road use Claimed maximum range 140 miles; current table associates this with Cruise Tune Eco at 15 mph Claimed acceleration 0–30 mph in 1.7 seconds Ride modes tested Eco, Normal, Sport and Hyper Wheels 17-inch tubeless Brakes Hydraulic discs with 220mm rotors Display TFT touchscreen Phone integration Apple CarPlay / Android Auto Other features Reverse, cruise control, regenerative braking, turn signals and alarm/key fob Advertised ready-to-ride weight Approximately 155 pounds

Sources: Onyx model and pricing overview⁠, RCR product page⁠, RCR feature page⁠ and Onyx’s brake and wheel description⁠.

Joseph Maldonado

Street, Dual Sport and getting it home

The Street and Dual Sport share the advertised motor and battery ratings. Their clearest hardware differences are the tires and fenders: Street has 4-inch street tires with optional fenders; Dual Sport has 4.5-inch tires with a more aggressive tread and fenders included. (See how the models compare at Onyx.⁠)

Neither arrives like a lightweight bicycle. The RCR is a heavy freight delivery that still needs final assembly, and I wouldn’t recommend unpacking it alone. At roughly 155 pounds ready to ride, it also demands some thought about storage before you order.

I live in a three-flight walk-up. That matters more to my daily experience than another few miles per hour at the top end.

Yes, the RCR has pedals. I doubt many people are spending nearly $5,000 because they’re looking forward to using them.

Joseph Maldonado

Small bike, serious performance

I’m 6 feet tall, around 260 pounds and usually carrying a backpack. The RCR has had no trouble moving me around.

Most of my riding has been between 15 and 35 mph, with plenty of time in Normal. I haven’t often felt the need for more. What I appreciate is the reserve power for acceleration and hills, rather than having to ask the bike for everything just to carry a heavier rider.

Seward made a similar point when we talked about the RCR’s development around San Francisco. Steep hills help explain why usable power matters beyond a top-speed claim.

His background also helps explain the bike. An industrial designer whose portfolio includes projects for Sonos and Bird, Seward founded Onyx to bring classic motorbike character to an electric machine. ⁠

He described a combination of motorcycle performance and BMX-style maneuverability. I grew up racing BMX, and I can relate to that influence. The RCR’s compact dimensions make it easy to move around underneath me and maneuver in tighter spaces. Its size is part of its appeal, although the weight is a reminder that this is a very different machine from a BMX bike.

“It’s like a blank canvas that you can customize… It’s not a BMX at all, but it definitely has some influence from when I was a kid,” says Seward.

Joseph Maldonado

The throttle changes the experience

With this much power, how it arrives matters.

On my test bike, Eco and Normal feel smoother and more forgiving. Sport and Hyper respond more immediately to wrist movement. Switching modes changes more than the available speed; it changes how carefully I need to feed in the throttle.

I like having that choice. Sometimes I want an easy cruise. Other times, I appreciate a quicker response. A gentler mode doesn’t eliminate the need for careful throttle control, but it makes the bike’s delivery better suited to how I want to ride.

These impressions apply to the software on my test bike. They aren’t a comparison of Onyx’s newer Cruise and Thrill tunes.

What I can say about range

I haven’t completed a controlled range test, so I don’t have a measured full-charge figure to give you.

What I do have is several hundred miles of use without range anxiety. On one ride from around 151st Street in Harlem to East 26th Street, the display showed a drop of about nine percentage points. My ride took me through Central Park, so we’re looking at about 9 miles. After longer outings through Queens and Brooklyn, I’ve returned with roughly 60% to 70% of the indicated charge remaining.

My much lighter teenage son also rode the RCR on an outing through those boroughs. I recall the indicated charge dropping by 17%, although that wasn’t a controlled comparison with my own riding.

One thing that continues to impress me about the Onyx RCR 80V is just how quiet its motor is. There’s none of that high-pitched whining or wheezing you sometimes hear from electric motors. Power delivery is equally impressive, remaining smooth and consistent whether I’m accelerating from a standstill or riding at higher speeds. I’ve also noticed how much the route itself can affect battery consumption. On a recent commute from 151st Street to East 26th Street, I took a different route instead of traveling entirely through Central Park and used just 6% of the battery compared with 9% on a previous ride. It’s a good reminder that real-world range isn’t simply about distance. Terrain, elevation changes, traffic, speed and riding conditions all influence how efficiently the bike uses energy.

Joseph Maldonado

Those readings describe what I saw on the display. They don’t establish that each percentage point equals a mile, or that the bike will travel 100 miles on a charge. Without recorded distances, consistent conditions and a fuller discharge test, that would be an extrapolation.

Rider weight, speed, acceleration and terrain all matter. My conclusion is narrower: the battery has comfortably covered the rides I’ve taken. Someone spending more time at high speed should expect a different experience.

Onyx itself recommends watching battery voltage for a better indication of remaining charge and range. That’s another reason to treat my percentage readings as observations rather than precision measurements. (Here’s Onyx’s battery guidance.⁠)

Joseph Maldonado

Comfortable suspension, with limits at the seat

The RCR fits me surprisingly well, and the suspension has done a good job taking the edge off New York’s potholes and broken pavement.

The seat is comfortable with good cushioning for shorter rides. After about 90 minutes, though, I start shifting around. The suspension helps with the road underneath me, but it doesn’t eliminate the discomfort that builds during a longer ride. That also could be due to my size; I’m far from a lightweight.

The brakes have also felt consistently strong. After a few hundred miles, lever travel still feels close to how it did at the start, and I haven’t noticed a meaningful decline in stopping performance. That’s a riding impression, not a measured stopping-distance or brake-wear test.

Cruise control and reverse were pleasant surprises

Cruise control sounded like a minor convenience until I used it. On the inclines I’ve encountered with it engaged, the RCR has held the selected speed even with my weight aboard. That has been a more useful demonstration of its available power than a top-speed run.

Discovering that it could also reverse was another pleasant surprise. On a machine this heavy, powered reverse is a feature I’m glad to have. Onyx documents both functions in its advanced controls guide.

Joseph Maldonado

CarPlay is a favorite feature — and a frustration

I didn’t expect to care this much about CarPlay. Having navigation and audio controls on the built-in display means I can leave my phone put away.

My main complaint is what happens to the motorbike’s own information. While using CarPlay, especially during a call, I want speed and battery status to remain easy to see. On my test bike, they aren’t presented as conveniently as I’d like.

Onyx told me it intends to address the display issue through a software update.

Navigation brings up another issue. I’d like routing that better reflects the vehicle I’m riding. Because it uses CarPlay, it offers driving directions. However, I would like the option to choose a different route if I choose to.

“Having Android Auto and CarPlay in the bike makes me want to ride more … Part of the new update will show stats like battery level and mode on the side while using it,” says Seward, who is also Onyx’s chief design officer.

Joseph Maldonado

Signals, lights and wet pavement

The turn signals sit close to the body, with less protruding hardware to catch on something. I like that design, but in sunny settings, the signals may not be as visible.

They don’t self-cancel. The display indicators help, but I’d prefer automatic cancellation to discovering I’ve announced a left turn for the last 20 blocks (a minor complaint). The Bluetooth connection indicator is another small, useful display detail.

The headlight has worked well for the nighttime riding I’ve done. The halo running light and main beam give the bike a distinctive look, with high beam available when needed.

Joseph Maldonado

I’ve also ridden in the rain and on wet pavement without noticing handling problems. That’s limited experience, not a comprehensive wet-weather test. The more immediate issue is spray, as my bike doesn’t have the optional fenders installed, and New York street water gets everywhere.

Fenders are high on my list before doing more wet-weather riding.

Tubeless tires and everyday maintenance

The tubeless setup matters to me because removing a motorized rear wheel to deal with a flat tube can become a project. I’d rather avoid that extra complication where possible.

Tubeless doesn’t mean puncture-proof, and I wouldn’t assume any roadside plug is a permanent repair suitable for motorcycle speeds. But it’s a great go-to when in a pinch. Not having to remove the wheel to make it to your destination is clutch.

“These are basically motorcycle wheels and tires, so if you get a nail, you can patch or plug it without taking the wheel off and replacing the whole tube,” says Seward.

Joseph Kaminski

Forget the fob and the bike stays put

I’ve kept the RCR in storage at my partner’s apartment because she has an elevator. I sometimes forget to leave the key fob with it, which works well until I arrive without the fob.

That experience made phone or NFC access more appealing. Seward told me Onyx is developing app-based diagnostics, firmware updates and service support, and we discussed possible phone access. I’d welcome it, along with integrated tracking or movement alerts.

For now, I keep an AirTag hidden in the bike. I’ve also found the rear-wheel locking behavior reassuring when the bike is secured, although that isn’t a substitute for a physical lock.

Onyx already links a Superpower BMS app for battery monitoring. That should be distinguished from the broader app and unlocking features we discussed; I haven’t established that those proposed functions are available. (See the Onyx product page.)

Joseph Maldonado

The pedals don’t settle the legal question

I think of the RCR as a compact electric motorcycle. That description doesn’t, by itself, establish whether a particular example can be registered for road use. But it can be insured.

New York’s legal definition of an electric-assist bicycle includes a motor below 750 watts and specified assistance-speed limits. The RCR’s advertised power and performance exceed those limits. Buyers shouldn’t assume that pedals or a lower-speed setting make it a legal e-bike. (See New York’s DMV definitions.)⁠

I haven’t verified New York registration eligibility for this exact model and configuration. That needs to be resolved with the DMV and the manufacturer before it can be presented as a straightforward street-legal commuting option. Bicycle lanes and walking routes should not be assumed available to it.

Joseph Maldonado

Beyond the ride: A conversation with Tim Seward

Seward’s explanation of Onyx starts with the products he no longer wanted to design. During our conversation, he described working on consumer electronics for brands including Sonos, HP and Samsung, only to watch products become disposable shortly after reaching the market. His experiences with furniture and old gas-powered mopeds suggested a different approach.

The following excerpts are edited for length and clarity from the interview transcript. Questions have been shortened, and the discussion has been reordered by topic. Future features are plans described during the interview, not confirmation that they are available today.

Joseph Maldonado

CNET: Is there anything about your background or the bike that people might not know?

Seward: Before Onyx, I was a big consumer-electronics designer. I worked on Sonos, HP, Samsung, and all sorts of products you would see at Best Buy. While I liked that job, I didn’t like that people were throwing away their products.

When I was customizing gas-powered mopeds, I realized I was working on vehicles 30 to 50 years old. Who knows how many hands it went through until it got to me? I was like, I need to make products like this. I need to make products that, even if Onyx dies tomorrow, the products will live on. I didn’t want to continue to create landfill.

Joseph Maldonado

If an owner keeps this bike for five years, what can they realistically expect for battery health?

With our extra layer of health protections, we are confident our battery pack will show only a 10% degradation in 10 years. So, at the five-year mark, you won’t even notice much of a difference, if any, in performance.

(That’s an ambitious prediction. Seward’s response didn’t include the testing, charging habits or usage conditions behind it, so I wouldn’t treat it as a guaranteed outcome or a warranty. It does give me something specific to follow up on as the bike ages.)

How committed is Onyx to supporting owners with replacement parts years down the road?

We strive to offer hard-to-find parts even for discontinued products that are 5 to 6 years old. Also, our newest model, the RCR 80V, uses many parts that are compatible with aftermarket upgrades, so you can modify or maintain it for decades to come.

(That gets to one of my biggest questions about an expensive electric vehicle: What happens when something breaks after the model is no longer current? Aftermarket compatibility could help keep the RCR running, although it isn’t a guarantee that every component will remain available.)

Joseph Maldonado

What sets Onyx apart from the growing number of electric motorcycle companies?

We are not just building a bike. We are building a community of riders who support each other across the globe.

(That connects with how I found my way to Onyx. I met John Angel while testing another bike, and he kept encouraging me to try an RCR. Before I spoke with the company, another rider had already shared his experience and got me interested.

The community side matters most when it becomes useful: Someone helping you understand a feature, troubleshoot a problem or figure out a modification. That’s the kind of owner involvement I’d like to see continue as Onyx grows.

Onyx also brings its community together through events like Onyx Week, where owners and enthusiasts participate in organized rides, meet members of the Onyx team, exchange ideas, and connect with other riders. Events have been organized in Los Angeles and New York, giving owners an opportunity to experience the community beyond online discussions and social media.)

Joseph Maldonado

What stays with me

The RCR has more power than I usually need and has covered my outings without battery anxiety. CarPlay and cruise control have become features I actually value. The seat can become less comfortable on longer rides, and the display should show the current speed and battery level while on a call.

Talking with Seward gave me a clearer understanding of the decisions behind those experiences. Customer feedback helped shape the 80V, while his experience with disposable electronics explains why he wants owners to keep these bikes running.

Joseph Maldonado

It’s nice to hear a company talk about making something you can keep for years instead of pushing you to buy a new model every year. That intention still has to be backed by replacement parts, documentation and service. Onyx’s published guidance says it doesn’t repair, refurbish or rebalance batteries, so long-term battery support remains an important question. (See Onyx’s battery support policy.)⁠

For me, that’s what makes this worth looking at beyond the review — understanding why the RCR was built this way, how owners influence what comes next and whether the support can live up to the design. Would I recommend getting one? Heck yeah!

Tech.title: A New Bird-Recognizing Feeder Under $100 Launches for Beginner Bird-Watchers
Tech.content:
Birdbuddy released its latest line of smart bird feeders equipped with cameras that can detect birds by species on Thursday, and it’s never been a better time to start birdwatching at your home. The reason is a new model called the Birdbuddy Nook, which starts at $99 and offers its AI features for free with no subscription needed.



Most of the smart bird feeders we’ve tested, including past Birdbuddy models, cost around $200 or more. The particularly affordable Nook includes a 2K-resolution camera with both portrait and landscape orientations, plus a 3.8-cup birdseed container. It wakes up via motion but can keep recording for longer periods of time when there’s lots of activity. All the alerts and species recognition features happen on your phone, via the Birdbuddy app.

More from CNET

The Nook comes in both a standard model for $99 and a model with a solar panel built into the roof for $159. I’ve tested many solar-powered security cameras, and these small panels really do help keep wireless batteries charged for long periods. Since the Nook’s battery is only rated for around a month, and the bird-feeder battery looks a bit more complicated to charge up, I highly recommend the solar model.

Along with the Nook, the company is releasing a Birdbuddy Home mode for $219, which is similar, except it has a larger 6-cup capacity and a wraparound bar for more perching space.

Where should you put the Nook?

The Nook holds nearly four cups of food. Birdbuddy

Feeders should be placed within 4 feet to 10 feet of shrubs or trees, which is close enough for birds to feel safe from predators, while still being far enough to deter squirrels, according to Mary Mack Gray, Birdbuddy’s in-house ornithologist, who told CNET the best placement options. “If using a pole, a height of 5 to 6 feet off the ground is ideal. Nook is designed for compact spaces like patios, balconies and small yards.”

If you’re worried about squirrels messing up your view or getting in the way, Gray suggests using safflower seeds and suet, which squirrels tend to ignore, and avoid feed like corn or peanuts that squirrels love.

How does the bird recognition feature work?

AI trained on birds has seen success in identifying species. Corin Cesaric-Epple/CNET

Birdbuddy uses AI that has been trained on bird species visits to feeders, so it can analyze shape, color, markings and other aspects to pull up a match if one is available. The camera needs a couple of moments to wake up and take a snapshot, as well as a Wi-Fi connection, so you don’t want to put the feeder out too far from your router.

Once a bird lands on the feeder, the feeder will send a snapshot to algorithms for analysis and return an identified species or label it as currently unknown. Birdbuddy doesn’t say if it’s all local AI or if processing is done in the cloud.

CNET’s previous birdwatching reviewer noted that, aside from an occasional misstep, the bird recognition was quite good and even self-corrected itself. That sounds like a handy package for someone who wants to get to know birds in the area while paying the minimum amount.
